name: Propaedeutics of Childhood Diseases
description: Complete study manual · 15 practical class topics

topics.title: Introduction to the propaedeutics of childhood diseases. The case history. Taking the history and general inspection of a sick child

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the subject, aim and tasks of the discipline, the periods of childhood;
the structure of the case history and the content of each of its sections;
the concept of emergency assessment (triage) and the danger signs;
the order of taking the history of present illness and the life history, and the features of talking with parents and with children of different ages;
the clinical criteria for assessing the severity of a sick child's condition;
the order of general inspection: general condition, consciousness, position, body build, stigmas of dysembryogenesis.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: establish contact with the child and the parents and take the history independently;
take the history of present illness and the life history according to the scheme and draw a conclusion;
assess the child rapidly (emergency assessment) and identify the danger signs;
perform a general inspection and assess the severity of the patient's condition;
record the data obtained correctly in the case history.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: A child is not a scaled-down copy of an adult. The child's body is constantly growing and developing, so each age period has its own anatomical and physiological features, its own normal values and its own specific course of disease. A pulse, respiratory rate or blood formula that is normal for an infant is pathological for an older child.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The order of questioning and examining a child can be remembered with the English acronym **HELP**: **H** (history) — the history; **E** (examination) — objective examination; **L** (logical deduction) — logical conclusion (syndromal diagnosis); **P** (plan of management) — the plan of investigation and treatment.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: If questioning reveals that an organ is affected, the physician pays more attention to it, but this **does not release him from the obligation to examine all systems fully**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The emergency signs are easy to check in the **ABCD** order: **A** (airway) — patency of the airway; **B** (breathing) — breathing (present or absent, severe respiratory distress, cyanosis); **C** (circulation; coma; convulsions) — circulation (shock), coma, convulsions; **D** (dehydration) — severe dehydration.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The specific feature of the history in pediatrics: the information is obtained mainly **from the parents** (or the child's caregiver) and is supplemented by questions addressed to the child only according to the child's age. In a child under 5 years of age the history is taken almost entirely from the parents.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **A short history** (from a few hours to 1–2 weeks) indicates an acute process, and **a long history** (weeks, months, years) a chronic disease. In a chronic disease the parents often confuse the duration of the disease with the duration of the last exacerbation — that is why the medical records should be reviewed.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Two main criteria** are used to assess the general condition: 1. **The degree of intoxication (toxicosis)** — the main criterion in acute diseases. 2. **The degree of functional impairment of organs and systems** (respiratory, cardiac, renal, hepatic failure) — the main criterion in chronic, long-lasting diseases. In blood diseases the blood count and myelogram, and in kidney diseases the urinalysis and functional tests, are also taken into account.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The general condition and well-being **are not the same thing**. The general condition is assessed objectively by the physician, and well-being subjectively by the patient. Even with many complaints the general condition may be satisfactory, and vice versa: for example, at the onset of severe poisoning a child may feel well.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Up to 5–6** stigmas in one child are considered borderline. If there are more stigmas (**the stigmatization threshold is exceeded**), malformations of the internal organs (heart, genitourinary system) and hereditary syndromes should be sought. The degree of stigmatization is assessed by their total number regardless of location.

sections.title: 1.1. The subject, aim and tasks of the discipline

blocks.text: **Propaedeutics** (Greek propaideuo — “I teach beforehand”) is an introduction to the study of a discipline, the part that gives its foundations. **The propaedeutics of childhood diseases** is the introductory branch of pediatrics; it teaches the age-specific features of the child's body, the methods of examining healthy and sick children, and the main signs of diseases.

parts.text: A child is not a scaled-down copy of an adult. The child's body is constantly growing and developing, so each age period has its own anatomical and physiological features, its own normal values and its own specific course of disease. A pulse, respiratory rate or blood formula that is normal for an infant is pathological for an older child.

blocks.text: The discipline consists of the following parts:

items: The anatomical and physiological features of the child's body and the laws of physical and neuropsychological development.
Methods of questioning the child (taking the history) and of objective examination.
The basic semiotics of childhood diseases — symptoms and syndromes.
The rules of feeding a healthy child and drawing up a menu.
Methods of child care and the basic medical procedures.

blocks.text: **The aim of the discipline** is to teach the student the features of the child's body according to age and the technique of examining it, and to develop the skill of evaluating the data obtained to identify the affected system and the main syndrome.
Tasks of the discipline:

items: to teach the anatomical and physiological features of children of different ages;
to master the technique of a complete objective examination of the child (inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation);
to teach the evaluation of laboratory and instrumental findings according to age;
to teach the identification of the main symptoms and syndromes and their combination into a syndromal diagnosis;
to develop the skills of feeding and caring for a healthy child and of writing a case history.

blocks.text: A brief history of pediatrics

The first information on children's medicine is found in Hippocrates' (4th century BC) work “On the Nature of the Child”. In the Middle Ages, scholars of the East made a great contribution to this field. **Abu Bakr al-Razi** (865–925) wrote “A Treatise on Smallpox and Measles” and “Diseases of Children”, and was the first to introduce keeping a daily record of the patient's condition in hospital — the basis of today's case history. **Abu Ali ibn Sina** (980–1037) devoted special chapters of the “Canon of Medicine” to the care of the newborn, breastfeeding, choosing a wet nurse and the treatment of childhood diseases.

Pediatrics took shape as an independent discipline in the 19th century. The founders of the Russian school of pediatrics are N.F. Filatov, N.P. Gundobin, A.A. Kisel, G.N. Speransky, M.S. Maslov and A.F. Tur. N.P. Gundobin created the classification of the periods of childhood that is still used today.

Professors R.S. Gershenovich, K.G. Titov, S.Sh. Shamsiyev, S.N. Yo‘ldosheva, M.A. Mirzamuhamedov, M.R. Nuritdinov, F.X. Nazarmuhamedov, O.S. Mahmudov, X.A. Yunusova and T.A. Daminov made a great contribution to the development of the school of pediatrics in Uzbekistan. Professor **S.Sh. Shamsiyev** headed departments of the propaedeutics of childhood diseases in 1951–1989 and is the author of works such as “Acute Pneumonia in Children” and “Clinical Electrocardiography in Children”. In 1972 the Central Asian Medical Pediatric Institute was opened.
Periods of childhood
Knowing the periods of childhood is necessary for taking the history and evaluating examination findings according to age. In pediatrics a modified classification of N.P. Gundobin is used.

rows: From the beginning of pregnancy until birth (280 days)

sections.title: 1.2. Medical ethics and deontology in pediatrics

blocks.text: The pediatrician works with two parties at the same time — the child and the parents. That is why the physician's communication skills directly affect the accuracy of the diagnosis.

items: Before the examination, **contact should be established** with the child: ask an older child about his name, school and interests; distract a small child with a toy.
A young child is **not asked for permission** to be examined (he usually says “no”) — the physician acts confidently but gently.
Words that convey a poor prognosis or that the treatment was wrong are not used in front of the child and the parents.
The child is addressed by name and the parents respectfully; accusatory phrases such as “Why didn't you bring him earlier?” are not used.
**Confidentiality** is maintained in conversations with adolescents; it is possible to talk first with the parents and then separately with the adolescent.
Before an examination with a group of students, the consent of the child (if older) or of the parents is obtained.

blocks.text: **The physician's appearance and hands:** a clean gown, hair under a cap, hands washed before examining each child, warm, with short nails. The physician should be patient, calm and kind.
The examination of a child is divided into two groups of methods:

items: **Main methods:** subjective — questioning (history); objective (physical) — inspection (inspectio), palpation (palpatio), percussion (percussio), auscultation (auscultatio).
**Additional methods:** laboratory (blood, urine and stool tests and others) and instrumental (radiography, ultrasound, ECG, endoscopy and others).

parts.text: The order of questioning and examining a child can be remembered with the English acronym **HELP**:

items: **H** (history) — the history;
**E** (examination) — objective examination;
**L** (logical deduction) — logical conclusion (syndromal diagnosis);
**P** (plan of management) — the plan of investigation and treatment.

blocks.text: The objective examination is carried out in the following sequence: general inspection → skin and subcutaneous fat → lymph nodes → musculoskeletal system → respiratory system → cardiovascular system → digestive system → urinary system → nervous system and sense organs → endocrine system. Each system is examined in the order **inspection → palpation → percussion → auscultation**.

parts.text: If questioning reveals that an organ is affected, the physician pays more attention to it, but this **does not release him from the obligation to examine all systems fully**.

blocks.text: Every sick child arriving at a hospital or an admission room is first assessed **rapidly — within 1–2 minutes**. The aim here is not a detailed diagnosis but the detection of a life-threatening condition and the setting of the order of care. This process is called **triage** (French trier — to sort). The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed the **ETAT** system for children (Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment).
As a result of triage, sick children are divided into three groups:

blocks.title: Table 1.2. Triage groups according to the WHO ETAT system
head: Group
Signs
Action
rows: Obstructed or absent breathing; severe respiratory distress; central cyanosis; signs of shock (cold hands, capillary refill time longer than 3 s, rapid and weak pulse); coma or convulsions; severe dehydration in a child with diarrhea (lethargy, sunken eyes, skin pinch goes back very slowly)
An infant under 2 months; high fever; trauma; severe pallor; poisoning; severe pain; respiratory distress; restlessness or lethargy; urgent referral; severe wasting; edema of both feet; burns
Seen first, without waiting in the queue

parts.text: The emergency signs are easy to check in the **ABCD** order:

items: **A** (airway) — patency of the airway;
**B** (breathing) — breathing (present or absent, severe respiratory distress, cyanosis);
**C** (circulation; coma; convulsions) — circulation (shock), coma, convulsions;
**D** (dehydration) — severe dehydration.

blocks.text: **Rapid assessment of consciousness — the AVPU scale.** In triage, consciousness is assessed with a simple four-level scale:

items: **A** (alert) — the child is alert and responds appropriately to the surroundings;
**V** (voice) — responds only to voice;
**P** (pain) — responds only to pain;
**U** (unresponsive) — does not respond to anything.

blocks.text: Responding only to pain (P) or not responding (U) is a sign of coma, that is, an emergency.

**General danger signs.** In the WHO and UNICEF Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) program, the following **general danger signs** are checked in every sick child aged 2 months to 5 years:

items: The child is unable to drink or breastfeed.
The child vomits everything.
The child has had convulsions during this illness.
The child is lethargic or unconscious.
The child is convulsing now.

parts.text: A child with at least one general danger sign is considered **severely ill**: he is given immediate care and urgently admitted to hospital. For example, if a 1-year-old child has fever and cough and refuses to breastfeed, this is not a simple cold but may be a sign of severe pneumonia or sepsis.

blocks.text: **The history (anamnesis)** (Greek anamnesis — recollection) is the body of information about the patient and the disease obtained by questioning the patient or a person who knows the patient well.

parts.text: The specific feature of the history in pediatrics: the information is obtained mainly **from the parents** (or the child's caregiver) and is supplemented by questions addressed to the child only according to the child's age. In a child under 5 years of age the history is taken almost entirely from the parents.

blocks.text: Components of the history:

items: Personal data.
Complaints — the main reason for seeking care.
History of present illness (anamnesis morbi).
Life history (anamnesis vitae): obstetric, neonatal, feeding, developmental, past illnesses, immunizations, allergic, hereditary (family), social and living conditions, and epidemiological history.

blocks.text: Personal data

Surname, first name and patronymic; date of birth (exact age — years, months, and days for a newborn); home address; the parents' names, ages, occupations and places of work; whether the child attends a kindergarten or school; date of admission; the diagnosis of the referring institution. The home address gives information about the epidemiological environment (water supply, sewerage), and the parents' occupation about the family's social level and occupational hazards.
Complaints

Complaints are the subjective signs of the disease. First the **main** and then the **general** complaints are recorded concisely; the complaints on admission and at the time of examination are indicated separately. Each complaint is clarified in detail: site, character, intensity, duration, when it appears, what makes it worse and what relieves it.
Difficulties in obtaining complaints from children:

items: a young child cannot express complaints because of age or impaired consciousness, and the parents only report that signs have appeared (for example, “he is crying and pulling his legs up to his tummy”);
adolescents may exaggerate their condition (aggravation), play it down (dissimulation) or feign a nonexistent disease (simulation).

blocks.text: Questions are asked in language the child and the parents understand; a question should not contain a ready answer (not “Does your tummy hurt on the right?” but “Where does it hurt? Can you show me?”).
History of present illness (anamnesis morbi)
The history of present illness establishes:

items: What the child was like before the illness.
When and how the illness began: **acutely** (within hours, 1–2 days) or **gradually**.
What the illness is thought to be associated with: chilling, contact with a sick person, a new food, taking a medicine, an injury.
The first signs and their subsequent course (dynamics).
What investigations were done and their results (the outpatient card and discharge summaries should be reviewed).
What treatment was received (including self-treatment) and its effect.
The present condition.

parts.text: **A short history** (from a few hours to 1–2 weeks) indicates an acute process, and **a long history** (weeks, months, years) a chronic disease. In a chronic disease the parents often confuse the duration of the disease with the duration of the last exacerbation — that is why the medical records should be reviewed.

blocks.text: After the history of present illness has been taken, a preliminary assumption is made about which organ or system is affected and about the course of the disease (acute or chronic).
Life history (anamnesis vitae)

The life history is taken in two ways depending on the child's age: **in young children (under 3 years)** in detail, starting from the mother's pregnancy and delivery, and in older children more briefly.
1. Obstetric (antenatal and intranatal) history:

items: from which pregnancy and which delivery the child was born; how previous pregnancies ended (abortion, miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm delivery);

how the first and second halves of pregnancy proceeded: toxicosis, gestosis, anemia, threatened miscarriage, the mother's illnesses (especially infections), medicines taken, harmful habits (smoking, alcohol), occupational hazards, nutrition;

the delivery: at term or preterm, its duration and complications, whether a cesarean section, obstetric forceps or a vacuum extractor was used, the duration of the period after rupture of the membranes.

parts.text: Spontaneous miscarriages in the mother and threatened abortion may indicate hereditary pathology or intrauterine infection. Gestosis, abnormal labor and a low Apgar score lead to cerebral hypoxia, which later becomes the basis for diseases of the nervous system.

blocks.text: **2. Neonatal period:** whether the child cried at once and what the cry was like (loud or weak); whether resuscitation was needed; the Apgar score; the birth weight, length and head and chest circumferences; when the baby was put to the breast and how he sucked; when the umbilical stump fell off and how the umbilical wound healed; the degree and duration of physiological jaundice; the physiological weight loss and its recovery; illnesses in the newborn period; on which day and with what weight the baby was discharged from the maternity hospital.

**3. Feeding history:** breast, mixed or formula feeding; for how many months the baby was exclusively breastfed; when he was weaned; the type and amount of formula; when and in what order complementary foods were introduced; whether vitamin D was given to prevent rickets; when the child moved to the family table; present diet, appetite.

parts.text: Early formula feeding, non-adapted formulas and failure to introduce complementary foods on time lead to allergic diseases, digestive diseases, anemia, rickets and hypotrophy. For example, in celiac disease the arrest of weight gain begins a few weeks (usually 1–2 months) after gluten-containing cereals are introduced.

blocks.text: **4. Physical and neuropsychological development:** when the birth weight doubled; the weight and length at 1 year; when the first teeth erupted and the number of teeth at 1 year; when the child began to hold up his head, smile, babble, roll over, sit, crawl, stand and walk; the first words and phrases; in an older child, school performance and behavior in a group.

**5. Past illnesses:** what illnesses the child had before and after 1 year of age, their severity and complications; rickets, anemia, diatheses; infectious diseases; operations, injuries, blood transfusions (risk of hepatitis B and C and HIV infection).

**6. Immunizations:** whether the child has been immunized according to the national immunization schedule; reactions and complications after vaccination; medical contraindications; the results of the Mantoux test.
**7. Allergic history:** reactions to drugs, foods, household and other allergens (rash, swelling, bronchospasm). This information is necessary for choosing drugs and preventing complications.

**8. Hereditary (family) history:** the parents' ages and health; chronic, hereditary, allergic, endocrine and mental diseases, tuberculosis, syphilis and alcoholism in the family; consanguineous marriage; the other children in the family and their health, children who have died and the causes of death. The hereditary history is drawn up as **a pedigree (family tree)** covering at least three generations.

**9. Social and living conditions:** the family's financial situation; housing conditions (area, lighting, dampness, heating, ventilation, number of occupants); who looks after the child; whether the child has a separate bed; daily routine, sleep, walks; bathing; smoking in the family.

**10. Epidemiological history:** contact with an infectious patient (influenza, ARVI, intestinal infections, tuberculosis, hepatitis) during the last 3 weeks; the quality of food products and water; whether the child has traveled recently. The epidemiological history completes the life history and decides to which ward the patient will be admitted.
Features of talking with the parents, the child and the adolescent

**Talking with the parents.** Parents describe signs mixed with their own emotions, so the information should be assessed objectively. For example, parents associate a chronic cough with “frequent colds” and do not think of the possibility of bronchial asthma. The conversation takes place in a friendly atmosphere; helping (open) questions are more effective. It is useful to ask at the end of the conversation, “Is there anything else you would like to tell me about your child?” — sometimes the real reason for the visit comes out at this moment.

**Talking with the child (5 years and older).** A child often describes symptoms more accurately than the parents. The conversation begins with an interesting, non-frightening topic (games, school, clothes). Then questions the child can understand are asked: “Show me where it hurts. Is the pain strong, or like a needle prick? Does the pain stay in one place or move somewhere else?”

**Talking with the adolescent.** An adolescent opens up when addressed respectfully, like an adult. The conversation should begin with his interests, friends and school. Confidentiality is guaranteed. Confrontation and long silences make the adolescent close up.
Conclusion from the history

After the history has been taken, a general conclusion is drawn: the presumed pathology, its nature (**hereditary, congenital or acquired**), its course (**acute or chronic**) and the **risk factors** that contributed to the development of the disease are indicated.

The case history is the main medical and legal document reflecting the process of examining, diagnosing and treating the patient. During the course the student writes a training case history according to the following scheme.

blocks.title: Table 1.3. Scheme of the training case history
head: Section
Content
rows: Full name, age, address, information about the parents, date of admission, diagnosis of the referring institution
Main and general complaints on admission and at the time of examination
Onset, development, investigations, treatment and its effect
Obstetric, neonatal, feeding, developmental, past illnesses, immunization, allergic, hereditary, social and epidemiological history; conclusion from the history
General inspection, physical development, examination by systems (inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation)
VI. Conclusion from the history and status
Laboratory and instrumental investigations and their interpretation
VIII. Justification of the syndromal diagnosis
Based on complaints + history + objective + additional data
Daily and single feed volumes, requirements for protein, fat, carbohydrate and energy, a one-day menu
X. Daily notes and temperature chart

blocks.text: The following conditions are met for examining a child:

items: the room is warm — air temperature **20–22 °C**; if the temperature is below 20 °C, the child is examined partly undressed;

the lighting is sufficient, preferably **natural daylight**; the child's face is turned toward the light source; in direct light the skin color is seen well, and in side lighting the movements on the body surface (pulsation, peristalsis);
the child is **fully undressed**: under 3 years — completely; school-age children (especially girls during puberty) are undressed gradually during the examination;
young children are examined **on a changing table**, older children lying or sitting on a couch or bed; having the parents nearby calms the child;
the physician stands **on the patient's right side**;
**a sleeping child is not woken**: during sleep the respiratory rate and pulse are counted and the abdomen is palpated;
procedures unpleasant for the child (inspection of the throat and ears, examination of a painful area, instrumental investigations) are performed **at the end of the examination**;
in a preschool child the examination is conducted not according to a strict scheme but according to the child's mood; a restless child is distracted with play.

blocks.text: The general inspection begins already during the conversation with the child and the mother: the physician notes the child's behavior, movements, voice and response to the surroundings. General inspection is of great diagnostic value — the direction toward the diagnosis is often obtained at first glance.
The general inspection assesses:

items: The general condition (degree of severity).
Well-being and mood.
The state of consciousness.
The patient's position (active, passive, forced).
Body build (constitution type), posture, gait.
Facial expression.
Stigmas of dysembryogenesis and visible malformations.
Physical development (see topic 2).

blocks.label: Figure 1.5
blocks.caption: Stages of general inspection in an older child: 1 — head, 2 — neck, 3 — trunk, 4 — limbs, 5 — oral cavity (inspected last) (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: The general condition and the criteria for assessing it

**The general condition** is the physician's **objective conclusion** based on the history and the findings of objective and additional investigations. It determines the scope and order of treatment, the need for additional investigations and where the patient is admitted (intensive care, isolation box, ordinary ward). The condition may change during the day, even within hours.
Grades of the general condition: **satisfactory, moderately severe, severe** and **extremely severe (terminal)**.

parts.text: **Two main criteria** are used to assess the general condition: 1. **The degree of intoxication (toxicosis)** — the main criterion in acute diseases. 2. **The degree of functional impairment of organs and systems** (respiratory, cardiac, renal, hepatic failure) — the main criterion in chronic, long-lasting diseases. In blood diseases the blood count and myelogram, and in kidney diseases the urinalysis and functional tests, are also taken into account.

blocks.title: Table 1.4. Criteria for assessing the severity of the general condition in acute diseases
head: Condition
Clinical description
rows: The child is active and interested in the surroundings; weakness and restlessness absent or mild; body temperature normal or subfebrile; skin pale pink or slightly flushed; changes in organs and systems absent or mild

Intoxication is evident: the child is weak, reluctant to communicate, drowsy; temperature 38–39 °C; skin flushed or pale-cyanotic; increased respiratory rate, tachycardia; vomiting, loose stools and, in young children, abdominal distension may occur; the functions of vital organs are subcompensated

Impaired consciousness (stupor, sopor, coma); convulsions may occur; temperature 39–40 °C; skin pale, gray or mottled (impaired microcirculation); dyspnea; tachycardia or bradyarrhythmia; repeated vomiting, intestinal paresis (distended abdomen), diarrhea; reduced diuresis; the main physiological systems are decompensated
Deepening of the above signs and signs directly threatening life; the patient is in the intensive care unit

blocks.text: Well-being

**Well-being** is the patient's **subjective** sensation. It is good, satisfactory or unsatisfactory and depends on mood. The mood may be even, calm, elevated, excited or unstable; the child's interest in the people around and in toys is noted.

parts.text: The general condition and well-being **are not the same thing**. The general condition is assessed objectively by the physician, and well-being subjectively by the patient. Even with many complaints the general condition may be satisfactory, and vice versa: for example, at the onset of severe poisoning a child may feel well.

blocks.text: State of consciousness

blocks.title: Table 1.5. Degrees of impaired consciousness
head: Degree
Description
rows: The child responds appropriately to the surroundings, willingly makes contact and answers questions correctly
There is a response to the surroundings, but it is slowed and reduced; the child answers questions correctly but with delay and sluggishly; responds to stimulation by crying
Consciousness is clouded, there is no response to the surroundings, the child does not answer questions or gives the same answer, but the response to pain is preserved
Unconscious, no active movements, no or a very weak response to pain, reflexes reduced or absent; divided into grades I–IV according to its depth

blocks.text: Consciousness may also be impaired in the form of **excitation**: euphoria, negativism, psychomotor agitation, delirium (with hallucinations). In young children intoxication often begins with **lethargy (apathy) and reduced movement (adynamia)**, alternating from time to time with restlessness, after which stupor, sopor, coma and convulsions develop.

parts.text: The appearance of drowsiness and lethargy in a young child is always a serious sign. The complaint “the child sleeps a lot” may hide the onset of neurotoxicosis, meningitis, severe dehydration or hypoglycemia.

blocks.text: The patient's position

items: **Active position** — the child moves freely and readily changes position at the physician's request or according to circumstances.
**Passive position** — in unconsciousness or extreme weakness: the patient is motionless, the head and limbs hang down, and he cannot change position himself.
**Forced position** — a specific position the patient adopts to relieve his condition.

blocks.title: Table 1.6. Examples of forced positions
head: Disease
Forced position
rows: Lying on the side with the head thrown back, the legs drawn up to the abdomen and the abdomen drawn in (the “pointer dog” or “cocked gun” position)
Sitting, propped with the hands on the edge of the bed or on the knees (orthopnea)
Lies on the affected side (the excursion of the healthy lung is preserved)
On the back with the legs bent, does not move — every movement causes pain

blocks.label: Figure 1.6
blocks.caption: Forced position of a child with meningitis: on the side, head thrown back, legs bent (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Body build (constitution), posture and gait
**Constitution** is the set of relatively stable morphological and functional features of the body formed under the influence of heredity and environment. Three types of body build are distinguished:

blocks.title: Table 1.7. Types of body build
head: Type
Signs
rows: The body is proportionally developed; the epigastric angle is about 90°
The length of the body predominates over its width; long limbs, a long and narrow chest; acute epigastric angle (less than 90°); poorly developed muscles and subcutaneous fat
The width of the body predominates over its length; relatively short limbs, a broad chest, a large abdomen; obtuse epigastric angle (more than 90°)

blocks.label: Figure 1.7
blocks.caption: Appearance of children with different body builds (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Posture and gait.** A healthy child holds the body upright, walks briskly, and moves freely. Stooping, scoliosis, limping, a “waddling” gait (hip dislocation, muscular dystrophy) and an ataxic gait (cerebellar damage) are noted.
Facial expression
The facial expression gives much information about the child's condition and some diseases. The face of a healthy child is calm, and the eyes are clear and curious.

items: **Suffering face** — in pain (otitis, abdominal pain).
**Hippocratic face** — sunken eyes and temples, a sharpened nose, gray skin, cold sweat — peritonitis, severe dehydration, a terminal state.
**Adenoid face** — mouth constantly open, puffy face, flattened nasolabial folds, no nasal breathing.
**Nephritic face** — edema of the face and eyelids, pale skin.
**Down syndrome** — slanting palpebral fissures (mongoloid slant), epicanthus, flat face, open mouth and a large tongue.
**Cushingoid (“moon”) face** — round, flushed face (glucocorticoid excess).
**“Sardonic smile”** — spasm of the facial muscles in tetanus.

blocks.text: Stigmas of dysembryogenesis
**Stigmas of dysembryogenesis** are minor anomalies in the shape or structure of an organ that do not impair its function. Several stigmas occur as a familial trait even in healthy people.

parts.text: **Up to 5–6** stigmas in one child are considered borderline. If there are more stigmas (**the stigmatization threshold is exceeded**), malformations of the internal organs (heart, genitourinary system) and hereditary syndromes should be sought. The degree of stigmatization is assessed by their total number regardless of location.

blocks.text: Assessing the newborn's condition: the Apgar score

The newborn's condition is assessed with the Apgar score **at 1 and 5 minutes** after birth. Each sign is scored 0, 1 or 2 points. The initial letters of the English names of the signs form the word “APGAR”.

blocks.title: Table 1.9. The Apgar score
head: Sign
0 points
1 point
2 points

blocks.text: Interpretation: **8–10 points** — satisfactory condition; **6–7 points** — mild asphyxia; **4–5 points** — moderate asphyxia; **0–3 points** — severe asphyxia. Respiratory distress is assessed with **the Silverman score** in preterm newborns and with **the Downes score** in term newborns (topic 2).
Recording the general inspection in the case history
The result of the general inspection is recorded in the case history in the following order:

items: General condition: satisfactory / moderately severe / severe.
Well-being and mood.
Consciousness: clear / somnolence / sopor / coma.
Response to the surroundings: appropriate / inappropriate.
Position: active / passive / forced (which one).
Body build: normosthenic / asthenic / hypersthenic.
Stigmas of dysembryogenesis: none found, or those found are listed.

blocks.text: Sample: “General condition moderately severe due to intoxication. Well-being unsatisfactory, mood unstable, capricious. Consciousness clear, response to the surroundings appropriate. Position active. Body build normosthenic. Stigmas of dysembryogenesis: Gothic palate, low-set ears (2).”
The history is half the diagnosis
Experienced pediatricians say that “a correctly taken history gives half the diagnosis”. The following examples show the practical value of the history:

items: **Relation to food.** If arrest of weight gain, an enlarging abdomen and large amounts of fatty stools began in a 9-month-old child 1–2 months after semolina porridge was introduced — celiac disease should be considered.
**Cough during feeding.** Attacks of coughing and cyanosis with every feed in a newborn are a sign of a tracheoesophageal fistula.
**Family history.** A dry night cough in a child whose parents and elder brother have allergic rhinitis and eczema is characteristic of bronchial asthma.

**Epidemiological history.** A child who had contact with a child with measles at the kindergarten and has developed fever and conjunctivitis is in the catarrhal period of measles; such a child is admitted to an isolation box ward.
**Birth history.** Delayed motor development later in a child born with severe asphyxia (Apgar 3 points) is a consequence of perinatal encephalopathy.

blocks.text: The importance of assessing severity correctly
Assessing the general condition is not just for the record — it determines where the patient is admitted, how quickly care is given and how he is monitored.

parts.text: **In an acute disease** the main criterion is intoxication. For example, if a child with ARVI has a fever of 39.5 °C, lethargy, mottled skin and cold hands and feet, the condition is severe (“white hyperthermia”, impaired microcirculation). **In a chronic disease** the main criterion is functional failure.
For example, in a child with a congenital heart defect, even without fever, dyspnea at rest and an enlarged liver (grade II heart failure) make the condition severe.

blocks.text: The forced position — a key to the diagnosis

The patient's position often points to the diagnosis already in the admission room: a febrile child lying with the head thrown back and the legs bent — meningitis; a child sitting propped on the hands and breathing with a wheeze — an asthma attack; a cyanotic child squatting — tetralogy of Fallot.

skills.title: Skill 1. Taking the history

items: Wash the hands, introduce yourself, establish contact with the parents (and the child) and obtain consent.
Establish the personal data.
Establish the main and general complaints; explore each complaint in detail (site, character, duration, aggravating and relieving factors).
Take the history of present illness: onset, cause, development, investigations, treatment and its effect.
Take the life history (appropriate to age): obstetric, neonatal, feeding, developmental, past illnesses, immunizations, allergic, hereditary, social and living conditions, epidemiological history.
Draw up a pedigree (at least three generations).
At the end of the conversation, give the parents the opportunity to ask further questions.
Draw a conclusion from the history: the presumed affected system, the nature and course of the disease, the risk factors.

skills.title: Skill 2. Emergency assessment (triage)

items: Assess the child immediately on arrival (within 1–2 minutes) by ABCD.
**A** — patency of the airway: stridor, signs of a foreign body.
**B** — breathing: present or absent, respiratory distress (accessory muscles, nasal flaring, chest indrawing), central cyanosis.

**C** — circulation: feel the temperature of the hands, determine the capillary refill time (press on the nail for 3 seconds and release; if the color returns more slowly than in 3 seconds — pathology), pulse; consciousness (AVPU) and convulsions.
**D** — dehydration in a child with diarrhea: lethargy, sunken eyes, how fast the skin pinch goes back.
If there is an emergency sign — start treatment immediately and call a senior physician; if there is a priority sign — send for examination without waiting; if there are no signs — the general queue.
In a child aged 2 months to 5 years, ask about and check the general danger signs.

skills.title: Skill 3. General inspection and assessment of severity

items: Ensure the conditions for examination: room temperature 20–22 °C, daylight, warm clean hands.
During the conversation, observe the child's behavior, movements, voice and response to the surroundings.
Undress the child appropriately for age and place him in a position convenient for examination.
Assess consciousness (answers to questions, response to voice and pain).
Determine the patient's position (active, passive, forced).
Assess the signs of intoxication: weakness, temperature, skin color, respiratory rate, pulse, vomiting, diuresis.
Identify the signs of functional impairment of organs (respiratory, heart failure and others).
Assess the body build, posture, gait and facial expression.
Look for and count the stigmas of dysembryogenesis in sequence: head, face, ears, mouth, neck, trunk, limbs.
Determine the grade of the general condition and record it in the case history.

skills.title: Skill 4. Drawing up a pedigree (family tree)

items: The sick child (proband) is marked — he is indicated with an arrow.
Males are indicated by a square and females by a circle; the symbol of an affected person is shaded; a line is drawn through the symbol of a deceased person.

Members of one generation are placed in one horizontal row in birth order starting from the left; generations are indicated by Roman numerals (I — grandparents, II — parents and their brothers and sisters, III — the proband and his brothers and sisters).
Spouses are joined by a horizontal line and their children by a vertical line; a consanguineous marriage is shown by a double line.
The disease of each person is recorded and a conclusion is drawn about hereditary predisposition.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A child aged 1 year 2 months was brought to the admission room. According to the mother, he has had a fever of 39 °C and a cough for 2 days. Since this morning he has not been breastfeeding and vomits the water he drinks. On examination the child is lethargic, barely opens his eyes and responds weakly to voice. Respiratory rate 58 per minute; the lower part of the chest is drawn in on inspiration.
cases.ask: 1) What general danger signs does the child have? 2) To which triage group does the child belong? 3) Assess his general condition.
cases.answer: 1) There are two general danger signs: the child is unable to breastfeed and vomits everything; in addition, lethargy is also a general danger sign. 2) Chest indrawing and tachypnea indicate severe respiratory distress, that is, an emergency (E) sign; lethargy is a priority sign. The child belongs to the emergency group, and treatment is started immediately. 3) The general condition is severe: obvious intoxication (lethargy, reduced consciousness — weak response to voice, V on AVPU) and signs of respiratory failure. Presumptive diagnosis — severe pneumonia; urgent hospital admission is necessary.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 10-year-old girl came with the complaint of “tummy ache”. Her mother is very anxious: her daughter says that her tummy hurts every morning before going to school. There is no pain at weekends. Objective examination revealed no changes; the condition is satisfactory.
cases.ask: 1) Which part of the history gives an important direction for the diagnosis? 2) How should the conversation with the child be organized? 3) Explain the difference between the condition and well-being.
cases.answer: 1) The appearance of pain only on school mornings and its absence at weekends suggest psychogenic (functional) pain; the social history (the school environment, performance, relations with classmates, the family situation) should be taken in detail. At the same time, organic causes (digestive diseases) are excluded. 2) The conversation begins with an interesting, non-frightening topic; it is also useful to talk with the child alone, without the mother; open questions are asked (“How does your day at school go? What upsets you?”); the child is asked to show where it hurts. 3) The condition (the physician's objective assessment) is satisfactory; the well-being (the girl's subjective sensation) may be unsatisfactory because of the pain. It is natural for these two concepts not to coincide.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: On assessing a newborn at 1 minute: the body is pink and the limbs bluish; heart rate 110 per minute; grimaces when a nasal catheter is inserted; the limbs are slightly flexed; breathing is slow and irregular, and the cry is weak.
cases.ask: 1) Score by the Apgar scale. 2) Draw a conclusion. 3) When is the reassessment performed?
cases.answer: 1) Skin color — 1 point, heart rate (more than 100) — 2 points, reflex irritability (grimace) — 1 point, muscle tone (slightly flexed) — 1 point, respiration (slow, irregular) — 1 point. Total: 6 points. 2) Mild asphyxia (6–7 points). 3) The reassessment is performed at 5 minutes; if the score is below 7, the assessment is continued every 5 minutes up to 20 minutes, and resuscitation measures are taken.

topics.title: Physical development of the child. The newborn and the preterm newborn

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the concept of physical development and the factors affecting it;
the technique of anthropometric measurements;
the patterns of change of length (height), weight, and head and chest circumferences with age, and the formulas for approximate calculation;
the methods of assessing physical development: sigma, centile, WHO Z-score method, indices;
the semiotics of disorders of physical development;
the anatomical and physiological features of the newborn and the borderline (transitional) states;
the degrees and signs of prematurity;
the features of examining a newborn, the Apgar and Silverman scores.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: measure the length (height), weight, and head and chest circumferences of children of different ages;
evaluate anthropometric indicators by formulas and centile tables and write a conclusion;
examine a newborn and distinguish transitional states from pathology;
identify the signs of prematurity;
assess respiratory distress by the Silverman score.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: All anthropometric measurements are made **in the morning, on an empty stomach**, after voiding urine and stool, with the same instruments. The measurements are repeated regularly: **under 1 year — every month; 1–3 years — every quarter; 3–7 years — twice a year; 7–17 years — once a year**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: For height, “**50 – 75 – 100 – 130 – 150**”: 50 cm at birth, 75 cm at 1 year, 100 cm at 4 years (“one meter”), 130 cm at 8 years, 150 cm at 12 years. Height **doubles by 4 years** and **triples by 12 years**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: For weight, the “**3 – 6 – 12**” rule: at 1 year the weight is **3 times** the birth weight; at 6–7 years it is **2 times** the weight at 1 year; at 12 years it is **3 times** the weight at 1 year.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Order of centile assessment: 1) determine into which corridor each of height, weight and chest circumference falls; 2) **the level of physical development is determined by the height corridor**; 3) **harmony** is assessed by the difference between the corridors: a difference of **0–1** corridor — harmonious; **2** corridors — disharmonious; **3 or more** — sharply disharmonious development. Corridors 2 and 6 are borderline (require follow-up); in corridors 1 and 7 the probability of pathology is high, and an in-depth examination is needed.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Main definitions: **Live born** — a baby that has breathed or shows other signs of life (heartbeat, pulsation of the umbilical vessels, voluntary muscle movement) (WHO). **Term** — born from **37 completed weeks to 42 weeks** of gestation (37^0^–41^6^ weeks). **Post-term** — born at **42 completed weeks or later**. **Preterm (premature)** — born **before 37 completed weeks**. **Gestational age** — the number of completed weeks from conception to birth.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Most transitional states follow the “**3–7 rule**”: they begin around **day 3** and pass by **days 7–10** (weight loss, jaundice, sexual crisis, uric acid infarction). An earlier onset or longer duration is a sign of pathology.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: On **the Apgar** score, the higher the score, the better the condition (10 — ideal). On **the Silverman** score it is the opposite: the higher the score, the more severe the respiratory distress (0 — ideal).

sections.title: 2.1. The concept of physical development and the factors affecting it

blocks.text: **Physical development** is the set of morphological and functional features reflecting the process of growth and maturation of the body. In clinical pediatrics it is understood as the child's growth in length, weight gain, development of body parts and biological maturation in the different periods of childhood. Physical development is one of the most important criteria of a child's health.
Four groups of signs of physical development are distinguished:

items: **Anthropometric** — length (height), weight, and the circumferences of the head, chest, arm, thigh and calf.
**Functional** — vital capacity of the lungs, hand grip and back strength, physical working capacity.
**Somatoscopic** — shape of the spine, degree of fat deposition, muscle development, posture, shape of the legs and feet.
**Biological** — dental formula, body proportions, ossification centers, secondary sexual characteristics.

blocks.title: Table 2.1. Factors affecting the child's growth and development
head: Factor
Effect
rows: More than 100 genes control the synthesis of growth hormones and factors; they determine the rate of growth and the final height
Somatotropic hormone (growth hormone) — the main growth hormone; thyroid hormones, insulin; sex hormones at puberty
Protein-energy malnutrition and deficiency of vitamins, amino acids and calcium impair growth
In hot climates and mountainous areas growth slows and puberty is accelerated
A daily routine, enough sleep and physical activity create good conditions for growth
Chronic and severe diseases slow or stop growth
The family's financial situation, the quality of care, the parents' harmful habits

blocks.text: Acceleration and retardation

**Acceleration** (Latin acceleratio — speeding up) is the speeding up of children's growth and biological maturation compared with previous generations. The term was introduced in 1935 by the German scientist E. Koch. In the 20th century the length of newborns increased by 1–2 cm, that of 1-year-old children by 4–5 cm, and that of 15-year-old adolescents by an average of 20 cm over 100 years. Early eruption of permanent teeth, early sexual maturation and early menarche in girls are also signs of acceleration.

items: **Harmonious acceleration** — growth in height and biological maturation speed up together.
**Disharmonious acceleration** — only one indicator speeds up (for example, height increases rapidly, while sexual maturation occurs on time).

blocks.text: **Retardation** is a slowing of the rate of physical development. Causes: reduced physical activity (sitting for long periods at a computer), the parents' smoking, alcohol and drug use (intrauterine growth restriction), children's harmful habits. The alternation of periods of acceleration and retardation is called **the secular trend**.

sections.title: 2.2. Methods of assessing physical development and the technique of anthropometry

blocks.text: Physical development is assessed by three methods:

items: **Somatoscopic** — visual assessment of body build and proportions.
**Somatometric (anthropometric)** — measuring body weight, length (height), and head and chest circumferences.
**Physiometric** — measuring functional indicators with instruments (spirometry, dynamometry).

parts.text: All anthropometric measurements are made **in the morning, on an empty stomach**, after voiding urine and stool, with the same instruments. The measurements are repeated regularly: **under 1 year — every month; 1–3 years — every quarter; 3–7 years — twice a year; 7–17 years — once a year**.

blocks.text: Measuring length (height)

The length of children **under 2 years** is measured **lying down with a horizontal length board** (a board 80 cm long and 40 cm wide). The child is placed on the back with the head touching the fixed headboard. The head is held so that the lower margin of the orbit and the upper margin of the tragus are **in one vertical plane**. An assistant or the mother holds the head. With the right hand the physician straightens the legs by pressing lightly on the knees, and with the left hand moves the sliding footboard against the heels (the feet flexed at a right angle). The distance between the two boards equals the child's length.

The height of children **over 2 years** is measured **standing with a vertical stadiometer**. The child stands with the back to the stadiometer, touching it with **the heels, buttocks, the area between the shoulder blades and the back of the head**; the arms hang along the body, the heels are together and the toes apart. The lower margin of the orbit and the upper margin of the tragus should be **in one horizontal plane**. The sliding headpiece is lowered without pressing on the head.

blocks.text: Measuring body weight

Children under 3 years are weighed on **electronic baby scales** with a maximum load of up to 15 kg. First a diaper is placed on the platform and the scale is set to zero (or the weight of the diaper is subtracted afterward), then the child is placed lying or sitting. Children over 3 years are weighed undressed on medical scales **to an accuracy of 50 g**; the child stands still in the middle of the platform.
Measuring the head and chest circumferences

items: **Head circumference** — the tape measure is passed at the back over **the occipital protuberance** and at the front over **the brow ridges**.

**Chest circumference** — the tape is passed at the back below **the lower angles of the shoulder blades** and at the front at the level of **the nipples**. In older children the chest circumference is measured three times — during quiet breathing, at maximal inspiration and at maximal expiration; the difference shows the chest excursion.

sections.title: 2.3. Changes in anthropometric indicators with age and their approximate calculation

blocks.text: Length (height)

**Length is the most stable and leading indicator of physical development.** In assessing physical development, length is relied on first. The length of a term newborn is **48–52 cm** (average 50 cm; range 46–56 cm).

blocks.title: Table 2.2. Growth in length in the first year
head: Quarter (months)
Per month
Per quarter

blocks.text: At 1 year the length is **75–77 cm**. In the second year the child grows 12–13 cm, and in the third year 7–8 cm.

blocks.title: Table 2.3. Formulas for the approximate calculation of height in children over 1 year
head: Age
Formula
Reference point
rows: 100 cm at 4 years (twice the birth length)

blocks.text: n — the child's age (years).

During puberty a **growth spurt** is seen: 8–10 (12) cm per year. The maximal growth occurs at **10–12 years in girls** and at **13.5–15.5 years in boys**. Growth in height ends at 16–17 years in girls and at 18–19 years in boys.

parts.text: For height, “**50 – 75 – 100 – 130 – 150**”: 50 cm at birth, 75 cm at 1 year, 100 cm at 4 years (“one meter”), 130 cm at 8 years, 150 cm at 12 years. Height **doubles by 4 years** and **triples by 12 years**.

blocks.text: Body weight

The weight of a term newborn is **2600–4200 g** (average 3500 g in boys and 3200 g in girls). A newborn heavier than 4000 g is considered **large**; a weight below 2500 g is characteristic of prematurity or intrauterine growth restriction.
After birth **physiological weight loss** is seen: the maximal loss occurs on **days 3–4** and amounts to **5–8%** (permissible limit up to 10%); the weight is regained by **days 7–10**.
Weight gain:

items: in the first half-year — on average **800 g** per month (25–30 g per day);
in the second half-year — on average **400 g** per month;
at 1 year the weight is on average **10.5 kg** — **3 times** the birth weight; the weight **doubles by 4.5–5 months**.

blocks.text: **Formula for calculating weight in the first year:** the weight of a 6-month-old child ≈ **8200 g**. For a child younger than 6 months, 800 g are subtracted for each missing month; for a child older than 6 months, 400 g are added for each subsequent month. Another method: 800 g for each month of the first half-year and 400 g for each month of the second half-year are added to the birth weight.

blocks.title: Table 2.4. Calculating weight in children over 1 year
head: Age
Formula or rule
rows: A height of 125 cm corresponds to 25 kg; 2 kg are subtracted for each missing 5 cm, and 3 kg (3.5 kg at puberty) are added for each extra 5 cm

parts.text: For weight, the “**3 – 6 – 12**” rule: at 1 year the weight is **3 times** the birth weight; at 6–7 years it is **2 times** the weight at 1 year; at 12 years it is **3 times** the weight at 1 year.

blocks.text: Head circumference

At birth the head circumference is **34–36 cm**. In the first year it grows by 2 cm per month at 0–3 months, by 1 cm per month at 4–6 months and by 0.5 cm per month at 7–12 months. At 1 year it is ≈ **46 cm**, at 5 years ≈ **50 cm**, at 10 years ≈ **55 cm**.

**Formulas:** in a 6-month-old child the head circumference is **43 cm**; 1.5 cm are subtracted for each missing month, and 0.5 cm are added for each subsequent month. In a child over 1 year it is **50 cm** at 5 years; 1 cm is subtracted for each missing year, and 0.6 cm is added for each subsequent year.
Chest circumference

At birth the chest circumference is **32–34 cm** — **1–2 cm smaller** than the head circumference. **At 3–4 months** the two circumferences become equal, after which the chest circumference grows faster. After 1 year the chest circumference exceeds the head circumference by approximately **n to 2n cm** (n — age).

**Formulas:** in a 6-month-old child the chest circumference is **45 cm**; 2 cm are subtracted for each missing month, and 0.5 cm are added for each subsequent month. At 10 years it is **63 cm**; 1.5 cm are subtracted for each missing year, and 3 cm are added for each subsequent year.

parts.text: In a newborn, a head circumference **more than 2 cm larger** than the chest circumference may be a sign of hydrocephalus (for example, perinatal damage to the central nervous system). A head circumference small for age is microcephaly. When measuring, the molding of the skull bones during delivery (configuration), the caput succedaneum and edema are taken into account.

blocks.text: Proportionality indices and body proportions

items: **The weight–length ratio** is the birth weight (g) / length (cm). In a healthy term newborn it is **60–80** (most often 60–65). **Less than 60** indicates intrauterine growth restriction (hypotrophy).
**Body mass index (BMI, Quetelet index)** = weight (kg) / height (m)^2^ — used in school-age children to assess nutritional status and obesity; it is evaluated with centile tables for age and sex.

blocks.text: **Body proportions change with age:** the height of the head is **1/4** of the body length in a newborn, **1/5** at 2 years, **1/6** at 6 years, **1/7** at 12 years and **1/8** in adults. The midpoint of the body lies above the umbilicus in a preterm newborn, at the umbilicus in a term newborn, between the umbilicus and the pubis at 6 years, and at the pubis in adults.

**Philippine test:** with the child's head upright, the child's right hand is placed across the top of the head, with the fingers reaching toward the left ear. If the fingertips reach the ear, the test is positive — the first “growth spurt” is complete and the child is biologically ready for school (usually at 5–8 years).

**The body surface area** of a child is large relative to that of an adult: in a newborn there are 0.06 m^2^ per 1 kg of weight, in an adult 0.02 m^2^. In a newborn the head accounts for 21% of the body surface, in an adult for 7.5%. That is why a child cools down and overheats quickly; the doses of many drugs are calculated per body surface area.

blocks.caption: Changes in body proportions in children of different ages: fetus at 2 and 5 months, newborn, 2, 6, 12 and 18 years (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Anthropometric indicators are assessed by the following methods: approximate formulas (above), **the sigma (parametric)** method, **the centile (nonparametric)** method, **the WHO growth standards (Z-score)** and regression analysis.
The sigma (parametric) method
The child's indicator is compared with the arithmetic mean (M) and the standard deviation (σ) for children of the same age and sex.

blocks.title: Table 2.5. Assessment by the sigma method
head: Range of the indicator
Assessment
rows: From M − 1σ to M − 2σ / from M + 1σ to M + 2σ
From M − 2σ to M − 3σ / from M + 2σ to M + 3σ

blocks.text: For development to be harmonious, the difference in sigma deviations between the indicators should not exceed 1σ.
The centile (nonparametric) method

Centile tables and charts show the distribution of an indicator in a population of children in percentages. The table has 7 centile columns (**3, 10, 25, 50, 75, 90, 97**); the intervals between them are called **corridors** (from 1 to 7).

blocks.title: Table 2.6. Centile corridors and their assessment
head: Corridor
Centile interval
Proportion of children
Assessment

parts.text: Order of centile assessment: 1) determine into which corridor each of height, weight and chest circumference falls; 2) **the level of physical development is determined by the height corridor**; 3) **harmony** is assessed by the difference between the corridors: a difference of **0–1** corridor — harmonious; **2** corridors — disharmonious; **3 or more** — sharply disharmonious development. Corridors 2 and 6 are borderline (require follow-up); in corridors 1 and 7 the probability of pathology is high, and an in-depth examination is needed.

blocks.text: The most important chart is the **weight-for-length** chart. Weight in the **10–25 / 75–90** centile indicates grade I underweight/overweight; in the **3–10 / 90–97** centile — grade II; **below 3 / above 97** — grade III.
The WHO growth standards (Z-score)

In Uzbekistan and many other countries the **WHO growth standards** (2006) are used for children under 5 years. The indicator is assessed by the Z-score (the number of standard deviations from the median).

blocks.title: Table 2.7. Interpretation of the Z-score according to the WHO standards
head: Z-score
Length/height-for-age
Weight-for-length/height
rows: Very tall (endocrine pathology to be excluded)

blocks.text: Writing the conclusion
The conclusion on physical development states three things: **the level** (by height), **harmony** and, if present, **the degree of underweight or overweight**.

Sample: “Boy aged 8 months. Length 68 cm (corridor 4), weight 9000 g (corridor 5), chest circumference 44 cm (corridor 4). Conclusion: physical development average, harmonious; weight-for-length in the 75–90 centile — grade I overweight.”

sections.title: 2.5. Semiotics of disorders of physical development

blocks.text: Changes in height
**Short stature** is a height markedly below that of children of the same age and sex (below the 3rd centile or −2 SD); severe short stature (**nanism, dwarfism**) is below −3 SD. Causes:

items: endocrine: growth hormone deficiency (pituitary dwarfism — usually detected at 2–4 years: a “doll face”, infantile body build), hypothyroidism, Cushing's disease, severe diabetes mellitus, precocious puberty (early closure of the growth zones);
chromosomal diseases: Shereshevsky–Turner syndrome and others;
skeletal dysplasias: achondroplasia, chondrodystrophy, severe rickets;
chronic somatic diseases (heart, lungs, kidneys, intestine), psychosocial deprivation;

constitutional (familial) short stature. **Tall stature (gigantism)** — growth hormone excess (pituitary tumor), hyperthyroidism, Marfan syndrome, Klinefelter syndrome (XXY); in families with tall parents, constitutional tall stature is considered normal.

blocks.text: Changes in weight
**Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR)** — the newborn's weight and/or length is below the 10th centile for gestational age.

items: **Symmetric (hypoplastic)** — both weight and length are equally reduced; the adverse factors acted in the first and second halves of pregnancy, and the changes are more severe.
**Asymmetric (hypotrophic)** — length is normal and only weight is reduced; the adverse factors acted in the second half of pregnancy.

blocks.label: Figure 2.7
blocks.caption: A newborn with intrauterine growth restriction (left) and a newborn with normal physical indicators (right) (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Acquired chronic nutritional disorders (dystrophies):** under 1 year they are called **hypotrophy** and **paratrophy**, and in children over 1 year **protein-energy malnutrition** and **obesity**.

blocks.title: Table 2.8. Degrees of hypotrophy
head: Sign
Grade I
Grade II
Grade III
rows: On the abdomen, trunk and limbs
Absent everywhere, even on the face
Sharply reduced, the skin hangs in folds

blocks.text: **Hypostature** — an equal lag of length and weight with a satisfactory nutritional status. It occurs in congenital heart defects, brain malformations, endocrine and hereditary diseases.

**Paratrophy** — a chronic nutritional disorder in children under 1 year with excess weight (5–10% or more); the main cause is excessive, one-sided (most often carbohydrate-rich) feeding. The children are flabby and pasty, the skin is pale, tissue turgor and muscle tone are reduced, and they fall ill frequently.

**Obesity** is excessive fat deposition. Excess weight relative to height: grade I — 15–24%, II — 25–49%, III — 50–99%, IV — more than 100%. **Primary** (alimentary-constitutional) and **secondary** (hypothyroidism, Itsenko–Cushing syndrome, hypothalamic syndrome, Prader–Willi and Laurence–Moon syndromes) obesity are distinguished.

blocks.label: Figure 2.8
blocks.caption: Boys aged 5 years: normal height (left) and short stature (right) (Navruzova, Geppe)

sections.title: 2.6. Anatomical and physiological features of the newborn

blocks.text: **The neonatal (newborn) period** is the period from birth to **28 days**; the period of the body's adaptation to extrauterine life. It is divided into the **early** (from tying of the cord to the end of day 7) and **late** (days 8–28) neonatal periods. **The perinatal period** — from the 22nd week of pregnancy to 7 days after birth.

parts.text: Main definitions:

items: **Live born** — a baby that has breathed or shows other signs of life (heartbeat, pulsation of the umbilical vessels, voluntary muscle movement) (WHO).
**Term** — born from **37 completed weeks to 42 weeks** of gestation (37^0^–41^6^ weeks).
**Post-term** — born at **42 completed weeks or later**.
**Preterm (premature)** — born **before 37 completed weeks**.
**Gestational age** — the number of completed weeks from conception to birth.

blocks.text: **A healthy newborn** — a baby born to a mother whose pregnancy and delivery were uncomplicated, with an Apgar score of 8–10, an average weight of 3200–3600 g, a weight–length ratio of 60–80, a normal adaptation period, a weight loss not exceeding 6–8%, and fed with breast milk.

blocks.title: Table 2.9. Features of the newborn by system
head: System
Features

blocks.caption: A newborn: physiological hypertonia of the flexor muscles (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Morphofunctional maturity** is the readiness of the newborn's organs and systems to support extrauterine life. A functionally mature newborn has sufficient motor activity, physiological hypertonia of the flexors, active sucking, a loud cry, adequate thermoregulation, a regular breathing rhythm (without attacks of apnea and cyanosis) and a regular heart rhythm.

sections.title: 2.7. Borderline (transitional) states of the newborn period

blocks.text: **Borderline (transitional) states** are states that arise at the border between intrauterine and extrauterine life and reflect the newborn's adaptation to the new conditions. They are **physiological** and pass on their own, but under unfavorable conditions they **may become pathological**.

parts.text: Most transitional states follow the “**3–7 rule**”: they begin around **day 3** and pass by **days 7–10** (weight loss, jaundice, sexual crisis, uric acid infarction). An earlier onset or longer duration is a sign of pathology.

blocks.text: **A preterm newborn** is a baby born **before 37 completed weeks** of pregnancy, usually with a weight **below 2500 g** and a length **below 45 cm**. The main criterion is **the gestational age**; assessment by weight alone is inaccurate (a term newborn with IUGR may also have a low weight).

head: Degree
Gestational age

rows: Less than 29 weeks (28 weeks or less)

blocks.text: By weight: **low birth weight** — 1500–2500 g; **very low birth weight** — 1000–1500 g; **extremely low birth weight** — less than 1000 g.

**Causes of preterm birth:** isthmic-cervical insufficiency, uterine malformations, extragenital diseases and infections of the mother, fetal pathology, pathology of pregnancy and labor, occupational hazards, the mother's age (under 20 and over 35), harmful habits.
