blocks.text: Signs of functional immaturity:

items: **nervous system:** lethargy, a weak cry or squeal, weak or absent sucking and swallowing reflexes, muscle hypotonia; the unconditioned reflexes appear from 1–2 months of age; psychomotor development lags by 1–3 months;
**thermoregulation:** prone to hypothermia, but also overheats easily (the temperature in the incubator must be strictly controlled);
**respiration:** RR 36–82, breathing shallow and irregular, attacks of **apnea**; surfactant deficiency — **respiratory distress syndrome** (atelectasis, hyaline membrane disease);
**cardiovascular:** HR 140–160, BP lower than in term babies (≈ 50–60/30 mm Hg); the fetal communications close anatomically later (at 2–8 weeks);
**digestion:** small stomach capacity (in the first 10 days 3 ml/kg × days of life), low enzyme activity;
**jaundice** appears on day 2, is maximal on days 5–8 and lasts up to 2–3 weeks.

blocks.text: Physical development of the preterm child

In the first year, the development of a preterm child is assessed by **postconceptional age** (gestational age + age after birth). For example, a child born at 27 weeks and now 9 weeks old has a postconceptional age of 36 weeks.

items: Length increases by 3.5–5 cm per month in the first 3 months; 27–38 cm are added in 1 year.

At 1–2 months the weight increases by 10–15 g per day for each 1 kg of birth weight. Babies born weighing 1001–1500 g double their weight by 2–3 months, triple it by 3.5–4 months and increase it 6–7 times by 1 year; those born weighing 1501–2000 g double it by 2.5–3 months, triple it by 4–4.5 months and increase it 5–6 times by 1 year.
The head and chest circumferences become equal (“cross over”) at 3–5 months.
The indicators catch up with those of term babies at about **2 years**.

blocks.label: Figure 2.10
blocks.caption: An extremely preterm newborn and an incubator (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Conditions:** ward temperature **22–26 °C**, **30 minutes after** a feed, in daylight, on a heated changing table. The condition is assessed at 1 and 5 minutes by **the Apgar score** (topic 1). The history establishes the obstetric history and risk factors.

**Inspection:** proportions, position (flexed in a term baby; on the back with the limbs extended in a preterm baby), spontaneous movements, eye movements, facial expressions and cry are assessed. Pathological positions: **the “frog position”** (limbs extended, thighs lying flat to the sides — hypotonia), **opisthotonus** (arching of the body supported on the head and heels).

items: **Skin:** a healthy newborn is pink; slight cyanosis of the hands, feet and around the mouth is normal if the rest of the body is pink.

**Head:** size, shape, fontanelles and sutures. **Caput succedaneum** — doughy, with indistinct borders, lies over several bones and disappears in a few days. **Cephalohematoma** (hemorrhage under the periosteum) — firmer, fluctuant, located **within the border of a single bone** (most often the parietal bone).
**Neck:** a firm mass in the sternocleidomastoid muscle (hemorrhage — a cause of torticollis); **the clavicle** is palpated (fracture — in breech delivery, with obstetric forceps).
**Chest:** shape, accessory nipples, respiratory movements, nasal flaring, retraction of the intercostal spaces and sternum.

**Abdomen:** distension (intestinal obstruction, ascites) or retraction (diaphragmatic hernia); **the umbilical stump falls off on days 4–10**; the state of the umbilical wound (hyperemia, discharge, palpable umbilical vessels).
**Spine:** a spinal hernia (meningocele, myelomeningocele) is sought.

**Limbs:** malformations, fractures, symmetry, number of digits; the state of **the hip joint** — **the Ortolani test**: with the newborn on the back, the hip and knee joints are flexed at a right angle and the thighs are abducted; a **“click”** felt as the femoral head slips into place is a sign of congenital dislocation (dysplasia) of the hip. Limited abduction of the thighs also raises suspicion of this.
**Stigmas of dysembryogenesis:** up to 5–7 stigmas are normal in a newborn.

blocks.text: **Palpation and percussion:** size, bulging or depression and pulsation of the fontanelles; liver size; pulsation of the femoral and brachial arteries (generally weak pulsation — left ventricular failure; absent femoral pulse — coarctation of the aorta). Because the chest is small, percussion is of limited value.

**Auscultation:** breathing is mainly weakened vesicular; HR 100–160. A murmur heard immediately after birth is not always a sign of a congenital heart defect — it often disappears during the neonatal period.
The Silverman score
The severity of respiratory distress is assessed with **the Silverman score** in preterm newborns and with **the Downes score** in term newborns. Each sign is scored 0–2 points.

blocks.title: Table 2.13. The Silverman score
head: Sign
0 points
1 point
2 points
rows: “Seesaw” — the chest sinks while the abdomen rises
The chin drops on inspiration with the mouth closed; slight nasal flaring
The chin drops with the mouth open; marked nasal flaring

blocks.text: Interpretation: **0 points** — no respiratory distress; **1–3 points** — initial (mild); **4–5 points** — moderate; **6 points or more** — severe respiratory distress syndrome.

parts.text: On **the Apgar** score, the higher the score, the better the condition (10 — ideal). On **the Silverman** score it is the opposite: the higher the score, the more severe the respiratory distress (0 — ideal).

blocks.text: Assessing physical development — a mirror of health
Regular assessment of physical development makes it possible to detect many diseases before their other signs appear.

items: **Arrest of weight gain** in infancy may be the first sign of insufficient breast milk (hypogalactia), urinary tract infection, celiac disease, a congenital heart defect or cystic fibrosis.
**Slowing of growth in height** is an early sign of hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, chronic kidney disease or Crohn's disease.
**Rapid enlargement of the head circumference** (more than 2 cm per month after 3 months) — hydrocephalus; neurosonography is needed.

**The dynamics matter, not a single measurement:** if a child has always grown along the 25th centile, this is his individual norm; if he was previously on the 75th centile and has “dropped” to the 25th, this is a sign of disease.

blocks.text: The newborn: the border between normal and pathology

parts.text: Distinguishing physiological jaundice from pathological jaundice is one of the most important tasks in practice. Jaundice **appearing on the first day of life** is never physiological — it is most often a sign of hemolytic disease (Rh or ABO incompatibility) and requires immediate measurement of bilirubin. Jaundice lasting longer than **2 weeks** in a term newborn and longer than **3 weeks** in a preterm newborn also requires investigation (hypothyroidism, biliary atresia, hepatitis).

blocks.text: Similarly, **if the weight falls by more than 10%** or is not regained in 2 weeks, insufficient breast milk, incorrect attachment to the breast or infection is sought.

skills.title: Skill 1. Measuring the length of an infant

items: Wash the hands, explain the procedure to the mother, spread a diaper on the length board.
Lay the child on the back; bring the head into contact with the fixed headboard.
Hold the head so that the lower margin of the orbit and the upper margin of the tragus are in one vertical plane (an assistant or the mother).
Straighten the legs by pressing lightly on the knees with the right hand.
With the left hand, move the sliding footboard against the heels (flexed at a right angle).
Read the result, pick up the child, record and evaluate the result.

skills.title: Skill 2. Measuring the height of a child over 2 years

items: Stand the child without shoes on the platform of the stadiometer with the back to it.
Make sure the heels, buttocks, the area between the shoulder blades and the back of the head touch the stadiometer; arms along the body, heels together.
Position the head so that the lower margin of the orbit and the upper margin of the tragus are in one horizontal plane.
Lower the headpiece without pressing on the head, read and record the result.

skills.title: Skill 3. Measuring the head and chest circumferences

items: Check and disinfect the tape measure.
**Head circumference:** pass the tape at the back over the occipital protuberance and at the front over the brow ridges, tighten slightly and read the result.

**Chest circumference:** the child raises the arms to the sides; pass the tape at the back below the lower angles of the shoulder blades; have the child lower the arms and pass the tape at the front at the level of the nipples; measure during quiet breathing (in an older child also at inspiration and expiration).
Record the results and compare them with the age norms.

skills.title: Skill 4. Assessing physical development by the centile method

items: Establish the child's age and sex; measure the height, weight and chest circumference.
Find the height corridor in the centile table for age and sex — determine **the level of development**.
Find the corridors for weight and chest circumference.
Calculate the maximal difference between the corridors — assess **harmony** (0–1 harmonious, 2 disharmonious, 3 or more sharply disharmonious).
Determine the degree of underweight or overweight from the weight-for-height chart.
Write the conclusion and, if necessary, refer for additional investigation.

skills.title: Skill 5. Examining a newborn

items: Prepare the conditions: temperature 22–26 °C, a heated changing table, 30 minutes after a feed, wash and warm the hands.
Review the obstetric history and the Apgar score.
General inspection: position, movements, cry, skin color, proportions.
Head: size, shape, fontanelles, sutures, caput succedaneum or cephalohematoma.
Face, eyes, mouth (integrity of the palate, frenulum of the tongue), neck, clavicles.
Chest: shape, RR (a full 1 minute), participation in breathing, retractions; auscultation of the heart and lungs.
Abdomen: shape, palpation of the liver and spleen, umbilical stump and umbilical wound.
Genitals, anus, spine.
Limbs, hip joints (Ortolani test).
Anthropometry, assessment of muscle tone and unconditioned reflexes (topic 3).
Identify the transitional states and write the conclusion.

skills.title: Skill 6. Assessment by the Silverman score

items: Undress the newborn and observe the movements of the chest and abdomen.

Assess the five signs in sequence: movement of the upper chest, intercostal retraction, sternal retraction, chin position and nasal flaring, expiratory grunting (with a stethoscope and at a distance).
Add up the points and interpret the result (0 — none; 1–3 — mild; 4–5 — moderate; 6 or more — severe).
Depending on the result, decide with a senior physician on oxygen therapy or transfer to the intensive care unit.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: An 8-month-old boy came to the polyclinic for a preventive checkup. At birth he weighed 3200 g and was 50 cm long. Now he weighs 9000 g and is 68 cm long.
cases.ask: 1) Calculate the normal length and weight. 2) Assess the physical development. 3) What advice will you give the mother?
cases.answer: 1) Normal length: 50 + 9 (1st quarter) + 7.5 (2nd quarter) + 3.5 (months 7–8, 1.5–2 cm per month) ≈ 70 cm (range 68–70 cm). Normal weight: 8200 + 400 × 2 = 9000 g. 2) His length and weight correspond to his age — physical development is average; a centile table is used for an exact assessment. If the weight-for-length is in the 75–90 centile — grade I overweight, harmonious development. 3) Check the feeding regimen (volume and composition of complementary foods, do not increase carbohydrate foods), physical activity, and continue the monthly control measurements.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A newborn on day 3: the mammary glands are engorged up to 1.5 cm on both sides with no changes in the overlying skin. The girl has a grayish-white mucous discharge from the genital slit. The skin is yellow; the jaundice appeared this morning; the baby is active and sucks well. The weight has fallen by 6% from the birth weight.
cases.ask: 1) What states are being observed? 2) Are they physiological? 3) What is recommended to the mother?
cases.answer: 1) Sexual (hormonal) crisis (physiological engorgement of the mammary glands, desquamative vulvovaginitis), physiological jaundice, physiological weight loss. 2) Yes, all of them are transitional (borderline) states: their timing (day 3), degree (weight loss 6%) and the unaffected condition of the baby indicate a physiological course. 3) Do not squeeze the mammary glands (risk of mastitis), genital hygiene, continue breastfeeding on demand; if the jaundice does not disappear by days 7–10 or increases — see a physician.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A baby was born at 31 weeks of pregnancy weighing 1400 g. The skin is thin and dark red, there is lanugo over the whole body, subcutaneous fat is almost absent, the posterior fontanelle is open, the auricles are soft, and the labia majora do not cover the labia minora. On inspiration there is marked retraction of the intercostal spaces and sternum, the chest moves in a “seesaw” fashion, there is marked nasal flaring, the chin drops with the mouth open, and expiratory grunting is heard at a distance.
cases.ask: 1) Determine the degree of prematurity. 2) Score by the Silverman scale. 3) What is the cause of the respiratory distress?
cases.answer: 1) 31 weeks and 1400 g — grade III prematurity (very low birth weight). 2) Chest movement — 2, intercostal retraction — 2, sternal retraction — 2, chin and nasal flaring — 2, grunting — 2; total 10 points — severe respiratory distress syndrome. 3) Immaturity of the surfactant system (hyaline membrane disease, atelectasis); the baby needs respiratory support and surfactant therapy in the intensive care unit.

topics.title: Neuropsychological development of children. Semiotics of nervous system damage. Body temperature, thermoregulation and fever

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the anatomical and physiological features of the nervous system in children;
the stages of development of statics, motor skills, speech, emotions and forms of communication;
the development of the sense organs (vision, hearing, taste, smell, skin sensation, vestibular apparatus);
the innate unconditioned reflexes of the newborn and the times of their disappearance;
the methods of examining the nervous system, the meningeal and encephalitic syndromes, pathological reflexes;
the features of thermoregulation in children, measuring body temperature, the types of fever.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: assess the child's neuropsychological development according to age;
elicit and assess the unconditioned reflexes in a newborn;
detect meningeal signs;
measure body temperature correctly, fill in a temperature chart and determine the type of fever.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Differentiation of nerve cells is completed **by 3 years**; **at 7–8 years** the structure of the cerebral cortex hardly differs from that of adults; the brain is fully formed anatomically **by 20 years**. The younger the nervous system, the faster it develops — especially **in the first 3 months**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The main motor milestones can be remembered with the series “**2 – 4 – 6 – 8 – 10 – 12**”: **2 months** — holds up the head; **4 months** — rolls over and grasps a toy; **6 months** — sits; **8 months** — stands; **10 months** — walks when supported; **12 months** — walks independently.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: NPD is considered appropriate for age if the child has acquired the skills **within 1 month (±15 days) in the first year**, **within a quarter in the second year**, **within half a year in the third year**, and **within a year after 3 years**. Lagging behind this means delayed development; being ahead means accelerated development.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Kernig's sign is physiological in children under 4 months** (because of flexor hypertonia) — at this age it is not a sign of meningitis. In infants the most reliable signs of meningitis are **a bulging anterior fontanelle and Lesage's sign**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The temperature in the delivery room should be **24–26 °C**; the newborn is immediately wrapped in a warm diaper, dried and placed on a radiant warmer table (the “warm chain”). Preterm babies weighing less than 1500 g are cared for **in an incubator** (34.5–35 °C).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The types of temperature curve are easy to remember by **the daily fluctuation**: **continuous — less than 1 °C**; **remittent — more than 1 °C, does not fall to normal**; **intermittent — falls to normal**; **hectic — 3–5 °C**.

sections.title: 3.1. Anatomical and physiological features of the nervous system

blocks.text: The nervous system connects the body with the external environment and maintains the internal balance (homeostasis). At birth the nervous system is not fully formed anatomically and functionally — this determines the specific features of the child's motor, sensory and mental life.

**The fetal period.** The nervous system begins to form from the ectoderm as the neural tube in the 3rd–4th week of intrauterine development. **The critical period of brain development is weeks 10–18 of pregnancy** (nerve cells divide most intensively). At birth the child has 25% of the cells of the CNS, and at 1 year 90–95%.

parts.text: Differentiation of nerve cells is completed **by 3 years**; **at 7–8 years** the structure of the cerebral cortex hardly differs from that of adults; the brain is fully formed anatomically **by 20 years**. The younger the nervous system, the faster it develops — especially **in the first 3 months**.

blocks.text: **Neuropsychological development (NPD)** is the age-related formation of the child's motor (locomotor) functions, sensation, speech, emotional and mental sphere and skills. Together with physical development, it is the main criterion of a child's health.

NPD is assessed in the following **leading lines**: visual and auditory reactions, emotions, gross movements, hand movements and actions with objects, active speech, understanding of speech, skills; in the second and third years — sensory development and play.
Development of statics and motor skills
Motor functions develop in a **“top-down”** (craniocaudal) direction: first the child holds up the head, then sits, then stands and walks.

blocks.text: Assessing neuropsychological development
NPD is assessed by observing the child during play, independent activity and carrying out adults' instructions.

parts.text: NPD is considered appropriate for age if the child has acquired the skills **within 1 month (±15 days) in the first year**, **within a quarter in the second year**, **within half a year in the third year**, and **within a year after 3 years**. Lagging behind this means delayed development; being ahead means accelerated development.

blocks.text: In older children, thinking and speech, movement (motor skills), attention and memory, social contacts and mental health are assessed. For example, a **4-year-old** child groups objects (furniture, dishes, clothes), jumps on both feet and buttons up; a **5-year-old** makes up a story from a picture and hops on one foot; a **6-year-old** does a standing long jump of at least 70 cm and counts to ten. **At 7 years** the child can think abstractly and is ready for school.

blocks.text: At birth all the sense organs work, but their reactions are generalized and undifferentiated.

**Vision.** The newborn's cornea is thick, the lens round and the eyeball short — **all newborns are farsighted (hypermetropic)**. In the first 2–3 weeks there is photophobia and no tears. At 2 weeks tears begin to be secreted and brief monocular fixation appears; at 3 weeks the baby looks binocularly at a stationary object; **at 2 months** he follows a bright toy; **at 3 months** binocular vision forms and he distinguishes red and yellow; at 6 months he distinguishes bright colors; at 3 years color discrimination is developed; visual acuity is low until 4–5 years. Transient strabismus and nystagmus are normal in the first months.

blocks.label: Figure 3.2
blocks.caption: Structure of the eye (diagram): 1 — pupil; 2 — cornea; 3 — lens; 4 — iris; 5 — ciliary body; 6 — sclera; 7 — choroid; 8 — vitreous body; 9 — retina; 10 — fovea; 11 — blind spot; 12 — optic nerve (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Hearing.** The auditory analyzer is anatomically and functionally formed at birth — the newborn responds to sound by startling or crying. The external auditory canal is narrow and short, the eardrum thick and horizontal, and **the Eustachian tube short and wide** — a tendency to otitis. From 7–8 weeks the baby turns the head toward a sound, and at 3–4 months recognizes the mother's voice. **Audiological screening** is performed on all newborns in the maternity hospital.

blocks.label: Figure 3.3
blocks.caption: Structure of the ear (diagram): 1 — auricle; 2 — external auditory canal; 3 — eardrum; 4 — malleus; 5 — incus; 6 — stapes; 7 — Eustachian tube; 8 — vestibular apparatus; 9 — cochlea; 10 — auditory nerve (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Taste** works from birth: the baby responds positively (sucks) to sweet taste and negatively to bitter, sour and salty tastes; taste is fully differentiated by 4–5 months.
**Smell:** the baby distinguishes strong odors from the 1st month, pleasant and unpleasant ones at 2–4 months, and faint odors at 7–8 months.

**Skin sensation:** tactile sensation appears before the other senses. The newborn responds to a touch on the skin with a generalized movement; at 7–8 months he shows precisely the place of the stimulus; he distinguishes pain points at 7–8 years. In the newborn the sensitivity to cold is higher than to heat.
**The vestibular apparatus** works at birth: when the newborn is rotated, nystagmus appears in the direction opposite to the rotation; rocking calms him.

sections.title: 3.4. Methods of examining the nervous system

blocks.text: **History:** complaints (headache, dizziness, impaired memory and mood, convulsions, sleep disturbance), pregnancy, delivery and the neonatal period, development of static and mental functions. The parents of a child older than 5–6 years are questioned in the child's absence.

**Inspection:** the child's response to the surroundings (indifference, drowsiness, excitability), facial expression, mimicry, behavior, consciousness, position, shape and size of the head, fontanelles and sutures, stigmas of dysembryogenesis, coordination of movements (finger-nose and heel-knee tests), gait, speech.

**The cranial nerves** (12 pairs) are examined by methods appropriate to the child's age: response to odors (I), response to light and following an object (II), eye movements, pupillary reaction, ptosis, strabismus (III, IV, VI), sucking and chewing (V), symmetry of the face at rest and when crying (VII), response to sound and the rotation reflex (VIII), sucking and swallowing (IX, X), turning the head (XI), movements of the tongue (XII).

**Muscle tone:** the newborn has physiological flexor hypertonia. When the child is pulled to sitting by the hands, the arms extend slightly at the elbows and the head follows the trunk. In older children the tone is assessed by the resistance to passive movements. Reduced tone is **hypotonia**, increased tone **hypertonia**, and alternating tone **dystonia**.

**Reflexes:** in the newborn and infant, the innate unconditioned reflexes (section 3.5); tendon reflexes (easily elicited and with a wide zone until 2 years), skin (abdominal) reflexes (weak in children).

**The autonomic nervous system — dermographism:** a line is drawn on the skin with a blunt object. **Red** dermographism — predominance of parasympathetic tone; **white** — predominance of sympathetic tone; **raised (urticarial)** — excessive vagal tone and increased vascular permeability; **mixed** — autonomic dystonia.

**Additional methods: lumbar puncture** and analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid (between LIII and LIV), **neurosonography** (ultrasound of the brain through the anterior fontanelle — in newborns and infants), electroencephalography, rheoencephalography, computed and magnetic resonance tomography, Doppler ultrasound of the cerebral vessels, electromyography.

The presence or absence of the reflexes, their symmetry and strength, and **their timely appearance and disappearance** are assessed.

blocks.text: **Suprasegmental reflexes: the upper Landau** reflex (from 4 months) — a baby held in the air by the abdomen raises the head and the upper part of the trunk and holds them in line; **the lower Landau** reflex (from 5–6 months) — also extends and raises the legs; **the labyrinthine reflex**.

parts.text: **Absent or weak reflexes** (in a newborn) may be a sign of perinatal CNS damage, hypoxia, prematurity or sepsis. **Failure of the reflexes to disappear on time** (for example, persistence of the Moro and grasp reflexes in a 6-month-old child) indicates delayed cortical control and is an early sign of cerebral palsy. **Asymmetry** (a reflex absent on one side) is characteristic of a brachial plexus injury (Erb–Duchenne palsy) or a clavicle fracture.

blocks.text: Main complaints and objective signs

Headache, dizziness, vomiting, convulsions, disturbed sleep and behavior, reduced intellect and memory, movement disorders. On inspection: indifference to the surroundings or excitability, a forced position (the “pointer dog” position — meningitis, opisthotonus), the shape and size of the head (hydrocephalus, microcephaly, “tower skull”), convulsions, muscle development and tone, impaired coordination, stigmas of dysembryogenesis (there should be no more than 5).

**Focal signs:** a difference in the width of the palpebral fissures, ptosis, strabismus (pairs III, IV, VI), drooping of the corner of the mouth and flattening of the nasolabial fold on one side (pair VII — facial nerve paresis), bulbar disorders (pairs IX–X); paresis and paralysis, tremor, hyperkinesis; ataxia, nystagmus; sensory disturbances.

blocks.text: Main syndromes

**Syndrome of reduced excitability (hypoexcitability)** — reduced motor and mental activity, a prolonged latent period of the reflexes, hyporeflexia, muscle hypotonia. It occurs in perinatal CNS damage, hereditary diseases (Down syndrome, phenylketonuria), metabolic disorders (hypoglycemia, acidosis) and severe somatic diseases.
**Hyperexcitability syndrome** — motor restlessness, emotional instability, sleep disturbance, enhanced innate reflexes, tremor, a tendency to convulsions, often muscle hypertonia.

**Hydrocephalic and hypertensive-hydrocephalic syndrome** — an increase in the volume of cerebrospinal fluid and dilation of the cerebral ventricles: rapid enlargement of the head, separation of the sutures, enlargement and bulging of the anterior fontanelle, dilated veins on the scalp, thinning of the skin of the temples, disproportion between the cranial and facial parts. When intracranial pressure rises, these are joined by a high-pitched, painful cry, vomiting, **Graefe's sign (“setting sun”)** — a strip of sclera visible above the pupil, convergent strabismus, horizontal nystagmus, and a “cracked pot” sound on percussion of the skull.

**Convulsive syndrome** — paroxysmal involuntary muscle contractions: **clonic** (short, successive contractions), **tonic** (prolonged contraction), **tonic-clonic**; generalized and partial (local). Causes:

items: in newborns: brain malformations, perinatal CNS damage (hypoxia, birth injury, hemorrhage), intrauterine infections, metabolic disorders (hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hyperbilirubinemia), withdrawal syndrome;
in infancy: neuroinfections, hyperthermia, spasmophilia;
in older children: epilepsy, brain tumors, hemorrhage.

blocks.text: **Febrile seizures** are convulsions, most often generalized tonic-clonic, that occur in children aged 6 months to 5 years against the background of fever (usually above 38 °C) without a neuroinfection. **Breath-holding spells** — cessation of breathing at the peak of a deep inspiration during intense crying or emotional stress, with cyanosis, brief loss of consciousness and sometimes convulsions.

**Movement disorder syndrome** — hypotonia, hypertonia, dystonia; **cerebral palsy (CP)** — hypotonia and hyporeflexia at birth, dystonia from the 2nd month, then muscle hypertonia (the arms internally rotated and extended, the fingers clenched in a fist, the legs crossed).

**Coma syndrome** (see topic 1, section 1.8) — grade I: eyes closed, uncoordinated defensive movements, pupillary reflexes preserved; grade II: no defensive reaction to pain and no pupillary reflexes, breathing and cardiac activity preserved; grade III: breathing impaired, pupils dilated and fixed, BP fallen.
**Syndrome of autonomic-visceral disorders** — mottled and pale skin, acrocyanosis, cold hands and feet, profuse sweating, prolonged subfebrile temperature without infection, emotional instability.
Meningeal syndrome
**The meningeal syndrome** is irritation of the meninges; it occurs in all forms of acute meningitis. It consists of three groups of signs:

items: **General cerebral signs:** fever, severe headache, vomiting that brings no relief, hyperesthesia (heightened sensitivity of the skin, to light and to sound), impaired consciousness, convulsions.
**Meningeal signs** (signs of the meninges).
**Changes in the cerebrospinal fluid** (increased pressure, cytosis, protein).

parts.text: **Kernig's sign is physiological in children under 4 months** (because of flexor hypertonia) — at this age it is not a sign of meningitis. In infants the most reliable signs of meningitis are **a bulging anterior fontanelle and Lesage's sign**.

blocks.text: **Meningism** — meningeal signs are present, but the cerebrospinal fluid is unchanged (only the pressure is slightly raised); it arises from a toxic effect in severe infections (influenza, pneumonia, intestinal infection).
Encephalitic syndrome
**The encephalitic syndrome** is damage to the brain substance (encephalitis, meningoencephalitis, toxic encephalopathy). Signs:

items: **General cerebral signs:** impaired consciousness (from somnolence to coma), psychomotor agitation, convulsions, headache, vomiting, fever.

**Focal signs:** paresis and paralysis (hemiparesis), cranial nerve damage (strabismus, ptosis, facial nerve paresis, bulbar disorders), hyperkinesis, ataxia, speech disturbance (aphasia), pathological reflexes.
**Cerebrospinal fluid:** pressure increased, protein slightly increased, lymphocytic cytosis slight or normal.

blocks.text: Pathological reflexes
In children over 2 years the following reflexes are signs of **damage to the pyramidal tract**:

items: **Babinski** — on stroke-like stimulation of the outer edge of the sole, the big toe extends and the others fan out;
**Oppenheim** — the same response when the fingers are run down the anterior edge of the tibia;
**Gordon** — on squeezing the calf muscle;
**Schaeffer** — on squeezing the Achilles tendon;
**Rossolimo** — flexion of the toes toward the sole when the tips of the toes are struck briskly;
**ankle clonus** — rhythmic contractions when the foot is sharply dorsiflexed.

blocks.text: **Signs of latent spasmophilia** (in hypocalcemia; in detail in topic 5): **Chvostek** — contraction of the eyelid and lip muscles when the zygomatic arch is tapped with a hammer; **Trousseau** — the “obstetrician's hand” when the upper arm is compressed; **Lust** — outward turning of the foot when tapped behind the head of the fibula (“ballerina's foot”).
Features of thermoregulation in children
Thermoregulation is the balance between heat production (**chemical thermoregulation**) and heat loss (**physical thermoregulation**). Its center is **the hypothalamus**.

items: The hypothalamic centers are immature — thermoregulation is **imperfect**, especially in newborns and preterm babies; the child **cools down and overheats quickly**.
The body surface area is large relative to weight (2–3 times that of adults) — heat loss is high.
Heat is produced mainly by **brown adipose tissue** (non-shivering thermogenesis); the newborn cannot produce heat by shivering.
The sweat glands work poorly (full function at 5–7 years) — heat loss is difficult in hot weather, and the newborn overheats easily.
The skin is rich in blood vessels, and the subcutaneous fat is thin (almost absent in preterm babies).
Newborns cannot produce a typical febrile reaction — in a severe infection (sepsis) the temperature may not rise or may even fall.

parts.text: The temperature in the delivery room should be **24–26 °C**; the newborn is immediately wrapped in a warm diaper, dried and placed on a radiant warmer table (the “warm chain”). Preterm babies weighing less than 1500 g are cared for **in an incubator** (34.5–35 °C).

blocks.text: Measuring body temperature

blocks.title: Table 3.10. Normal values of body temperature
head: Site of measurement
Normal
Note

blocks.text: The temperature is measured twice a day — **in the morning at 7–8 am and in the evening at 5–7 pm** — and recorded on **the temperature chart** as a curve. In a healthy child the daily fluctuation **does not exceed 1 °C** (lower in the morning, higher in the evening). The axilla should be dry; a mercury thermometer is held for 5–10 minutes, and an electronic thermometer until the signal. The temperature rises slightly when the child moves, cries, and after meals and bathing.
**Hypothermia** — an axillary temperature below 36.0 °C (below 36.5 °C in newborns): prematurity, chilling, severe infection, hypothyroidism, collapse.

**Fever (febris)** is a rise in body temperature resulting from an **upward shift of the “set point”** of the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center under the action of pyrogens. It is a protective-adaptive reaction of the body: the production of interferon and antibodies increases, and the multiplication of many microbes slows.

**Hyperthermia (overheating)** differs from fever: the set point does not change, and the temperature rises because of impaired heat loss (a hot room, heavy wrapping, dehydration, heatstroke). Antipyretic drugs are ineffective here — the child must be cooled.
Degrees of fever

blocks.title: Table 3.11. Types of fever by height (axillary temperature)
head: Type
Temperature

blocks.text: Stages of fever

items: **Rise of temperature** (stadium incrementi) — heat production exceeds heat loss: the skin is pale and cold, shivering, “goose bumps”, the child feels cold.
**Plateau of high temperature** (stadium fastigii) — the skin is hot and flushed, tachycardia, tachypnea, headache.

**Fall of temperature** (stadium decrementi) — heat loss predominates, profuse sweating. The fall occurs by **crisis** (sharply within a few hours — risk of collapse) or by **lysis** (gradually over several days).

parts.text: The types of temperature curve are easy to remember by **the daily fluctuation**: **continuous — less than 1 °C**; **remittent — more than 1 °C, does not fall to normal**; **intermittent — falls to normal**; **hectic — 3–5 °C**.

blocks.title: Table 3.13. “Pink” and “white” fever
head: Sign
“Pink” (red) fever

rows: Cold, acrocyanosis, bluish nails and lips

Severe: lethargy or agitation, tachycardia, risk of convulsions

parts.text: Antipyretic treatment is not necessary in every fever. In previously healthy children over 3 months, the temperature is usually lowered when it is **above 39.0–39.5 °C** or when the child feels unwell. **In the risk group** (children under 3 months, a history of febrile seizures, neurological and heart diseases) and **in “white” fever** the temperature is lowered from **38.0–38.5 °C**. In children only **paracetamol** and **ibuprofen** are recommended; acetylsalicylic acid (risk of Reye syndrome) and metamizole (risk of agranulocytosis) are not used. In “white” fever, warming of the limbs and vasodilator drugs are also needed.

blocks.text: Delayed development — the first sign of disease
Regular assessment of NPD makes it possible to detect many diseases early:

items: If a 3-month-old child **does not hold up the head** and **does not smile** — perinatal CNS damage, hypothyroidism, a visual or hearing defect should be considered.
If **the grasp and Moro reflexes persist** in a 6-month-old child and the muscle tone is increased — risk of cerebral palsy.
If a 1-year-old child **does not respond to sound**, does not coo or babble — a hearing defect; an audiological examination is needed.
If a 2-year-old child does not speak, does not make eye contact and does not respond to his name — autism spectrum disorder, a hearing defect or intellectual delay.
**Loss of acquired skills (regression)** is always a serious sign: a neurodegenerative disease, severe hypotrophy, encephalitis.

blocks.text: Fever and danger signs

parts.text: In a febrile child the following **“red flag”** signs require urgent admission: age under 3 months; lethargy, barely opening the eyes; incessant vomiting; convulsions; a bulging fontanelle or neck stiffness; a hemorrhagic rash that does not fade on pressure (meningococcal infection); “white” fever; respiratory distress; signs of dehydration.

skills.title: Skill 1. Assessing neuropsychological development

items: Establish the child's age (in preterm children — the corrected age).
Observe the child during play and independent activity, and ask the mother when the skills appeared.
Assess by the leading lines: visual and auditory reactions, emotions, gross movements, hand movements, understanding of speech, active speech, skills.
Compare the result with the age norm (±1 month in the 1st year, ±1 quarter in the 2nd year, ±half a year in the 3rd year).
Conclusion: NPD appropriate for age / delayed (in which lines) / advanced.

skills.title: Skill 2. Examining the unconditioned reflexes in a newborn

items: Conditions: a warm room (22–26 °C), 30–60 minutes after a feed, the baby calm and awake.
**In the supine position:** the search, sucking, proboscis, Babkin, grasp, Moro, tonic neck and Babinski reflexes.
**In the vertical position:** the support and automatic walking reflexes.
**In the prone position:** the protective, crawling (Bauer), Galant and Perez reflexes.
Assess the presence, strength, symmetry and age-appropriateness of each reflex.
Assess the muscle tone (the baby's posture, the pull-to-sit test); record the result.

skills.title: Skill 3. Detecting meningeal signs

items: Lay the child on the back on a flat surface and remove the pillow.
**Neck stiffness:** place the left hand under the child's head and passively flex the head toward the chest.
**Upper Brudzinski:** at the same time watch for flexion of the legs.
**Kernig:** flex the leg to 90° at the hip and knee and try to extend it at the knee (on both sides).
**Lower Brudzinski:** watch the other leg while testing Kernig's sign.
**Middle Brudzinski:** press on the pubic region.
In infants: palpate **the anterior fontanelle** and test **Lesage's sign**.
Record the result (taking into account that Kernig's sign is physiological under 4 months).

skills.title: Skill 4. Measuring the axillary temperature and filling in the temperature chart

items: Check and disinfect the thermometer; shake a mercury thermometer down below 35 °C.
Wipe the axilla dry.
Place the tip of the thermometer deep in the axilla; hold the child's arm pressed against the chest (in a young child the mother holds it).
Wait 5–10 minutes with a mercury thermometer, or until the signal with an electronic thermometer.
Read the result and disinfect the thermometer.
Mark the result on the temperature chart with a dot (in the morning “M” or evening “E” column) and join it to the previous dot with a line.
Determine the type of fever from the curve.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A mother brought her child for a preventive checkup. When placed on the abdomen, the child raises the head and chest supported on the forearms, rolls onto the side, grasps a hanging toy and examines it, laughs out loud, recognizes the mother and coos in a prolonged sing-song way. The grasp, Babkin, support and automatic walking reflexes cannot be elicited; the upper Landau reflex is present.
cases.ask: 1) Determine the child's approximate age. 2) Is the NPD appropriate for age? 3) Which reflex is expected to appear in 1–2 months?
cases.answer: 1) About 4 months: leaning on the forearms on the abdomen, rolling onto the side, grasping a toy, loud laughter, recognizing the mother, sing-song cooing and the upper Landau reflex are characteristic of 4 months. 2) Yes, the NPD is appropriate for age: the grasp, Babkin, support and automatic walking reflexes have disappeared on time. 3) The lower Landau reflex (at 5–6 months) — when held in the air by the abdomen, the child also extends and raises the legs.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: An 8-month-old child was brought to hospital with fever (39.4 °C) for 2 days and repeated vomiting. On examination the child is lethargic and gives a high-pitched, monotonous cry when stimulated. The anterior fontanelle is bulging and tense, with increased pulsation. When lifted under the arms, he draws the legs up to the abdomen and holds them there. The neck muscles are stiff.
cases.ask: 1) Which syndrome should be considered? 2) Indicate the symptoms. 3) What investigation is needed to establish the diagnosis, and what result is expected?
cases.answer: 1) The meningeal syndrome — acute meningitis is suspected. 2) General cerebral signs (fever, repeated vomiting, lethargy, monotonous cry) and meningeal signs: a bulging anterior fontanelle, a positive Lesage's sign, neck stiffness. 3) Lumbar puncture and analysis of the cerebrospinal fluid: the pressure is increased; in purulent meningitis the fluid is turbid, the cytosis is in the thousands with predominance of neutrophils, and the protein is sharply increased; in serous meningitis the fluid is clear with lymphocytic cytosis. A blood count and CSF culture; the child is treated urgently.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 2-year-old child has ARVI. Temperature 39.2 °C. The child is lethargic, the skin is pale and mottled, the hands and feet are cold, the nails bluish, HR 160 per minute. According to the mother, he had a seizure against the background of fever at 1 year of age.
cases.ask: 1) Determine the degree and clinical type of fever. 2) Why should the child be included in the risk group? 3) What is the physician's management?
cases.answer: 1) High fever (39.1–41.0 °C); clinical type — “white” (pale) fever: spasm of the peripheral vessels (mottled skin, cold limbs, acrocyanosis, tachycardia). 2) There is a history of a febrile seizure (within the age range of 6 months – 5 years) and “white” fever — the risk of a recurrent seizure is high. 3) Lower the temperature immediately (paracetamol or ibuprofen at the age-appropriate dose) and at the same time warm the limbs and relieve the vascular spasm (vasodilator drugs prescribed by the physician); monitor the condition and decide on hospital admission.

topics.title: The skin, subcutaneous fat and lymphatic system: anatomical and physiological features, methods of examination, semiotics

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the anatomical and physiological features of children's skin, the skin appendages (hair, nails, glands) and the subcutaneous fat;
the primary and secondary morphological elements of the skin;
the skin changes characteristic of the newborn period;
the main signs and syndromes of damage to the skin and subcutaneous fat;
the anatomical and physiological features of the lymphatic system (lymph nodes, spleen, thymus) and the methods of examining it;
the semiotics of lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly and lymphatic-hypoplastic diathesis.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: inspect the skin and its appendages and describe a rash correctly;
determine the moisture, temperature and elasticity of the skin by palpation; perform the capillary fragility tests and test dermographism;
assess the thickness, distribution and consistency of the subcutaneous fat and the tissue turgor; detect edema;
palpate and describe all groups of peripheral lymph nodes;
palpate and percuss the spleen, and percuss the thymus;
write the corresponding sections of the case history.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: A child's skin is **thin, delicate, rich in vessels, highly absorptive and weakly protective**. That is why it needs strict hygiene and a proper temperature regimen, and ointments are used with caution (for example, ointments containing boric acid, hormones or phenol may cause poisoning).

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Remember the solid elements in order of depth: **“Macule — Papule — Tubercle — Node”** — from the skin surface downward. The cavitary elements by size and contents: **vesicle < 5 mm < bulla**, **pustule — pus**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **An erosion heals without a trace, whereas an ulcer heals with a scar** — this is the main criterion for distinguishing them. Small scars remain after chickenpox, irregular deep scars after tuberculosis, and star-shaped scars after a syphilitic gumma.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Physiological** jaundice of the newborn appears **on days 2–3** and disappears **by days 7–10** (up to 2–3 weeks in preterm babies). Jaundice appearing **on the 1st day** or persisting **longer than 2 weeks** is always **pathological** (hemolytic disease, infection, biliary atresia).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: **Carotene jaundice** (from eating large amounts of carrots, pumpkin or tangerines) — only **the palms and soles** turn yellow; **the sclerae and mucous membranes never turn yellow**. This is the main difference from true jaundice.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Physiological acrocyanosis in the newborn** (bluish palms and soles) is normal in the first 1–2 days and in the cold. If **cyanosis around the mouth** (perioral) increases with crying, sucking and coughing, cardiac or pulmonary pathology should be excluded.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Fat **is deposited: face → limbs → trunk → abdomen**, and **disappears in the reverse order: abdomen → trunk → limbs → face**. That is why in hypotrophy the face loses weight last (“Bichat's fat pads” persist for a long time).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Skin **elasticity** concerns only the skin fold (rapid smoothing); **turgor** is the resistance of all soft tissues; **the thickness of the skin fold** reflects the development of the fat layer. Do not confuse these three concepts.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In a healthy child **no more than 3 groups** are palpable — usually among the **submandibular, cervical, axillary and inguinal** groups: single, no larger than a pea, soft-elastic, mobile, painless. **The submental, supraclavicular and infraclavicular, thoracic, cubital and popliteal** nodes are normally **not palpable**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The groups not palpable normally: **“S-S-I-T-C-P”** — **S**ubmental, **S**upraclavicular, **I**nfraclavicular, **T**horacic, **C**ubital, **P**opliteal.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In newborns and infants the pole of the spleen may be palpable **up to 1 cm** below the costal margin (the abdominal muscles are lax, and the organ is relatively large). In older children a palpable spleen is always **pathological**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The rule of percussion: percussion proceeds **from the resonant (clear) note toward the dull note**, and the border is marked along the edge of the finger **facing the resonant note**. The spleen — **quiet percussion**, because it is surrounded by hollow organs that give tympany.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Causes of splenomegaly — **“HILTA”**: **H**emolysis, **I**nfection, **L**iver (portal hypertension), **T**umor (leukemia, lymphoma), **A**utoimmune and storage diseases.

sections.title: 4.1. Anatomical and physiological features of the skin

blocks.text: The skin is the organ that covers the body from the outside and performs the functions of a barrier between the internal and external environment, metabolism, thermoregulation, respiration and sensation. It consists of three layers: **the epidermis**, **the dermis** (papillary and reticular layers) and **the subcutaneous fat** (hypodermis).

blocks.label: Figure 4.1
blocks.caption: Structure of the skin. I — epidermis: 1 — horny, 2 — lucid, 3 — granular, 4 — spinous, 5 — basal layer; II — dermis: 6 — papillary, 7 — reticular layer; III — subcutaneous fat; 8 — sweat glands, 9 — hair follicle, 10 — sebaceous glands (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Structural features:

items: In children under 3 years the skin layers are **1.5–3 times thinner** than in adults; they approach those of adults only **at 7 years**.
The epidermal cells lie far apart, and the structure is loose; in the newborn the horny layer consists of 2–3 rows and is easily shed.
The granular layer is poorly developed — the newborn's skin is **translucent and pale pink**.

**The connection between the epidermis and the dermis is very delicate** (the basement membrane and connective fibers are weak) — in various diseases the epidermis is easily detached and **blisters** form.
The pH of the skin surface in the newborn is close to neutral and falls by the end of the 1st month; the bactericidal activity of the secretion is weak.
The capillary network is extensive and well developed — the skin is pink, and absorption and heat loss are high.
The nerve endings are morphologically immature but functionally mature — pain, tactile and temperature sensation are complete.

blocks.title: Table 4.1. Functional features of children's skin
head: Function
Feature in children
rows: Weak: the horny layer is thin, keratinization and the connection with the dermis are insufficient; pH close to neutral; local immunity not formed — a tendency to infection and injury
Immature — weak stimulation of the melanocytes; sensitive to sunlight
High — the horny layer is thin and rich in vessels; ointments containing hormones or toxic substances have a systemic effect
Weak: heat loss exceeds heat production — the child overheats and cools down quickly
Several times stronger than in adults
Complete from weeks 3–4: vitamin D~3~ is synthesized under the action of UV rays
Complete from birth; the newborn first recognizes the mother through tactile sensation

blocks.text: Skin appendages:

items: **The sebaceous glands** work already in the fetal period and produce **the cheese-like coating** (vernix caseosa) — it protects the skin from the amniotic fluid and eases passage through the birth canal. The glands work intensively in the 1st year, then their activity decreases and increases again at puberty (acne).

**The sweat glands** (eccrine) are not fully formed at birth, and their ducts are closed by epithelium. Sweating begins **from weeks 3–4** and is incomplete until 3–4 months; until 3 years sweating occurs only at high temperatures. The sweat glands and the thermoregulatory center mature fully **at 5–7 years**. The apocrine glands begin to work at puberty.

**Hair.** The newborn has downy hair — **lanugo** — on the shoulders and back (abundant in preterm babies). The hair follicles are poorly developed — furuncles hardly occur in newborns (pseudofurunculosis occurs instead). The eyebrows and eyelashes are poorly developed.
**The nails** reach the fingertips in a term newborn (a sign of maturity); in the first days of life their growth slows and a “physiological line” forms.

parts.text: A child's skin is **thin, delicate, rich in vessels, highly absorptive and weakly protective**. That is why it needs strict hygiene and a proper temperature regimen, and ointments are used with caution (for example, ointments containing boric acid, hormones or phenol may cause poisoning).

blocks.text: The examination is carried out by **questioning, inspection, palpation and special tests**.
Questioning

The time of appearance of changes in color, a rash, itching, sweating or edema; their relation to food, drugs, infections and chemicals; whether similar episodes have occurred before; allergic and skin diseases in the family are established.
Inspection

Inspection is carried out, as far as possible, **in natural daylight** in a warm room. The skin is inspected in sequence **from top to bottom**: the hairy part of the head, face, neck, trunk, **natural folds**, inguinal and femoral regions, palms and soles, the spaces between the fingers.
Inspection assesses:

items: the **color** of the skin and its evenness;
**moisture**;
**cleanness** (absence of rash, scaling, scratch marks, hemorrhages);
the state of the **skin vessels** (venous network);
the **integrity** of the skin;
the skin **appendages** — hair and nails.

blocks.text: **When a rash is found**, the following are established: the time of appearance; relation to any factor; the morphological type; size (mm, cm); number (single, few — can be counted, many — cannot be counted); shape (round, oval, star-shaped, annular); color; location (extensor or flexor surfaces, folds) and extent; the skin background (hyperemic or unchanged); the stages and course of the eruption; the secondary elements left (scaling, pigmentation, crusts).
Primary morphological elements of the skin

**Primary elements** appear on unchanged skin. They are **solid** (macule, papule, tubercle, node, wheal) and **cavitary** — filled with serous, hemorrhagic or purulent fluid (vesicle, bulla, pustule).

blocks.title: Table 4.2. Primary morphological elements of the skin
head: Element
Description
rows: A circumscribed change of color that is not raised above the skin surface and has unchanged consistency. An inflammatory macule results from dilation of the dermal vessels and disappears when pressed with glass (diascopy): roseola — up to 5 mm (numerous roseolas of 1–2 mm — a fine punctate rash); macula — 6–20 mm (5–10 mm — a small-spotted rash, >10 mm — a large-spotted rash); erythema — an area of reddening larger than 20–30 mm. Non-inflammatory macules: pigmented (nevus, freckle, chloasma, vitiligo), vascular (hemangioma, telangiectasia), hemorrhagic (petechia — punctate, purpura — small and numerous, ecchymosis — >20 mm) — they do not disappear on pressure
A solid element raised above the skin surface; located in the epidermis and the superficial dermis; heals without a scar. Miliary — 1–1.5 mm, lenticular — 2–3 mm, plaque — larger than 1 cm
A circumscribed firm raised element, 5–10 mm; formed by an inflammatory granuloma in the dermis; may leave an ulcer and a scar (tuberculosis, leprosy)
A round or oval formation located in the deep dermis or the subcutaneous fat; the result of inflammation or a tumor; may heal without a trace, ulcerate, or leave a scar or atrophy
A solid raised element formed by edema of the papillary layer, larger than 3–4 mm; itchy; transient — lasts from a few minutes to hours and disappears without a trace (urticaria)
A cavitary element up to 5 mm containing serous or serous-hemorrhagic fluid; dries to form a crust or ruptures to leave an erosion (chickenpox, herpes, eczema)
A cavitary element larger than 0.5 cm filled with serous, hemorrhagic or purulent fluid (pemphigus, epidermolysis bullosa, burns)
An element from 1–2 mm to 10 mm filled with pus, with a ring of hyperemia around it; superficial or deep (vesiculopustulosis, folliculitis)

blocks.text: Secondary morphological elements
**Secondary elements** appear as a result of the evolution of primary elements and help to diagnose the disease retrospectively.

parts.text: **An erosion heals without a trace, whereas an ulcer heals with a scar** — this is the main criterion for distinguishing them. Small scars remain after chickenpox, irregular deep scars after tuberculosis, and star-shaped scars after a syphilitic gumma.

blocks.text: Palpation
Palpation is carried out from top to bottom, carefully over affected areas.

items: **Moisture** is determined by stroking symmetric areas of the body (palms, soles, axillae, groins) with the palm. Normally the skin is slightly shiny and moderately moist.
**Temperature** is determined by touching symmetric areas with the back of the hand; a local rise in temperature is characteristic of inflammation.

**Elasticity** — in an area where subcutaneous fat is poorly developed (front of the chest, back of the hand, elbow crease), a fold of **skin only** is picked up with the thumb and index finger. If it smooths out immediately after release, elasticity is preserved; if it smooths out slowly, it is **reduced**.

blocks.label: Figure 4.18
blocks.caption: Determining skin elasticity (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Special tests
**The state (fragility) of the vessel wall** is assessed by three signs:

items: **The tourniquet sign (Konchalovsky–Rumpel–Leede).** A tourniquet (or a sphygmomanometer cuff) is applied to the middle third of the upper arm so that the venous outflow stops but the radial pulse is preserved. **After 3–5 minutes** the petechiae on the elbow crease and the inner surface of the forearm are counted. **More than 5 petechiae** is pathological (impaired vascular permeability or platelet deficiency).

**The pinch sign.** A fold of skin on the front or side of the chest is picked up with the fingers of both hands (2–3 mm apart) and shifted in opposite directions; if a hemorrhage appears in the area of the fold, the sign is positive.
**The hammer sign.** The sternum is tapped with a percussion hammer without causing pain; if hemorrhages appear on the skin, the sign is positive.

blocks.text: **Dermographism** is an assessment of the tone of the skin vessels. Several lines are drawn on the skin of the chest or abdomen with a fingernail or the tip of a spatula:

items: normally **after 5–20 seconds** a **white line** appears (white dermographism — sympathetic effect), which is replaced **after 1–10 minutes** by a **red line** (parasympathetic effect);

a rapidly appearing, broad, long-lasting **red** dermographism indicates parasympathetic predominance (vagotonia); a **white**, long-lasting one — sympathicotonia; a raised one — **urticarial** dermographism (allergic predisposition).

blocks.label: Figure 4.19
blocks.caption: Eliciting dermographism (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.label: Figure 4.20
blocks.caption: Red dermographism (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Other methods:** diascopy (pressing a macule with glass — an inflammatory macule disappears, a hemorrhagic one does not); skin biopsy; smears and scrapings (fungi, scabies burrow); the tuberculin (**Mantoux**) test and skin tests with allergens.

blocks.label: Figure 4.21
blocks.caption: The Mantoux reaction: a papule with surrounding hyperemia (Navruzova, Geppe)

parts.text: **Physiological** jaundice of the newborn appears **on days 2–3** and disappears **by days 7–10** (up to 2–3 weeks in preterm babies). Jaundice appearing **on the 1st day** or persisting **longer than 2 weeks** is always **pathological** (hemolytic disease, infection, biliary atresia).

blocks.text: Changes in skin color

**Pallor.** Diffuse pallor of the skin, visible mucous membranes and conjunctivae is a sign of **anemia**. Pallor also occurs in vascular spasm: aortic defects, hypertensive crisis, collapse, “white” fever, shock. Specific tints: **waxy (alabaster)** — chlorosis and kidney diseases; **earthy** — malignant tumors; **“café-au-lait”** — infective endocarditis.

**Hyperemia (redness)** — dilation of the peripheral vessels (fever, overheating, vasodilators, inflammation, burns, excitement, physical exertion) or erythrocytosis (polycythemia — a dark red-bluish tint). In carbon monoxide poisoning the skin is **bright red (cherry red)**. In Itsenko–Cushing syndrome redness of the cheeks gives a **“matron face”**.

blocks.label: Figure 4.23
blocks.caption: The “butterfly” erythema on the face in systemic lupus erythematosus (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.label: Figure 4.24
blocks.caption: Erythema of the face and eyelids in juvenile dermatomyositis (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.label: Figure 4.25

blocks.text: Pigmentation disorders:

items: **Hyperpigmentation** — congenital pigmented spots (nevus), “café-au-lait” spots (neurofibromatosis — more than 6, >5 mm), a bronze color (adrenal insufficiency — Addison's disease; at friction sites), pigmentation after measles, hemochromatosis, porphyria, heavy metal poisoning.

**Hypopigmentation** — albinism (complete absence of pigment), **vitiligo** (white spots of various shapes), areas after burns and rashes. In scleroderma, areas of hyper- and hypopigmentation occur together.

blocks.label: Figure 4.26
blocks.caption: A giant congenital pigmented nevus (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Jaundice (icterus)** is the accumulation of bilirubin in the tissues. First **the sclerae, the soft palate and the area under the tongue** turn yellow. Causes: hemolysis (hemolytic disease of the newborn, hemolytic anemias), damage to the liver parenchyma (viral hepatitis), obstruction of the bile ducts, hereditary disorders of bilirubin metabolism (Gilbert, Crigler–Najjar syndromes), metabolic diseases (galactosemia, tyrosinemia, cystic fibrosis). Tints: **lemon-yellow** — hemolytic; **orange (deep yellow)** — parenchymal; **green-yellow** — obstructive jaundice.

parts.text: **Carotene jaundice** (from eating large amounts of carrots, pumpkin or tangerines) — only **the palms and soles** turn yellow; **the sclerae and mucous membranes never turn yellow**. This is the main difference from true jaundice.

blocks.text: **Cyanosis** is a bluish tint of the skin and mucous membranes; it appears when **reduced hemoglobin in capillary blood exceeds 50 g/l**. It is first seen where the epidermis is thin — the lips, nails, earlobes and oral mucosa.

blocks.title: Table 4.5. Types of cyanosis
head: Type
Mechanism and causes
Clinical difference
rows: Oxygenation of arterial blood is impaired: pneumonia, atelectasis, bronchial obstruction, air or fluid in the pleural cavity, damage to the respiratory center and muscles; “blue” congenital heart defects with a right-to-left shunt (tetralogy of Fallot); methemoglobinemia (nitrates, aniline)
The tongue and lips are also blue; the limbs are warm; in heart defects it does not decrease with oxygen
Peripheral blood flow slows and the tissues extract more oxygen: heart failure, shock, cold exposure
The tip of the nose, ears and fingers are blue; the limbs are cold; the tongue is pink
Venous thrombosis or compression (superior vena cava syndrome — upper body, neck, arms), Raynaud syndrome, autonomic dystonia

parts.text: **Physiological acrocyanosis in the newborn** (bluish palms and soles) is normal in the first 1–2 days and in the cold. If **cyanosis around the mouth** (perioral) increases with crying, sucking and coughing, cardiac or pulmonary pathology should be excluded.

blocks.text: Skin integrity, blood vessels and peeling

items: **Trophic ulcers** — in chronic circulatory failure, diseases of the spinal cord and peripheral nerves, arterial thrombosis, vasculitis. In bedridden patients, **bedsores** on the buttocks, sacrum and shoulder blades.
**Striae** — broad pink-purple lines: **Itsenko–Cushing syndrome** and long-term glucocorticoid therapy; thin whitish striae may be physiological during rapid growth at puberty.

**Dilation of the venous network:** on the hairy part of the head — **hydrocephalus**; on the upper chest and between the shoulder blades — enlarged bronchopulmonary lymph nodes; on the anterior abdominal wall the **“caput medusae”** — liver cirrhosis (portal hypertension).

**Spider angiomas** and **“liver palms”** — chronic liver diseases. **Hemangioma** — a pink or dark red spot, sometimes raised, formed by proliferation of capillaries. **Livedo** — a net-like bluish pattern (vasculitis, antiphospholipid syndrome).

blocks.text: Changes in moisture, temperature and elasticity

items: **Hyperhidrosis** — overheating, fever (stage of defervescence), physical and mental stress, **hypoglycemia**, **thyrotoxicosis**, autonomic dystonia (palms and axillae — in adolescents), **the initial period of rickets** (sour-smelling sweat on the nape, rubbing against the pillow — bald patch on the nape).
**Dry skin** — dehydration (hypohidrosis), chronic intoxication, dystrophy, hypovitaminosis A and PP, ichthyosis, **hypothyroidism**.
**A local rise in temperature** — inflammation of the skin, muscle or joint; a local fall — vascular spasm (Raynaud syndrome, autonomic dystonia).
**Reduced elasticity** — rapid dehydration (vomiting, diarrhea), severe dystrophy, chronic infections, hypothyroidism.

parts.text: **Fever + a hemorrhagic rash that does not disappear on pressure** is regarded as meningococcal infection until another diagnosis is proven. Such a child is given an antibiotic (for example, ceftriaxone) at the prehospital stage and urgently admitted. The rash can be checked with the “glass test”: if the spot does not disappear when a transparent glass is pressed on it, it is hemorrhagic.

blocks.text: Main skin diseases in children (in brief)

items: **Pyodermas of the newborn:** vesiculopustulosis, pseudofurunculosis (Figner), epidemic pemphigus of the newborn, exfoliative dermatitis (Ritter) — blisters form easily because of the weak connection between the epidermis and dermis. **Omphalitis** — redness, infiltration and discharge of the umbilical ring.
**Streptoderma** — impetigo (purulent vesicles, yellow “honey” crusts), erysipelas.
**Viral:** herpes (grouped vesicles), molluscum contagiosum (pearly papules with a depressed center).
**Fungal:** trichophytosis, microsporia, candidiasis; **parasitic:** scabies (paired papulovesicles, itching at night, between the fingers), pediculosis.

**Allergic:** seborrheic dermatitis, **atopic dermatitis** (cheeks, flexor surfaces, itching), strophulus, urticaria, **Quincke's edema** (lips, eyelids, tongue, larynx — risk of respiratory obstruction).
**Hereditary:** epidermolysis bullosa (blisters from trivial injury), ichthyosis, acrodermatitis enteropathica (impaired zinc metabolism).

blocks.text: **Sample case-history entry (normal):** “The skin is pale pink, clean, moderately moist, warm, with preserved elasticity. No rash, hemorrhages or peeling. The subcutaneous venous network is not visible. Dermographism red, appears after 10 seconds and disappears in 2 minutes. The tourniquet and pinch signs are negative. The hair is shiny and evenly grown; the nails are pink and smooth.”
Anatomical and physiological features

Adipose tissue consists mainly of **white fat** and partly of **brown fat**. In brown fat cells oxidation is uncoupled from phosphorylation — energy is converted not into ATP but into **heat** (**non-shivering thermogenesis**).

blocks.title: Table 4.10. Features of adipose tissue in children
head: Indicator
Feature
rows: ≈16% of the body mass in a term newborn; relatively increases by 1 year (rounded body shape, deep folds); low in preterm babies

Accumulates intensively in utero from the 7th month; grows rapidly until 9 months (the volume of the fat cell increases 5 times), then decreases; 2 times less at 5 years; increases again at puberty (more in girls)

At birth well developed on the face (Bichat's fat pads — make sucking easier), limbs and chest; very scanty in the thoracic and abdominal cavities and the retroperitoneal space (the internal organs are mobile — risk of intussusception and renal ptosis)
The fat cells are small with large nuclei; with age the cell enlarges and the nucleus becomes smaller
Relatively firm with a high melting point — rich in palmitic and stearic (saturated) fatty acids, poor in oleic acid. Tends to harden on cooling (sclerema, scleredema)

1–3% of the body mass in the newborn: back of the neck, axillae, between the shoulder blades, around the thyroid gland and kidneys, along the aorta. Protects the newborn from mild cold for 1–2 days; decreases in the 1st year

parts.text: Fat **is deposited: face → limbs → trunk → abdomen**, and **disappears in the reverse order: abdomen → trunk → limbs → face**. That is why in hypotrophy the face loses weight last (“Bichat's fat pads” persist for a long time).

blocks.text: Methods of examination

**The degree of development** is assessed by the thickness of the skin fold. A fold of **skin together with the subcutaneous fat** (without muscle) is picked up with the thumb and index finger. Where the fold is measured:

items: **on the abdomen** — at the level of the umbilicus, to the left or right of it;
**on the chest** — at the edge of the sternum;
**on the back** — below the shoulder blades;
**on the limbs** — the back of the upper arm (over the triceps), the inner surface of the thigh;
**on the face** — in the cheek area.

blocks.label: Figure 4.36
blocks.caption: Technique of assessing the thickness of the subcutaneous fat: taking a fold on the abdomen, chest, upper arm and thigh (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.title: Table 4.11. Average thickness of the abdominal skin fold (A.F. Tur)
head: Age
Thickness, cm

blocks.text: For an accurate objective assessment, the skin fold is measured with **a caliper** at 4 points — biceps, triceps, subscapular and suprailiac — and the sum is compared with centile tables.

**Distribution** — even or uneven (accumulation on the face, neck, upper body, abdomen). In boys the fat is relatively evenly distributed; in pubertal girls it accumulates on the abdomen, thighs, buttocks and breasts.
**Consistency** — normally finely granular, uniform and soft; hardening (sclerema), areas of atrophy and nodules are detected.

**Tissue turgor** — on the inner surface of the upper arm or thigh (upper 1/3), all the soft tissues (skin, fat, muscle) are squeezed with the thumb and index finger and **the resistance** is assessed: tense, with strong resistance — satisfactory turgor; soft, flabby — **reduced**.

**Edema** — the anterior surface of the shin, the ankle, the sternum, the face (eyelids) and the lumbar region are pressed with a finger for 5–10 seconds: if **a pit** remains, there is edema (pastosity — mild). In young children edema is also seen as deepening of the skin folds and marks left by clothing and socks.

parts.text: Skin **elasticity** concerns only the skin fold (rapid smoothing); **turgor** is the resistance of all soft tissues; **the thickness of the skin fold** reflects the development of the fat layer. Do not confuse these three concepts.

blocks.text: Semiotics of changes in the subcutaneous fat

**Deficiency of the fat layer.** In young children — **hypotrophy** (topic 2), at an older age — **dystrophy**, the most severe degree — **cachexia**. Causes: constitutional (asthenic type), insufficient or unbalanced nutrition, digestive diseases (malabsorption), prolonged intoxication, chronic infections (tuberculosis), helminthic invasion, CNS pathology, endocrine diseases (thyrotoxicosis, diabetes mellitus), malignant tumors.

**Excessive deposition (obesity).** If the body mass exceeds the mass appropriate for height by **more than 15%**, it is obesity (the degrees are in topic 2; it is now also assessed by BMI centiles: **≥95th centile** or, by WHO, **Z-score > +2**). It most often develops **before 4 years and at 7–11 years**.

items: **Primary (exogenous-constitutional)** — overeating, low activity; the fat is evenly distributed, the height is appropriate for age or tall.

**Secondary** — endocrine (hypothyroidism, Itsenko–Cushing, hypogonadism), hypothalamic (tumor, craniopharyngioma, after a neuroinfection), hereditary syndromes (Prader–Willi, Laurence–Moon–Bardet–Biedl, Down).

**In Itsenko–Cushing syndrome** fat accumulates on **the face** (“moon face”), **the back of the neck** (“buffalo neck”), the upper body and the abdomen, while the limbs are thin; pink-purple striae, hyperemic cheeks.
**Paratrophy** — with incorrect (carbohydrate-rich) feeding: the mass is excessive, but the turgor is reduced, the tissues are hydrophilic and pale.

blocks.text: **Lipodystrophy (lipoatrophy)** — generalized (congenital generalized) or partial absence of the fat layer (Barraquer–Simons disease — in the upper body); local lipoatrophy **at insulin injection sites**. **Lipomatosis** — excessive diffuse or tumor-like accumulation of fat (Madelung and Dercum diseases).
Hardening:

items: **Scleredema** — hardening of the skin and subcutaneous fat together with **doughy edema** in preterm and weak newborns on days 3–4; **a pit remains** on pressure; it begins on the legs and lower abdomen.

**Sclerema** — **diffuse hardening** of the skin and subcutaneous fat; **no pit remains** on pressure, and the skin cannot be picked up in a fold; the palms, soles and genitals are not affected; the child's condition is severe (cold exposure, sepsis), and movements are restricted.
**Subcutaneous fat necrosis of the newborn** — circumscribed firm nodules after birth trauma.
**Scleroderma** — induration of the skin and subcutaneous fat followed by atrophy; areas of hyper- and hypopigmentation.

blocks.label: Figure 4.40
blocks.caption: Juvenile scleroderma: areas of pigmentation and atrophy (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Edema

Edema is the accumulation of fluid in the interstitial spaces. Mechanisms of **generalized edema**: venous congestion (heart failure), activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system, **hypoproteinemia** (reduced oncotic pressure — nephrotic syndrome, liver diseases, protein deficiency, malabsorption, exudative enteropathy), reduced renal filtration, increased vascular permeability (glomerulonephritis, vasculitis). **Local edema:** Quincke's edema, acute inflammation (phlegmon, erysipelas, osteomyelitis), impaired venous or lymphatic outflow, toxic diphtheria (edema of the cervical subcutaneous fat), mumps (in front of the ear), dermatomyositis (firm edema over the affected muscles).

blocks.text: **Myxedema** (hypothyroidism) — a firm edema **that leaves no pit on pressure** (accumulation of mucopolysaccharides); on the face, the anterior surface of the shins, the backs of the hands and the supraclavicular fossae.

sections.title: 4.6. Anatomical and physiological features of the lymphatic system

blocks.text: The lymphatic system includes **the thymus, the spleen, the lymph nodes**, circulating lymphocytes and the lymphoid aggregates of the mucous membranes (tonsils, adenoids, Peyer's patches of the ileum, the appendix). The thymus and bone marrow are **central**, and the rest **peripheral**, lymphoid organs.
The thymus

items: It lies in the upper mediastinum behind the sternum; it develops **from the 6th week** of intrauterine life from the 3rd–4th pairs of pharyngeal pouches; it forms **before the other lymphoid organs**.
In the newborn its mass is **10–15 g** (the largest relative to body mass); the cortex predominates over the medulla.
Its absolute mass increases **until puberty (9–12 years)** (≈30–40 g), after which **age-related involution** begins — the lymphoid tissue is replaced by fat, but the gland persists throughout life.
Its function is **the differentiation of T lymphocytes** and the production of thymic hormones (thymosin, thymopoietin).

Under the influence of adverse factors (infection, stress, antibiotics, glucocorticoids, cytostatics) **accidental (reversible) involution** may occur — at an early age it leads to secondary immunodeficiency.

blocks.text: The spleen

items: It lies in the left hypochondrium of the abdominal cavity at the level of ribs IX–XI; its long axis runs along rib X from back to front and downward.
It is not fully formed at birth: the trabeculae and capsule are weak, the shape is round and lobulated.
Mass: newborn — **11 g**, 1 year — **26 g**, 12 years — **94 g**, adults — **150 g** (0.25–0.3% of the body mass — constant).
Functions: immune (formation of T and B lymphocytes and antibodies), destruction of aged erythrocytes and platelets, blood depot; hematopoiesis in the fetal period.

blocks.text: Lymph nodes

Lymph nodes are oval formations located in groups where large lymphatic vessels converge; they are the site of tissue fluid drainage, **a barrier** against infection and the multiplication of lymphocytes. The node is covered on the outside by **a capsule** from which **trabeculae** extend inward; under the capsule lies **the marginal sinus**, and in the cortex the **follicles** (B zone), the paracortical (T zone) region and **the medulla**.

blocks.caption: Structure of a lymph node: capsule, trabecula, marginal sinus, cortex and medulla, follicles, afferent and efferent vessels (Navruzova, Geppe)

The barrier function is well developed — infection is retained in the nodes

sections.title: 4.7. Methods of examining the lymphatic system

blocks.text: Questioning and inspection

**Questioning:** enlargement of lymph nodes, redness and pain over them, the time of appearance, possible causes (recent tonsillitis, skin infection, cat scratch, vaccination, contact with tuberculosis), accompanying signs — fever, sweating (especially at night), weight loss, weakness, itching, bone pain, bleeding.
**Inspection:** markedly enlarged nodes (change in the configuration of the neck), hyperemia of the skin over them, edema, fistulas and scars; the state of the tonsils.
Palpation of the lymph nodes

Palpation is performed with the tips of fingers II–IV of **both hands**, simultaneously on **symmetric** areas, with sliding circular movements, pressing the node against a firm base (bone). **Order — from top to bottom:**

blocks.text: Criteria for describing lymph nodes
For each palpated group the following are recorded:

items: **Location** (group) and **symmetry**.
**Number: single** — up to 3 in a group; **multiple** — more than 3.
**Size** — in mm or cm, or by comparison. Normally up to **0.3–0.5 cm** (up to 0.5–1 cm according to Kildiyarova).
**Consistency:** normally **soft-elastic**; in pathology dense, hard (“pebble”) or softened (fluctuation — suppuration).
**Mobility:** normally mobile; in pathology poorly mobile, immobile.
**Relation to the surrounding tissues and to each other:** normally not adherent to each other or to the skin; in pathology they form **a “packet”** (conglomerate).
**Pain:** normally painless.
**Overlying skin:** normally unchanged; in inflammation hyperemia, warmth, edema, fistula.
