parts.text: In a healthy child **no more than 3 groups** are palpable — usually among the **submandibular, cervical, axillary and inguinal** groups: single, no larger than a pea, soft-elastic, mobile, painless. **The submental, supraclavicular and infraclavicular, thoracic, cubital and popliteal** nodes are normally **not palpable**.
The groups not palpable normally: **“S-S-I-T-C-P”** — **S**ubmental, **S**upraclavicular, **I**nfraclavicular, **T**horacic, **C**ubital, **P**opliteal.

blocks.text: Examination of the spleen
**Palpation** — deep sliding palpation according to N.D. Strazhesko:

items: The child lies on the back with the legs slightly bent at the knees and the arms along the body; the doctor sits on the child's right side.
The doctor places **the left hand** on the left half of the child's chest in the area of ribs VII–X and squeezes it slightly (restricting respiratory movement).

The fingers of **the right hand**, slightly bent, are placed perpendicular to the left costal arch, below it — **starting from below** (from the level of the umbilicus, so as not to miss an enlarged spleen).

During the child's expiration a skin fold is formed with the fingers and they are pressed deep into the abdominal cavity; **on deep inspiration** the descending pole of the spleen strikes the fingers.

If there is no result, the fingers are moved upward and the maneuver is repeated. If the spleen is not detected in the supine position, it is palpated with the child lying **on the right side** (right leg extended, left leg bent at the knee and hip joints) — the abdominal muscles relax and the spleen moves forward.

blocks.text: **In a healthy child the spleen is not palpable** (its anterior edge falls 3–4 cm short of the costal arch). If it is palpable, it is **enlarged 1.5–2 times**. When it is detected, the following are assessed: how far it projects below the costal arch (cm), the edge (sharp/blunt, notches), the consistency (soft, dense, hard), the surface, mobility and tenderness.

parts.text: In newborns and infants the pole of the spleen may be palpable **up to 1 cm** below the costal margin (the abdominal muscles are lax, and the organ is relatively large). In older children a palpable spleen is always **pathological**.

blocks.text: **Percussion** — **quiet (soft)** percussion (the spleen borders the intestine and stomach, which give a tympanic sound):

items: The child lies **on the right side** or stands; the left arm is on the head.

**Determining the length:** the pleximeter finger is placed along rib X, parallel to it. **Anterior border** — percussion is performed from the costal arch backward along rib X; a mark is made where the dull sound appears (along the edge facing the resonant sound). **Posterior border** — percussion is performed from the posterior axillary line forward along rib X. The distance between the two points is the **length** of the spleen.

**Determining the width:** a line perpendicular to rib X is drawn from the middle of the length; with the pleximeter parallel to rib X, percussion is performed toward the center of the spleen **from above** (two intercostal spaces higher) and **from below** (from the costal arch). The borders are marked along the edge on the side of the resonant sound.

parts.text: The rule of percussion: percussion proceeds **from the resonant (clear) note toward the dull note**, and the border is marked along the edge of the finger **facing the resonant note**. The spleen — **quiet percussion**, because it is surrounded by hollow organs that give tympany.

blocks.text: Percussion of the thymus
It is performed in young children to detect **thymomegaly**:

items: The child lies on the back or sits.

Using **quiet direct or finger-to-finger** percussion, the **1st and 2nd intercostal spaces** are percussed to the right and left of the manubrium of the sternum, and also from the midclavicular line toward the sternum (the pleximeter finger parallel to the edge of the sternum).
**Normally** there is **no** dullness beyond the borders of the sternum (or only up to the edge of the sternum).
Dullness beyond the edge of the sternum on the right and left (widening of the vascular bundle area) suggests **thymic enlargement**. Confirmation — **chest X-ray** and **ultrasound**.

blocks.text: Lymphadenopathy

**Lymphadenopathy** — enlargement of the lymph nodes (inflammatory and non-inflammatory). **Lymphadenitis** — inflammation of a node: enlarged, **painful**, the overlying skin red, warm and swollen; **fluctuation** when it suppurates. **Micropolyadenia** — small (3–5 mm), dense, mobile, painless nodes in many groups (chronic intoxication, lymphatic diathesis).
**Local (regional) lymphadenopathy** — a process in the area drained by the node: an infected wound, furuncle, folliculitis, pyoderma, dental caries, stomatitis.

items: **Cervical nodes:** tonsillitis (angina), chronic tonsillitis, scarlet fever, diphtheria, adenoiditis; tuberculosis (a dense painless “packet” adherent to the skin, **caseous breakdown and a fistula**, followed by irregular **“stellate” scars**); the initial stage of lymphogranulomatosis (dense-elastic conglomerates fused together — **“a sack of potatoes”**, painless); lymphosarcoma (very hard, painless, enlarges rapidly).
**Occipital and mastoid: rubella** (before the rash!), infections of the hairy part of the head, pediculosis.
**Preauricular:** mumps, conjunctivitis.
**Axillary and cubital: “cat scratch” disease** (bartonellosis — a hand injury), infections of the arm and hand, BCG vaccination complication (left axilla).
Enlargement of **the supraclavicular** nodes is always a serious sign (lymphoma, mediastinal and abdominal tumors).

blocks.text: **Generalized lymphadenopathy** — enlargement of 2 or more non-adjacent groups.

blocks.title: Table 4.19. Causes of generalized lymphadenopathy
head: Group
Diseases and features of the nodes
rows: Infectious mononucleosis (all groups, especially cervical — the configuration of the neck changes, “packet”; the spleen is enlarged, atypical mononuclear cells); rubella (occipital, mastoid); measles (cervical, occipital); adenovirus and parainfluenza (cervical, occipital — slight); yersiniosis, pseudotuberculosis

Toxoplasmosis (marked enlargement, the size of a nut, painless); chronic tuberculous intoxication (many small hard “pebbles” in all groups); brucellosis (1–1.5 cm, with splenic enlargement); HIV/AIDS (an early sign, up to 2–3 cm)
Acute leukemia (all groups, hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, hemorrhagic syndrome, bone pain); lymphogranulomatosis (Hodgkin lymphoma); non-Hodgkin lymphomas; neuroblastoma metastases
Diffuse connective tissue diseases (SLE), the systemic form of juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (Still's disease), serum sickness, drug reactions, lymphatic-hypoplastic diathesis

parts.text: **“Alarming” signs of lymphadenopathy** (a biopsy or an oncohematologist consultation is needed): a node **>2 cm** that does not shrink within 4–6 weeks; **supraclavicular** location; **hard, immobile**, fused conglomerate; **general signs** — prolonged fever, night sweats, weight loss (B symptoms), hepatosplenomegaly, cytopenia or blasts in the blood.

blocks.text: Splenomegaly
**Splenomegaly** — persistent enlargement of the spleen. **Primary** — diseases of the spleen itself (cyst, tumor, congenital anomalies) — rare. **Secondary** — most often:

items: **infections** — infectious mononucleosis, sepsis, bacterial endocarditis, malaria, leishmaniasis, tuberculosis, brucellosis, viral hepatitis, congenital infections (CMV, toxoplasmosis, rubella);
**hemolytic anemias** (“work” hypertrophy) — microspherocytosis, thalassemia, hemolytic disease of the newborn;
**liver diseases and portal hypertension** — liver cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis, portal vein thrombosis (after umbilical vein catheterization);
**tumor and infiltrative processes** — leukemias, lymphomas, histiocytosis, storage diseases (Gaucher, Niemann–Pick);
**autoimmune** — SLE, the systemic form of juvenile arthritis.

blocks.text: **Hypersplenism** — enlargement of the spleen together with excessive destruction of blood cells: **splenomegaly + anemia + leukopenia (neutropenia) + thrombocytopenia + compensatory hyperplasia of the bone marrow**. It is seen in all diseases with portal hypertension.

parts.text: Causes of splenomegaly — **“HILTA”**: **H**emolysis, **I**nfection, **L**iver (portal hypertension), **T**umor (leukemia, lymphoma), **A**utoimmune and storage diseases.

blocks.text: Lymphatic-hypoplastic diathesis

**Lymphatic-hypoplastic diathesis** — a constitutional anomaly with **generalized hyperplasia** of the lymphoid tissue, reduced function of the endocrine system (adrenal glands) and reduced adaptability. Signs may be present from the first months (especially with thymomegaly), but are most often pronounced at **2–5 years**.
Signs:

items: **thymomegaly** (widening of the vascular bundle area on percussion, enlarged thymic shadow on X-ray);
generalized **lymphadenopathy**, hyperplasia of the **adenoids** and tonsils;
**hepatosplenomegaly**;
appearance: **pastose**, pale, sluggish, low muscle tone, well-developed fat layer but reduced turgor, long limbs (disproportionate build);
in the blood — moderate **leukocytosis and lymphocytosis**, neutropenia; arterial hypotension;
frequent ARVI, reduced adaptation to stress (infection, surgery, anesthesia, vaccination) — **risk of sudden death** due to adrenal insufficiency;
an enlarged thymus at an early age may cause **respiratory disturbances** (dyspnea, stridor, apnea) and compression of the esophagus.

parts.text: Before anesthesia, surgery or a severe infection in a child with thymomegaly, the pediatrician and anesthesiologist are warned — because of the risk of adrenal insufficiency a glucocorticoid should be kept ready.

blocks.text: A child with a rash — diagnostic approach
When examining a child with a rash, the answers to three questions are sought:

items: **What is the element?** (macule, papule, vesicle, hemorrhagic) — examined by diascopy.

**In what order and where did it appear?** (in stages — measles; simultaneously — rubella, scarlet fever; polymorphic — chickenpox; dense in the folds — scarlet fever; symmetric on the legs — Henoch–Schönlein).
**What is the general condition and what are the accompanying signs?** (fever, lymph nodes, mucous membranes, meningeal signs).

parts.text: Description of a hemorrhagic rash: in **thrombocytopenia** (Werlhof) — petechiae and ecchymoses are **asymmetric, “leopard skin”**, bleeding from the mucous membranes; in **vasculitis** (Henoch–Schönlein) — a **symmetric, palpable** papular-hemorrhagic rash, often with joint and abdominal pain; platelets are normal; in **meningococcemia** — stellate, necrotic, against a background of fever and intoxication.

blocks.text: Assessment of dehydration by skin signs

According to WHO (IMCI), **the return of the skin pinch** is an important sign of dehydration: the abdominal skin halfway between the umbilicus and the side of the abdomen is pinched in a vertical direction with the thumb and index finger and released. If it goes back **slowly (less than 2 seconds)** — a sign of **some** dehydration; **very slowly (≥2 seconds)** — of **severe** dehydration (assessed together with other signs: condition, eyes, thirst).
A child with lymphadenopathy — algorithm

items: Determine whether it is local or generalized (palpate all groups!).
If local — carefully examine the drainage area (tonsils, teeth, skin, scratches).
Features of the node: painful, warm, red — **inflammation**; dense, painless, adherent — **tuberculosis, tumor**.
Examine the spleen and liver.
Complete blood count — the first test; then targeted investigations.

skills.title: Skill 1. Inspection of the skin and its appendages

items: A warm room, daylight; wash and warm the hands; talk to the child, obtain the mother's consent.
Undress the child step by step.
Inspect the skin from top to bottom: head, face, neck, trunk, limbs, folds, palms and soles, between the fingers, perineum.
Assess the color, moisture, cleanliness, venous network and integrity.
If there is a rash — describe it by all criteria; examine it by diascopy.
Inspect the hair and nails.
Record the result in the case history.

skills.title: Skill 2. Palpation of the skin and special tests

items: Determine moisture by stroking symmetric areas with the palm.
Determine temperature with the back of the hand.
Elasticity — pick up a skin fold on the front of the chest or the back of the hand and assess how quickly it smooths out.

**Tourniquet sign:** place a sphygmomanometer cuff on the upper arm, raise the pressure to midway between systolic and diastolic (or to a level at which venous outflow stops but the pulse is preserved), hold for 3–5 minutes; count the petechiae in the antecubital area (within a circle 2.5 cm in diameter); **>5 — positive**.
**Pinch sign:** pick up a fold in the subclavian area and shift it; assess for hemorrhage.
**Dermographism:** draw lines on the skin of the chest with a spatula; record the time of appearance, color, width and time of disappearance.

skills.title: Skill 3. Assessment of the subcutaneous fat and turgor

items: Pick up a skin-fat fold on the abdomen (at the level of the umbilicus), chest, below the shoulder blade, the back of the upper arm, the inner thigh and the face; measure the thickness (with a caliper or ruler).
Compare the result with the age norm; assess the distribution (even/uneven).
Consistency — by palpation (soft, finely granular, foci of hardening).
Turgor — squeeze all the soft tissues on the inner surface of the thigh and assess the resistance.
Detect edema: press on the sternum, the anterior surface of the shin, the ankle and the lumbar region for 5–10 seconds.
Conclusion: “The subcutaneous fat is sufficiently (insufficiently / excessively) developed, evenly distributed, soft-elastic in consistency, turgor preserved, no edema.”

skills.title: Skill 4. Palpation of the peripheral lymph nodes

items: The child sits or stands, the doctor in front of or behind the child.
Palpate symmetrically with the fingertips of both hands, with light circular movements, pressing the nodes against the bony base.

Order: occipital → preauricular → mastoid → submandibular → submental → anterior cervical and tonsillar → posterior cervical → supraclavicular → infraclavicular → axillary → thoracic → cubital → inguinal → popliteal.
For each group: number, size, consistency, mobility, adhesion, tenderness, state of the overlying skin.
Conclusion: normal / micropolyadenia / regional or generalized lymphadenopathy / lymphadenitis.

skills.title: Skill 5. Palpation and percussion of the spleen

items: The child lies on the back with the legs slightly bent; the doctor is on the right side.

The left hand fixes the lower left part of the chest; the fingers of the right hand, starting from the level of the umbilicus toward the left costal arch, are pressed deeper during expiration, and the pole of the spleen is sought on deep inspiration.
If it is not found — repeat with the child lying on the right side (left leg bent).
When it is found: assess the distance below the costal arch, consistency, edge and tenderness.

Percussion: on the right side, with quiet percussion along rib X determine the anterior and posterior borders (length), then along a perpendicular line the upper and lower borders (width); compare with the age norm.

skills.title: Skill 6. Percussion of the thymus

items: The child lies on the back or sits.
**Quiet** percussion in the 1st and 2nd intercostal spaces from the midclavicular line toward the sternum, with the pleximeter finger parallel to the edge of the sternum.
Mark the border of dullness along the edge on the side of the resonant sound.
Normally the dullness does not extend beyond the edge of the sternum; if it does — suspect thymomegaly and confirm radiologically.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 7-year-old child has had a temperature of 38.7 °C and a sore throat for 2 days. This morning a rash appeared on the skin. On examination: flushed cheeks, a pale nasolabial triangle. A fine punctate rash on a hyperemic background, denser in the axillae, groin and antecubital folds; dark red lines in the folds. The tonsils are red with a purulent coating; the submandibular and anterior cervical lymph nodes are 1.5 cm, painful, mobile.
cases.ask: 1) Which morphological element is the rash? 2) Which disease should be considered? 3) How do you assess the changes in the lymph nodes? 4) What skin changes are expected after 2 weeks?
cases.answer: 1) Roseola — inflammatory spots of 1–2 mm (fine punctate rash) on a hyperemic background. 2) Scarlet fever: tonsillitis, a fine punctate rash dense in the folds (Pastia's sign — lines in the folds), a pale nasolabial triangle (Filatov). 3) Regional lymphadenitis — the submandibular and anterior cervical nodes are enlarged (close to degree V), painful — an inflammatory reaction related to lymph drainage from the tonsils. 4) Large lamellar peeling on the palms and soles, branny peeling on the trunk.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 5-year-old girl has been weak, with poor appetite and pallor, for 3 weeks. Her mother noticed “bruises” on her legs and nosebleeds. On examination: pale skin and mucous membranes, petechiae and ecchymoses of various sizes on the legs and trunk, asymmetric. Peripheral lymph nodes of all groups are enlarged (cervical nodes 2–3 cm, dense, painless, poorly mobile). The liver projects 4 cm and the spleen 5 cm below the costal arch, dense. There is bone pain.
cases.ask: 1) Which syndromes do you identify? 2) What type of lymphadenopathy is it? 3) Which disease should be considered, and what is the first-line investigation?
cases.answer: 1) Anemic syndrome (pallor, weakness), hemorrhagic syndrome (petechiae, ecchymoses — thrombocytopenic type, nosebleeds), generalized lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, ossalgia (bone pain) — i.e., hyperplastic (lymphoproliferative) syndrome. 2) Generalized, “alarming” lymphadenopathy: nodes >2 cm, dense, painless, poorly mobile. 3) Acute leukemia is highly likely. The first investigation is a complete blood count (anemia, thrombocytopenia, blasts, “leukemic hiatus”); confirmation — bone marrow aspiration (myelogram).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A preterm (34 weeks) newborn, 4 days old, was kept in a cold ward. The condition is severe, lethargic, the sucking reflex weakened, body temperature 35.2 °C. On the shins, thighs and lower abdomen the skin and subcutaneous fat are swollen and hardened; a pit remains on pressure with a finger; the skin is cold, pale-cyanotic.
cases.ask: 1) What do you call the change in the subcutaneous fat? 2) How does it differ from sclerema? 3) Which feature of the newborn's subcutaneous fat predisposes to this condition?
cases.answer: 1) Scleredema of the newborn — hardening of the skin and subcutaneous fat together with edema (a pit remains on pressure) in a weak preterm newborn against a background of cold exposure. 2) In sclerema the hardening is diffuse, no pit remains, the skin cannot be picked up in a fold, the palms, soles and genitals are not affected, and the condition is very severe. 3) Newborn fat is rich in saturated (palmitic, stearic) fatty acids and poor in oleic acid — its melting point is high and it hardens easily in the cold; in addition, thermoregulation is imperfect, and preterm babies have little brown fat.

cards.back: Physiological erythema, erythema toxicum (day 3–5), marbled skin, harlequin syndrome, Mongolian spot, milia, physiological jaundice (day 2–3 → day 7–10)
Lemon-yellow — hemolytic; orange (saffron) — parenchymal; greenish-yellow — obstructive
Central (tongue and lips blue, warm limbs); peripheral/acrocyanosis (cold limbs, pink tongue); local (one area)
Scarlet fever — fine punctate, dense in the folds, Filatov's triangle, lamellar peeling; measles — maculopapular, over 3 days face→trunk→legs, Filatov–Koplik spots, pigmentation

topics.title: The bones and muscles: anatomical and physiological features, methods of examination, semiotics and syndromes

goals.text: The student should know:

items: anatomical and physiological features of bone tissue, the parts of the skeleton (skull, spine, chest, pelvis, limbs), joints and teeth in children;
age-related changes in body proportions;
age-related features of the muscular system, physiological hypertonia;
methods of examining the bones, joints and muscles and additional investigations;
the main signs and syndromes of involvement of the osteoarticular and muscular systems (rickets, arthritis, myopathy, hypo- and hypertonia, tetany).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: inspect and palpate the head, chest, spine and limbs; measure the anterior fontanelle;
determine the number of teeth and assess whether it matches the age;
examine the joints and assess the range of motion; perform the tests for detecting developmental dysplasia of the hip;
assess the degree of muscle development, tone and strength;
write the “Musculoskeletal system” section of the case history.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Early closure** of the anterior fontanelle (before 3 months) — microcephaly, craniostenosis, hypervitaminosis D; **late closure** (after 1.5–2 years) — **rickets**, hydrocephalus, hypothyroidism. **Bulging** — raised intracranial pressure (meningitis, hydrocephalus); **sunken** — **dehydration**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Primary teeth: **“they start at 6 months, 8 at 1 year, 20 at 2 years”**; formulas: primary — **“months minus 4”**, permanent — **“4 × age minus 20”**. Delayed teething (the first tooth after 10 months) may be a sign of **rickets**, hypothyroidism or Down syndrome.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In the newborn **the midpoint of the body is at the umbilicus**, in adults — **at the pubic symphysis**; the ratio of the head to the height decreases **from 1/4 to 1/8**. This explains the “big head, short legs” appearance of the newborn.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Chronology of the signs of rickets: **up to 3 months** — sweating, bald nape, restlessness; **3–6 months** — **craniotabes** (the earliest bone sign); **from 6 months** — **bosses, “rosary”, “bracelets”** (osteoid hyperplasia); **after 1 year** (when the child begins to stand) — **leg deformities**.

sections.title: 5.1. Anatomical and physiological features of bone tissue

blocks.text: **Development.** Bones form in two ways: **intramembranous osteogenesis** — directly from connective tissue (the bones of the cranial vault, the facial bones, part of the clavicle) and **endochondral osteogenesis** — first a cartilage model, then bone in its place (tubular bones, vertebrae, pelvis). The skeleton is mainly formed in **weeks 8–9** of intrauterine life.
**Growth.** Bone grows in length through the **epiphyseal (growth) cartilage** and in width through **the periosteum**.

blocks.label: Figure 5.1
blocks.caption: Skeleton of the newborn: a — the skull consists of separate bones; b — the chest is conical, the ribs horizontal; c — the pelvis is narrow, funnel-shaped (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.label: Figure 5.2
blocks.caption: Development of a tubular bone: primary ossification center in the diaphysis and secondary centers in the epiphyses, growth zone, thick periosteum (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.title: Table 5.1. Features of children's bone tissue and their clinical significance
head: Feature
Clinical significance
rows: The structure is coarse-fibered (woven); by 3–4 years it becomes lamellar (Haversian)
The bone is porous and flexible
Few mineral substances, much organic matter and water
The bones are flexible and deform quickly (rickets, incorrect posture), but break rarely
The periosteum is thick, functionally active and well supplied with blood
Subperiosteal fractures of the “greenstick” type; fractures heal quickly
Remodeling is intensive: in the 1st year 50–70% of the bone tissue is renewed (≈5% per year in adults)
High need for calcium, phosphorus and vitamin D; rickets develops quickly when they are deficient
Abundant blood supply; the vessels of the diaphysis and epiphysis are connected
Hematogenous osteomyelitis is most often in the metaphysis; infection easily spreads into the joint
Red bone marrow in all bones (in the fetus and at an early age)
The hematopoietic zone is wide; in adults it remains only in the flat bones and epiphyses
The bone surface is smooth; tuberosities form as the muscles develop

blocks.text: **By 12 years** the bones approach those of adults in their external and histological structure.

**Bone age.** The order in which the ossification nuclei appear is an indicator of biological maturity — **bone age**. In the wrist area: **the 1st nucleus at 6 months, the 2nd at 1 year**, then **one each year** (approximately age + 1); by 12–13 years all the nuclei of the wrist bones are formed. In a term newborn there are nuclei in the distal epiphysis of the femur and the proximal epiphysis of the tibia, and in the calcaneus, talus and cuboid bones — **a sign of maturity**.

blocks.label: Figure 5.3
blocks.caption: Radiological determination of bone age: a — 2 nuclei (1–2 years) (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.label: Figure 5.4
blocks.caption: b — 6 nuclei (6–7 years) (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.label: Figure 5.5
blocks.caption: c — 11–12 years: all nuclei are formed (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Phosphorus-calcium metabolism** is regulated by parathyroid hormone, vitamin D (active form — 1,25(OH)~2~D~3~) and calcitonin. Vitamin D~3~ (cholecalciferol) is synthesized in the skin under UV light, D~2~ (ergocalciferol) comes with food; in the liver it is converted to 25(OH)D and in the kidney to active 1,25(OH)2D. It increases the absorption of calcium and phosphorus in the intestine.

sections.title: 5.2. Features of the parts of the skeleton

blocks.text: The skull

items: At birth the skull consists of many separate bones; **the sutures** (coronal, sagittal, lambdoid) are open — the head **molds** in the birth canal. The sutures begin to close at 3–4 months and fully close at **3–5 years**.

**The anterior fontanelle** — at the junction of the coronal and sagittal sutures, diamond-shaped; its size at birth is **from 1.5×2 to 3×3 cm** (measured between the midpoints of opposite edges); it closes at **1–1.5 years**.
**The posterior fontanelle** — between the sagittal and lambdoid sutures, triangular; it is closed at birth in **75%** of term babies, and closes at **1–2 months** in the rest.
**The lateral fontanelles** (sphenoid and mastoid) are closed in the term newborn.

**The cerebral part of the skull is 8 times larger than the facial part** (2 times in adults). The orbits are relatively wide, the frontal bone has two halves, there are no superciliary arches or frontal sinus, and the jaws are undeveloped.

In the 1st year the skull grows rapidly and the thickness of the bones increases 3 times; at 2–3 years growth of the facial part accelerates (teething, chewing); the skull base grows actively until 7 years.

blocks.label: Figure 5.6
blocks.caption: Skull of the newborn from the side: 1 — posterior fontanelle, 2 — parietal bone, 3 — anterior fontanelle, 4 — coronal suture, 5 — temporal bone (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.label: Figure 5.7
blocks.caption: Skull of the newborn from above: 1 — posterior fontanelle, 2 — sagittal suture, 3 — parietal bone, 4 — anterior fontanelle, 5 — frontal bone (Navruzova, Geppe)

parts.text: **Early closure** of the anterior fontanelle (before 3 months) — microcephaly, craniostenosis, hypervitaminosis D; **late closure** (after 1.5–2 years) — **rickets**, hydrocephalus, hypothyroidism. **Bulging** — raised intracranial pressure (meningitis, hydrocephalus); **sunken** — **dehydration**.

blocks.text: The spine
In the newborn the spine has **no physiological curves**; it is shaped like an arc concave anteriorly (only the sacral kyphosis is marked). The curves form with the static functions:

blocks.title: Table 5.2. Formation of the physiological curves of the spine
head: Curve
Time of appearance
Related skill
rows: Beginning to hold the head up

blocks.text: The curves become stable at **6–7 years** and fully fixed **in adolescence** (14–17 years). Because the vertebrae and the muscles supporting them are poorly developed, children easily develop **scoliosis** and **postural disorders** (incorrect sitting, a heavy bag).

blocks.label: Figure 5.8
blocks.caption: Physiological curves of the spine: 1 — cervical lordosis, 2 — thoracic kyphosis, 3 — lumbar lordosis, 4 — sacral kyphosis (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: The chest

items: In the newborn it is **conical (barrel-shaped)**; the anteroposterior dimension is greater than or equal to the transverse one; the ribs leave the spine **at a right angle, horizontally** — **breathing is abdominal (diaphragmatic)**, and chest excursion is small.

Once the child begins to walk, the sternum descends and the ribs become oblique; **at 3 years** the anteroposterior and transverse dimensions become equal; at school age the transverse dimension predominates and the chest flattens.
From school age its shape depends on the constitution: **conical** (hypersthenic), **cylindrical** (normosthenic), **flat** (asthenic).

blocks.text: The pelvis and limbs

items: At an early age the pelvis is **funnel-shaped** and narrow; sex differences become noticeable **from 9 years** (wider in girls). In the newborn **the acetabulum** is shallow and oval, and a large part of the femoral head lies outside the socket — **predisposition to developmental dysplasia and congenital dislocation of the hip**.
In the newborn the limbs are relatively **short**; later the legs grow faster than the arms.
**The foot** is flat until 1 year (fat pad); the arch forms with standing and walking — **flat feet are physiological up to 2 years**.

blocks.text: The joints

At birth the articular-ligamentous apparatus is anatomically formed. The epiphyses are cartilaginous, **the ligaments are extensible but not strong** — the range of motion in the joints is large, and **dislocations and subluxations** occur easily (at 2–4 years a sharp pull on the arm causes **subluxation of the radial head**). Full formation of the articular surfaces, capsule and ligaments is completed at **13–16 years**.
Teeth
There are 20 **primary teeth**; they begin to erupt **from 6–7 months** (5–7 months), and teeth of the same name erupt in pairs.

blocks.title: Table 5.3. Eruption times of the primary teeth
head: Teeth
Eruption time

blocks.text: **Approximate calculation of the number of primary teeth** (up to 2 years): **X = n – 4**, where n is the age in months (e.g., 6 teeth at 10 months).

There are 32 **permanent teeth**; they begin to erupt **from 5–6 years**: 5–7 years — first molars; 7–8 — central incisors; 8–9 — lateral incisors; 10–11 — first premolars; 11–12 — second premolars and canines; 10–14 — second molars; 18–25 — wisdom teeth. **Number of permanent teeth: X = 4n – 20** (n is the age in years).

blocks.label: Figure 5.9
blocks.caption: Order of eruption of the primary and permanent teeth (Navruzova, Geppe)

parts.text: Primary teeth: **“they start at 6 months, 8 at 1 year, 20 at 2 years”**; formulas: primary — **“months minus 4”**, permanent — **“4 × age minus 20”**. Delayed teething (the first tooth after 10 months) may be a sign of **rickets**, hypothyroidism or Down syndrome.

blocks.text: A child's growth is uneven: first the head, then the trunk, and then the limbs grow relatively fast. Therefore the body proportions change with age.

blocks.title: Table 5.4. Age-related changes in body proportions

blocks.text: Disturbed body proportions are of diagnostic importance: **short limbs with a normal trunk** (disproportionate short stature) — **chondrodystrophy (achondroplasia)**; **long limbs and long thin fingers** — **Marfan syndrome**; proportionate short stature — pituitary dwarfism; persistence of “infantile” proportions — **hypothyroidism**.

parts.text: In the newborn **the midpoint of the body is at the umbilicus**, in adults — **at the pubic symphysis**; the ratio of the head to the height decreases **from 1/4 to 1/8**. This explains the “big head, short legs” appearance of the newborn.

sections.title: 5.4. Methods of examining the osteoarticular system

blocks.text: Questioning

**Complaints:** pain in the bones and joints (location, character, time of appearance, morning or evening, relation to movement, provoking factor); deformity; restricted movement and **morning stiffness**; change in gait; joint swelling.

**History:** osteoarticular, rheumatic and autoimmune diseases in relatives; relation to injury or infection (tonsillitis — rheumatic fever; intestinal and urinary tract infections — reactive arthritis); feeding in the 1st year and **vitamin D prophylaxis**, the age of walking.
Inspection
Inspection is performed **from top to bottom**, with the child **lying, standing and moving**.
Head:

items: **shape** — round; **tower-shaped** (craniostenosis), “square” — enlarged **frontal and parietal bosses** (**rickets**), **flattening of the occiput** (rickets), **hydrocephalic** (overhanging forehead, small facial part), **microcephaly**;
**symmetry**;
**size** (head circumference — topic 2);

state of **the upper and lower jaws**, number and condition of the teeth, **the bite (occlusion)**: primary bite — **orthognathic**, permanent — orthognathic; pathological — progenia, prognathia, open bite; “**gothic palate**” (high, narrow).

blocks.text: Chest:

items: **shape** — conical, cylindrical, flat, **barrel-shaped** (emphysema, bronchial asthma);
**symmetry**;
**the epigastric angle**: **≈90°** — normosthenic; **obtuse** — hypersthenic; **acute** — asthenic;

**deformities**: **“pigeon chest”** (forward protrusion of the sternum — rickets), **funnel chest (“cobbler's chest”)** — inward depression of the lower sternum (congenital or rickets), **Harrison's groove** (an inward depression at the attachment of the diaphragm, with the costal arches flared forward — rickets), **cardiac hump** (congenital heart defect), **rachitic “rosary”** (thickenings at the costochondral junctions of the ribs).

blocks.label: Figure 5.10
blocks.caption: Funnel chest (“cobbler's chest”) (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Spine:** physiological curves and how marked they are (hyperlordosis, hyperkyphosis, **rachitic kyphosis** — in the 1st year, prominent when sitting; **tuberculous spondylitis** — sharp-angled kyphosis — **gibbus**), **scoliosis** (lateral curvature), postural disorders. The child is examined from behind while standing: the symmetry of **the levels of the shoulders and the angles of the shoulder blades, the waist triangles** (the space between the arm and the trunk) and **the iliac crests**. For scoliosis, the line of the spinous processes and **the rib hump** are assessed with the child **bending forward**.

blocks.label: Figure 5.11
blocks.caption: Examination of the spine: 1 — lateral curvature of the spine, 2 — symmetry of the angles of the shoulder blades, 3 — waist triangle, 4 — symmetry of the iliac crests (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Limbs:** straightness and symmetry of the contours (fracture, pseudarthrosis), relative length (proportions), shape — **X-shaped (valgus)** and **O-shaped (varus)** deformity of the legs (rickets), **saber-shaped** curvature of the tibia (rickets, congenital syphilis); **flat feet** (pathological after 2 years); **“bracelets”** (thickening of the distal metaphysis of the radius) and **“strings of pearls”** (finger phalanges) — rickets; **“drumstick fingers”** — chronic hypoxia.
Gait:

items: **antalgic** — the child quickly shifts from the painful leg to the healthy one (involvement of the hip, knee or foot, back pain);
**“duck gait”** (waddling) — congenital dislocation of **both hips**, myopathies;
**limping** — unilateral dislocation, Perthes disease, leg length discrepancy;
with heel pain (talalgia) — the child walks on tiptoe.

blocks.text: Palpation

items: **Head:** the sutures, the anterior fontanelle (size, edges, bulging or depression), **craniotabes** — softening of separate areas of the occipital and parietal bones (they bend like parchment when pressed with a finger) — **an initial sign of rickets** (3–6 months).
**Ribs:** in a healthy child the thickening at the costochondral junction is hardly noticeable; distinct hemispherical thickenings (ribs V–VIII) — **rachitic “rosary”**.
**Limbs:** “bracelets”, “strings of pearls”, pain (periostitis, osteomyelitis, tumor, leukemia), pathological fractures.
**Spine: enthesopathies** (pain at the sites where tendons and ligaments attach to bone), depression or protrusion of the spinous processes, pain.
**Tapping (percussion):** **pain** when the flat and tubular bones (sternum, ribs, vertebrae, tibia) are tapped with a finger — blood diseases (**leukemia**), bone metastases.

blocks.text: Examination of the joints

**On inspection:** shape, size, symmetry, color of the overlying skin; **swelling**, **defiguration** (a reversible change due to intra-articular fluid and thickening of the synovial membrane), **deformity** (a persistent change due to proliferative and destructive processes — subluxation, ankylosis, contracture), hyperemia, pigmentation.
**On palpation:** local temperature, pain, swelling of the soft tissues, intra-articular fluid (**ballottement** of the patella — on pressure over the patella it “floats” in the fluid), crepitus.

Disease

Reactive arthritis, Reiter disease, psoriatic arthritis

blocks.text: **Joint function** — the range of active and passive movements (precise measurement — with **a goniometer**):

items: **Fingers:** making a full fist (the fingers should touch the palm).
**Wrist joint:** bringing the palms together (“prayer position”) and the backs of the hands together, bent at a right angle to the forearm.
**Elbow:** fully extending the arm and bending it so that the fingers touch the shoulder.
**Shoulder:** raising the arms forward and to the side, internal and external rotation; touching the opposite shoulder blade and the opposite ear with the hand.
**Temporomandibular:** opening the mouth as wide as possible, moving the jaw forward and to the sides.
**Hip:** flexion (pulling the knee to the chest), **spreading (abduction — normally 40–45°)** the legs to the side, internal and external rotation (≈35–45°).
**Knee:** touching the buttock with the heel and fully extending the leg (inability to extend — flexion contracture).
**Ankle:** passive flexion and extension; Achillobursitis (swelling in the area of the Achilles tendon).

**Spine:** cervical — touching the chest with the chin, throwing the head back, touching the shoulder with the ear, turning the head; **general rigidity** — bending forward without bending the knees and touching the floor with the fingers (normally the distance is **less than 5 cm**); **Ott's test** (thoracic part): a mark on the 7th cervical vertebra and another 30 cm below it — on bending the distance increases by **4–5 cm**; **Schober's test** (lumbar part): a mark on LV and another 10 cm above it — on bending it increases by **4–5 cm**. In rigidity the change does not exceed 1–2 cm.

blocks.text: Detecting developmental dysplasia of the hip (newborn and infant)
All newborns are examined:

items: **Asymmetry of the skin folds** — the thigh, inguinal and gluteal folds are at different levels and of different depth.
**Relative shortening of the leg** — in a child lying on the back with the legs bent at the hips and knees, the knees are at different heights.

**Restricted spreading (abduction) of the thighs** — when the thighs flexed at 90° are spread apart, they do not reach the table surface (normally 80–90° at 1 month). At an early age physiological hypertonia also causes slight restriction.

**“Slipping” (dislocation-reduction) sign — the Marx–Ortolani test**: the child lies on the back with the legs flexed at 90° at the hips and knees; the doctor places the thumbs on the inner surface of the thighs and the other fingers on the outer (greater trochanter) surface and slowly spreads the thighs apart — as the dislocated femoral head enters the socket, **a “click”** is felt.
External rotation of the foot.
Confirmation — **hip ultrasound** (Graf method, at 1–3 months), and X-ray in older children.

parts.text: Detecting developmental dysplasia of the hip **in the first weeks of life** and treating it with wide swaddling or special splints (the Pavlik harness) ensures full recovery of the joint. If it is detected late (after the child starts walking) — limping, “duck gait”, and surgical treatment is needed.

blocks.text: Additional methods of examination

items: **X-ray** — fractures, anomalies, inflammation, tumors, degenerative processes; **bone age** (wrist); in rickets **cup-shaped widening** of the metaphyses, osteoporosis.
**Ultrasound** (developmental dysplasia of the hip, intra-articular fluid), **CT, MRI**, **densitometry** (bone mineral density), scintigraphy.

**Biochemistry:** serum **calcium** (total 2.25–2.75 mmol/l; ionized 1.1–1.3), **phosphorus** (1.3–2.3 mmol/l at 1–2 years), **alkaline phosphatase** (raised in rickets), **25(OH)D**, parathyroid hormone; urinary calcium and phosphorus (Sulkowitch test).
**Immunological:** CRP, rheumatoid factor, ASO, antinuclear antibodies, HLA-B27.
Analysis of **synovial fluid**, **biopsy** of the synovial membrane and bone.

blocks.label: Figure 5.24
blocks.caption: X-ray of the hip joint: a — normal; b — arthritis (narrowing of the joint space, osteoporosis, erosion of the femoral head) (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.label: Figure 5.25
blocks.caption: X-ray of the hand in rickets: cup-shaped widening of the metaphyses, osteoporosis (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Skeletal developmental anomalies

items: **Skull:** craniostenosis (premature closure of the sutures), “wolf's palate” (non-fusion of the maxillary and palatine bones), micro- and macrocephaly.
**Vertebrae:** non-fusion of the vertebral arch — **spina bifida** (most often lumbosacral), sacralization, lumbarization.
**Ribs:** an extra cervical rib, absent or fused ribs, clefts of the sternum.
**Limbs: congenital dislocation of the hip** (the most common), amelia (absence of a limb), phocomelia, poly- and syndactyly, **congenital clubfoot**, underdevelopment of the clavicle.
**Systemic skeletal dysplasias: achondroplasia** (short limbs, large head, depressed nasal bridge), **osteogenesis imperfecta** (brittle bones — multiple fractures, **blue sclerae**, deafness).

blocks.text: Bone and joint pain

items: **Ossalgia** (bone pain) — fracture, **osteomyelitis**, tumor, **leukemia** (night pain, pain on tapping).
**“Growing pains”** — at 4–12 years, in the evening and at night in the legs (shins, popliteal area), bilateral; they pass by morning; there are no local changes and no changes in the blood count.
**Arthralgia** — joint pain without objective changes (infections, onset of rheumatic diseases).
**Perthes disease** — aseptic necrosis of the femoral head: hip pain increasing with load, limping, the child feels well.
**Enthesopathies** — Osgood–Schlatter disease (tibial tuberosity), juvenile spondyloarthritis, reactive arthritis.

blocks.text: Rickets

**Rickets** — a disorder of bone formation and mineralization in the growing body due to **vitamin D deficiency** and disturbed phosphorus-calcium metabolism. Most often **from 2 months to 2 years**. The bones show signs of **softening (osteomalacia)** and **osteoid tissue hyperplasia**.

blocks.title: Table 5.6. Bone and other signs of rickets
head: Area
Signs of osteomalacia (softening)
Signs of osteoid hyperplasia
rows: Softening of the edges of the anterior fontanelle, craniotabes, flattening of the occiput, skull asymmetry
Frontal and parietal bosses (“square head”, “Socrates' forehead”)
Harrison's groove, lateral compression of the chest, “pigeon chest”, “cobbler's chest”
O-shaped and X-shaped deformity, flat pelvis
Late and irregular eruption, enamel defects, caries

Restlessness, startling, sour-smelling sweat on the nape and a bald nape (hair loss), muscle hypotonia (“frog belly”, “loose joints”, the “pocket-knife” sign — the child easily brings the foot to the face), delayed static functions

blocks.label: Figure 5.26
blocks.caption: Muscle hypotonia and joint laxity in a child with rickets: the “pocket-knife” sign (Navruzova, Geppe)

parts.text: Chronology of the signs of rickets: **up to 3 months** — sweating, bald nape, restlessness; **3–6 months** — **craniotabes** (the earliest bone sign); **from 6 months** — **bosses, “rosary”, “bracelets”** (osteoid hyperplasia); **after 1 year** (when the child begins to stand) — **leg deformities**.

blocks.text: **Rickets-like diseases** (vitamin D-resistant rickets, de Toni–Debré–Fanconi syndrome, renal tubular acidosis) — tubulopathies developing after 2 years that do not respond to usual doses of vitamin D, with impaired intestinal absorption of calcium or urinary loss of calcium and phosphorus.
Spasmophilia (infantile tetany)

In the initial period of rickets or during recovery (most often in spring, from 6 months to 2 years), **neuromuscular excitability increases** as a result of **a fall in ionized calcium** in the blood.
Signs of **latent tetany**:

items: **Chvostek's sign** — contraction of the facial muscles (lip, nasal ala, eyelid) when the area between the zygomatic arch and the corner of the mouth (where the facial nerve emerges) is tapped with a hammer;
**Trousseau's sign** — when the neurovascular bundle of the upper arm is compressed (with a cuff) for 2–3 minutes, the hand goes into spasm and takes the **“obstetrician's hand”** position;
**Lust's sign** — outward turning and flexion of the foot when the area below the head of the fibula (n. peroneus) is tapped with a hammer;
**Maslov's sign** — a brief arrest of breathing when the skin is lightly pricked with a needle.

blocks.text: **Manifest tetany** — **laryngospasm** (crowing inspiration like a “rooster's crow”, cyanosis), **carpopedal spasm** (spasm of the hands and feet), generalized **eclamptic seizures**.

parts.text: Emergency care for laryngospasm and seizures: lay the child down, splash cold water on the face, fresh air, clear the mouth and nose; **10% calcium gluconate** (or calcium chloride) slowly intravenously; if the seizures continue — diazepam. Vitamin D must not be prescribed without calcium preparations (it worsens the seizures).

blocks.text: Hypermobility

**Joint hypermobility** — a range of motion greater than normal: **connective tissue dysplasias** (Ehlers–Danlos and Marfan syndromes), muscle hypotonia (rickets, Down syndrome). It is assessed by the Beighton criteria (bending the little finger back more than 90°, touching the forearm with the thumb, hyperextension of the elbow and knee by more than 10°, placing the palms on the floor without bending the knees).
Arthritis

Signs of **arthritis**: **defiguration and/or deformity** of the joint, **swelling** of the soft tissues, local **hyperemia and hyperthermia**, **pain** on palpation, **restriction** of active and passive movements.

blocks.title: Table 5.7. Main types of arthritis in children
head: Arthritis
Features
rows: Most often one large joint; acute pain, all the signs of inflammation, purulent exudate, hectic fever, intoxication
2–4 weeks after an intestinal or genitourinary infection; asymmetric oligoarthritis (2–3 joints), most often of the legs; talalgia, enthesitis, conjunctivitis, urethritis
Symmetric polyarthritis with new joints added progressively; morning stiffness, “fusiform” fingers, deformities, contractures, subluxations; lasts more than 6 weeks
Migratory (flitting), non-erosive polyarthritis of the large joints; passes quickly and completely; with carditis
Joints of the legs, enthesopathies, spinal rigidity, HLA-B27

blocks.caption: Deformity of the right knee joint, flexion contracture (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Osteomyelitis, fractures, tumors

items: **Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis** — purulent inflammation of the bone marrow and bone; most often **the metaphyses** of the femur and tibia; acute local pain, the child does not move the leg (“pseudoparalysis”), swelling, high fever, intoxication. X-ray changes appear only **after 10–14 days** (early diagnosis — MRI, scintigraphy).
**Periostitis** — inflammation of the periosteum: local thickening, pain, unevenness (tuberculosis, syphilis, tumors).

**Fractures:** pain, swelling, deformity, crepitus, hemorrhage, impaired function; at an early age **“greenstick”** and subperiosteal fractures; fractures through the growth zone may disturb growth. Multiple fractures from trivial trauma — osteogenesis imperfecta; multiple fractures at different stages of healing — possible **child abuse**.
**Bone tumors** — osteosarcoma, **Ewing sarcoma**, osteochondroma, **osteoid osteoma** (night pain, relieved by aspirin).

blocks.label: Figure 5.28
blocks.caption: Fracture of the humerus, callus (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Dental pathology

items: **Developmental anomalies:** supernumerary teeth, **adentia**, malposition, **Hutchinson's teeth** (“screwdriver-shaped” upper incisors with a crescent-shaped notch — congenital syphilis).
**Enamel hypoplasia** — disturbed mineral and protein metabolism in the fetus and at an early age (rickets, prematurity).
**Caries** — demineralization of the enamel (Streptococcus mutans + carbohydrates; a sweet formula and a pacifier at night — “bottle caries”).
**Fluorosis** — chalky spots on the enamel from excessive fluoride intake.
**Premature loss** of primary teeth — hypovitaminosis C, hypophosphatasia, diabetes mellitus, leukemia, histiocytosis, mercury poisoning.
**Late eruption** — rickets, hypothyroidism, Down syndrome, pituitary dwarfism.

blocks.text: Anatomical and physiological features

items: In the newborn the number of muscles is the same as in adults (more than 600), but **the muscle mass** is **≈23–25%** of the body mass (27% at 8 years, **32–33%** at 15 years, **40–44%** in adults). The mass increases not through the number of muscle fibers but through their **thickening**.
The muscle fibers are thin and multinucleated, with few contractile proteins and preserved **fetal myosin**; they contain much water and little protein, fat and minerals.

The muscle relief is smooth and becomes defined at 5–7 years; **the fasciae** are delicate and the aponeuroses weak — in the newborn cephalohematoma, **umbilical hernia** (the umbilical ring is not fully closed), forward protrusion of the abdomen (until 3–5 years).
In the newborn the muscles **do not relax even during sleep** — this produces heat and stimulates the development of muscle tissue.

**Physiological hypertonia** — in the first 2–4 months **the tone of the flexor muscles** predominates over the extensors: it persists in the arms **until 2–2.5 months** and in the legs **until 3–4 months**. That is why the newborn lies in the “fetal position”.

In preterm babies (less than 30 weeks) — **generalized hypotonia**: the limbs are extended; at 30–34 weeks the legs flex, and flexion of the arms after 34 weeks — one of the criteria for assessing **gestational age**.

Muscle development is uneven: first the muscles of **the shoulder and forearm**, then the muscles of the hand (hand movements become well coordinated **at 6–7 years** — readiness for writing). The muscles holding the body upright grow rapidly from 7 years, especially **at 12–16 years**. Precision of movement improves from 10 years and speed at 14 years.
Muscle strength is higher in boys; relative strength changes little until 6–7 years and increases rapidly **at 13–14 years**.

blocks.text: Examination of the muscular system

**Complaints:** muscle pain (**myalgia**), weakness, rapid fatigue, reduced muscle strength, difficulty walking, frequent falls, inability to climb stairs. **History:** muscle diseases in the family, relation to infection, injury or medication.
**1. Degree of development** (inspection and palpation — symmetric areas at the same level are compared):

items: **good** — at rest the contours of the muscles of the trunk and limbs are clearly visible, the abdomen is drawn in, and the shoulder blades are close to the chest; on tension the relief becomes more pronounced;
**moderate** — the trunk muscles are moderately and the limb muscles well developed;
**poor** — at rest the contours are not visible and hardly change on tension; the lower abdomen sags, **the shoulder blades lag behind the chest (“winged scapulae”)**.

blocks.text: To detect asymmetry, the circumference of the limbs is measured with a tape at the same level.
**2. Muscle tone** — assessed by the resistance to passive movements (the limb should be maximally relaxed). The first impression is obtained from **the child's posture**.

blocks.title: Table 5.8. Tests for assessing muscle tone in the newborn and infant
head: Test

The legs quickly return to the previous flexed position — normal/hypertonia; they do not return — hypotonia

Normally the arms first extend (1st phase), then flex and the child pulls up (2nd phase). In hypertonia the 1st phase is absent, in hypotonia the 2nd phase is absent (the arms extend and the head lags behind)
The child is lifted up, held under the arms

blocks.text: **Hypotonia** — reduced resistance to passive movements, soft muscles, increased range of motion in the joints (excessive flexibility); the child is like a “rag doll”.

**3. Muscle strength** — assessed with movements in which the child actively resists: in a small child, pulling away a toy held in the hand; in an older child, resistance to extension of the bent arm (leg); sitting, standing, climbing stairs, getting up from the floor (**Gowers' sign** — in myopathy the child “climbs up” his own legs with his hands). Objectively — **dynamometry** (in children over 5 years, 3 times, the highest result). Strength is also graded on a **0–5 point** scale.

blocks.text: **Additional investigations:** blood **creatine phosphokinase (CPK)**, LDH, transaminases, myoglobin, creatine; autoantibodies; **electromyography** (to distinguish primary muscle from nerve involvement), chronaximetry, ergography; muscle **biopsy**, genetic testing.
Semiotics of muscular system involvement

**Hypotrophy and atrophy:** a sedentary lifestyle, after surgery, severe somatic disease, dystrophy, poliomyelitis (paralytic form), hereditary muscular dystrophies, chronic infections, long-term glucocorticoid therapy; **local** — joint diseases, nerve damage, immobilization.
Causes of hypotonia:

items: in newborns — CNS damage (hypoxia, hemorrhage), prematurity, **hyperbilirubinemia**, sepsis, hypothyroidism, **Down syndrome**, spinal muscular atrophy;
at an early age — **rickets**, grade II–III hypotrophy;
at an older age — **rheumatic chorea**, cerebellar damage, myopathies;
**hypokalemia** (vomiting, diarrhea, diuretics), endocrine diseases.

blocks.text: **Causes of hypertonia:** damage to the pyramidal tract (**cerebral palsy**, Little disease), brain and spinal cord injuries, meningitis and encephalitis, **tetanus**, hypocalcemia (tetany), Thomsen myotonia.

blocks.label: Figure 5.34
blocks.caption: Hypertonia in cerebral palsy (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Myalgias:** infections (influenza, enterovirus — Bornholm disease, leptospirosis, brucellosis), inflammation (**myositis, dermatomyositis**, trichinellosis — pain and induration), ischemia; after physical exertion — metabolic myopathies. Stone-like indurations in the muscles (calcinosis) — dermatomyositis, myositis ossificans.

**Muscle weakness: proximal** (thigh, shoulder girdle) — **myopathies, dermatomyositis**; **distal** — polyneuropathies, myotonic dystrophy; worsening after exertion — **myasthenia**, metabolic myopathy; endocrine — hypocortisolism, thyrotoxicosis, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism.
Main diseases:

items: **Progressive muscular dystrophies** (Duchenne — impaired dystrophin synthesis, boys, from 3–5 years, “duck gait”, **Gowers' sign**, **pseudohypertrophy** of the calf muscles, sharply raised CPK);
**Inflammatory myopathies** — infectious (bacterial, viral, parasitic), autoimmune (**dermatomyositis** — proximal weakness, violaceous erythema of the eyelids, Gottron's papules);
**Drug-induced myopathies** (glucocorticoids, penicillamine, etc.);
**Myotonia** — inability of a muscle to relax for several seconds after contraction (Thomsen disease);
**Myasthenia** — autoantibodies to acetylcholine receptors; **ptosis, diplopia**, weakness increasing toward the end of the day; neonatal (from the mother) and congenital forms;
**Paralyses (pareses): peripheral** — reduced tone, atrophy, absent reflexes; **central** — **spastic hypertonia**, hyperreflexia, pathological reflexes;
**Congenital anomalies** — **muscular torticollis** (underdevelopment or injury of the sternocleidomastoid muscle), diaphragmatic hernia, absence of the pectoral muscle (Poland syndrome).

blocks.text: A child suspected of rickets

Rickets is diagnosed on the basis of clinical signs (sweating, bald nape, hypotonia, bone changes) and confirmed by **biochemistry** (reduced calcium and phosphorus, **raised alkaline phosphatase**, reduced 25(OH)D) and **X-ray** (wrist: cup-shaped widening of the metaphyses, a “fringed” border of the growth zone, osteoporosis).

parts.text: **Prevention of rickets:** during pregnancy — fresh air, proper nutrition and vitamin D for the mother; after birth — **breast milk**, walks, massage and gymnastics; for term babies from 1 month of age **vitamin D 400–500 IU/day** (according to Uzbekistan and WHO recommendations, doses are set by the local protocol), more for preterm babies.

blocks.text: Joint syndrome — diagnostic approach

items: **How many joints?** Mono- (1), oligo- (2–4), polyarthritis (≥5).
**Is it symmetric?** Symmetric — JRA, SLE; asymmetric — reactive, septic.
**What is the course?** Migratory — rheumatic fever; persistent, progressive — JRA.
**Additional signs:** fever, rash (SLE, Still's disease, vasculitis), conjunctivitis (Reiter), heart murmur (rheumatic fever), preceding infection.
**Laboratory:** CBC, CRP, ESR, ASO, rheumatoid factor, ANA, HLA-B27, synovial fluid.

blocks.text: A newborn with muscle hypotonia

Hypotonia is “not a disease but a sign”. Its causes are **central** (CNS damage, hypoxia, syndromes) and **peripheral** (spinal muscular atrophy, myopathies, myasthenia). In central hypotonia the reflexes are preserved or increased; in peripheral hypotonia they are **reduced or absent**, and muscle weakness is pronounced.

skills.title: Skill 1. Measuring the anterior fontanelle and palpating the head

items: Wash and warm the hands; calm the child, on the mother's lap or lying down.
Palpate the skull bones and sutures and determine whether they are closed.
Find the anterior fontanelle; measure the distance between **the midpoints of opposite sides** in two directions with a tape (not the diagonals!).
Assess the edges of the fontanelle (firm/soft), its level (at the level of the skull/bulging/sunken) and its pulsation.
Test for craniotabes by pressing on the occipital and parietal bones with a finger.
Compare the result with the age norm and record it.

skills.title: Skill 2. Inspection of the chest and spine

items: The child is undressed and stands (arms along the body).
From the front: shape and symmetry of the chest, deformities, the epigastric angle (placing the edges of the palms on the costal arches).
From the side: how marked the physiological curves are.
From behind: symmetry of the shoulders, the angles of the shoulder blades, the waist triangles and the iliac crests; the line of the spinous processes.
The child bends forward — to detect scoliosis and a rib hump.
Palpate the ribs for the “rosary”, and the wrists and phalanges for “bracelets” and “strings of pearls”.

skills.title: Skill 3. Examination of the joints

items: Observe the gait.
Inspect each joint symmetrically: shape, swelling, defiguration, deformity, skin color.
Palpation: temperature (comparing with the back of the hand), pain, swelling, fluid (ballottement of the patella), crepitus.
Assess the range of active, then passive movements with functional tests; record pain and restriction.
Mobility of the spine (finger-to-floor distance, Ott's and Schober's tests).
Conclusion: the shape of the joints is unchanged, there are no signs of inflammation, movements are in full range and painless (or the changes found).

skills.title: Skill 4. Testing for developmental dysplasia of the hip (newborn)

items: The child lies on the back on a warm table, calm.
Assess the symmetry of the thigh, inguinal and gluteal folds (gluteal folds — with the child prone).
Bend the legs at the hips and knees and compare the levels of the knees (relative shortening).
Flex the thighs to 90° and slowly spread them apart; assess the abduction angle.
Marx–Ortolani test: determine whether a “click” is felt while the thighs are spread.
If there is any suspicion — orthopedic consultation and hip ultrasound.

skills.title: Skill 5. Assessment of the muscular system

items: Inspection: degree of development, relief, symmetry; measure the limb circumference if necessary.
Palpation: consistency, pain, indurations.
Tone: the child's posture; resistance to passive flexion-extension; in the newborn, the recoil, traction and “loose shoulders” tests.
Strength: movements against resistance; dynamometry in an older child.
Range of active and passive movements.
Conclusion: “The muscles are moderately developed, symmetric, tone normal, strength appropriate for age, painless, movements in full range.”

skills.title: Skill 6. Testing for the signs of latent tetany

items: **Chvostek:** tap with a hammer or finger below the zygomatic arch, in front of the ear, where the facial nerve emerges; watch for contraction of the corner of the mouth, the nasal ala and the eyelid.
**Trousseau:** place a sphygmomanometer cuff on the upper arm, inflate it slightly above systolic pressure and hold for 2–3 minutes; watch for the “obstetrician's hand”.
**Lust:** tap with a hammer below the head of the fibula; watch for outward turning and dorsal flexion of the foot.
Record the result; if positive — refer for a blood calcium test.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 5-month-old child. Born in winter, mixed-fed, vitamin D prophylaxis was not given. According to the mother, the child is restless, startles, sweats a lot (especially when feeding and during sleep), and has lost hair on the nape. On examination: anterior fontanelle 3×3.5 cm with soft edges; the occiput is flattened, and areas of softening are found on the occipital and parietal bones on pressure with a finger. Muscle tone is reduced, the abdomen is “frog-shaped”. No teeth.
cases.ask: 1) Which disease do you suspect? 2) Which signs are typical of osteomalacia? 3) Which investigations are needed to confirm the diagnosis? 4) What complication is there a risk of, and how do you test for its latent signs?
cases.answer: 1) Rickets (onset of the peak period): risk factors — birth in winter, mixed feeding, no prophylaxis; neurovegetative signs (restlessness, sweating, bald nape), muscle hypotonia, bone changes. 2) Craniotabes, flattening of the occiput, softening and enlargement of the edges of the anterior fontanelle. 3) Blood calcium, phosphorus (reduced), alkaline phosphatase (raised), 25(OH)D; wrist X-ray (cup-shaped widening of the metaphyses, osteoporosis). 4) Spasmophilia (especially in spring, when treatment is started) — the Chvostek, Trousseau and Lust signs are tested.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 9-year-old boy has complained of pain and swelling in the left knee and right ankle joints for 3 days. He had an intestinal infection (diarrhea) 3 weeks ago. On examination: the left knee joint is defigured, the skin over it is warm, ballottement of the patella is positive; the right ankle joint is swollen and painful; the 2nd toe of the right foot is swollen along its whole length and red. The conjunctivae of both eyes are red. There is heel pain.
cases.ask: 1) Describe the joint syndrome. 2) What is the change in the toe called? 3) Presumptive diagnosis? 4) Which investigations are needed?
cases.answer: 1) Asymmetric oligoarthritis (2 joints) of the legs; in the left knee — defiguration, local hyperthermia, intra-articular fluid (positive ballottement); talalgia (enthesitis). 2) A “sausage” toe (dactylitis). 3) Reactive arthritis (Reiter disease) — after an intestinal infection, arthritis + conjunctivitis (urethritis may also be present). 4) CBC, CRP, ESR, HLA-B27, pathogens (Yersinia, Salmonella, Shigella; Chlamydia) or antibodies in the stool and urine, ultrasound and X-ray of the joints, and synovial fluid analysis if necessary.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 1-month-old girl came for a preventive check-up. The delivery was a breech presentation. On examination: the left thigh and gluteal folds are higher and deeper than on the right; when the legs are flexed at the hips and knees the left knee is lower; abduction of the left thigh is limited to 50° (80° on the right); during abduction a “click” is felt on the left.
cases.ask: 1) Which pathology do you suspect? 2) Name the signs found. 3) How is it confirmed? 4) What will be the consequence if treatment is not given in time?
cases.answer: 1) Developmental dysplasia (congenital dislocation) of the left hip; risk factors — breech presentation, female sex. 2) Asymmetry of the skin folds, relative shortening of the left leg, limited abduction, positive “slipping” sign (Marx–Ortolani). 3) Hip ultrasound (Graf method), orthopedic consultation; after 3–4 months — X-ray. 4) Limping when the child begins to walk, leg shortening, lumbar hyperlordosis, later coxarthrosis; need for surgical treatment.

topics.title: The respiratory system: anatomical and physiological features, the first breath, history taking, inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation

goals.text: The student should know:

items: anatomical and physiological features of children's respiratory organs (nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs, pleura, chest) and their clinical significance;
the mechanism of the first breath, the importance of surfactant, age-related features of the regulation of breathing;
age norms for respiratory rate, type and rhythm of breathing;
the rules of comparative and topographic percussion, the lung borders;
age-specific breath sounds and adventitious breath sounds.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: take complaints and history from a child with a respiratory disease;
inspect the chest, count the respiratory rate and determine the type of dyspnea;
palpate the chest: determine pain, resistance and vocal fremitus;
perform comparative and topographic percussion and determine the excursion of the lower lung edge;
auscultate the lungs and assess the results.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The right main bronchus** leaves the trachea at a small angle and is its continuation — this is why **foreign bodies most often enter the right bronchus**. The glottis is at the level of **C~IV~** in children and **C~VII~** in adults.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Density conducts, fluid and air block”**: dense tissue (pneumonia) **increases** vocal fremitus, bronchophony and bronchial breathing; fluid or air in the pleura and an obstructed bronchus **weaken** them.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Lower lung border: **“6-7-8-9-10-11”** — it increases by one rib at each line from the midclavicular line toward the paravertebral line.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Weakened → puerile → vesicular”** = **0–6 months → 6 months–7 years → 7+ years**. Hearing puerile breathing in an older child is not a pathology in itself; it is increased vesicular breathing (dyspnea, fever).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In infants with a blocked nose or accumulated mucus, **transmitted (nasopharyngeal) rales** are heard over all areas of the lungs and may lead to a wrong diagnosis. Clear the nose, make the child cough and listen again: transmitted rales disappear or change, while focal rales in the lung remain in place.

sections.title: 6.1. Anatomical and physiological features of the respiratory organs

blocks.text: **Main idea:** in the child all the airways are **narrow, soft, rich in blood and lymph vessels and poor in elastic fibers**. For this reason the mucosa swells quickly, the airways become obstructed quickly, and atelectasis and pneumonia are common.
The airways are divided into three parts: **upper** (nose, paranasal sinuses, pharynx), **middle** (larynx, trachea, main, lobar and segmental bronchi), **lower** (bronchioles, alveoli).

blocks.title: Table 6.1. Age-related features of the respiratory organs and their clinical significance
head: Organ
Feature in children
Clinical significance
rows: Small, narrow nasal passages; no inferior nasal meatus (forms at 4 years); the mucosa is rich in blood vessels; no cavernous tissue (develops at 8–9 years)
With a runny nose, nasal breathing is quickly impaired and feeding becomes difficult; nosebleeds are rare
The maxillary and ethmoid sinuses are present at birth but small; the frontal and sphenoid sinuses develop from 6–7 years and grow until 15–20 years
Sinusitis is rare at an early age; ethmoiditis may occur
Infection easily passes from the nose to the eye (conjunctivitis)
Otitis develops quickly with a runny nose
Small, narrow; the tonsils are undeveloped until 1 year and well developed at 4–5 years
Tonsillitis is rare before 1 year; adenoids — mouth breathing
Funnel-shaped, located high (the glottis at the level of the 4th cervical vertebra, the 7th in adults); the cartilages are soft, the glottis is narrow, the loose subglottic tissue is prone to edema
Funnel-shaped; ≈4 cm long in the newborn (12 cm in adults); soft cartilage, few elastic fibers
Short, narrow, soft cartilage, few muscle and elastic fibers, weak mucociliary clearance; the right main bronchus is a continuation of the trachea, short and wide
Foreign bodies and pneumonia more often on the right; bronchiolitis and obstruction before 1 year
50–60 g in the newborn; less airy, rich in blood, few elastic fibers, much interstitial tissue; the acinus is not fully mature (grows until 8 years)
Atelectasis, emphysema and pneumonia develop quickly
Thin, delicate, the parietal layer loosely attached
When fluid accumulates, the mediastinal organs shift easily
Barrel-shaped in the newborn, ribs horizontal, epigastric angle obtuse; respiratory muscles weak, the diaphragm high
Breathing is shallow and rapid, mainly diaphragmatic; meteorism makes breathing difficult

parts.text: **The right main bronchus** leaves the trachea at a small angle and is its continuation — this is why **foreign bodies most often enter the right bronchus**. The glottis is at the level of **C~IV~** in children and **C~VII~** in adults.

blocks.text: **Lung segments:** right lung — **10** segments (3 in the upper lobe, 2 in the middle lobe, 5 in the lower lobe); left lung — **9** segments. In children pneumonia most often occurs in **segments 6, 2 and 10** (poor drainage, the child lies for a long time). The bronchi of **segments 4 and 5** are long and narrow, with lymph nodes nearby — “**middle lobe syndrome**” (chronic atelectasis) may develop.
Stages of lung development (A.I. Strukov):

items: **0–2 years** — the number of alveoli increases rapidly;
**2–5 years** — elastic and muscle fibers and peribronchial and perivascular lymphoid tissue grow (pneumonia tends to become chronic);
**5–7 years** — formation of the acinar structure is completed;
**7–12 years** — lung mass increases mainly through maturation of the lung tissue.

blocks.text: Functional features:

items: Breathing is **shallow and rapid**; the minute volume of breathing relative to body mass is higher than in adults; the oxygen demand is high.
Gas exchange in the alveoli is intensive (the lungs are rich in blood), but **the respiratory reserve is small** — respiratory failure develops quickly.
**Local defense** is weak: little secretory IgA, lysozyme and interferon; the ciliated epithelium is immature; the cough reflex is weak (especially in preterm babies).

blocks.text: **Main idea:** clamping of the cord → **hypoxia + hypercapnia + acidosis** → chemoreceptors → respiratory center → **sharp contraction of the diaphragm** → the lungs expand, and surfactant keeps them open.

items: **The chemical (humoral) factor is the most important.** When the cord is clamped, pO~2~ falls from 80 to ≈15 mm Hg, pCO~2~ rises from 40 to ≈70 mm, and pH falls below 7.35. The central chemoreceptors are sensitive to pH, the peripheral (carotid, aortic) chemoreceptors to O~2~ and CO~2~.
**Physical (external) stimuli:** cold, light, stimulation of skin receptors, gravity → reticular formation → the excitability of the respiratory center increases.
**Removing inhibiting factors:** suctioning mucus and amniotic fluid from the mouth and nose.

**Mechanics:** the diaphragm contracts and creates negative intrathoracic pressure (≈80 mm H~2~O); the volume of the first breath exceeds 80 ml. Lung fluid is absorbed into the lymphatics and capillaries. A healthy baby takes the first breath with **a loud cry**.

blocks.label: Figure 6.4
blocks.caption: Mechanism of the first breath: birth → clamping of the cord → rise in pCO~2~ → stimulation of the aortic and carotid chemoreceptors → respiratory center and muscle tone centers → contraction of the diaphragm and skeletal muscles → entry of air → expansion of the lungs (with the participation of surfactant) → absorption of lung fluid (Kildiyarova, Figure 8.1; figure labels in Russian)

blocks.text: **Surfactant** — a surface-active substance covering the alveolar surface (90% lipid, mainly phosphatidylcholine; 10% protein). It is synthesized by **type II alveolocytes**. It prevents the alveoli from collapsing on expiration and has a bactericidal effect. Synthesis enzymes: methyltransferase — active **from week 22–24**, phosphocholine transferase — **from week 35**. Surfactant deficiency causes **respiratory distress syndrome** (hyaline membrane disease), mainly in preterm babies.

parts.text: If there is a risk of preterm birth (before 34 weeks), the mother is given **glucocorticoids** (dexamethasone or betamethasone) — they accelerate surfactant synthesis in the fetal lungs. Exogenous surfactant is given intratracheally to the preterm newborn.

blocks.text: **The respiratory center** (medulla oblongata and pons): the medullary part (alternation of inspiration and expiration), the apneustic part (inspiratory spasm), the pneumotaxic part (inhibits the apneustic part). The pneumotaxic part matures **by the end of the 1st year** — at an early age breathing is **arrhythmic**; **apnea** occurs in preterm babies. Up to 3 months, pauses in breathing of **up to 8–10 seconds** are physiological; apnea longer than 20 seconds or accompanied by bradycardia and cyanosis is pathological.
**Main idea:** the leading sign of respiratory disease is **cough**; its character often indicates the level of the lesion.

**Main complaints:** runny nose (nasal congestion, discharge), cough, sputum, dyspnea and attacks of suffocation, chest pain, hemoptysis, fever, weakness, headache, change of voice; in small children — refusal to feed, restlessness, vomiting.

blocks.text: **Sputum:** amount, color (yellowish — purulent, green — stagnant pus, **rusty** — lobar pneumonia), odor (fetid — bronchiectasis, abscess, gangrene), consistency (viscous, glassy — asthma). Small children swallow the sputum. **Hemoptysis** — blood from the lungs is **bright red and frothy**.
**Voice:** nasal speech — adenoids, cleft palate, paralysis of the soft palate; aphonia — true croup (diphtheria). False croup begins **suddenly** (often at night), true croup **gradually**.

**History of the present illness:** when and how it began (acutely or gradually), the cause (ARVI, chilling, foreign body — sudden cough during play), the course, the effect of treatment. At an early age pneumonia often develops after ARVI.

**Life history:** prematurity, whether mechanical ventilation was given; respiratory diseases in the family and contact with **tuberculosis**; past measles or whooping cough; vaccinations; rickets, hypotrophy, allergy (predisposition to asthma); passive smoking; home conditions (dampness, mold, animals).
**Main idea:** five things are assessed on inspection — **skin color, chest shape, type of breathing, respiratory rate and rhythm, signs of dyspnea**.

**General inspection:** cyanosis (lips, nasolabial triangle, around the eyes), pallor; **flaring of the nasal alae** (pneumonia in an infant); froth at the corner of the mouth (pneumonia in the newborn); herpes on the lips (ARVI, lobar pneumonia); redness of one cheek (lobar pneumonia on that side); “**drumstick fingers**” and “**watch-glass**” nails (chronic hypoxia); forced position — **orthopnea** (in an asthma attack the child sits leaning on the hands), in pleurisy the patient lies on the affected side. Nasal discharge, nasal breathing. Inspection of the pharynx and tonsils is performed **last** so as not to upset the child.

**Chest shape.** In the newborn it is barrel-shaped (the sagittal dimension equals the transverse one); with age the transverse dimension increases. In an older child there are three types: **normosthenic** (conical, epigastric angle ≈90°), **asthenic** (long, narrow, angle <90°, winged scapulae), **hypersthenic** (cylindrical, angle >90°). Pathological shapes: **barrel-shaped (emphysematous)** — asthma, emphysema; **funnel chest** and “**pigeon chest**”, **Harrison's groove** — rickets; **asymmetric** — in exudative pleurisy the affected side bulges, in chronic pneumonia and pneumofibrosis it sinks.

blocks.text: The **symmetric** participation of both halves of the chest in breathing is checked (the angles of the shoulder blades are watched). Lagging of one side — pleurisy, atelectasis, pneumonia. **Excursion** is measured with a tape (in front over the nipples, behind under the angles of the shoulder blades): at rest, at maximal inspiration and expiration; the difference in older children is 5–8 cm.

**The respiratory rate (RR)** is counted unnoticed while the child is calm or asleep (with a hand on the chest or abdomen, with a stethoscope held near the nose, or during auscultation). **Up to 3 months — for 1 full minute** (because of arrhythmia and apnea).

parts.text: According to WHO (IMCI), the cut-offs for **tachypnea** (a sign of pneumonia) are: **up to 2 months — ≥60**, **2–12 months — ≥50**, **1–5 years — ≥40** breaths per minute. Lower chest wall indrawing is a sign of **severe pneumonia**.

blocks.text: In respiratory diseases the respiration/pulse ratio narrows to **1:2 or 1:3**. **Tachypnea** — rapid breathing (fever, excitement, lung and heart diseases, anemia, acidosis); **bradypnea** — slow breathing (coma, poisoning with sleeping pills, raised intracranial pressure).
**Dyspnea** — a disturbance of the rate, depth and rhythm of breathing with increased work of the respiratory muscles.

What is difficult

When
rows: Flaring of the nasal alae; retraction of the intercostal spaces and the suprasternal and supraclavicular fossae; noisy breathing (stridor)
Narrowing of the upper airways: croup, foreign body, retropharyngeal abscess
The chest is in the “inspiratory” position, expiration is prolonged, the abdominal muscles take part, whistling breathing, wheezing heard at a distance
