blocks.text: **Congenital stridor** — a noise on inspiration resembling a cat's purr or a pigeon's “cooing”; it increases with crying and decreases in sleep; it is related to softness of the laryngeal cartilages (laryngomalacia) and disappears **at 2–3 years**. Thymic enlargement and bronchoadenitis must be excluded. Up to 3 months, slight retraction of the intercostal spaces at the attachment of the diaphragm is normal.
**Pathological types of breathing** (severe disturbance of the respiratory center):

items: **Cheyne–Stokes** — the depth of breathing gradually increases, then decreases and ends with a pause (meningitis, encephalitis, severe poisoning, heart failure); it may occur in sleep in preterm babies.
**Biot** — breaths of the same depth suddenly begin and are suddenly replaced by a long pause (cerebrovascular disorders, meningitis).
**Grocco** — wave-like breathing without pauses (similar to Cheyne–Stokes, but with shallow breaths instead of the pause).
**Kussmaul** — deep, noisy, infrequent breathing (the breathing of a “hunted animal”) — diabetic coma, metabolic acidosis, uremia.

blocks.label: Figure 6.6
blocks.caption: Pathological types of breathing (spirogram): 1 — Grocco; 2 — Cheyne–Stokes; 3 — Biot; 4 — Kussmaul (Kildiyarova, Figure 8.10)

blocks.text: **Main idea:** palpation confirms the findings of inspection; it is performed with both hands over **symmetric** areas.
Palpation determines:

items: **Tenderness** — superficial (muscle, rib, nerve — myositis, neuralgia) or deep pleural. Pleural pain increases with breathing and decreases when the chest is compressed and when bending toward the affected side (in neuralgia it increases instead). **Mussy's sign** — pain on pressure between the heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle — diaphragmatic pleurisy.
**Skin fold thickness** — thickening on the affected side (**Filatov's sign**) — exudative pleurisy, pneumonia.

**Resistance (elasticity)** — assessed by compressing the chest with the palms front-to-back and from the sides. If it compresses easily — elastic (normal; increased in rickets); if it does not compress — **rigid** (exudative pleurisy, tumor, ossification of the costal cartilages at an older age).
**Vocal fremitus (fremitus vocalis)** — transmission of the vibration of the vocal cords to the chest wall.

**In addition:** smoothing and bulging of the intercostal spaces (exudative pleurisy), rachitic “rosary”, subcutaneous **crepitus** (subcutaneous emphysema — crunching like snow), pleural friction felt by hand.

blocks.text: **Technique of testing vocal fremitus:** both palms are placed on symmetric areas of the chest and moved alternately from the apices to the lower parts. The child says **words with the letter “R”** (“tractor”, “thirty-three”, “ninety-nine”). In an infant who does not speak — during crying or screaming (low accuracy). Normally it is **the same** on both sides.

Fluid (exudative pleurisy, hydrothorax) or air (pneumothorax) in the pleural cavity, bronchial obstruction (obstructive atelectasis), emphysema, obesity

parts.text: **“Density conducts, fluid and air block”**: dense tissue (pneumonia) **increases** vocal fremitus, bronchophony and bronchial breathing; fluid or air in the pleura and an obstructed bronchus **weaken** them.

blocks.text: **Main idea:** in the child the stroke is **light (quiet)**, because the chest is thin and elastic — with a strong stroke distant tissues also vibrate and small foci are “lost”. Percussion is always performed **from the clear sound toward the dull sound**.

**General rules:** a quiet, warm room; the doctor's hands warm and dry, nails short. For anterior percussion the doctor stands on the child's right side, for posterior percussion on the left side. The child's position: over 2 years — standing or sitting; the mother holds an infant upright; up to 2–3 months — lying on the back for the front, and lying with the abdomen on the doctor's palm for the back. For posterior percussion the child bends the head slightly and crosses the arms in front (the shoulder blades move apart); for the lateral areas the hands are placed on the back of the neck. If the child cries — percuss during the deep inspiration between cries. The child's body must be straight and symmetric (otherwise the sound will be asymmetric).
Methods:

items: **Indirect (finger-to-finger)** — the 3rd finger of the left hand (pleximeter finger) is placed firmly in the intercostal space **parallel** to the ribs; the 3rd finger of the right hand (plessor finger) gives 2 short strokes on the middle phalanx of the pleximeter; movement only at the wrist joint.

**Direct** — the fingertip strikes the chest wall directly; used in infants and in hypotrophy. **Obraztsov's method** — the index finger of the right hand slips off the middle finger and strikes the chest.

blocks.text: Comparative percussion
The sound is compared at **symmetric** points of the chest; normally it is the same. A difference is a sign of pathology.
Order:

items: **From the front:** the supraclavicular fossa (finger parallel to the clavicle), directly over the clavicle, infraclavicular; along the midclavicular line in the 2nd–3rd intercostal spaces (lower down on the left is the heart — only on the right).
**From the sides:** along the midaxillary lines (hands on the back of the neck).
**From behind:** suprascapular (finger horizontal), interscapular (finger **parallel to the spine**), subscapular (finger horizontal along the intercostal spaces).

blocks.text: Topographic percussion

Purpose — to determine the lung borders. **Rules:** the pleximeter finger is placed **parallel** to the border sought; it is moved from the clear sound toward the dull sound; the border is marked along **the edge of the finger facing the clear sound**; quiet percussion is used.
**Height of the lung apices** (in children over 5–7 years; in younger children the apices lie behind the clavicle and cannot be determined):

items: **From the front** — the finger is placed in the supraclavicular fossa parallel to the clavicle and moved upward and medially. Normal: **2–4 cm above the clavicle**.
**From behind** — from the middle of the spine of the scapula toward the spinous process of **the 7th cervical vertebra**. Normal: **at the level of the C~VII~ process**.

**Krönig's field** — the strip of clear sound over the apex. The finger is placed at the middle of the edge of the trapezius muscle and percussion is performed alternately toward the neck and toward the shoulder until dullness appears. Normal: **3–5 cm** (4–6 cm according to Arzikulov).

blocks.text: **Lower lung borders** (at school age; at preschool age approximately **one rib higher**). Up to 3 years they are determined along the midclavicular (right), midaxillary and scapular lines.

parts.text: Lower lung border: **“6-7-8-9-10-11”** — it increases by one rib at each line from the midclavicular line toward the paravertebral line.

blocks.text: **Changes in the borders:** downward displacement — emphysema, asthma attack, low position of the diaphragm (visceroptosis). Upward displacement — shrinkage of the lung (pneumofibrosis, atelectasis), fluid or air in the pleura, raised abdominal pressure (hepatosplenomegaly, meteorism, ascites).

**Mobility (excursion) of the lower edge** — in children who can hold their breath: the border is determined on the middle or posterior axillary line during quiet breathing → the child takes a deep breath and holds it, the border is found → the child breathes out deeply and holds it, it is found again. The distance between the two marks is the excursion, normally **2–6 cm** (depending on age). It is reduced in emphysema, asthma, pneumofibrosis, inflammation, pleural adhesions; it is absent with fluid or air in the pleura, complete fusion of the pleural layers, diaphragmatic paralysis.

blocks.text: **Main idea:** auscultation is performed **in the order** of comparative percussion, at symmetric points, listening to **2–3 breaths** at each point; it is essential to know the type of breathing typical of the child's age.
Technique and rules:

items: Complete quiet; the clothes are removed (rustling of clothes interferes).
The child stands or sits; a seriously ill patient lies. In a crying child — during the deep inspiration between cries (crying also helps).
In small children the diaphragm of the stethoscope **should not be larger than 2 cm in diameter**; it is placed in the intercostal space.

First listen during breathing through the nose, then during deep breathing through the mouth (adventitious sounds become louder). To induce a deep breath in an infant: close the nose for a few seconds, tickle, press lightly on the trachea.
Listening points: the apices, the anterior surface, the axillae, suprascapular, interscapular, subscapular and paravertebral areas.

blocks.text: **Areas requiring special attention in children:** the axillae (in segmental pneumonia bronchial breathing appears early); paravertebral and suprascapular (segments 2, 6, 10 — foci of pneumonia); interscapular (lung root); subscapular (crepitation is heard early); the cardiac area (left lingula).

parts.text: **“Weakened → puerile → vesicular”** = **0–6 months → 6 months–7 years → 7+ years**. Hearing puerile breathing in an older child is not a pathology in itself; it is increased vesicular breathing (dyspnea, fever).

blocks.text: **Bronchophony** — whispered words (“sixty-six”, “ninety-nine”) heard over the chest wall. Normally the words are not clearly distinguished. **Increased** — over pneumonia and atelectasis (if the bronchus is open), a cavern (metallic); **weakened** — fluid or air in the pleura, obesity. The logic is the same as for vocal fremitus.
Adventitious breath sounds

**Main idea: rales** — from the bronchi (air + fluid or mucus), **crepitation** — from the alveoli (only at the end of inspiration), **pleural friction rub** — from the pleura (in both phases, superficial).

**Dry rales (rhonchi).** They arise from vibration of strands of thick mucus on the bronchial wall in the air flow, or from narrowing of the bronchial lumen due to edema and spasm. They are heard in both phases and change after coughing.

blocks.text: **Moist rales.** There is liquid secretion (sputum, blood, transudate) in the bronchi, and **bubbles burst** as air passes. Their caliber depends on the caliber of the bronchus.

blocks.text: **Consonant** (loud, distinct) moist rales — the lung around the bronchus is consolidated (pneumonia); **non-consonant** — only the bronchus is affected (bronchitis). In infants rales are hard to hear because chest excursion is small; they are better detected during the deep inspiration while crying.

**Crepitation.** When there is a small amount of exudate in the alveoli, the stuck-together alveolar walls separate **at the very peak of inspiration**. The sound is a fine uniform crackling, like rubbing hair between the fingers near the ear. **Only at the end of inspiration**, unchanged after coughing. An important sign of pneumonia:

items: **crepitatio indux** — days 1–3 of lobar pneumonia (period of exudate accumulation);
on days 4–6 it is not heard (the alveoli are filled with exudate — bronchial breathing);
**crepitatio redux** — days 7–10 (resorption of the exudate — a sign of recovery).

blocks.text: **Pleural friction rub** — friction of the parietal and visceral layers when they become rough and covered with fibrin: **dry pleurisy**, the beginning and end of exudative pleurisy, tuberculosis, tumor, severe dehydration. The sound is like crunching snow or rubbing paper or leather. Most often in **the lower part of the midaxillary line**, together with pain.

parts.text: In infants with a blocked nose or accumulated mucus, **transmitted (nasopharyngeal) rales** are heard over all areas of the lungs and may lead to a wrong diagnosis. Clear the nose, make the child cough and listen again: transmitted rales disappear or change, while focal rales in the lung remain in place.

blocks.text: Foreign body aspiration

parts.text: Choking and a severe coughing fit that begin **suddenly during play or eating** in a previously healthy child are considered foreign body aspiration until proven otherwise. It most often enters the **right** bronchus. Signs: unilateral weakening of breathing, localized whistling rales, later atelectasis or recurrent pneumonia. Diagnosis and treatment — **bronchoscopy**. Emergency care for a child who cannot cough or speak: under 1 year — 5 back blows between the shoulder blades + 5 chest thrusts; in older children — **the Heimlich maneuver**.

blocks.text: Clinical detection of pneumonia

In small children the first signs of pneumonia are often not physical but **general and respiratory**: fever lasting more than 3 days, **tachypnea**, flaring of the nasal alae, perioral cyanosis, chest indrawing, “grunting” expiration, intoxication. Physical changes (shortened sound, fine-bubbling consonant rales, crepitation) may not be detected if the focus is small — confirmation is by **X-ray**.

skills.title: Skill 1. Counting the respiratory rate and assessing dyspnea

items: Observe the child unnoticed at rest (if possible, asleep).
Place a hand on the child's chest or abdomen (or observe visually).
Count the respiratory movements for 1 minute (up to 3 months — always a full minute).
Assess the rhythm, depth and type of breathing.
Look for signs of dyspnea: flaring of the nasal alae, accessory muscles, retraction of the intercostal spaces and the suprasternal area, stridor, prolonged expiration.
Compare the result with the age norm, calculate the ratio to the pulse, and record it.

skills.title: Skill 2. Determining vocal fremitus

items: The child stands or sits; the doctor's hands are warm.
Place the palms on symmetric areas: supra- and infraclavicular, lateral areas, suprascapular, interscapular, subscapular.
Ask the child to say words with the letter “R” (in an infant — during crying).
Compare the two sides at each pair of points; if necessary, swap the hands and repeat.
Conclusion: equal / increased / weakened (in which area).

skills.title: Skill 3. Comparative percussion

items: The child stands straight and symmetrically; for anterior percussion the doctor stands on the right.
Place the pleximeter finger firmly in the intercostal space parallel to the ribs.
With a quiet stroke, percuss the supraclavicular, clavicular and infraclavicular areas, then the lateral areas.
From behind: the suprascapular, interscapular (finger parallel to the spine) and subscapular areas.
Compare the sound at each pair of symmetric points.
Conclusion: clear pulmonary sound over the whole lung / site and type of change.

skills.title: Skill 4. Topographic percussion

items: Height of the apices (from 5–7 years): from the front — relative to the clavicle, from behind — relative to CVII; Krönig's field.
Lower borders: on the right starting from the parasternal line, finger parallel to the ribs, from top to bottom, from the clear sound toward the dull sound; along each topographic line.
On the left — starting from the anterior axillary line.
Mark the border along the edge of the finger facing the clear sound; count the ribs or vertebrae.
Determine the excursion of the lower edge on the midaxillary line.
Compare the result with the age norm.

skills.title: Skill 5. Auscultation of the lungs

items: A quiet, warm room; the child undressed; a warm stethoscope.
Listen symmetrically at the points of comparative percussion, 2–3 breaths at each point.
Determine the basic breath sound and compare it with the age norm.
Detect adventitious sounds: type, phase of breathing, location, change after coughing.
Test bronchophony.
Conclusion: “Puerile (vesicular) breathing in the lungs, no rales” or the changes found.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 6-year-old child has complained of fever (39.2 °C), cough and right-sided chest pain for 4 days. On examination: the right cheek is flushed, herpes on the lips, flaring of the nasal alae, RR 36/min. The right half of the chest lags behind during breathing. Below the right shoulder blade vocal fremitus is increased; percussion gives a dull sound; on auscultation bronchial breathing and crepitation are heard, and bronchophony is increased.
cases.ask: 1) Which syndrome do you identify? 2) Why is vocal fremitus increased? 3) Presumptive diagnosis? 4) Is the respiratory rate appropriate for the age?
cases.answer: 1) The syndrome of consolidation (infiltration) of lung tissue: dull sound, increased vocal fremitus and bronchophony, bronchial breathing, crepitation. 2) Consolidated lung tissue (with an open bronchus) conducts sound vibrations better than air-filled tissue. 3) Right-sided lower lobe lobar pneumonia — flushing of one cheek, herpes and pleural pain are characteristic. 4) No, the norm at 6 years is 20–25/min — tachypnea (a sign of respiratory failure).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: An 8-month-old child has had a runny nose and cough for 2 days, and last night breathing became difficult. On examination: restless, cyanosis of the nasolabial triangle, RR 64/min. Expiration is prolonged and noisy, the intercostal spaces and the area below the sternum are retracted, and the chest is distended. Percussion gives a box-like sound. On auscultation expiration is prolonged, with diffuse whistling dry rales and many fine-bubbling moist rales on both sides.
cases.ask: 1) What type of dyspnea is it? 2) Which syndrome? 3) Presumptive diagnosis? 4) What does the box-like sound on percussion indicate?
cases.answer: 1) Expiratory dyspnea (mixed with expiratory predominance). 2) Bronchial obstruction syndrome and respiratory failure. 3) Acute bronchiolitis (8 months old, after ARVI, diffuse whistling and fine-bubbling rales, marked tachypnea). 4) Hyperinflation of the lungs (acute emphysema) — because of the obstruction, air does not manage to leave on expiration.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 10-year-old child has complained of fever, dry cough and left-sided pain that increases with breathing for 1 week; in the last 2 days the pain has decreased, but the dyspnea has increased. On examination: prefers to lie on the left side, the left half of the chest is enlarged and lags behind during breathing, the intercostal spaces are smoothed. Low on the left, vocal fremitus cannot be detected; percussion gives a dull sound with an oblique upper border; breath sounds are not heard.
cases.ask: 1) Which syndrome? 2) What is the oblique border found on percussion called? 3) How do you explain the decrease in pain and increase in dyspnea? 4) Which investigations are needed to confirm the diagnosis?
cases.answer: 1) The syndrome of fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity (left-sided exudative pleurisy). 2) The Damoiseau (Sokolov–Damoiseau) line. 3) It began as dry (fibrinous) pleurisy — the rubbing of the pleural layers caused pain; when fluid accumulated, the layers separated and the pain decreased, but the lung was compressed and respiratory failure increased. 4) Chest X-ray (opacity with a horizontal or oblique level, mediastinal shift toward the healthy side), pleural ultrasound, pleural puncture and fluid analysis (exudate or transudate).

topics.title: Instrumental and laboratory methods of examining the respiratory system. Semiotics and syndromes of respiratory involvement

goals.text: The student should know:

items: functional (spirometry, spirography, pneumotachometry, peak flowmetry, breath-holding tests, blood gases, pulse oximetry), radiological (X-ray, tomography, CT, bronchography, fluorography), endoscopic and laboratory methods of examining the respiratory system, their indications and age limitations;
the semiotics of the main respiratory symptoms;

the syndromes of upper airway involvement, croup, bronchial obstruction, consolidation (infiltration) of lung tissue, atelectasis, fluid and air in the pleural cavity, a cavity in the lung, respiratory disorders in newborns, pulmonary edema;
the types and degrees of severity of respiratory failure.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: assess spirogram and peak flowmetry results and determine the type of ventilatory disorder;
“read” a chest X-ray in order;
assess sputum and pleural fluid analyses;
identify the leading syndrome on the basis of the physical examination findings;
determine the degree of respiratory failure.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **Restrictive — “the volume is small”** (VC ↓, Tiffeneau normal); **obstructive — “the speed is small”** (FEV~1~ and Tiffeneau ↓). An increase in FEV~1~ of **more than 12%** in a bronchodilator (salbutamol) test is a sign of reversible obstruction (bronchial asthma).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The key to distinguishing consolidation from atelectasis is **the state of the bronchus**: an open bronchus (pneumonia) — sound is conducted well (vocal fremitus ↑, bronchial breathing); a closed bronchus (atelectasis) — sound is not conducted (vocal fremitus ↓, breath sounds not heard). On X-ray, in pneumonia the mediastinum stays in place; in atelectasis it is pulled **toward the affected side**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In Kildiyarova's textbook, the signs of pleurisy (dull sound, fluid level) were mistakenly repeated in the pneumothorax section. The correct signs of pneumothorax are given here — **tympanitis** and, on X-ray, **absence of the lung markings** (consistent with Arzikulov's textbook and general clinical data).

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In Arzikulov's textbook the degrees of RF are also given by **blood oxygen saturation**: I — normal or down to 90%; II — 70–80%; III — <70%; IV (hypoxemic coma) — <50%. These are old cut-offs; in practice the SpO~2~ values in the table above are used. In a healthy child arterial blood saturation is **94–98%**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **Four rules:** 1) **Dense tissue + open bronchus** → sound is conducted well → vocal fremitus and bronchophony ↑, bronchial breathing. 2) **Fluid or air in the pleura, or an obstructed bronchus** → sound is blocked → everything ↓. 3) The mediastinum **moves away from what “pushes”** (fluid, air → toward the healthy side) and **toward what “pulls”** (atelectasis → toward the affected side). 4) **Upper airways → inspiration is difficult** (croup), **small bronchi → expiration is difficult** (asthma, bronchiolitis).

blocks.text: **Main idea:** functional tests require the child's **active participation** — spirography and pneumotachometry are usually performed **after 5 years**; in small children respiratory failure is assessed by clinical signs, pulse oximetry and blood gases.
Breath-holding tests
Performed sitting, with the nose pinched:

items: **Stange test** — breath-holding time after a deep inspiration;
**Genche test** — breath-holding time after expiration (in pediatrics, after 3 deep breaths).

blocks.title: Table 7.1. Age norms for breath-holding tests (Kildiyarova)
head: Age
Genche, s (boys / girls)
Stange, s (boys / girls)

blocks.text: Shortening of the test times indicates reduced reserve of the cardiorespiratory system (respiratory or heart failure, anemia, detraining).
Spirometry

**Spirometry** — a method of determining **the vital capacity (VC)** (with a Hutchinson spirometer or a portable spirometer). The child, standing or sitting, takes a maximal breath, pinches the nose and slowly breathes all the air out into the spirometer through the mouthpiece. The measurement is repeated 2–3 times, the highest result is taken and compared with **the predicted value (for age, height and sex)**. A decrease of **more than 15–20%** from the predicted value is pathological.
Spirography

**Spirography** — graphic recording of respiratory movements, reflecting changes in lung volumes. It is performed in the morning on an empty stomach after 10–15 minutes of rest; the child breathes through a mouthpiece (with a nose clip) or a mask. First 3–5 minutes of quiet breathing and the VC are recorded, then the forced tests.
Main parameters:

items: **TV** — tidal volume (the volume of air in one respiratory cycle);
**MV** — minute volume of breathing = RR × TV; it increases in lung and heart diseases and thyrotoxicosis, and decreases when the respiratory center is depressed;
**VC** — vital capacity = TV + inspiratory reserve volume + expiratory reserve volume;
**FVC** — forced vital capacity (a sharp expiration after a maximal deep breath);
**FEV~1~** — forced expiratory volume in the 1st second; **Tiffeneau index** = FEV~1~ / VC × 100%, normally **≥70%**;
**MVV** — maximal voluntary ventilation of the lungs (the maximal volume of air that can be ventilated in 1 minute; calculated from a 10–15-second recording);
**Breathing reserve** = MVV – MV; it decreases in respiratory failure.

blocks.text: A deviation of **±20%** from the predicted values is considered acceptable.

parts.text: **Restrictive — “the volume is small”** (VC ↓, Tiffeneau normal); **obstructive — “the speed is small”** (FEV~1~ and Tiffeneau ↓). An increase in FEV~1~ of **more than 12%** in a bronchodilator (salbutamol) test is a sign of reversible obstruction (bronchial asthma).

blocks.text: Pneumotachometry

**Pneumotachometry** — assessment of bronchial patency: **the peak air flow rate** on inspiration and expiration is measured (from 5–6 years). First a tube 20 mm in diameter is used, then one of 10 mm; the test is repeated 3–4 times and the highest result is taken. A reduced expiratory rate indicates bronchial obstruction (bronchospasm, mucosal edema, secretions).
Peak flowmetry

**Peak flowmetry** — determining **the peak expiratory flow (PEF)** with a portable device, the peak flow meter. It is simple, cheap and done at home — the main method of **monitoring bronchial asthma** and its control. The child stands, takes a deep breath, seals the lips tightly around the mouthpiece and breathes out **sharply and quickly**; this is repeated 3 times and the highest result is recorded. Measurements are taken **2 times a day** — in the morning (before taking medication) and in the evening.

items: **Daily variability >20%** or a **“morning dip”** — bronchial **hyperreactivity** (uncontrolled asthma).
The result is compared with the norm for the child's height: 107 cm — ≈140, 130 cm — ≈250, 152 cm — ≈360, 175 cm — ≈480 l/min.
**The “traffic light” system: green zone** — ≥80% of the personal best (good control); **yellow** — 50–80% (step up treatment); **red** — <50% (emergency care).

blocks.text: Blood gases and pulse oximetry

items: **Blood gases** (capillary or arterial blood, micro-Astrup apparatus): **PaO~2~** (normal in children 80–100 mm Hg), **PaCO~2~** (35–45 mm), **pH** (7.35–7.45), buffer bases (BE).

**Pulse oximetry (oxyhemometry)** — continuous, painless transcutaneous measurement of blood oxygen saturation (**SpO~2~**); **94–98%** in a healthy child. **SpO~2~ <92–94%** is an indication for oxygen therapy (pneumonia, bronchiolitis, asthma attack).

**Chest X-ray** — the most widely used instrumental method; in frontal (anterior) and lateral projections. It detects pneumonia, pleurisy, pneumothorax, atelectasis, foreign bodies (radiopaque), thymomegaly and developmental defects.
**Fluoroscopy** — real-time observation of diaphragmatic movement and mediastinal shift (high radiation dose — rarely used).
**Tomography** (layer-by-layer) — the lung root, lymph nodes, cavities.
**Computed tomography** (spiral, high-resolution CT) — the most accurate method: bronchiectasis, interstitial changes, small foci, tumors; with contrast when necessary.
**Bronchography** — X-ray after injecting a contrast medium into the bronchi: **bronchiectasis**, bronchial defects, tumors (now mostly replaced by CT).
**Angiopulmonography**, **radioisotope scanning (scintigraphy)** — pulmonary circulation and ventilation.
**X-ray of the paranasal sinuses** — sinusitis.
**Ultrasound of the pleural cavity and lungs** — detecting fluid, marking the puncture site.
**Fluorography** — mass preventive screening (tuberculosis, tumor); because of the high radiation dose only **after 15 years**.

blocks.text: Order of reading an X-ray:

items: Determine the projection (frontal, lateral).
Correct positioning of the child — the clavicles at the same level, the spinous processes in the middle of the sternum.
Exposure of the X-ray — if the disc between the 3rd and 4th thoracic vertebrae is visible — normal.
The chest skeleton (ribs, spine, clavicles).
**Transparency** of the lung fields on both sides.
Position of the diaphragmatic domes, the costophrenic sinuses, the gastric air bubble.
**Lung roots** — normally from the anterior end of rib II to rib IV, structured.
**Lung markings** — normally visible in the inner 2/3 of the lung field; when increased they reach the periphery.
Pleura.
Mediastinum (cardiac shadow, thymus, position of the trachea).
Conclusion. **Reduced transparency (opacity)** — pneumonia, atelectasis, pleurisy, tumor; **increased transparency (lucency)** — emphysema, pneumothorax, bronchial obstruction.

blocks.label: Figure 7.2
blocks.caption: Normal chest X-ray of a child (Kildiyarova, Figure 8.8)

items: **Rhinoscopy** (anterior and posterior) and **pharyngoscopy** — the nose, adenoids, pharynx.
**Laryngoscopy** — at an early age direct laryngoscopy (often under anesthesia), in older children indirect (with a mirror); croup, laryngeal anomalies, papillomatosis.

**Bronchoscopy** — **up to 3–4 years** with a rigid bronchoscope **under anesthesia**, in older children **fiberoptic bronchoscopy** under local anesthesia. Its possibilities: viewing the inner surface of the trachea and bronchi; removing **a foreign body**; suctioning pus, blood and mucus (sanitation); detecting tumors and defects; **biopsy**; obtaining bronchial washings (bronchoalveolar lavage); direct administration of drugs.
**Thoracoscopy** — viewing the pleural cavity (pleural biopsy, treatment of empyema).

blocks.label: Figure 7.3
blocks.caption: Bronchogram in chronic bronchitis: bronchiectasis (Kildiyarova, Figure 8.9)

items: **Complete blood count:** in bacterial pneumonia **neutrophilic leukocytosis**, a left shift, raised ESR; in viral infection — leukopenia or normal, lymphocytosis; in bronchial asthma and helminthiasis — **eosinophilia**; in whooping cough — marked **leukocytosis and lymphocytosis**.
**Inflammatory markers:** C-reactive protein, procalcitonin (bacterial infection).

**Microbiological examination:** culture and bacterioscopy of nasopharyngeal swabs (including for diphtheria — Loeffler's bacillus), sputum, bronchial secretions and pleural fluid; antibiotic sensitivity; PCR and rapid tests for viruses; for tuberculosis — mycobacteria in sputum or gastric washings.
**Sweat test** — sweat electrolytes (chloride >60 mmol/l) — diagnosis of **cystic fibrosis**.
**Allergological:** skin tests (scarification, prick test, intradermal), provocation tests; total and specific **IgE** in the blood.
**Diagnosis of tuberculosis:** Mantoux test, Diaskintest, QuantiFERON test.

sections.title: 7.5. Semiotics of the main respiratory symptoms

blocks.text: **Main idea:** cough indicates **the level of the lesion** (pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchus, pleura), while its timing and sputum indicate **the nature of the process**.

**Runny nose:** the discharge is serous, mucous, mucopurulent or blood-stained. Nasal congestion without discharge — viral and allergic disease, adenoids. **Unilateral purulent, fetid discharge** in a small child — **a foreign body in the nose**. **Nosebleeds** — hemorrhagic diatheses, leukemia, hypoplastic anemia, arterial hypertension, nasal polyps.

blocks.title: Table 7.4. Character of the cough by level of the lesion
head: Site of the lesion
Character of the cough
rows: Dry, exhausting, with a scratchy throat
Harsh, “as if coughing into a barrel”, retrosternal pain
Dry at first, then moist, productive
Paroxysmal, with reprises, at night, with facial flushing and vomiting
Paroxysmal, dry; viscous sputum after the attack

blocks.text: Timing of the cough:

items: **morning** — a cavity in the lung (abscess, bronchiectasis, cavern), chronic bronchitis: sputum accumulated overnight moves when the position changes;
**evening** — acute bronchitis, pneumonia;

**night** — tuberculosis, lymphogranulomatosis, tumors (the lymph nodes irritate the bifurcation, and vagal tone rises at night), bronchial asthma (attacks at 4–6 a.m.), adenoiditis (mucus runs down the posterior pharyngeal wall);
**related to eating** — tracheoesophageal fistula, gastroesophageal reflux, esophageal diverticulum.

blocks.text: If an infrequent cough becomes **frequent and moist** during an illness, this indicates that bronchiolitis or pneumonia has developed. A cough lasting **more than 3–4 weeks** requires exclusion of a chronic disease (asthma, tuberculosis, cystic fibrosis, foreign body, reflux).

**Sputum:** “a mouthful” of purulent sputum — rupture of an abscess or a suppurating cyst into a bronchus, bronchiectasis. **Hemoptysis** — destructive pneumonia, tuberculous cavern, tumor, hemorrhagic diathesis, pulmonary hemosiderosis.
**Voice:** a weak squealing cry or no cry in a newborn — asphyxia, CNS damage; hoarse voice and aphonia — acute laryngitis, diphtheria; nasal speech — adenoids; a low “croaky” voice — hypothyroidism.

**Dyspnea:** inspiratory — narrowing of the upper airways (croup, foreign body, retropharyngeal abscess); expiratory — bronchial obstruction (asthma, obstructive bronchitis, bronchiolitis); mixed — pneumonia, pleurisy, respiratory failure, heart failure.

**Chest pain:** increased by deep breathing and coughing — pleurisy, lobar pneumonia (pleuropneumonia); localized, painful on pressure — myositis, intercostal neuralgia, rib injury; in diaphragmatic pleurisy and lower lobe pneumonia the pain **radiates to the abdomen** (risk of mistaking it for acute appendicitis).

**Cyanosis:** of the nasolabial triangle and around the eyes — mild to moderate respiratory failure; diffuse, gray-marbled — severe respiratory failure. **“Drumstick fingers”** and **“watch-glass” nails** — chronic hypoxia (bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis).

sections.title: 7.6. Syndromes of consolidation (infiltration) of lung tissue and atelectasis

blocks.text: **Main idea: consolidation** (open bronchus) → vocal fremitus and bronchophony are **increased**, bronchial breathing; **atelectasis** (closed bronchus) → they are **weakened**, breathing is faint. On percussion the sound is shortened in both.
Infiltration syndrome
It occurs in: **pneumonia**, pulmonary infarction, pulmonary hemorrhage, tuberculous infiltrate, eosinophilic infiltrate.

blocks.caption: Diagram of the syndromes: a — normal; b — pneumothorax; c — obstructive atelectasis; d — lobar consolidation (lobar pneumonia); e — focal consolidation (bronchopneumonia); f — bronchial narrowing (Arzikulov)

parts.text: In small children the most reliable clinical signs of pneumonia are **tachypnea**, **lower chest wall indrawing**, fever lasting more than 3 days and **a fall in SpO~2~**. Physical signs may not be pronounced with small foci — if in doubt, an X-ray is taken.

blocks.text: Atelectasis syndrome

**Atelectasis** — loss of air and collapse of part of the lung: obstruction of the airway (thick mucus, foreign body, tumor, an enlarged lymph node compressing from outside) or compression of the lung from outside (fluid, air). Predisposition: narrow bronchi, surfactant deficiency, weak cough reflex; newborns also have **primary (physiological) atelectasis**.

blocks.title: Table 7.6. Signs of obstructive atelectasis
head: Method
Signs
rows: With a large atelectasis the condition worsens; tachypnea, tachycardia, cyanosis; the chest on the affected side is flattened (sunken) and lags behind during breathing
Breathing weakened or not heard, no rales
Triad: a homogeneous triangular shadow (base at the periphery, apex at the lung root) + mediastinal shift toward the affected side + elevation of the diaphragm on the affected side

blocks.label: Figure 7.6
blocks.caption: Chest X-ray in atelectasis (Kildiyarova, Figure 8.13)

parts.text: The key to distinguishing consolidation from atelectasis is **the state of the bronchus**: an open bronchus (pneumonia) — sound is conducted well (vocal fremitus ↑, bronchial breathing); a closed bronchus (atelectasis) — sound is not conducted (vocal fremitus ↓, breath sounds not heard). On X-ray, in pneumonia the mediastinum stays in place; in atelectasis it is pulled **toward the affected side**.

blocks.text: **Main idea:** in the pleura **both fluid and air** block sound — vocal fremitus, bronchophony and breathing are **weakened or absent**; the difference is in percussion: fluid — **dull**, air — **tympanic**. In both, the mediastinum shifts **toward the healthy side**.
Dry (fibrinous) pleurisy

The pleural layers are covered with fibrin. Signs: **stabbing pain** that increases with breathing and coughing; the child lies on the affected side (to restrict movement); the affected side lags behind during breathing; percussion is almost unchanged (mobility of the lower edge is restricted); breathing is weakened because of the pain; **pleural friction rub** (mainly low on the midaxillary line). In diaphragmatic pleurisy — pain radiating to the abdomen and shoulder, hiccups, **Mussy's sign**.
Syndrome of fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity
It occurs in: exudative pleurisy (parapneumonic, tuberculous), **empyema** (purulent), hydrothorax (heart failure, nephrotic syndrome), hemothorax, chylothorax.

blocks.title: Table 7.7. Signs of the syndrome of fluid in the pleural cavity
head: Method
Signs
rows: Respiratory failure increases, dyspnea, cyanosis, tachypnea, tachycardia; the pain decreases as fluid accumulates
Forced position — lies on the affected side; the chest is asymmetric, the affected side enlarged and lagging behind during breathing; the intercostal spaces are smoothed or bulging
The affected side is rigid; vocal fremitus is not transmitted; the skin fold is thickened (Filatov)

Dull (“thigh”) sound; in older children the Damoiseau (Sokolov–Damoiseau) line — the oblique upper border of the fluid (highest on the posterior axillary line); Garland's triangle — on the same side next to the spine, a shortened-tympanic sound over the compressed lung; the Rauchfuss–Grocco triangle — on the opposite side next to the spine, dullness due to the displaced mediastinum
Breathing sharply weakened or not heard; bronchophony weakened; bronchial breathing may be heard at the border of the compressed lung above the fluid

Homogeneous opacity with an oblique upper border (or horizontal — if there is fluid and air), the costophrenic sinus obliterated, the mediastinum shifted toward the healthy side; in the lateral decubitus position the shape of the shadow changes

blocks.label: Figure 7.7
blocks.caption: Right-sided pleurisy: fluid level in the upright position (Kildiyarova, Figure 8.14)

blocks.text: **Pleural puncture** — for diagnosis and treatment, at the site of the dullest sound (under ultrasound guidance), most often along the posterior axillary or scapular line **in the 7th–8th intercostal space, along the upper edge of the lower rib** (so as not to injure the neurovascular bundle under the rib).

blocks.title: Table 7.8. Differences between exudate and transudate
head: Sign
Exudate (inflammatory)
Transudate (non-inflammatory)
rows: Rivalta test (turbidity in acetic acid solution)
Many: neutrophils in acute infection, lymphocytes in tuberculosis

blocks.text: Accumulation of air in the pleural cavity — pneumothorax

Causes: lung destruction (**staphylococcal pneumonia**), rupture of a bulla or cyst, injury, complications of mechanical ventilation, a complication of pleural puncture. **Valvular (tension) pneumothorax** is the most dangerous: with each breath the air increases and compresses the lung and mediastinum; urgent pleural puncture is required. **Pyopneumothorax** — pus and air in the pleura.

blocks.title: Table 7.9. Signs of pneumothorax
head: Method
Signs
rows: Sudden chest pain, sharp dyspnea, cyanosis, tachycardia, restlessness
The affected side is enlarged, does not take part in breathing, the intercostal spaces are smoothed
Tympanic sound; the cardiac borders are shifted toward the healthy side
Breathing not heard or sharply weakened; bronchophony weakened
On the affected side a lucent field without lung markings, the lung collapsed toward the root, the mediastinum shifted toward the healthy side

blocks.label: Figure 7.8
blocks.caption: Left-sided pneumothorax (Kildiyarova, Figure 8.15)

parts.text: In Kildiyarova's textbook, the signs of pleurisy (dull sound, fluid level) were mistakenly repeated in the pneumothorax section. The correct signs of pneumothorax are given here — **tympanitis** and, on X-ray, **absence of the lung markings** (consistent with Arzikulov's textbook and general clinical data).

blocks.text: **Main idea: narrowing of the upper airways** → **inspiratory** dyspnea (croup); **narrowing of the small bronchi** → **expiratory** dyspnea, box-like sound, whistling rales (obstruction).
Syndrome of upper airway involvement

In rhinitis, nasopharyngitis, pharyngitis, laryngitis and tracheitis: runny nose (serous-watery at first, then thick), pain on swallowing, a scratchy throat; **dry cough**; hyperemia and granularity of the posterior pharyngeal wall; fever, intoxication. Palpation is unchanged; percussion gives a clear pulmonary sound; breathing is **harsh**, and the rales are **transmitted** in character — **they disappear after coughing**.

**Adenoid facies** (enlargement of the nasopharyngeal tonsil): a puffy face, the mouth always open, no nasal breathing, snoring and apnea in sleep, malocclusion, a high “gothic” palate, nasal speech, hearing loss (otitis), frequent colds, reduced attention and memory from prolonged hypoxia.
Croup syndrome

**Croup** — narrowing (stenosis) of the laryngeal lumen. At an early age (6 months – 3 years) it is most often **false croup** — **stenosing laryngotracheitis** in influenza, parainfluenza and adenovirus infection (edema of the loose tissue below the vocal cords). **The croup triad: barking cough + hoarse voice + inspiratory dyspnea (stridor)**; in addition: restlessness, tachycardia, participation of the accessory muscles, retraction of the suprasternal area and intercostal spaces.

blocks.title: Table 7.10. Differences between false and true croup
head: Sign
False croup (ARVI)
True croup (laryngeal diphtheria)
rows: Edema + fibrinous membrane on the vocal cords
Loeffler's bacillus in a nasopharyngeal swab
The stenosis progresses, risk of asphyxia; complications (myocarditis, nephritis)

blocks.title: Table 7.11. Degrees of laryngeal stenosis
head: Degree
Signs
rows: Dyspnea and stridor only when the child is upset, absent at rest
Stridor even at rest, retraction of the intercostal spaces and the suprasternal area, perioral cyanosis, tachycardia
Marked dyspnea, generalized cyanosis, severe restlessness or lethargy, paradoxical pulse, weakened breathing
Unconscious, shallow breathing, bradycardia, seizures, risk of cardiac arrest

parts.text: In false croup: calm the child (crying worsens the stenosis), fresh moist air, **inhaled budesonide** or **dexamethasone** (orally or IM), from grade II **adrenaline inhalation**; in grade II–III — urgent hospitalization. Forcible inspection of the pharynx with a spatula **must not** be done (reflex laryngospasm; in epiglottitis — risk of complete obstruction).

blocks.text: Bronchial obstruction syndrome

It occurs in: an attack of bronchial asthma, obstructive bronchitis, **bronchiolitis**, cystic fibrosis, foreign body, bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Mechanism: **spasm of the bronchial smooth muscle + mucosal edema + mucus hypersecretion**; at an early age **edema and hypersecretion** mainly predominate (which is why bronchodilators are less effective).

blocks.title: Table 7.12. Signs of the bronchial obstruction syndrome
head: Method
Signs
rows: Dry, paroxysmal cough; restlessness, respiratory failure; tachypnea (up to 60–80/min in bronchiolitis)

Expiratory dyspnea, whistling breathing heard at a distance; accessory muscles, flaring of the nasal alae; cyanosis of the nasolabial triangle; distended (barrel-shaped) chest; orthopnea in an asthma attack

Box-like sound; the lower lung border shifted downward, its excursion reduced; the borders of relative cardiac dullness reduced; the liver and spleen displaced downward (should not be mistaken for enlargement)
Breathing harsh or weakened, prolonged expiration; dry whistling rales on expiration; in bronchiolitis + many fine-bubbling moist rales and crepitation
FEV~1~, Tiffeneau index, peak flow and small airway flows reduced — obstructive type; daily PEF variability >20%
The lungs are hyperinflated (increased transparency), the ribs horizontal, the diaphragm low and flattened, increased bronchovascular markings

blocks.label: Figure 7.9
blocks.caption: X-ray in the obstructive syndrome: increased transparency of the lung fields, horizontal ribs, increased bronchovascular markings (Kildiyarova, Figure 8.11)

blocks.text: **Emphysema** (persistent increase in lung airiness): barrel chest, widened intercostal spaces, reduced excursion; weakened vocal fremitus; **box-like** sound, lowered lower borders; **weakened** breathing; on X-ray increased lung transparency, a flattened and low diaphragm. Local (unilateral) emphysema — foreign body (valve mechanism), congenital lobar emphysema.
Syndrome of a cavity in the lung

An (emptied) abscess, tuberculous cavern, bronchiectasis, suppurated cyst, bullae in destructive (staphylococcal) pneumonia. Signs: restricted respiratory movement on the affected side; vocal fremitus **increased** (if there is a dense inflammatory ridge around the cavity); **tympanic** sound on percussion (shortened if the cavity is small or deep); **amphoric** breathing; **coarse-bubbling consonant** moist rales; increased bronchophony (metallic). X-ray — **a ring-shaped shadow**, possibly with air and a fluid level inside. When an abscess ruptures into a bronchus — “a mouthful” of purulent, fetid sputum.
Syndrome of respiratory disorders in newborns (respiratory distress)

Pneumopathies: atelectasis of the newborn, **hyaline membrane disease**, edematous-hemorrhagic syndrome, meconium aspiration, transient tachypnea of the newborn; mainly **in preterm babies** (surfactant deficiency). Signs: restlessness or lethargy, cyanosis, **frothy discharge on the lips**, retraction of the compliant parts of the chest (sternum, intercostal spaces), **“seesaw” breathing** (thoracoabdominal asynchrony), respiratory arrhythmia and **apnea**, **“grunting” expiration**, weakened breathing, scattered fine-bubbling rales and crepitation, tachycardia, muffled heart sounds, muscle hypotonia, seizures. Severity is assessed with the **Silverman** (preterm) and **Downes** (term) scales (see topic 2).
Pulmonary edema

Escape of fluid from the capillaries into the interstitium and the alveoli: **cardiac** (left ventricular failure, mitral stenosis) and **noncardiac** (drowning, toxic gases, severe pneumonia, sepsis, rapid and large-volume infusion, nephrotic and nephritic syndromes) causes. Signs: restlessness, fear of death, orthopnea, **cough with frothy, sometimes pink sputum**, rapidly increasing dyspnea and cyanosis, cold sweat, a rapid weak pulse; on percussion a shortened sound in the lower posterior parts; on auscultation **many bilateral fine-bubbling non-consonant** rales, later medium- and coarse-bubbling (“boiling samovar” breathing).

**Main idea:** RF is a condition in which the normal gas composition of the blood is not maintained, or is maintained only **through strain** of the external respiratory apparatus. The cut-offs in children: **PaO~2~ <80 mm Hg**, **PaCO~2~ >40–45 mm Hg**. RF accompanies any respiratory disease and diseases of other organs (CNS, heart, muscles).
Types (by pathogenesis):

items: **Ventilatory (hypercapnic)** — lung ventilation is insufficient: PaO~2~ low, **PaCO~2~ high**; the clinical picture is related to **hypercapnia**: headache, sweating, tachycardia, arterial hypertension, drowsiness, tremor, later cerebral edema and coma.

**Parenchymal (diffusion, hypoxemic)** — the ventilation-perfusion ratio or alveolar-capillary diffusion is disturbed: PaO~2~ low, PaCO~2~ normal or low; the clinical picture is related to **hypoxemia**: cyanosis, restlessness → CNS depression, tachycardia, arrhythmia, muffled heart sounds, arterial hypotension.

blocks.text: Causes of acute RF:

items: **Obstructive (mechanical)** — upper airway obstruction (croup, epiglottitis, foreign body, tongue falling back in unconsciousness), bronchospasm (asthma), viscous secretions (cystic fibrosis), exudate in the bronchi (bronchitis, bronchiolitis, aspiration).
**Restrictive** — reduced compliance of the lungs and chest wall: pneumonia, pleurisy, pneumothorax, atelectasis, pulmonary edema, meteorism and a high diaphragm, rib injury.

**Neuromuscular** — depression of the respiratory center (CNS injury, neuroinfection, drug poisoning), paralysis of the respiratory muscles (poliomyelitis, myasthenia, botulism, muscular dystrophies).
**Diffusion disorder** — pulmonary edema, interstitial pneumonia, fibrosing alveolitis.

blocks.title: Table 7.13. Degrees of severity of acute respiratory failure
head: Sign
Grade I
Grade II
Grade III
rows: >50% above normal, or bradypnea, arrhythmic breathing
Pale; cyanosis of the nasolabial triangle on exertion
Pale, cyanosis of the nasolabial area and around the eyes at rest, acrocyanosis
Gray, marbled, generalized cyanosis; does not decrease with oxygen
Markedly rapid or bradycardia, BP reduced

blocks.text: **Grade IV — hypoxic coma:** unconscious; the respiration-pulse ratio is severely disturbed; the skin is gray with purple-blue patches; pathological types of breathing; dilated pupils, seizures; PaO~2~ <50 mm, pH <7.2.

parts.text: In Arzikulov's textbook the degrees of RF are also given by **blood oxygen saturation**: I — normal or down to 90%; II — 70–80%; III — <70%; IV (hypoxemic coma) — <50%. These are old cut-offs; in practice the SpO~2~ values in the table above are used. In a healthy child arterial blood saturation is **94–98%**.

blocks.text: Distinguishing the syndromes in one table

blocks.title: Table 7.14. Physical and X-ray signs of the main respiratory syndromes
head: Syndrome
The chest
Vocal fremitus
Percussion
Respiration
Adventitious sound
Mediastinum (X-ray)
rows: Pleural friction rub at the beginning and end

parts.text: **Four rules:** 1) **Dense tissue + open bronchus** → sound is conducted well → vocal fremitus and bronchophony ↑, bronchial breathing. 2) **Fluid or air in the pleura, or an obstructed bronchus** → sound is blocked → everything ↓. 3) The mediastinum **moves away from what “pushes”** (fluid, air → toward the healthy side) and **toward what “pulls”** (atelectasis → toward the affected side). 4) **Upper airways → inspiration is difficult** (croup), **small bronchi → expiration is difficult** (asthma, bronchiolitis).

blocks.text: A child in an attack of bronchial asthma

Bronchial asthma is chronic allergic inflammation and hyperreactivity of the bronchi with recurrent attacks of reversible obstruction. Signs of an attack: expiratory dyspnea, whistling breathing heard at a distance, orthopnea, dry cough, box-like sound, dry whistling rales. Diagnosis: history (allergy, heredity, recurrent attacks), reversible obstruction on spirometry (FEV~1~ ↑ ≥12% after salbutamol), daily variability >20% on peak flowmetry, eosinophilia, raised IgE, Curschmann spirals and Charcot–Leyden crystals in the sputum.

parts.text: In an asthma attack, **a “silent chest”** (breath sounds and rales are no longer heard), inability to speak, cyanosis, lethargy and SpO~2~ <90% are signs of **a life-threatening** attack: urgent oxygen, salbutamol inhalation (via a spacer or nebulizer), systemic glucocorticoids, admission to the intensive care unit.

skills.title: Skill 1. Performing and assessing peak flowmetry

items: Set the peak flow meter pointer to zero; show the child the technique.
The child stands and holds the peak flow meter horizontally (the fingers should not touch the scale).
The child takes a deep breath, seals the lips tightly around the mouthpiece and breathes out **sharply and quickly**.
Record the result; repeat 3 times and note the highest.
Measure in the morning and evening; calculate the daily variability: (evening – morning) / mean × 100%.
Compare the result with the norm for height and the personal best (the “traffic light” zones).

skills.title: Skill 2. Assessing a spirogram

items: Determine the child's data (age, sex, height) and find the predicted values.
Compare the actual values of VC, FEV~1~, Tiffeneau index and MVV with the predicted values (in %).
Determine the type of ventilatory disorder: restrictive (VC ↓, Tiffeneau normal), obstructive (FEV~1~, Tiffeneau ↓), mixed.
If there is a bronchodilator test — calculate the increase in FEV~1~ (≥12% — reversible obstruction).
Write the conclusion.

skills.title: Skill 3. “Reading” a chest X-ray

items: Check the patient's details, the date and the projection.
Assess the child's positioning and the exposure of the X-ray.
Skeleton, soft tissues.
Compare the transparency of the lung fields on both sides; detect foci of opacity or lucency (location, size, shape, homogeneity).
Lung markings and roots.
Diaphragm, sinuses, pleura.
Position and displacement of the mediastinum.
Conclusion (e.g., “right lower lobe infiltration”, “left-sided exudative pleurisy”).

skills.title: Skill 4. Performing pulse oximetry

items: Place the pulse oximeter sensor on the child's finger (in a newborn — on the hand or foot).
The child should be calm and the hand warm (a cold hand or movement gives an erroneous result).
Once the pulse wave has stabilized (15–30 s), record the SpO~2~ and pulse rate.
Assessment: ≥95% — normal; 92–94% — borderline; <92% — hypoxemia, oxygen therapy.

skills.title: Skill 5. Identifying the syndrome on the basis of physical examination findings

items: Inspection data: type of dyspnea, symmetry of the chest, its participation in breathing.
Palpation: vocal fremitus increased / weakened.
Percussion: dull, shortened, tympanic, box-like sound.
Auscultation: type of breathing, rales, crepitation, pleural friction rub, bronchophony.
Compare the signs with the table of syndromes and identify the leading syndrome.
Plan confirmatory investigations (X-ray, blood tests, puncture, etc.).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 2-year-old child suddenly woke at night with a harsh “barking” cough and noisy breathing. In the evening there was a runny nose and a temperature of 37.8 °C. On examination: the child is restless, the voice is hoarse, noisy inspiration (stridor) is heard even at rest, the suprasternal area and intercostal spaces retract on inspiration, perioral cyanosis, RR 42/min, pulse 140/min. In the lungs harsh breathing, transmitted rales.
cases.ask: 1) Which syndrome? 2) Determine the type of dyspnea and the degree of stenosis. 3) False or true croup? Justify. 4) What are the emergency measures?
cases.answer: 1) Croup syndrome (acute stenosing laryngotracheitis). 2) Inspiratory dyspnea; stridor at rest, retractions and perioral cyanosis — grade II (subcompensated) stenosis. 3) False croup: against a background of ARVI, sudden onset at night, hoarse voice (not aphonia), little intoxication. 4) Calm the child, moist fresh air, budesonide inhalation or dexamethasone, adrenaline inhalation, hospitalization; do not forcibly inspect the pharynx.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 12-year-old adolescent complains of cough and attacks of shortness of breath; the attacks worsen in spring, during the flowering season and after playing with a cat. The mother has pollinosis. Spirography: VC — 88% of predicted, FEV~1~ — 62%, Tiffeneau index 58%. After salbutamol inhalation FEV~1~ increased by 20%. Daily variability on peak flowmetry is 28%. Blood eosinophils 9%.
cases.ask: 1) Determine the type of ventilatory disorder. 2) Assess the result of the bronchodilator test. 3) Presumptive diagnosis? 4) What may be found in the sputum?
cases.answer: 1) Obstructive type: FEV~1~ and the Tiffeneau index (<70%) markedly reduced, VC almost normal. 2) An increase in FEV~1~ of ≥12% is a sign of reversible obstruction (bronchospasm). 3) Bronchial asthma (atopic): allergen-related attacks, hereditary predisposition, reversible obstruction, PEF variability >20%, eosinophilia. 4) Eosinophils, Curschmann spirals, Charcot–Leyden crystals.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 3-year-old child has been treated for pneumonia for 5 days. Today the condition suddenly became much worse: restless, marked dyspnea (RR 60/min), generalized cyanosis, pulse 160/min, SpO~2~ 84%. The right half of the chest is enlarged and does not take part in breathing. On the right vocal fremitus cannot be detected, percussion gives a tympanic sound, breath sounds are not heard. The heart sounds are shifted to the left. X-ray: on the right a lucency without lung markings, the lung collapsed toward the root, the mediastinum shifted to the left; there are destruction cavities in the lung.
cases.ask: 1) Which complication has developed? 2) What could be its cause? 3) Determine the degree of respiratory failure. 4) Emergency measures?
cases.answer: 1) Right-sided pneumothorax (probably valvular — the mediastinum is shifted and the condition is very severe). 2) Destructive (most often staphylococcal) pneumonia — rupture of a bulla or abscess into the pleural cavity (it may also be pyopneumothorax). 3) Grade III RF: RR >50% above normal (25–30 at 3 years), generalized cyanosis, SpO~2~ <85%, marked tachycardia. 4) Oxygen, urgent pleural puncture (2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line) and drainage of the pleural cavity, transfer to the surgical department.

topics.title: The cardiovascular system: anatomical and physiological features, fetal and neonatal circulation, inspection, palpation, percussion, X-ray and cardiometry

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the intrauterine development of the heart and the features of the fetal circulation;
the postnatal reorganization of the circulation and the closure times of the fetal communications;
the age-related anatomical and physiological features of children's heart and blood vessels;
the methods of history taking, inspection, palpation and percussion of the cardiovascular system;
the age norms for the borders of relative and absolute cardiac dullness;
the basic principles of radiological examination, cardiometry (cardiothoracic index), ECG and echocardiography.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: take complaints and history from a child with cardiovascular disease;
inspect the cardiac area and the vessels;
palpate and describe the apex beat, detect a “cat's purr”, examine the pulse in the peripheral arteries;
determine the borders of relative cardiac dullness by percussion and compare them with the age norm;
calculate the cardiothoracic index on a chest X-ray.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The fetus lives **under conditions of hypoxia**, but is adapted to it: the respiratory surface of the placenta is large, the blood flow is rapid, fetal blood contains **much hemoglobin and many erythrocytes**, **HbF** has a greater affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin, and the tissues need little oxygen.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In the neonatal period, with hypoxia, acidosis, cold exposure, pneumonia or RDS, pulmonary vascular resistance may rise again and **the fetal communications may reopen** — the **“persistent fetal circulation” syndrome** (pulmonary hypertension, right-to-left shunt, cyanosis). A hemodynamically insignificant patent foramen ovale is considered **a minor cardiac anomaly**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: With age the heart **“becomes smaller and descends”**: **the upper border rib II → 2nd intercostal space → rib III**; **the right border from the parasternal line → to the edge of the sternum**; **the left border from 2 cm outside the midclavicular line → to the midclavicular line**. The numbers: **“2 – 1 – 0”** cm outside (0–2, 2–7, 7+ years).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In the newborn, **weak pulses in the femoral arteries** are a sign of **coarctation of the aorta**; when the ductus arteriosus closes (in the 1st–2nd weeks of life) the child's condition may deteriorate sharply (“duct-dependent” defects). Checking the femoral pulses is mandatory at every examination of a newborn.

sections.title: 8.1. Development of the heart and the fetal circulation

blocks.text: The heart forms from the mesoderm as a tube in **the 3rd week** of intrauterine development and begins to contract **from day 22**. The division of the heart into atria and ventricles and the formation of the valves take place in **weeks 2–8** — this is **the critical period** for the formation of **congenital heart defects** (viruses, especially rubella, drugs, alcohol, ionizing radiation, maternal diabetes mellitus).
Features of the fetal circulation:

items: there is **a placental circulation**: gas exchange takes place not in the lungs but in the placenta;
**the pulmonary circulation hardly works** — only **≈10%** of the cardiac output passes through the lungs;
blood passes from both ventricles into the systemic circulation through **three shunts**: **the ductus venosus (Arantius)**, **the foramen ovale**, **the ductus arteriosus (Botallo)**;

the fetal organs are supplied with **mixed blood**; the most oxygenated blood goes to **the liver, brain and arms** (branches close to the superior vena cava), and the lower part of the body receives less oxygenated blood;
the pressure in the pulmonary artery and the aorta is almost the same and low.

blocks.text: **The path of the blood:** oxygen-rich blood comes from the placenta to the fetus via **the umbilical vein** → half to the liver (portal vein), the rest via **the ductus venosus** to the inferior vena cava → right atrium. Most of the blood from the inferior vena cava passes, with the help of the Eustachian valve, through **the foramen ovale** to the left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → head and arms. Blood from the superior vena cava goes to the right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → via **the ductus arteriosus** to the descending aorta (pulmonary vascular resistance is high). From the aorta blood returns to the placenta via **the two umbilical arteries**.

parts.text: The fetus lives **under conditions of hypoxia**, but is adapted to it: the respiratory surface of the placenta is large, the blood flow is rapid, fetal blood contains **much hemoglobin and many erythrocytes**, **HbF** has a greater affinity for oxygen than adult hemoglobin, and the tissues need little oxygen.

blocks.caption: Fetal circulation (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.label: Figure 8.2
blocks.caption: Neonatal circulation (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: After birth the circulatory system is fundamentally reorganized:

items: **the placental circulation stops**; the umbilical vessels close;
with **the first breath** the lungs expand, pulmonary vascular resistance falls sharply and pulmonary blood flow increases **≈5 times** — **the pulmonary circulation starts working**;
venous return to the left atrium increases, and the pressure in the left atrium exceeds that in the right atrium — **the valve of the foramen ovale closes**;
under the influence of increased blood oxygen and decreased prostaglandins, the smooth muscle of **the ductus arteriosus** contracts and it closes;
the systemic and pulmonary circulations begin to work **in series**; the load on the left ventricle increases.

A hemodynamically insignificant patent foramen ovale is considered **a minor cardiac anomaly**.

sections.title: 8.3. Anatomical and physiological features of the heart and blood vessels

blocks.title: Table 8.2. Anatomical features of the newborn's heart
head: Indicator
Feature
rows: ≈20–25 g, 0.8% of the body mass (0.4–0.5% in adults); it increases 2 times by 1 year, 3 times by 2–3 years and 10 times by 15–16 years
Spherical (round) — the atria are relatively large, the ventricles insufficiently developed; after 6 years oval as in adults
The walls of the right and left ventricles are almost the same thickness (1.4:1); later the left ventricle develops rapidly (3 times heavier at 16 years)

blocks.text: **Growth rate:** heart volume increases fastest **in the first 2 years of life, at 5–9 years and in puberty**. Up to 2 years mainly **the atria** grow, at 2–10 years the whole heart, and after 10 years mainly **the ventricles**.
Blood vessels:

items: the arteries are relatively **wide**, with thin walls and poorly developed muscle and elastic fibers; their structure becomes similar to that of adults **by 12 years**;
the ratio of the arterial and venous lumens in the child is **1:1** (1:2 in adults); the veins later grow faster and at 15–16 years are 2 times wider than the arteries;
in the newborn the pulmonary artery is wider than the aorta (21 and 16 mm); they become equal at 12 years, and in puberty the aorta is wider;
**the capillaries are wide, short and tortuous**, with higher permeability than in adults — predisposition to **edema** in infections, **exsicosis** in toxicosis, and vascular insufficiency;
there are **many anastomoses** between the coronary arteries — myocardial infarction is very rare.

blocks.text: **Innervation:** at an early age the **sympathetic** influence predominates — physiological **tachycardia**. Myelination of the vagus nerve is completed **at 3–4 years**; after that the heart rate (HR) decreases and **respiratory arrhythmia** appears (HR increases on inspiration and slows on expiration); it is maximal **at 4–12 years**.
Functional features:

items: **physiological tachycardia** — small heart volume, high oxygen demand, sympathicotonia;
HR is **labile** — it changes quickly with movement, crying, fever and excitement;
stroke and minute volume increase with age, but the minute volume relative to body mass is **greater** in the child;
**arterial pressure is low** — the arteries are wide, the pumping force of the heart small and the peripheral resistance low; it rises gradually with age;
the circulation rate is high (a full circulation ≈12 s in the newborn, 22 s in adults).

HR, per minute

blocks.text: **Variants of the adolescent heart** (puberty): **the “drop” (small) heart** — with rapid growth in height the heart seems to hang on the vessels; rapid fatigue, dizziness, low BP, a functional systolic murmur, fainting; **the “hypertrophic” heart** — more often in boys, the left ventricle enlarged, BP slightly raised; **“mitral” configuration** — only on X-ray (the left contour is flattened).
Complaints:

items: **weakness, rapid fatigue** on physical exertion; in the newborn — **tiring during feeding**, stopping feeding to rest, sweating, poor weight gain;
**dyspnea** — on exertion or at rest;
**cyanosis** (lips, nails, generalized) — on exertion or constant; **hypercyanotic spells**;
**edema** (legs, lower back, face);
**palpitations**, a feeling of “skipped beats”;
**pain in the heart area** (location, character, duration, radiation, relation to exertion or excitement, relief with medication);
**fainting**, dizziness, headache;
pain in the calf muscles on exertion (intermittent claudication) — insufficient arterial circulation in the legs;
frequent bronchopulmonary diseases (in defects with increased pulmonary blood flow).

blocks.text: **History of the present illness:** when the complaints appeared (since birth — congenital defect; 1–3 weeks after tonsillitis or ARVI — rheumatic fever, myocarditis), relation to exertion, the course.

**Life history:** the mother's pregnancy (infections, drugs, alcohol and diabetes in the 1st trimester, occupational hazards); in the family — **congenital heart defects**, cardiomyopathies, rheumatic fever, cases of **early (before 50 years) sudden death**, arterial hypertension; the child's past illnesses (frequent tonsillitis, scarlet fever), previous ECG and echocardiography results.
General inspection

items: **Position:** in heart failure the child lies with the head raised, often on the right side; in a severe condition — **orthopnea** (sitting with the legs hanging down); in exudative pericarditis — sits leaning forward or in the **knee-elbow** position; in **tetralogy of Fallot** — **squats** after exertion (the “squatting” position); in acute vascular insufficiency — horizontal, head low.

**Skin color: pallor** (vascular insufficiency, aortic defects, “white”-type defects, rheumatic fever); **acrocyanosis** (right ventricular failure, slowed peripheral circulation); **generalized (central) cyanosis** — “blue” congenital defects (right-to-left shunt), pulmonary hypertension; **differential cyanosis** — only in the legs or only in the arms (defects of the great vessels); crimson cheeks — mitral stenosis.
**“Drumstick fingers”** and **“watch-glass” nails** — chronic hypoxia (“blue” defects, infective endocarditis).

**Edema** — right ventricular failure: first on the feet and ankles, increasing in the evening; then the shins, thighs, lower back and abdomen; in a lying child — the sacrum and lower back; in infants — the face and scrotum.
**Physical development:** hypotrophy, short stature (congenital defects); **disproportion between the upper and lower body** (an “athletic” shoulder girdle, thin legs) — **coarctation of the aorta**.
**Precapillary pulse (Quincke)** — a change in the color of the nail bed in time with the pulse when the tip of the nail is lightly pressed — **aortic valve insufficiency**.

blocks.label: Figure 8.3
blocks.caption: “Drumstick fingers” and “watch-glass” nails in a congenital heart defect (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Inspection of the cardiac area

items: **The apex beat** — the rhythmic impact of the apex of the heart on the chest wall; it is visible in thin children.

**The cardiac impulse** — diffuse pulsation in the cardiac area (at the left sternal edge and in the epigastrium); only in pathology (right ventricular hypertrophy, cardiomegaly) or on physical exertion, in thin children.
**“Cardiac hump”** — bulging of the chest in the cardiac area; a sign of **cardiomegaly** that developed at an early age (the chest is soft): congenital defects, early carditis.
Smoothing of the intercostal spaces — pericarditis with a large effusion.
Epigastric pulsation, pulsation in the 2nd intercostal space to the right and left of the sternum.

blocks.text: Inspection of the blood vessels

items: **Strong pulsation of the carotid arteries (“carotid dance”)** and nodding of the head in time with the pulse (**de Musset's sign**) — aortic valve insufficiency.

**Distension and pulsation of the neck veins** — right ventricular failure, tricuspid valve insufficiency, exudative pericarditis, compression of the superior vena cava (**“Stokes' collar”** — edema of the face and neck).
Subcutaneous venous collaterals (occlusion of the venae cavae), pulsation of the intercostal arteries (coarctation of the aorta).
Signs of impaired arterial circulation in the limbs: coldness, pallor, trophic changes.

blocks.text: The apex beat

**Technique:** the child lies on the back or sits; the doctor stands on the right. The base of the right palm is placed on the sternum and the fingers on the cardiac area toward the anterior axillary line along the intercostal spaces (in girls the breast is moved upward). Once the pulsation is found, its exact location, area, height and force are determined with the tips of the 2nd–3rd fingers. If it cannot be found in the supine position, the child is turned on the left side or leans forward.

blocks.caption: Determining the apex beat (Kildiyarova, Figure 9.3)

blocks.text: The “cat's purr” and pulsations
**The “cat's purr”** — a **thrill** felt with the palm, produced by turbulent blood flow at the site of an altered valve apparatus:

items: **systolic** — in the 2nd intercostal space to the right of the sternum (aortic stenosis), to the left (pulmonary stenosis), in the 3rd–4th intercostal space at the left sternal edge (**ventricular septal defect**), at the base of the heart (**patent ductus arteriosus** — systolic-diastolic);
**diastolic** — at the apex of the heart (**mitral stenosis**).

blocks.text: **Epigastric pulsation** is best detected at the end of a deep inspiration: right ventricular hypertrophy or dilatation (directed from above downward, increases on inspiration); pulsation of the abdominal aorta (from front to back, normal in thin children).
**Palpation of the great vessels:** in the 2nd intercostal space to the right (aorta) and left (pulmonary artery) of the sternum, in the jugular notch (normally only weak pulsation).

blocks.label: Figure 8.5
blocks.caption: Detecting pulsation: a — in the epigastric area; b — in the jugular notch (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Pulse in the peripheral arteries

The pulse is examined and compared **in both arms and legs**: the radial, brachial, carotid (at the inner edge of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at the level of the thyroid cartilage), temporal, femoral (at the middle of the inguinal ligament), popliteal, posterior tibial (behind the medial malleolus) and dorsalis pedis arteries. In the newborn **the femoral pulses** must be checked — weak or absent pulses are a sign of **coarctation of the aorta**. The characteristics of the pulse are given in detail in topic 9.

blocks.label: Figure 8.6
blocks.caption: Points for detecting the pulse in the peripheral arteries: radial, brachial, carotid, temporal, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Percussion determines:** the size of the heart (the borders of relative and absolute dullness), its configuration, position, and the width of the vascular bundle.
Rules:

items: percussion should be **quiet** or **very quiet**;
the pleximeter finger is placed **parallel** to the border sought;
the pleximeter step is small (not more than the width of a finger);
the stroke is directed **strictly from front to back**;
the border is marked along **the outer edge of the finger (facing the clear sound)**;

in children over 4 years the technique is as in adults; at an early age, direct percussion is done **with one finger only**, and in indirect percussion the pleximeter finger is placed **with the 1st phalanx only**; in infants the most reliable method of determining the left border is **orthopercussion** (strictly in the sagittal direction, with the pleximeter finger placed on its lateral edge).

blocks.text: Order of determining the borders of relative dullness:

items: **Right border.** First, percussing from top to bottom along the right midclavicular line, find **the upper border of liver dullness** (usually rib V–VI). Then move up one intercostal space (the 4th intercostal space), place the finger parallel to the sternum and percuss **from outside inward** — from the clear sound until dullness appears. The right border is formed by **the right atrium**.

**Upper border.** The finger is placed along the left parasternal line in the 1st intercostal space parallel to the ribs, and percussion is performed **from top to bottom**; the border is marked along the upper edge of the finger. The upper border is formed by **the pulmonary artery cone and the left atrial appendage**.

**Left border.** First find the apex beat; in the same intercostal space place the finger **1–1.5 cm outside** the beat (or from the anterior axillary line), perpendicular to the ribs (parallel to the midclavicular line), and percuss **from outside toward the heart**. The left border is formed by **the left ventricle**.

parts.text: With age the heart **“becomes smaller and descends”**: **the upper border rib II → 2nd intercostal space → rib III**; **the right border from the parasternal line → to the edge of the sternum**; **the left border from 2 cm outside the midclavicular line → to the midclavicular line**. The numbers: **“2 – 1 – 0”** cm outside (0–2, 2–7, 7+ years).

blocks.text: **Absolute dullness** — the part of the heart not covered by the lungs (mainly **the right ventricle**); it is determined by very quiet percussion and is rarely determined in children.

**Cardiac configuration** — by the borders of relative dullness; in addition, the border is determined in the 3rd intercostal space on the right and the 4th on the left. Normally there is an obtuse angle between the vascular bundle and the left ventricular contour — **the “cardiac waist”**.

**Width of the vascular bundle** — very quiet percussion in the 1st (2nd at school age) intercostal space from the right and left parasternal lines toward the sternum; normally equal to the width of the manubrium (does not extend beyond the sternum).

blocks.text: **Chest X-ray** (in frontal and lateral projections, and if necessary in oblique projections with esophageal contrast) gives information on the size, shape (configuration) and position of the heart, the state of the great vessels and **the pulmonary blood flow** (increased or reduced lung markings).
**The normal cardiac shadow** in the frontal projection:

items: **right contour** — 2 arcs: above, the superior vena cava (and the ascending aorta), below, the right atrium;
**left contour** — 4 arcs: the aortic arch, the pulmonary artery, the left atrial appendage, the left ventricle.

blocks.text: In the newborn the cardiac shadow is relatively large, spherical and horizontally positioned, with a wide vascular bundle (thymus); with age it becomes elongated and oblique.

blocks.text: **Cardiometry** — measuring the dimensions of the heart on an X-ray. The most widely used parameter is **the cardiothoracic index (CTI)**:

**CTI = (CE + ED) / AB**, where CE is the distance from the midline to the outermost point of the right cardiac contour, ED — from the midline to the outermost point of the left contour, AB — the inner transverse diameter of the chest at the level of the diaphragmatic dome.
**Normal:** **≤0.55** in young children, **≤0.5** in older children. An increased index means **cardiomegaly**.

blocks.label: Figure 8.12
blocks.caption: Determining the cardiothoracic index: CTI = (CE + ED)/AB (Kildiyarova, Figure 9.12)

blocks.text: Pathological configurations:

items: **mitral** — the “cardiac waist” is flattened (the arcs of the pulmonary artery and the left atrial appendage bulge): mitral stenosis and insufficiency;
**aortic** — the “cardiac waist” is deepened, the left ventricle enlarged, the apex displaced downward and to the left (“sitting duck”): aortic defects, arterial hypertension;
**spherical or triangular (“trapezoid”)** — exudative pericarditis;
**“wooden shoe” (“Dutch clog”)** — **tetralogy of Fallot** (raised apex, deep “cardiac waist”, reduced lung markings);
**“egg-shaped”** — transposition of the great arteries; **“snowman” (“figure 8”)** — total anomalous pulmonary venous drainage.
