blocks.text: **Electrocardiography (ECG)** — recording of the electrophysiological processes in the heart; it gives information on the rhythm, HR, conduction, hypertrophy of the heart chambers and the state of the myocardium. 12 standard leads: 3 standard (I, II, III), 3 augmented (aVR, aVL, aVF) and 6 chest (V~1~–V~6~) leads.

items: **P wave** — atrial excitation;
**PQ interval** — conduction of the impulse from the atria to the ventricles;
**QRS complex** — ventricular excitation (depolarization);
**ST segment and T wave** — ventricular repolarization;
**QT interval** — electrical systole of the ventricles.

blocks.text: HR = 60 / RR (in seconds). The age-related features of the ECG in children (right axis deviation, short waves and intervals, negative T waves) are given in detail in topic 9.
**Echocardiography** — ultrasound examination of the structure and function of the heart (2.5–7.5 MHz probe); **the main method in pediatric cardiology**. Its possibilities:

items: the size of the heart chambers, wall thickness, **contractility** (ejection fraction, normally ≥55–60%);
the structure and movement of the valves, **regurgitation** and **stenosis** (Doppler echocardiography);
**congenital defects** (septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot, etc.) — the direction and volume of the shunt;
pulmonary artery pressure;
the state of the pericardium and **fluid in the pericardial cavity**;
intracardiac formations (thrombus, tumor, vegetations — infective endocarditis, false chords).

parts.text: For early detection of congenital heart defects in newborns, **pulse oximetry screening** is carried out: SpO~2~ is measured on the right hand and a foot at 24–48 hours of life. If **SpO~2~ <95%** or the difference between the hand and the foot is **>3%**, the baby is referred for echocardiography.

blocks.text: Suspicion of a congenital heart defect in a newborn

Parents' complaints and “alarming” signs on examination: rapid tiring and sweating during feeding, poor weight gain, tachypnea at rest, cyanosis (especially increasing with crying), cold limbs, a strong cardiac impulse, a “cardiac hump”, liver enlargement, weak or absent femoral pulses, a BP difference between the arms and legs.

parts.text: In the newborn, **weak pulses in the femoral arteries** are a sign of **coarctation of the aorta**; when the ductus arteriosus closes (in the 1st–2nd weeks of life) the child's condition may deteriorate sharply (“duct-dependent” defects). Checking the femoral pulses is mandatory at every examination of a newborn.

blocks.text: Physical detection of cardiomegaly

Signs of cardiomegaly: “cardiac hump”, a diffuse and displaced apex beat, a cardiac impulse, widening of the borders of relative dullness on percussion. Confirmation — an increased **CTI** on X-ray and **echocardiography**.

skills.title: Skill 1. Palpation of the apex beat

items: Wash and warm the hands; the child lies on the back or sits, the doctor on the right.
Place the right palm on the sternum and the fingers along the left intercostal spaces toward the anterior axillary line.
Where the pulsation is felt, find the outermost and lowest point with the tips of the 2nd–3rd fingers.
Determine its location (relative to the intercostal space and the midclavicular line), area, height and force.
Check the cardiac area for a “cat's purr” with the palm and determine whether it coincides with systole or diastole (comparing with the carotid pulse).
Compare the result with the age norm and record it.

skills.title: Skill 2. Determining the borders of relative cardiac dullness

items: The child stands or lies, the doctor on the right.
Find the upper border of liver dullness along the right midclavicular line.
One intercostal space higher, place the finger parallel to the sternum and determine the right border from outside inward.
Determine the upper border along the left parasternal line from the 1st intercostal space downward.
Determine the left border in the intercostal space of the apex beat from outside inward.
Mark the borders along the edge of the finger facing the clear sound; measure the transverse diameter.
Compare the result with the age norm.

skills.title: Skill 3. Examining the pulse in the peripheral arteries

items: Check the synchrony and equality of the pulse in the radial arteries of both arms simultaneously.
Examine the pulse symmetrically in the carotid, brachial, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis arteries.
Compare the pulse in the arms and legs (weak femoral pulse — coarctation).
Record the result.

skills.title: Skill 4. Calculating the cardiothoracic index

items: On a frontal X-ray draw the midline (along the spinous processes).
Measure the distance from the midline to the outermost point of the right contour (CE) and to the outermost point of the left contour (ED).
Measure the inner transverse diameter of the chest at the level of the diaphragmatic dome (AB).
Calculate CTI = (CE + ED) / AB.
Assessment: ≤0.55 at an early age, ≤0.5 in older children — normal; if increased — cardiomegaly.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 3-month-old child. The mother complains that the baby tires quickly during feeding, stops feeding to rest, sweats a lot and is not gaining weight well. On examination: pale skin, RR 56/min, HR 165/min. There is a bulge over the cardiac area on the left half of the chest. The apex beat is in the 5th intercostal space, 3 cm outside the midclavicular line, diffuse. A systolic thrill is detected at the left sternal edge in the 3rd–4th intercostal space. On percussion the cardiac borders are enlarged in all directions. The liver projects 3 cm below the costal arch.
cases.ask: 1) What is the bulge on the chest called and what does it indicate? 2) Assess the apex beat and percussion findings. 3) Which defect is the systolic thrill typical of? 4) Which investigations are needed?
cases.answer: 1) “Cardiac hump” — cardiomegaly developed at an early age. 2) The apex beat is displaced downward and to the left and diffuse (the norm in a 3-month-old is the 4th intercostal space, 1–2 cm outside the midclavicular line); the cardiac borders are enlarged — cardiomegaly. 3) A systolic thrill in the 3rd–4th intercostal space at the left sternal edge — ventricular septal defect. There are also signs of heart failure: tachycardia, tachypnea, sweating, liver enlargement. 4) Echocardiography (size of the defect, shunt, pulmonary pressure), ECG, chest X-ray (CTI, lung markings).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: When examining an 8-year-old girl, the doctor determined the cardiac borders: right border — 0.5 cm outside the right sternal edge, upper border — rib III, left border — 0.5 cm inside the left midclavicular line. The apex beat is in the 5th intercostal space, 1 cm inside the midclavicular line, area 1.5 cm², of moderate force. HR 84/min, increasing on inspiration and slowing on expiration.
cases.ask: 1) Are the cardiac borders appropriate for the age? 2) Assess the apex beat. 3) How do you assess the HR variability?
cases.answer: 1) Yes, they correspond to the norm for 7–12 years (right — sternal edge, upper — rib III, left — along the midclavicular line or 0.5–1 cm inside it). 2) The location, area and force of the apex beat are normal. 3) The HR is normal for 8 years (80–85); the change related to breathing is physiological respiratory (sinus) arrhythmia, most pronounced at 4–12 years; it disappears when the breath is held.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 12-year-old boy complains of rapid fatigue, headache and leg pain when running. On examination: the shoulder girdle is well developed, the legs are thin. The neck vessels pulsate strongly. BP in the arms is 150/90 mm Hg, in the legs 100/70. The femoral pulses are weak and delayed. The apex beat is displaced to the left and increased. On X-ray “usuration” (notching) of the lower edges of the ribs is found.
cases.ask: 1) Presumptive diagnosis? 2) Which signs confirm it? 3) Explain the change in the apex beat. 4) What is the normal ratio of BP in the arms and legs?
cases.answer: 1) Coarctation of the aorta. 2) Disproportion between the upper and lower body, arterial hypertension in the arms, hypotension in the legs, weak femoral pulses, intermittent leg pain (ischemia), rib notching from the pressure of the intercostal collateral arteries. 3) Left ventricular hypertrophy (working against the narrowed aorta) — an increased apex beat displaced to the left. 4) Normally BP in the legs is 10–20 mm Hg higher than in the arms.

topics.title: Auscultation of the heart, pulse and arterial pressure. Functional and instrumental examinations of the cardiovascular system, age-related features of the ECG, and semiotics

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the rules of cardiac auscultation, the listening points and their order;
the formation of the heart sounds and their age-related features;
the classification of heart murmurs, the difference between functional and organic murmurs;
the characteristics of the pulse and the age norms for arterial pressure;
the possibilities of functional tests (Martinet, Shalkov, clinoorthostatic), ECG, Holter monitoring and echocardiography;
the age-related features of the ECG, the main arrhythmias and the signs of hypertrophy;
the semiotics of changes in heart sounds, murmurs, pulse and arterial pressure.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: auscultate the heart at all points and describe the sounds and murmurs;
distinguish a functional murmur from an organic one;
examine the pulse for all its characteristics;
measure arterial pressure correctly in the arms and legs and assess it against the age norm (formula, centiles);
perform and assess a functional test;
“read” a child's ECG by the main parameters.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The order of auscultation — **“Mitral – Aortic – Pulmonary – Tricuspid – Botkin”** = **“MAPTB”**: it starts with the valve most often affected by heart disease.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **A diastolic murmur is never functional.** A functional murmur is **“soft, short, systolic, variable, non-radiating”**. A functional systolic murmur is heard at various ages in 50–70% of healthy children.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: By location of the murmur: **apex** — mitral (systolic — insufficiency, diastolic — stenosis); **2nd space on the right** — aortic stenosis; **Botkin's point** — aortic insufficiency (diastolic); **2nd space on the left** — pulmonary stenosis, ASD, PDA (“machinery”); **3rd–4th space at the left sternal edge** — VSD.

blocks.text: Rules:

items: a quiet, warm room; the doctor stands on **the child's right side**;
auscultation is performed **in different positions**: lying on the back, on the left side, standing; if necessary after physical exertion (at school age);
the results are compared during normal breathing and while holding the breath (after expiration);
a small-diameter stethoscope is used in small children; when the child cries, listen between breaths;
auscultation is performed **in a strict order**, then the whole cardiac area, the axilla, the infraclavicular area, the epigastrium and the interscapular area are listened to;
first the rhythm and HR are assessed, then the sounds, then the murmurs.

blocks.text: Listening points and their order:

items: **Apex of the heart** — **mitral valve**.
**2nd intercostal space, right of the sternum** — **aortic valve**.
**2nd intercostal space, left of the sternum** — **pulmonary valve**.
**The lower end of the sternum, the base of the xiphoid process** (slightly to the right) — **tricuspid valve**.
**Botkin–Erb point** — the attachment of ribs III–IV to the left sternal edge — **aortic (and mitral) valve**.

parts.text: The order of auscultation — **“Mitral – Aortic – Pulmonary – Tricuspid – Botkin”** = **“MAPTB”**: it starts with the valve most often affected by heart disease.

blocks.text: Heart sounds

blocks.title: Table 9.1. Description of the heart sounds
head: Sound
Formation
Time and place of hearing
rows: At the start of ventricular systole: closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves (valvular component), contraction of the ventricular myocardium (muscular), vibration of the initial parts of the aorta and pulmonary artery (vascular), atrial contraction (atrial component)
After the long pause; simultaneous with the apex beat and the carotid pulse; best heard at the apex
At the start of diastole: closure of the semilunar valves of the aorta and pulmonary artery and vibration of the vessel walls
After the short pause; best heard at the base of the heart (in the 2nd intercostal space)
At the start of diastole: rapid filling of the ventricles and vibration of their walls
After S2; may be heard in thin children and adolescents lying down (physiological)
Atrial contraction at the end of diastole
Before S1; may be present in athletic adolescents

blocks.text: At the apex the sounds are heard as **“LUB-dup”**, at the base as **“lub-DUP”** (Lang). The pause between S1 and S2 (systole) is shorter than the pause between S2 and S1 (diastole).

blocks.label: Figure 9.3
blocks.caption: Formation of the heart sounds (diagram): components of S1, S2, S3 and S4 (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Age-related features of the heart sounds:

items: **Embryocardia** — a pendulum rhythm: S1 and S2 are identical and the pauses equal. In the newborn it is considered normal **in the first 2 weeks** of life (because of tachycardia); in an older child — **pathological** (acute heart failure, paroxysmal tachycardia, high fever).
In the neonatal period the sounds may be slightly muffled; later in children the sounds are **louder than in adults** (thin chest wall).
In **the first 2–3 days** of life S2 is louder than S1 at the apex and at Botkin's point, then they become equal; **from 2–3 months** S1 predominates at the apex.
In the 1st year S1 is heard better at the base of the heart, then they become equal; **from 2 years** S2 is stronger.

**From 2 to 12 years** S2 is stronger **over the pulmonary artery** than over the aorta — **a physiological accentuation of S2 over the pulmonary artery**; at 12 years they become equal, and later it is stronger over the aorta.
In children **physiological splitting of S1 and S2** (at the end of inspiration, changing with body position) and **S3** are frequently heard.

blocks.text: **Splitting and reduplication:** if there is an imperceptible pause between the two components of a sound — **splitting** (“TRA-ta”); if the pause is distinct — **reduplication**. Physiological splitting is variable and depends on body position and the phase of breathing.
Heart murmurs

**A murmur** is a longer sound, heard in addition to the heart sounds, resulting from turbulent blood flow. Turbulence depends on changes in **the diameter of the valve orifice or vessel**, **the blood flow velocity** and **the blood viscosity**.
Classification:

items: **intracardiac** and **extracardiac** murmurs (pericardial friction rub, pleuropericardial murmur);
**organic** (anatomical changes in the valves, septa and vessels — congenital and acquired defects, endocarditis) and **inorganic**;

according to P.S. Moshchich's classification: **organic**, **organic-functional** (impaired cardiac function in myocarditis and arrhythmias — relative valvular insufficiency), **functional** (in extracardiac diseases: anemia, fever, thyrotoxicosis, autonomic dysfunction) and **physiological (innocent)** — in a healthy child.

blocks.text: **Describing a murmur:** 1) phase of the cardiac cycle (systolic, diastolic; early, mid, late, pansystolic); 2) duration; 3) loudness (intensity, grade 1–6); 4) timbre (soft, blowing, harsh, scraping, musical); 5) the place where it is best heard (epicenter, punctum maximum); 6) radiation (axilla, neck, interscapular area); 7) relation to the heart sounds; 8) change with body position, breathing and exertion.

blocks.title: Table 9.2. Differences between functional and organic murmurs
head: Sign
Functional (physiological) murmur
Organic murmur
rows: Long, often the whole of systole (pansystolic)
Not related to the sounds, the sounds are unchanged
Often related to S1; the sounds are changed
In a limited area (often at the apex or over the pulmonary artery)
A distinct epicenter at a particular point
Radiates to the axilla, neck, interscapular area
Variable: increases lying down, decreases or disappears when standing and after exertion
Cardiac borders, ECG, echocardiography normal; no circulatory failure
Cardiomegaly, ECG and echocardiographic changes, signs of failure

parts.text: **A diastolic murmur is never functional.** A functional murmur is **“soft, short, systolic, variable, non-radiating”**. A functional systolic murmur is heard at various ages in 50–70% of healthy children.

blocks.text: Extracardiac murmurs:

items: **pericardial friction rub** — “creaking”, “scraping”, at the base of the heart or in the area of absolute dullness, **does not radiate anywhere**, variable, does not fully coincide with systole and diastole, **increases on leaning forward and on pressure with the stethoscope**, **persists** when the breath is held;
**pleuropericardial murmur** — at the left border of the heart, increases at the peak of inspiration, **disappears when the breath is held**.

blocks.text: Auscultation of the blood vessels

In a healthy child two sounds are heard over **the carotid and subclavian arteries**, and sometimes S1 over **the femoral artery**; no sounds are heard over other arteries. Over the neck veins (especially on the right, with the head turned) a **“humming top”** is heard — a normal venous hum (increased in anemia). Murmurs are heard over vessels when arteries are narrowed or dilated and in aortic and valvular defects; a murmur over the abdominal aorta and renal arteries — renal artery stenosis (a cause of arterial hypertension).

blocks.label: Figure 9.4
blocks.caption: Points for listening to the vessels (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: In children **over 2 years** the pulse is examined mainly at **the radial artery** (in younger children — at the temporal, carotid, brachial or femoral arteries). The most accurate information is obtained in the morning, after the child wakes up, at rest (**basal pulse**). First the pulse is examined **in both arms simultaneously** (synchrony and equality), then in one arm for 1 minute.

blocks.title: Table 9.3. Characteristics of the pulse
head: Feature
Description and changes
rows: Corresponds to the HR; faster than the age norm — tachycardia, slower — bradycardia; pulse deficit — pulse lower than the HR (atrial fibrillation, extrasystole)

Regular or irregular; in children respiratory arrhythmia is normal (faster on inspiration, slower on expiration, disappears when the breath is held) — maximal at 4–12 years, may increase in adolescents (“adolescent arrhythmia”)
The pressure needed to stop the pulse — related to BP and vascular tone: hard (tense) — arterial hypertension; soft — hypotension
Depends on the stroke volume and the amount of blood: full, satisfactory, empty (blood loss, collapse)
Depends on tension and filling: large (aortic insufficiency), small; thready pulse — shock, collapse
The speed of rise and fall of the pulse wave: rapid, bounding (aortic insufficiency, patent ductus arteriosus, thyrotoxicosis), slow, low (aortic stenosis)
The same in both arms; a difference — vascular defect or aortoarteritis

blocks.text: In a healthy child with fever, the pulse increases by **8–10 beats** for each **1 °C** rise in temperature. At an early age there are **3–3.5** heartbeats per breath, in adults **4**.

blocks.title: Table 9.4. Changes in the pulse and their diagnostic significance
head: Type of pulse
When it occurs
rows: Physiological — newborn and early age, physical and mental stress; pathological — fever, anemia, thyrotoxicosis, pain, myocarditis, heart failure, hypovolemia
Physiological — in sleep, in athletes; pathological — AV blocks, sick sinus, raised intracranial pressure, hypothyroidism, obstructive jaundice, dystrophy, some infections (typhoid fever)
Weak or absent in both legs
Weak or absent in one arm or leg
Severe heart failure, severe myocardial damage — a poor prognostic sign
Exudative pericarditis (tamponade), severe asthma attack, grade III croup

blocks.text: **Systolic BP** — the maximal pressure in the arteries during left ventricular systole (depends on the stroke volume and the elasticity of the aorta); **diastolic BP** — the minimal pressure in diastole (depends on the tone of the peripheral arterioles); **pulse pressure** — the difference between them (≈40 mm in the newborn, ≈50 mm at 14–15 years).
Technique of measurement (Korotkov method)

items: The child sits quietly for **5 minutes** (small children lying down); there should be no food or active play for 30 minutes before the measurement.

**The cuff size must be appropriate for age**: the width of the rubber bladder should cover **≈40%** of the arm circumference and its length **80–100%** (newborn — 3–5 cm, infant — 5–8 cm, preschool — 9–10 cm, school age — 12–13 cm, adolescents — adult cuff). A narrow cuff **overestimates** BP, a wide cuff **underestimates** it.
The arm on the table, palm up, muscles relaxed; the heart, the cuff and the zero point of the manometer **at the same level**.
The deflated cuff is placed on the upper arm **2 cm above** the antecubital fossa so that 1–2 fingers can pass under it.
The brachial artery is found by palpation in the antecubital fossa, and the stethoscope is placed over it.
Air is pumped into the cuff to **30–40 mm Hg** above the level at which the radial pulse disappears.

The pressure is released slowly (**2–3 mm** per second): **the first clear sound** — systolic BP (Korotkov phase I), **disappearance of the sounds** — diastolic BP (phase V). In small children the sounds may be heard down to zero — then the point of sharp muffling of the sounds (phase IV) is taken.

The measurement is repeated **2–3 times** at 2–3-minute intervals and the average is taken; the first time it is measured **in both arms** and **in the legs** (in the leg — with a wide cuff on the thigh, listening over the popliteal artery).

blocks.caption: Measuring arterial pressure (Kildiyarova, Figure 9.8)

blocks.text: Age norms

blocks.title: Table 9.5. Average arterial pressure by age
head: Age
Systolic BP, mm Hg
Diastolic BP

blocks.text: Approximate formulas:

items: **Up to 1 year:** systolic BP = **76 + 2n** (n — number of months); diastolic = **1/2–2/3** of systolic;
**Over 1 year** (average for boys): systolic = **90 + 2n**, diastolic = **60 + n** (n — number of years);
upper limit: systolic = 105 + 2n, diastolic = 75 + n; lower limit: systolic = 75 + 2n, diastolic = 45 + n;
**in girls** **5 mm** is subtracted from the values obtained.

blocks.text: **In the legs** BP is **10–20 mm Hg higher** than in the arms; higher BP in the arms is a sign of coarctation of the aorta.

**Centile assessment** (tables by sex, age and height): **<10th centile** — low; **10–90** — normal; **90–95** — high normal (risk of hypertension); **≥95th centile** (on 3 measurements) — **arterial hypertension**; **<5th centile** — **arterial hypotension**.

parts.text: Arterial hypertension is diagnosed only on the basis of BP measured **at least 3 times, on different days**. To exclude “white coat hypertension”, **24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM)** is performed.

blocks.text: Functional tests are performed to determine the adaptation of the cardiovascular system to exertion, the possibility of extending the regimen, and the physical education group.

**Martinet test (orthostatic).** The child lies for 5–10 minutes and the pulse and BP are measured; then they are measured again standing or after **20 squats** (within 30 seconds), and recovery is observed every minute. **Favorable reaction:** the pulse rises by **≤25% (–50%)**, systolic BP rises by **5–10 mm** (up to 20 mm), diastolic is unchanged or falls slightly, the parameters recover **in 3 minutes**, no complaints.

**Graded exercise test according to N.A. Shalkov.** HR, RR and BP are measured at rest; the child is given a load (loads 1–3 — sitting up and lying down in bed for patients on bed rest; 4–6 — 5, 10, 20 deep squats or climbing 10–30 steps; 7–8 — exercise and sports loads), and the reaction is assessed.

blocks.title: Table 9.6. Assessment of the reaction to exertion
head: Indicator
Favorable reaction
Unfavorable reaction

blocks.text: **Clinoorthostatic test (COT).** The child lies for 10–15 minutes and HR and BP are measured; then the child stands up and stands without leaning for 10 minutes — measured every minute; then lies down again and is observed for 4 minutes. **Normal reaction:** no complaints, HR rises by **20–40%**, systolic and diastolic BP rise slightly (+5…+20 mm), the decrease in pulse pressure does not exceed 50%. The test is used to determine **autonomic support** (sympathicotonic, hyperdiastolic, asympathicotonic, asthenosympathetic and other variants).
**Pharmacological tests:** atropine (sinus node function, vagal influence), potassium and Obsidan (propranolol) tests (to determine the origin of ST-T changes).
**Bicycle ergometry, treadmill test** — in older children, to assess physical working capacity and exercise-related arrhythmias and ischemia.
Electrocardiography

**ECG protocol:** 1) voltage (1 mV = 10 mm); 2) rhythm source (sinus — a positive P before each QRS); 3) HR (= 60/RR); 4) electrical axis; 5) amplitude and width of the waves; 6) intervals (PQ, QRS, QT); 7) **systolic index** (QT/RR × 100%); 8) ST segment and T wave; 9) age-related features; 10) conclusion.

Newborn
Until 2 years
7–15 years

Positive in II, may be negative or biphasic in III
May be notched in lead III; tall R and deep S in the right chest leads
May be M- or W-shaped in III; R low in V~1–2~, tall in V~5–6~
Low, biphasic or negative in V~1~–V~4~
Width of the waves and QRS

blocks.text: Main features of children's ECG:

items: the waves and intervals are **short** (the impulse is conducted quickly, HR is high);
**sinus respiratory arrhythmia** is frequent;
at an early age **right axis deviation** (relative predominance of the right ventricle), which changes to a normal axis with age;
**negative T waves** in the right chest leads (V~1~–V~3~, sometimes V~4~) may be normal;
a deep Q in standard lead III;
in some children **incomplete right bundle branch block** (a normal variant);
**early repolarization syndrome** — slight ST elevation in adolescents (often a normal variant).

blocks.label: Figure 9.7
blocks.caption: ECG of sinus (a) and respiratory (b) arrhythmia: RR shortens on inspiration (Kildiyarova, Figure 9.15)

blocks.text: Other electrophysiological methods:

items: **Holter monitoring** — continuous ECG recording for 24 hours (or longer): HR dynamics, arrhythmias and their associations, ischemic changes. Indications: fainting, life-threatening arrhythmias, any arrhythmia at an early age, sudden death at a young age in relatives.
**24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring (ABPM)** — with a portable monitor under natural conditions.
**Cardiointervalography (CIG)** — mathematical analysis of 100 cardiac cycles; assessment of autonomic tone (sympathetic or parasympathetic predominance) and reactivity.
**Phonocardiography (PCG)** — graphic recording of heart sounds and murmurs; objective determination of the phase, shape and frequency of a murmur.
**Echocardiography** (see topic 8) and **Doppler echocardiography** — the direction and velocity of blood flow, regurgitation, gradients.
**Rheovasography, Doppler ultrasound** — the state of the peripheral vessels.
**CT, MRI, angiocardiography, cardiac catheterization** — complex defects and preoperative examination.

blocks.text: **Laboratory methods:** markers of myocardial damage (CK-MB, troponins, LDH), natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP — heart failure), CRP, ASO (streptococcal infection), blood culture (infective endocarditis), lipid profile.
Changes in the heart sounds

Complete AV block (when the atria and ventricles contract simultaneously)

blocks.text: Organic murmurs

blocks.title: Table 9.9. Main organic murmurs
head: Murmur
In which pathology, features
rows: Aortic stenosis — 2nd intercostal space right of the sternum (and at Botkin's point), harsh, radiates to the carotid arteries, systolic thrill; pulmonary stenosis — 2nd intercostal space on the left, radiates to the left clavicle and the interscapular area; atrial septal defect — 2nd–3rd intercostal space on the left, low-medium intensity (relative pulmonary stenosis), S2 splitting; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy

Mitral insufficiency — at the apex, blowing, merged with S1, radiates to the left axilla, increases lying on the left side, S1 weakened; ventricular septal defect — 3rd–4th intercostal space at the left sternal edge, harsh, loud, widely radiating (also to the back), systolic thrill; tricuspid insufficiency — at the base of the xiphoid process, increases on inspiration

Aortic valve insufficiency — a “pouring” blowing murmur beginning with S2, at the Botkin–Erb point and along the left sternal edge, best heard with the child leaning forward; pulmonary valve insufficiency (in pulmonary hypertension — the Graham Steell murmur)

Mitral stenosis — at the apex, low-frequency “rumbling”, with presystolic accentuation, best heard on the left side and on expiration, does not radiate; relative mitral stenosis (Austin Flint murmur — in aortic insufficiency)
Patent ductus arteriosus — 2nd intercostal space on the left and below the clavicle; before 1 year only the systolic component may be heard

parts.text: By location of the murmur: **apex** — mitral (systolic — insufficiency, diastolic — stenosis); **2nd space on the right** — aortic stenosis; **Botkin's point** — aortic insufficiency (diastolic); **2nd space on the left** — pulmonary stenosis, ASD, PDA (“machinery”); **3rd–4th space at the left sternal edge** — VSD.

blocks.label: Figure 9.8
blocks.caption: Position of murmurs in the cardiac cycle: a — presystolic; b — protosystolic; c — midsystolic; d — late systolic; e — protodiastolic; f — mid-diastolic (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Causes of functional murmurs

items: **physiological (innocent)** — uneven growth of the parts of the heart and the valve rings, false chords (minor cardiac anomalies), a “vibratory” murmur over the pulmonary artery;
**autonomic dysfunction** — changes in the tone of the papillary muscles (in adolescents);
**dystrophic changes in the myocardium**, relative valvular insufficiency (organic-functional);
**increased blood flow velocity** — fever, thyrotoxicosis, physical and mental stress;
**reduced blood viscosity** — **anemia**.

blocks.text: ECG semiotics
Arrhythmias:

items: **Sinus tachycardia** — HR above the age norm, the rhythm source is the sinus node; causes: exertion, fever, anemia, hypoxia, thyrotoxicosis, myocarditis, heart failure, “drop” heart.
**Sinus bradycardia** — HR below the age norm; vagotonia, athletes, hypothyroidism, raised intracranial pressure, sick sinus syndrome.
**Sinus (respiratory) arrhythmia** — the RR intervals change with the phase of breathing; it disappears when the breath is held — normal.

**Extrasystole** — premature contractions: **atrial** (deformed P, narrow QRS, incomplete compensatory pause), **AV nodal**, **ventricular** (wide, deformed QRS without P, discordant ST and T, **complete compensatory pause**). In children it is often functional (autonomic), but also occurs in myocarditis and cardiomyopathy.

**Paroxysmal tachycardia** — a sharp increase in HR that begins and ends suddenly (160–200 in older children, up to 200–300 at an early age); **supraventricular** (narrow QRS) and **ventricular** (wide QRS — dangerous) forms; the child is restless and pale, and heart failure may develop quickly.
**Atrial flutter and fibrillation** — rare in children (heart defects, after surgery).
**WPW syndrome** (Wolff–Parkinson–White) — an accessory pathway: short PQ (<0.1 s), **delta wave** at the start of QRS, widened QRS; predisposition to paroxysmal tachycardia.

**Blocks:** sinoatrial; **AV blocks** — 1st degree (prolonged PQ), 2nd degree (some QRS complexes are dropped — Mobitz I/II), 3rd degree (complete — the atria and ventricles contract independently, marked bradycardia, Morgagni–Adams–Stokes attacks; congenital — associated with maternal SLE); **bundle branch blocks**.
**Long QT syndrome** — congenital or drug-induced; risk of fainting and sudden death.

blocks.text: Signs of hypertrophy:

items: **left ventricle** — left axis deviation (relative to the age norm), tall R in V~5–6~, deep S in V~1–2~, ST depression and negative T in the left chest leads;
**right ventricle** — marked right axis deviation, tall R (qR) in V~1–2~, deep S in V~5–6~;
**left atrium** — wide, double-humped P (“**P mitrale**”) in I, II, aVL;
**right atrium** — tall, pointed P (“**P pulmonale**”) in II, III, aVF.

blocks.text: **Signs of myocardial damage:** reduced voltage of the waves, QRS deformation, arrhythmias and blocks, ST depression of more than 1 mm below the isoline, flattening or inversion of the T wave.
Changes in arterial pressure

items: **Arterial hypertension** — **primary (essential)** — most often in adolescents, with obesity and hereditary predisposition; **secondary (symptomatic)** — kidney diseases (glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, polycystic disease, renal artery stenosis — the most common cause in children), **coarctation of the aorta**, endocrine diseases (Itsenko–Cushing, pheochromocytoma, thyrotoxicosis, hyperaldosteronism), CNS damage (tumor, injury, encephalitis), drugs (glucocorticoids).

**Arterial hypotension** — primary (constitutional, autonomic dysfunction — vagotonia) and secondary: adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, pituitary insufficiency, aortic stenosis, shock, collapse, blood loss, dehydration, anaphylaxis.

blocks.text: In more detail — in topic 10 (dystonia syndrome).
A child with a murmur — diagnostic approach

items: **Determine the phase of the murmur:** diastolic or continuous — **organic**; systolic — continue.
**Assess its features:** soft, short, non-radiating, position-dependent — most likely functional; harsh, long, radiating, with a thrill — organic.
**Additional signs:** changes in the heart sounds, cardiomegaly, cyanosis, signs of failure, changes in the peripheral pulses, an arm–leg BP difference — organic.
**Exclude extracardiac causes**: anemia (CBC), fever, thyrotoxicosis.
**Investigations:** ECG, **echocardiography** (the main one), X-ray if necessary.

parts.text: In an infant, **any murmur**, and also a murmur accompanied by **dyspnea, cyanosis, poor weight gain or sweating**, requires a cardiology consultation and echocardiography. In large defects (e.g., a large VSD) there may be **no** murmur in the first weeks of life, because pulmonary vascular resistance is still high.

blocks.text: A child who has fainted

Types of fainting (syncope): **vasovagal** (the most common — prolonged standing, pain, fear, a stuffy room; preceded by nausea, sweating, pallor), **orthostatic** (on standing up abruptly), **sinocarotid**, **post-tussive**, **cardiogenic** (aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, tetralogy of Fallot, arrhythmias — complete AV block, long QT, paroxysmal tachycardia). **Dangerous signs of cardiogenic syncope:** fainting during physical exertion, preceding palpitations, fainting while lying down, sudden death at a young age in the family — ECG, Holter and echocardiography are needed.

skills.title: Skill 1. Auscultation of the heart

items: A warm, quiet room; warm the stethoscope; the child lies on the back, the doctor on the right.
Assess the rhythm and HR (if necessary, palpate the pulse simultaneously to detect a pulse deficit).
Listen in order: apex → 2nd space right → 2nd space left → base of the xiphoid process → Botkin–Erb point.
At each point identify S1 and S2 (S1 coincides with the carotid pulse) and assess their loudness and ratio, splitting and extra sounds.
If there is a murmur — describe it by all criteria.
Repeat auscultation lying on the left side, standing, and after exertion.
Listen over the great vessels (carotid and subclavian arteries, neck veins).
Write the conclusion.

skills.title: Skill 2. Examining the pulse

items: Palpate both radial arteries simultaneously with the 2nd–4th fingers and assess synchrony and equality.
Count the rate in one arm for 1 minute.
Assess the rhythm; in arrhythmia repeat while the breath is held.
Determine the tension, filling, size and shape.
Compare the result with the age norm and record it.

skills.title: Skill 3. Measuring arterial pressure

items: Choose an age-appropriate cuff; the child has been sitting quietly for 5 minutes.
Place the cuff 2 cm above the antecubital fossa; the arm at heart level.
Find the brachial artery and place the stethoscope.
Inflate to 30–40 mm above the point at which the radial pulse disappears; deflate at 2–3 mm per second.
Record the systolic and diastolic BP; repeat 2–3 times and take the average.
Measure in the other arm and in the legs.
Assess by the formula and centile tables.

skills.title: Skill 4. Performing the Martinet (or Shalkov) functional test

items: Measure the pulse (over 10 seconds) and BP at rest.
Ask the child to do 20 deep squats in 30 seconds (or the age-appropriate Shalkov load).
Measure the pulse and BP immediately after the exercise, then repeat every minute for 3–5 minutes.
Calculate the percentage increase in pulse, the change in BP and the recovery time.
Assess the reaction as favorable or unfavorable and write the conclusion.

skills.title: Skill 5. Analyzing an ECG

items: Check the voltage and paper speed.
Determine the rhythm source (is there a P before each QRS).
Calculate the HR from the RR interval.
Determine the electrical axis (from the QRS in standard leads I and III).
Measure the duration of P, PQ, QRS and QT; assess ST and T.
Compare the results with the age norm and write the conclusion (e.g., “Sinus rhythm, HR 92/min, respiratory arrhythmia, normal electrical axis — age norm”).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 7-year-old child at a preventive check-up. No complaints, physical development appropriate for age. The cardiac borders are normal. On auscultation a short, soft systolic murmur of musical timbre is heard at the apex and at Botkin's point, not radiating anywhere; it is heard well lying down and becomes much weaker on standing and after 10 squats. The heart sounds are clear. ECG — age norm. CBC — Hb 128 g/l.
cases.ask: 1) How do you assess the murmur? 2) Which signs confirm this conclusion? 3) With which investigation can it be definitively confirmed?
cases.answer: 1) A functional (innocent, physiological) systolic murmur. 2) Only systolic, short, soft, of musical timbre, non-radiating, changing with body position and exertion (decreasing on standing and after exertion), the heart sounds and cardiac borders are unchanged, the ECG is normal, no complaints, no anemia. 3) Echocardiography — confirms the absence of organic changes (minor anomalies, e.g., a false chord, may be found).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: An 11-year-old girl had tonsillitis 2 weeks ago. She now complains of weakness, dyspnea and unpleasant sensations in the heart area. On examination: pale skin, HR 118/min (temperature 37.2 °C), soft pulse. The apex beat is weakened, diffuse and displaced to the left. The cardiac border is enlarged 1.5 cm to the left. The heart sounds are muffled, S1 weakened at the apex, “gallop” rhythm, a soft systolic murmur at the apex. ECG: PQ 0.22 s, ST depression, negative T in V~5–6~.
cases.ask: 1) Which syndrome? 2) How do you assess the tachycardia? 3) What is the origin of the murmur? 4) Explain the ECG changes.
cases.answer: 1) The syndrome of myocardial damage (myocarditis, probably rheumatic — after tonsillitis). 2) The tachycardia does not correspond to the temperature (at 37.2 °C the pulse should be only slightly raised) — typical of myocarditis. 3) An organic-functional (muscular) murmur — relative mitral insufficiency due to left ventricular dilatation and reduced tone of the papillary muscles. 4) 1st-degree AV block (PQ longer than normal for 11 years), ST depression and negative T — disturbed repolarization in the myocardium (inflammatory and dystrophic changes).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a 14-year-old adolescent, BP of 142/88 mm Hg was found at a school medical check-up. On repeated measurement 3 times (on different days) the result was 138–145/85–90 mm. Height 168 cm, weight 82 kg. Complains of morning headaches. His father has hypertension. The pulses in the arms and legs are equal, BP in the legs is 155/90. Urinalysis is normal.
cases.ask: 1) How do you assess the BP? 2) Which investigations are needed? 3) Is the hypertension likely to be primary or secondary? Justify.
cases.answer: 1) The average BP for 14 years is ≈118/74 mm; the values obtained are above the 95th centile and confirmed 3 times — arterial hypertension. 2) ABPM (to exclude “white coat”), ECG and echocardiography (left ventricular hypertrophy), fundoscopy, ultrasound (Doppler) of the kidneys and renal arteries, blood creatinine, electrolytes, glucose, lipids, thyroid hormones. 3) Primary (essential) is likely: adolescence, obesity (BMI ≈29), hereditary predisposition, BP in the legs higher than in the arms (no coarctation), urine unchanged. But secondary causes (renal, endocrine) must be excluded by investigation.

topics.title: Syndromes of cardiovascular involvement: carditis (endocardium, myocardium, pericardium), dystonia, congenital heart defects, heart and vascular failure

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the carditis syndrome and its components — the syndromes of endocardial, myocardial and pericardial involvement;
the main physical signs of acquired heart defects;
arterial hypertension and hypotension, the autonomic dystonia syndrome;
the classification of congenital heart defects, the main and additional diagnostic criteria, the clinical picture of the most common defects;
the causes, types and stages of heart failure;
the signs of acute vascular insufficiency (fainting, collapse, shock).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: identify the leading cardiological syndrome on the basis of physical and instrumental findings;
determine the hemodynamic group of a congenital heart defect;
determine the type and stage of heart failure;
show first-aid measures in a hypercyanotic spell, fainting and collapse.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: The most important early signs of myocarditis are **tachycardia out of proportion to the temperature**, **muffled heart sounds (especially S1)** and **a gallop rhythm**. An ECG must be taken in weakness, dyspnea and tachycardia that appear 1–3 weeks after tonsillitis or a viral infection.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In an infant the **earliest signs** of heart failure are **tachypnea**, **tachycardia** and **liver enlargement**; peripheral edema appears late and rarely at this age. Early signs: tiring during feeding, sweating (especially of the head), poor weight gain.

blocks.text: **Carditis** — inflammatory involvement of the heart; the three layers of the heart — **endocardium, myocardium and pericardium** — may be affected separately or together. Simultaneous involvement of all layers is **pancarditis**.

**Causes:** rheumatic (acute rheumatic fever — after group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infection), nonspecific (viral — Coxsackie B, ECHO, adenoviruses, influenza; bacterial — diphtheria), infective endocarditis, autoimmune diseases (SLE, juvenile arthritis), toxic and allergic damage.
Syndrome of endocardial involvement

It is seen in infective or rheumatic **endocarditis** and **acquired heart defects**. As a result of inflammation the valves become deformed: **insufficiency** (incomplete closure of the cusps, backward flow of blood — regurgitation) or **stenosis** (narrowing of the orifice) develops. The clinical picture mainly reflects involvement of **the mitral** and **aortic** valves.

blocks.text: **Distinguishing endocarditis from an established acquired defect** is important: endocarditis is an ongoing process, the murmur is less long-lasting and regresses with treatment, the heart chambers are unchanged, it lasts up to 6–8 weeks; **an acquired defect** forms **8–12 months** after the onset of endocarditis — the murmur is long-lasting and widely radiating, and dilatation and hypertrophy of the heart chambers develop.

Signs of **infective endocarditis**: prolonged fever, chills, sweating, weakness, weight loss, pallor (“café-au-lait” color), a new or changed murmur, splenomegaly, petechiae, **Osler nodes** (painful nodules on the fingertips), **Janeway lesions**, **“drumstick fingers”**, emboli; the pathogen in blood culture, **vegetations** on the valves on echocardiography. Risk group — congenital and acquired defects, prosthetic valves, central venous catheters.
Syndrome of myocardial involvement
In **myocarditis** of various etiologies (rheumatic, viral — especially enteroviral, diphtheria), dystrophic and toxic damage, and cardiomyopathies.
**Complaints:** pain in the heart area (at an early age — restlessness), palpitations, “skipped beats”, dyspnea, weakness, rapid fatigue; in infants — refusal to feed, sweating, vomiting.
Physical signs:

items: **pulse changes** — **tachycardia out of proportion to the temperature**, less often bradycardia, arrhythmia;
the apex beat **weakened, diffuse**, displaced outward;
the cardiac borders **enlarged** (cardiomegaly);
**muffled heart sounds**, especially S1 at the apex; splitting, **“gallop” rhythm**;
**an organic-functional (muscular) systolic murmur** at the apex — relative mitral insufficiency;
reduced BP;
signs of heart failure (dyspnea, liver enlargement, edema).

blocks.text: **Instrumental signs:** ECG — reduced voltage of the waves, QRS deformation, rhythm and conduction disorders (sinus tachycardia, extrasystole, AV blocks, bundle branch block), **ST depression of more than 1 mm**, deformation and inversion of the T wave; X-ray — **CTI >0.5** (>0.55 at an early age); echocardiography — left ventricular dilatation, **reduced ejection fraction**; blood — raised **CK-MB and troponins**.

parts.text: The most important early signs of myocarditis are **tachycardia out of proportion to the temperature**, **muffled heart sounds (especially S1)** and **a gallop rhythm**. An ECG must be taken in weakness, dyspnea and tachycardia that appear 1–3 weeks after tonsillitis or a viral infection.

blocks.text: Syndrome of pericardial involvement
In pericarditis of various etiologies (viral, bacterial, tuberculous, rheumatic, uremic, SLE), accumulation of fluid (blood, transudate) in the pericardial cavity, and systemic diseases.
Dry (fibrinous) pericarditis:

items: **severe stabbing** or sharp pain behind the sternum (often in its middle part), **increased by movement, coughing and deep breathing**, decreased on leaning forward; it radiates to the left shoulder and neck;

**pericardial friction rub** — “creaking”, “scraping”, at the base of the heart or in the area of absolute dullness, **does not radiate anywhere**, variable, increases on leaning forward and on pressure with the stethoscope, **persists when the breath is held**;
ECG — **ST elevation** in all leads (concordant), then T inversion.

blocks.text: Exudative pericarditis:

items: dyspnea, a feeling of heaviness; **forced position** — sitting leaning forward or the knee-elbow position;
smoothing of the intercostal spaces, distension of the neck veins;
the apex beat **weakened or not detected**; the apex beat lies **inside** the percussion border;
cardiac dullness **enlarged in all directions**, **the difference between relative and absolute dullness disappears**;
**markedly muffled heart sounds**; the friction rub disappears as the fluid increases;
the pulse rapid, small, **paradoxical**; BP reduced, venous pressure raised;

X-ray — the cardiac shadow **spherical or triangular**, its arcs smoothed; ECG — **a sharp decrease in the voltage of all waves**; echocardiography — **fluid** in the pericardial cavity (the main diagnostic method).

blocks.text: **Cardiac tamponade** — fluid accumulates rapidly and compresses the heart: marked dyspnea, cyanosis, tachycardia, paradoxical pulse, a fall in BP, distended neck veins, muffled heart sounds (**Beck's triad**: hypotension + raised venous pressure + muffled heart sounds) — **urgent pericardiocentesis** is required.

**Constrictive (adhesive) pericarditis** — the pericardial layers thicken and fuse: the heart cannot expand in diastole — ascites, liver enlargement, edema, distended neck veins; **systolic retraction at the site of the apex beat**.

blocks.label: Figure 10.1
blocks.caption: Exudative pericarditis: the cardiac shadow is spherical, its arcs smoothed (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Acute rheumatic fever and carditis

Acute rheumatic fever is a systemic autoimmune disease that develops **2–3 weeks** after a group A β-hemolytic streptococcal infection (tonsillitis, pharyngitis, scarlet fever) and mainly affects **the heart** and joints; most often **at 7–15 years**.

blocks.title: Table 10.2. Diagnostic criteria of acute rheumatic fever (Kisel–Jones, revised)
head: Major criteria
Minor criteria
rows: Carditis (most often with mitral valve involvement)

blocks.text: The diagnosis requires **2 major** or **1 major + 2 minor** criteria and **evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection** (raised ASO titer, streptococcus in a throat swab).
**Dystonia syndrome** — a disturbance of the regulation of vascular tone; it may occur with a rise or a fall in arterial pressure.
Arterial hypertension syndrome
**Definition:** systolic and/or diastolic BP **above the 95th centile** for sex, age and height (measured at least 3 times, on different days).

**Clinical picture:** morning **headache** (often a feeling of pressure in the occiput), dizziness, tinnitus, rapid fatigue, “flies” before the eyes; it often has no symptoms and is found by chance. Physical — the apex beat increased, **S2 accentuated over the aorta**; ECG — first increased left ventricular potentials, then **left ventricular hypertrophy**; fundus — narrowing of the arteries, dilatation of the veins.
Types:

items: **primary (essential)** — in adolescents, with obesity, low activity, high salt intake, stress and hereditary predisposition;

**secondary (symptomatic)** — **renal** (glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, polycystic disease, hydronephrosis, renal artery stenosis — the most common cause in children), **cardiovascular** (coarctation of the aorta, aortic valve insufficiency), **endocrine** (pheochromocytoma, Itsenko–Cushing syndrome, adrenogenital syndrome, hyperaldosteronism, thyrotoxicosis), **neurogenic** (brain tumors, injury, encephalitis), drugs (glucocorticoids, sympathomimetics).

blocks.text: **Hypertensive crisis** — a sudden sharp rise in BP: the general condition suddenly worsens, severe headache, visual disturbance (flies, a veil), nausea, vomiting, trembling, pallor or flushing of the face, a feeling of fear; seizures may occur.

parts.text: In a young child (especially under 10 years) severe arterial hypertension is almost always **secondary** — first of all, kidney diseases and coarctation of the aorta must be excluded (urinalysis, renal ultrasound and Doppler, arm–leg BP difference).

blocks.text: Arterial hypotension syndrome

**Definition:** BP **below the 5th–10th centile**. **Signs:** weakness, rapid fatigue, sensitivity to cold, dizziness and headache (especially in the morning, on exertion, in a stuffy room), a tendency to faint, pallor, cold and moist palms and soles, tachycardia; on auscultation sometimes a “gallop” rhythm; on ECG ST depression, flattened T.

**Causes:** constitutional (predominance of parasympathetic tone — vagotonia), cardiac (aortic hypoplasia, aortic stenosis), endocrine (hypoglycemia, **adrenal insufficiency** — Addison disease, hypothyroidism, pituitary insufficiency), blood loss, dehydration, intoxication, anaphylaxis, drugs.
Autonomic dystonia syndrome (autonomic dysfunction)

A disturbance of the balance between the sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions of the autonomic nervous system; most often in adolescence (prepubertal and pubertal periods), more often in girls. Cardiovascular disturbances (palpitations, cardialgia, labile BP, fainting) are often leading.

blocks.title: Table 10.3. Signs of the two types of autonomic tone
head: Sign
Sympathicotonia
Vagotonia (parasympathicotonia)
rows: Marbled, moist, acrocyanosis; red, persistent dermographism; sweating
Nausea, tendency to diarrhea, much saliva
Tendency to obesity, dislikes stuffy rooms, tendency to faint, allergic reactions

blocks.text: The diagnosis is made by exclusion (organic heart, endocrine and neurological diseases are excluded); **the clinoorthostatic test** and **cardiointervalography** help to assess autonomic tone, reactivity and support.
Congenital heart defects (CHD) are anatomical defects of the heart and great vessels formed in utero; they occur in **6–8** of every 1000 live births; more than 90 variants are known.
Diagnostic criteria

blocks.title: Table 10.4. Main and additional diagnostic criteria of congenital heart defects (Kildiyarova)
head: Criteria
Manifestation
rows: Dyspnea, cyanosis or pallor, weight deficit, frequent bronchopulmonary diseases
Change in skin color, hypercyanotic spells, chest deformity (“cardiac hump”), changes in the characteristics of the pulse, cardiomegaly or displacement of the cardiac borders, organic murmurs
Strain or hypertrophy of the chambers on ECG; a shunt on echocardiography; cardiomegaly, an anomaly of cardiac position, altered pulmonary blood flow, pulmonary hypertension on X-ray

Delayed growth and statomotor development (hypoxia), late teething, sweating on exertion; the shade of cyanosis (crimson — pulmonary hypertension, Ebstein anomaly; bluish — single ventricle, tetralogy of Fallot; violet — Eisenmenger syndrome; dark blue — transposition of the great vessels); the location of cyanosis (only in the legs — preductal coarctation; only in the arms — transposition and aortic hypoplasia); sites of thrill, extracardiac radiation of the murmur

blocks.text: Classification
The classification of CHD is based on **the hemodynamic disturbance** and **the presence or absence of cyanosis**.

blocks.title: Table 10.5. Hemodynamic classification of congenital heart defects
head: Hemodynamics
Acyanotic (“white”)
Cyanotic (“blue”)
rows: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), ventricular septal defect (VSD), atrial septal defect (ASD), atrioventricular canal
Transposition of the great arteries, truncus arteriosus, Eisenmenger complex
Tetralogy of Fallot, tricuspid atresia, transposition with pulmonary stenosis, Ebstein anomaly

Dextrocardia, aortic arch anomalies, a small VSD in the muscular part (Tolochinov–Roger disease)

blocks.text: The five defects most common in clinical practice: **VSD, ASD, PDA, coarctation of the aorta, tetralogy of Fallot**.

blocks.label: Figure 10.2
blocks.caption: Pathological changes in congenital heart defects (diagram) (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Defects with a left-to-right shunt (VSD, ASD, PDA) — common signs

items: frequent and prolonged **bronchopulmonary diseases** at an early age (pulmonary plethora);
**hypotrophy**, lagging physical development;
dyspnea, tiring and sweating during feeding;
crimson acrocyanosis (in pulmonary hypertension);
**cardiomegaly** (“cardiac hump”, a diffuse cardiac impulse, borders enlarged in all directions), a **systolic thrill** to the left of the sternum;
**accentuation and splitting of S2 over the pulmonary artery**;
on X-ray **increased lung markings** (arterial hypervolemia), bulging of the pulmonary artery arc, an enlarged cardiac shadow.

blocks.text: Tetralogy of Fallot
**Tetralogy of Fallot** — the most common **“blue”** defect; it consists of four components:

items: **pulmonary stenosis** (narrowing of the right ventricular outflow tract);
**a large VSD**;
**right ventricular hypertrophy**;
**dextroposition of the aorta** (the aorta “overrides” the ventricular septum).

blocks.text: Hemodynamics: reduced pulmonary blood flow, mixed (venous) blood enters the systemic circulation — **central cyanosis**.
Diagnostic criteria:

items: **marked cyanosis** (usually increasing from 3–6 months), **hypercyanotic spells**;
forced position — **squatting** (or lying with the legs drawn up to the abdomen) — systemic resistance rises and pulmonary blood flow increases;
**“drumstick fingers”** and **“watch-glass” nails**;
**weakening of S2** over the pulmonary artery;
**a harsh systolic murmur** over the pulmonary artery (2nd–3rd intercostal space on the left) (stenosis);
**polycythemia** in the blood (Hb up to 250 g/l, erythrocytes up to 8×10^12^/l), raised hematocrit;
ECG — **right ventricular hypertrophy**, right axis deviation;
X-ray — a heart shaped like **a “wooden shoe” (“Dutch clog”)** (raised apex, deep “cardiac waist”), **reduced lung markings**.

blocks.label: Figure 10.3
blocks.caption: X-ray in tetralogy of Fallot: a “wooden shoe”-shaped heart, reduced lung markings (Kildiyarova, Figure 9.25)

blocks.text: **The hypercyanotic spell** is the most dangerous complication of tetralogy of Fallot; most often **at 2–5 years** (from 6 months), provoked by exertion, crying, feeding, defecation, minor surgical procedures, excitement. Mechanism — **spasm** of the right ventricular outflow tract → almost all the venous blood enters the aorta → CNS hypoxia. Signs: restlessness, **marked cyanosis** and dyspnea (deep rapid breathing), tachycardia, **weakening or disappearance** of the murmur (pulmonary blood flow sharply reduced), a fall in BP; in a severe spell — fainting, seizures, coma.

parts.text: **First aid in a hypercyanotic spell:** calm the child, put the child in **the knee-chest position** (pressing the knees to the chest — peripheral resistance increases), **humidified oxygen**, on the doctor's order **morphine** (or promedol) IM or IV, **sodium bicarbonate** (correction of acidosis), **β-blockers** (propranolol); infusion. Cardiac glycosides **must not be given** (they increase the spasm).

blocks.text: Coarctation of the aorta

**Coarctation of the aorta** — narrowing in the aortic isthmus (at the transition from the arch to the descending part). There are **two regimes** in the hemodynamics: **arterial hypertension** in the upper part of the body and **hypotension** in the lower part.

**Diagnostic criteria:** in the newborn poor weight gain, early heart failure (worsening sharply when the ductus arteriosus closes); at an older age — headache, nosebleeds, pain and coldness in the legs; **an “athletic” shoulder girdle, thin legs**; **a BP gradient between the arms and legs** (high in the arms, low in the legs); **weak or absent femoral pulses**; pulsation of the intercostal arteries; a systolic murmur between the shoulder blades and in the 2nd intercostal space on the left; ECG — **left ventricular hypertrophy**; X-ray — a dilated ascending aorta, an enlarged left ventricle, **rib notching** from 8–10 years; echocardiography — the narrowing and turbulent flow.
Transposition of the great arteries

The aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle — the systemic and pulmonary circulations work **in parallel**; life is possible only thanks to mixing of blood through a patent foramen ovale, PDA or VSD. **Marked generalized cyanosis from birth** (not decreasing with oxygen), dyspnea, rapidly developing heart failure; on X-ray an **“egg on its side”**-shaped heart with a narrow vascular bundle. Urgent surgical treatment (or balloon atrial septostomy) is required.

**Heart failure** — the inability of the heart to supply the organs and tissues with the required amount of blood at a normal or increased venous return; the inability of the heart to convert the venous inflow into an adequate cardiac output.

blocks.title: Table 10.7. Main diseases with heart failure by age (Kildiyarova)
head: Age
Diseases
rows: CHD (hypoplastic left heart syndrome, coarctation of the aorta, complex defects), persistent fetal circulation, respiratory distress syndrome
CHD (transposition of the great arteries, coarctation of the aorta, defects with a left-to-right shunt), fibroelastosis, nonspecific myocarditis
CHD (VSD, PDA, coarctation of the aorta), nonspecific myocarditis, rhythm and conduction disorders
Myocarditis (nonspecific, rheumatic), congenital and acquired defects, cardiomyopathies, infective endocarditis, arrhythmias, diseases of other organs (lung, liver, kidney, endocrine)

blocks.text: **Types:** by rate of development — **acute** and **chronic**; by the chamber mainly affected — **left ventricular** and **right ventricular** failure.
Left ventricular failure
The left atrium and ventricle are affected — **congestion in the pulmonary circulation**: the respiratory surface of the lungs and oxygen diffusion decrease, and hypoxia and acidosis increase.

items: nonspecific signs: restlessness, irritability, disturbed sleep, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, sometimes abdominal pain;

**dyspnea** — the earliest, and in infants **the main** sign; it decreases with oxygen and with the head raised; flaring of the nasal alae, participation of the accessory muscles; **cough** (a dry night cough is an early sign), orthopnea in a severe condition;
**tachycardia** — progressive, **out of proportion to the temperature, persisting in sleep**, resistant to treatment other than cardiac glycosides;
peripheral or central cyanosis;

**congestive rales** in the lungs — **fine-bubbling non-consonant moist rales**, symmetric, **in the posterior lower parts**, not disappearing after coughing; the percussion sound is shortened in these areas;
the cardiac borders enlarged to the left, muffled heart sounds, **“gallop” rhythm**, accentuation or splitting of S2 over the pulmonary artery;
in a severe condition — **pulmonary edema** (frothy, pink sputum, moist rales over the whole lung);
X-ray — increased lung markings (venous congestion), reduced transparency in the area of the lung roots.

blocks.text: Right ventricular failure
The right atrium and ventricle are affected — **congestion in the systemic circulation**.

items: rapid fatigue, lethargy, weakness, reduced appetite, sweating;
dyspnea, tachycardia, cyanosis;

**liver enlargement** — the earliest and most constant sign (first the left lobe, then the right); the liver is soft, elastic, **tender**; **Plesch's sign** (distension of the neck veins increases on pressure over the liver);
**distension of the neck veins** (increases in the horizontal position);

**edema** — first in the legs (in a lying child the sacrum and lower back, in infants the face and scrotum), then generalized — **anasarca**, **ascites**, hydrothorax, hydropericardium; diuresis decreases (**oliguria**).

parts.text: In an infant the **earliest signs** of heart failure are **tachypnea**, **tachycardia** and **liver enlargement**; peripheral edema appears late and rarely at this age. Early signs: tiring during feeding, sweating (especially of the head), poor weight gain.

blocks.text: Stages of chronic heart failure
Chronic heart failure usually involves disturbances in **both circulations**; its severity is assessed by stages based on the N.D. Strazhesko–V.Kh. Vasilenko classification.

blocks.title: Table 10.8. Stages of circulatory failure in children (Makarova V.I., Babikova I.V., 2010)
head: Signs
I
IIA
IIB
III
rows: Irreversible changes in the internal organs

blocks.title: Table 10.9. Degrees of heart failure (Belozerov Yu.M. et al., 1994)
head: Degree
Signs
rows: Tachycardia (HR 20–30% above normal) and dyspnea (RR 30–50% above normal) at rest; mucosal cyanosis disappearing with oxygen; muffled heart sounds, enlarged borders
HR 30–50%, RR 50–70% above normal; mucosal cyanosis, acrocyanosis, periorbital edema; the liver projects 2–3 cm below the costal arch; stroke volume reduced by 20–30%
The above + pulmonary congestion, oliguria, peripheral edema
HR 50–60%, RR 70–100% above normal; incipient pulmonary edema, hepatomegaly, peripheral edema, ascites; in the terminal period — bradypnea, bradycardia, a fall in BP, muscle hypotonia, areflexia

blocks.text: Three clinical forms of acute vascular insufficiency: **fainting (syncope), collapse, shock**.
**Fainting** — a brief loss of consciousness due to acute cerebral hypoxia:

items: **prodromal period:** general weakness, darkening before the eyes, ringing in the ears, nausea, sweating — if the child is laid down at this time, fainting can be prevented;
**sudden brief loss of consciousness** (seconds, minutes), marked pallor, weakening of breathing and circulation;
dilated pupils, BP sharply reduced, muffled heart sounds, weak pulse; tonic-clonic seizures may occur.

blocks.text: **Collapse** — an acute fall in vascular tone:

items: the condition suddenly worsens, marked weakness, apathy; **consciousness is preserved**, but the child is indifferent;
pale skin, acrocyanosis, cold clammy sweat; breathing shallow and rapid;
**the pulse small, rapid, barely detectable**; **BP sharply reduced** (systolic and diastolic); the veins collapsed; the heart sounds loud at first, then muffled.

blocks.text: The main sign distinguishing fainting from collapse — **in fainting consciousness is lost, in collapse it is preserved**.

**Shock** — an acutely developing life-threatening condition caused by an extremely strong stimulus (injury, infection — septic shock, allergen — anaphylactic shock, blood loss — hypovolemic shock, heart — cardiogenic shock): a severe disturbance of organ perfusion; it has **compensated** (BP normal, tachycardia, cold limbs, capillary refill >2 s, oliguria) and **decompensated** (hypotension, impaired consciousness) stages; its severity is assessed by BP and the character of the pulse.

parts.text: **First aid in fainting:** lay the child horizontally, **raise the legs by 30–40 cm**, loosen the collar and belt, fresh air, splash cold water on the face, hold ammonia (smelling salts) to the nose. If the child does not regain consciousness or fainting recurs — exclude a cardiogenic cause (ECG, echocardiography, Holter).

blocks.text: Distinguishing cardiological syndromes

blocks.title: Table 10.10. Distinguishing signs of the syndromes of endocardial, myocardial and pericardial involvement
head: Sign
Endocarditis
Myocarditis
Pericarditis (exudative)
rows: Often few; fever, intoxication in infective endocarditis
Normal (changes once the defect has formed)
Weakened or absent, inside the border
Organic, constant, at the valve-specific site
Reduced voltage, arrhythmia, blocks, ST-T changes
Sharply reduced voltage, ST elevation (in dry pericarditis)

blocks.text: A cyanotic newborn: heart or lung?

**Hyperoxia test:** if PaO~2~ (SpO~2~) rises significantly (PaO~2~ >150 mm) after breathing 100% oxygen for 10–15 minutes — **a pulmonary cause**; if it hardly rises (PaO~2~ <100 mm) — **a “blue” congenital heart defect** (right-to-left shunt). In addition: in lung disease — dyspnea, rales, lung changes on X-ray; in a heart defect — cyanosis with no or little dyspnea, a murmur, changes in the cardiac shadow and lung markings on X-ray.

skills.title: Skill 1. Examining a cardiac patient and identifying the leading syndrome

items: Take the complaints and history (preceding infection, heredity, signs since birth).
General inspection: position, color, edema, “drumstick fingers”, physical development.
Inspect the cardiac area and vessels, palpate the apex beat, detect a thrill.
Percuss the cardiac borders.
Auscultation: heart sounds, extra sounds, murmurs, pericardial friction rub.
Examine the pulse and BP in the arms and legs.
Liver size, neck veins, rales at the lung bases.
Group the signs found into syndromes; plan ECG, echocardiography and X-ray.

skills.title: Skill 2. Determining the stage of heart failure

items: Count the RR and HR and calculate the percentage above the age norm.
Detect cyanosis, acrocyanosis, cough, moist rales in the lungs.
Determine the liver size (cm below the costal arch); test Plesch's sign.
Assess the neck veins, peripheral edema, pastosity, ascites; determine diuresis.
Compare the data with the table of stages and determine the stage and type (left, right, total).

skills.title: Skill 3. First aid in a hypercyanotic spell and fainting

items: Calm the child and eliminate the provoking factor.
In a hypercyanotic spell — the knee-chest position; in fainting — horizontal, with the legs raised.
Fresh air, humidified oxygen.
Monitor the pulse, RR, SpO~2~ and BP.
Medications on the doctor's order (in a hypercyanotic spell — morphine, sodium bicarbonate, propranolol).
Decide on hospitalization.

skills.title: Skill 4. Determining the BP gradient between the arms and legs

items: Measure BP on the upper arm with an age-appropriate cuff.
Measure BP on the thigh with a wide cuff (the child lying prone), listening over the popliteal artery.
Palpate the femoral and radial pulses simultaneously to detect delay or weakness.
Assessment: normally BP in the legs is 10–20 mm higher; if it is lower in the legs — suspect coarctation of the aorta.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 2.5-year-old child. Since birth the lips have turned blue when crying, and from 6 months the cyanosis has become constant. The child tires quickly when walking and rests by squatting. This morning, while crying, the child suddenly became restless, turned markedly blue, breathed rapidly, then became lethargic. On examination: generalized cyanosis, “drumstick fingers”, “watch-glass” nails. S2 weakened over the pulmonary artery, a harsh systolic murmur in the 2nd–3rd intercostal space on the left (weakened during the spell). CBC: Hb 210 g/l, erythrocytes 7.2×10^12^/l.
cases.ask: 1) Presumptive diagnosis and today's condition? 2) Name the four components of the defect. 3) What is the meaning of squatting? 4) What X-ray changes are expected? 5) First aid in the spell?
cases.answer: 1) Tetralogy of Fallot; today — a hypercyanotic spell. 2) Pulmonary stenosis, a large VSD, right ventricular hypertrophy, dextroposition of the aorta. 3) Squatting compresses the systemic arteries and increases peripheral resistance — the right-to-left shunt decreases, more blood goes to the lungs, and cyanosis decreases. 4) A “wooden shoe”-shaped heart, reduced lung markings. 5) Calming, the knee-chest position, humidified oxygen, on the doctor's order morphine, sodium bicarbonate, propranolol; cardiac glycosides must not be given; urgent hospitalization.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 9-year-old child had tonsillitis 3 weeks ago. For 5 days: fever 38 °C, pain and swelling in the knee and ankle joints (in turn), weakness, dyspnea. On examination: pale skin, HR 124/min. The cardiac border is enlarged 1 cm to the left. At the apex S1 is weakened and there is a blowing systolic murmur radiating to the left axilla. ECG: PQ 0.20 s. ESR 45 mm/h, CRP strongly positive, ASO 800 IU/ml.
cases.ask: 1) Which disease? Justify the diagnosis with the criteria. 2) Which cardiological syndromes are present? 3) What complication is there a risk of in the future?
cases.answer: 1) Acute rheumatic fever: major criteria — carditis, migratory polyarthritis; minor criteria — fever, raised ESR and CRP, prolonged PQ; evidence of a streptococcal infection — a history of tonsillitis and a high ASO titer. 2) Endocardial involvement (signs of mitral valve insufficiency — a systolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, weakened S1) and myocardial involvement (tachycardia, enlarged border, prolonged PQ) — rheumatic carditis. 3) Formation of an acquired heart defect (mitral insufficiency) in 8–12 months, recurrences; therefore long-term bicillin prophylaxis is needed.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 5-month-old child. The mother complains that the baby tires quickly when feeding, sweats a lot, gains weight poorly and often has bronchitis. On examination: pale skin, RR 62/min, HR 168/min. “Cardiac hump”, a diffuse cardiac impulse. A systolic thrill and a harsh loud pansystolic murmur in the 3rd–4th intercostal space at the left sternal edge, widely radiating. S2 accentuated over the pulmonary artery. Fine-bubbling non-consonant moist rales in the lower posterior parts of the lungs. The liver projects 3.5 cm below the costal arch, the neck veins are distended, pastosity of the legs.
cases.ask: 1) Presumptive diagnosis? 2) Type and stage of heart failure? 3) What X-ray changes are expected? 4) What does the accentuation of S2 over the pulmonary artery indicate?
cases.answer: 1) Ventricular septal defect (large) — an acyanotic defect with a left-to-right shunt and increased pulmonary blood flow. 2) Total (left and right ventricular) chronic heart failure, stage IIB: HR ≈30% above the norm for 5 months (≈130), RR more than 70% above (≈35), congestive rales in the lungs, liver 3–4 cm, distended neck veins, pastosity. 3) Increased lung markings (arterial hypervolemia), bulging of the pulmonary artery arc, cardiomegaly (CTI >0.55). 4) Pulmonary hypertension.
