topics.title: The hematopoietic system: anatomical and physiological features, age-related features of peripheral blood, the complete blood count, semiotics and syndromes (anemic, hemorrhagic, lymphoproliferative)

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the periods of intrauterine and postnatal hematopoiesis, the types of hemoglobin;
the basic concepts of hematopoietic factors, iron metabolism and the hemostatic system;
the age-related features of peripheral blood parameters, the physiological crossovers of the leukocyte differential;
the methods of examining the blood system, the parameters of the complete blood count and the coagulogram;
the semiotics of changes in erythrocytes, leukocytes, platelets and hemostasis;
the anemic, sideropenic, hemorrhagic and lymphoproliferative syndromes and the leukemia syndrome.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: take complaints and history from a child with a blood disease, and perform inspection and palpation;
assess a complete blood count by comparing it with the age norms, and calculate the color index;
classify anemia by severity, color index and regeneration;
determine the bleeding time and clotting time, and perform the endothelial tests;
determine the type of hemorrhagic syndrome on the basis of clinical signs.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In young children with iron deficiency, intestinal iron absorption **does not increase compensatorily** (unlike adults) — this is why they are the group most prone to iron deficiency anemia.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The crossovers: **“5 days — 5 years”**. Between the two crossovers (**from 5 days to 5 years**) **lymphocytes predominate** in the differential — this is normal for children and is not regarded as “lymphocytosis”.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: The laboratory triad of iron deficiency anemia: **hypochromia** (color index <0.85, MCH ↓) + **microcytosis** (MCV <80 fl) + **reduced ferritin and serum iron** (raised TIBC). In the blood smear — **the “PHA” syndrome**: poikilocytosis, hypochromia, anisocytosis.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: **“Hemophilia — hematoma, Werlhof — petechiae, Henoch–Schönlein — symmetric purpura”**. In hemophilia **the clotting time** is prolonged, in thrombocytopenia **the bleeding time** is prolonged.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Acute leukemia must be distinguished from **a leukemoid reaction**: in a leukemoid reaction there is no “leukemic hiatus”, intermediate and mature forms are present, there are no specific clinical signs (bone pain, leukemids), and the blood picture recovers after the underlying disease is treated. If in doubt — **bone marrow aspiration**.

blocks.text: **Blood** is a liquid tissue; it consists of plasma and formed elements — **erythrocytes, leukocytes and platelets**. It supplies the tissues with oxygen and nutrients and performs metabolic and protective functions.
The three periods of intrauterine hematopoiesis:

items: **The embryonic (megaloblastic, yolk sac) period** — from **the 2nd–3rd week** of pregnancy; in the blood islands of the yolk sac, large nucleated cells — **megaloblasts** (primary erythroblasts) with embryonic hemoglobin — are formed.

**The hepatic period** — begins **from week 6–7** and reaches its maximum **at 5 months**; erythroblasts and erythrocytes are formed in the liver. **From 3–4 months the spleen** also joins in (erythro-, granulo-, megakaryocytopoiesis); active lymphopoiesis **from week 20**.
**The bone marrow (medullary) period** — forms **from 4–5 months** and gradually becomes the main hematopoietic organ.

blocks.text: In line with these periods there are **three types of hemoglobin**: **embryonic (HbP)**, **fetal (HbF)** and **adult (HbA)**. HbP and HbF have **a high affinity for oxygen** — this facilitates the transfer of oxygen to the fetus. At birth HbF makes up **60–85%** of the total hemoglobin and is gradually replaced by HbA: **≈15% at 1 year**, **≤2% at 3 years**.

blocks.label: Figure 11.1
blocks.caption: Intrauterine succession of the hematopoietic organs and the types of hemoglobin (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.label: Figure 11.2
blocks.caption: Diagram of hematopoiesis: from the stem cell to mature blood cells (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **After birth** hematopoiesis in the liver stops; in the spleen only lymphocytes and monocytes are formed, and it destroys aged erythrocytes and platelets. The main organ forming all the formed elements except lymphocytes is **the red bone marrow**.

items: In the newborn **all the flat and tubular bones** are filled with red bone marrow; from the first months of life the red marrow is gradually replaced by **yellow (fatty)** marrow; **at 12–15 years** hematopoiesis persists only in **the flat bones** and the epiphyses of the tubular bones.

In the newborn and young child the bone marrow is **functionally labile**: under adverse influences (severe infection, anemia) it is quickly exhausted or **hematopoiesis may revert to the embryonic type** (extramedullary foci — enlargement of the liver and spleen, young cells in the peripheral blood).

blocks.text: **Sites of bone marrow aspiration:** in the newborn — **the calcaneus**; up to 1 year — **the (proximal) epiphysis of the tibia**; in older children — **the iliac crest**. Sternal puncture is now rarely used in children. **Trephine biopsy** (from the ilium, under anesthesia) gives more accurate information on the structure of the bone marrow.

**Life span of blood cells:** erythrocytes — **≈120 days** (in the newborn, erythrocytes with HbF — 60–90 days); platelets — **9–11 days**; neutrophils — a few hours in the blood, ≈14 days in total; eosinophils — 8–12 days; monocytes circulate in the blood for ≈12 hours and become macrophages in the tissues; lymphocytes — from a few days to years.
Hematopoietic factors:

items: **erythropoietin** — a glycoprotein hormone, **90% produced in the kidneys** in response to hypoxia; it stimulates the proliferation of erythroid cells and hemoglobin synthesis;
**thrombopoietin** — accelerates megakaryocytopoiesis; **colony-stimulating factors** and interleukins regulate leukopoiesis;
**folic acid and vitamin B~12~** — necessary for DNA synthesis; vitamin B~12~ is absorbed in the small intestine with the help of **the gastric intrinsic factor of Castle**;
**iron** — part of heme, ensures oxygen transport, is a component of many enzymes, and is necessary for immune function.

blocks.text: **The iron store** accumulates in the fetus from the mother via the placenta, especially at **weeks 28–32** of pregnancy, unidirectionally against the concentration gradient. For this reason the store is small in **preterm babies**, twins and those born after a complicated pregnancy. After birth the main sources of iron are food (in the 1st half-year — **breast milk**, from which up to **50%** of the iron is absorbed) and endogenous stores. A child's daily requirement is **0.5–1.2 mg** (more in adolescents).

**Stages of iron metabolism:** Fe^2+^ is absorbed in the intestine → oxidized to Fe^3+^ → bound to **transferrin** and transported to the bone marrow, depots and enzymes → in the bone marrow **Fe + protoporphyrin = heme; heme + globin = hemoglobin**. The store — in the form of **ferritin** and **hemosiderin** in the liver, muscles and bone marrow macrophages.

parts.text: In young children with iron deficiency, intestinal iron absorption **does not increase compensatorily** (unlike adults) — this is why they are the group most prone to iron deficiency anemia.

blocks.text: **Hemostasis** — the system that keeps the blood in a liquid state and stops bleeding when a vessel is damaged. Three main components:

items: **The vascular component** — reflex **local angiospasm** on injury; the endothelium normally produces prostacyclin and prevents platelet adhesion.

**The platelet component** — platelet attachment to the damaged endothelium (**adhesion**) and to each other (**aggregation**) — the primary platelet plug; platelets contain more than 10 clotting factors (designated by Arabic numerals).
**The plasma (coagulation) component** — **13 plasma factors** (designated by Roman numerals) are activated in sequence and a **fibrin** clot forms.

blocks.text: Then **retraction** of the clot (normally 0.3–0.5, i.e., 60–75%) and **fibrinolysis** — dissolution of the clot and restoration of vascular patency — take place. The anticoagulant system — antithrombin III, proteins C and S, heparin.

**Features of hemostasis in newborns:** in the first days of life **the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X)**, as well as factors XI and XII, the physiological anticoagulants and the components of fibrinolysis are **physiologically reduced**; the system is balanced, but at a low level. In preterm babies these parameters are even lower — hemorrhagic and thrombotic syndromes, especially **DIC syndrome**, develop quickly. Early cord clamping and late first breastfeeding further reduce the vitamin K-dependent factors.

parts.text: **Hemorrhagic disease** of the newborn (vitamin K deficiency) presents on days 2–5 of life with melena, blood in vomit, and bleeding from the umbilicus and into the skin. To prevent it, all newborns are given **vitamin K (phytomenadione) intramuscularly** after birth.

blocks.text: Blood of the newborn

items: **The blood volume** in the newborn is **≈80–90 ml/kg** (≈8–9% of body mass; 90–100 ml/kg in preterm babies), in adults **≈65–70 ml/kg** (≈7%). Some older textbooks give 14–15% for the newborn.

In **the first days** of life hemoglobin (**180–240 g/l**), erythrocytes (**5–7×10^12^/l**), the color index (**up to 1.1**) and hematocrit (**≈54%**) are high — the result of intensive erythropoiesis in response to hypoxia in utero and during delivery.

After birth external respiration is established and hypoxia is replaced by hyperoxia → erythropoietin decreases → erythropoiesis slows; erythrocytes with HbF have a short life span and are easily hemolyzed → **physiological jaundice** (from day 2–3).

The erythrocytes are polychromatophilic, **anisocytosis** (macrocytes predominate); **normoblasts** may be present in the blood; **reticulocytes** are **2.2–4.2%** in the first days (later 0.6–0.8% — 1%).
**Leukocytes** are **10–30×10^9^/l** in the first days, 10–12×10^9^/l after 2 weeks; the differential shows **neutrophilia** and a left shift (down to myelocytes).
Platelets **150–400×10^9^/l**; **ESR low — 1–2 mm/h**; the bleeding time is as in adults; the clotting time is slightly faster or normal.

blocks.text: Physiological crossovers of the leukocyte differential

At birth neutrophils are **60–65%**, lymphocytes **20–30%**. Neutrophils decrease rapidly and lymphocytes increase, and on **days 4–6** they **become equal** (40–45%) — **the first physiological crossover**. Then lymphocytes predominate (up to 60–65% until 1 year, 50–60% until 5 years). From 3–4 years neutrophils gradually increase and **at 4–6 years (on average at 5 years)** they become equal again — **the second physiological crossover**; then neutrophils predominate, and at 12–14 years the differential approaches that of adults (neutrophils 60–65%, lymphocytes 25–30%).

blocks.label: Figure 11.3
blocks.caption: Changes in the numbers of neutrophils and lymphocytes in different periods of childhood: crossovers at 4–5 days and at 5 years (Navruzova, Geppe)

parts.text: The crossovers: **“5 days — 5 years”**. Between the two crossovers (**from 5 days to 5 years**) **lymphocytes predominate** in the differential — this is normal for children and is not regarded as “lymphocytosis”.

blocks.text: Blood of children under 1 year and older children

items: In the 1st year erythrocytes fall to **3.5–4.5×10^12^/l**, hemoglobin to **110–120 g/l**, and the color index below 1.0; **at 3–6 months** the parameters may fall to their lowest values — **physiological (early) anemia** (rapid growth, increase in blood volume, relative immaturity of erythropoiesis, low iron in the diet).

**Early anemia in preterm babies** (at 1.5–2 months; low erythropoietin, rapidly increasing blood volume) and **late anemia** (at 4–5 months; iron deficiency — hypochromic) develop; late anemia can be prevented with iron preparations.
In the 1st year leukocytes are **8–12×10^9^/l**, with lymphocytes predominating in the differential; ESR **4–7 (5–8) mm/h**.
**From 2 years to adolescence** the composition of peripheral blood approaches that of adults: hemoglobin **120–140 g/l**, erythrocytes **4.0–4.5×10^12^/l**.

sections.title: 11.5. Methods of examining the blood system

blocks.text: Questioning

**Specific complaints:** bleeding (from the nose, gums, gastrointestinal tract, menstrual), hemorrhages (“bruises” on the skin, hematomas, hemarthroses), enlarged lymph nodes, pallor of the skin and mucous membranes. **Nonspecific complaints:** weakness, rapid fatigue, dizziness, headache, dyspnea on exertion, reduced appetite, **distorted taste and smell** (eating chalk, soil, ice; liking the smell of gasoline, paint), hair loss, brittle nails, bone and joint pain, fever, sweating, weight loss.

**History:** the neonatal period (term birth, weight, neonatal jaundice — onset, degree, duration); feeding (breast milk, timing of complementary foods, early feeding with cow's milk, meat intake); past illnesses, medication; **family history** — blood diseases, jaundice, gallstone disease, splenectomy, hemorrhagic syndrome in relatives (hemophilia — in the mother's male relatives), early (before 50 years) infarction and stroke (thrombophilia).
Inspection and palpation

items: **General condition:** impaired consciousness (with a rapid fall in Hb or blood volume — anemic coma, hypovolemic shock), ongoing bleeding.

**Color of the skin and mucous membranes: pallor** (anemia; marked pallor — acute blood loss); pallor + **a lemon-yellow tint** (hemolytic anemia, B~12~ deficiency); waxy pallor (leukemia); **cherry-red** (polycythemia); perioral cyanosis (hypoxia in severe anemia).
**Hemorrhagic rash:** type (petechiae, purpura, ecchymoses, hematoma), location, symmetry, color (different colors — different ages), circumstances of appearance.

**Skin appendages and mucous membranes:** dry skin, brittle hair and nails, **koilonychia**, angular stomatitis (“cheilitis”), **a “lacquered” or “geographic” tongue**, glossitis, gum hyperplasia and bleeding (leukemia).
**Lymph nodes, liver and spleen** (by the methods of topic 4): enlargement, consistency, adhesion; **hepatosplenomegaly** — systemic blood diseases.
**Joints:** hemarthrosis (hemophilia), joint syndrome (hemorrhagic vasculitis, leukemia).
**Bones:** pain on tapping (sternum, ribs, spine, tibia — leukemia).
**Cardiovascular:** tachycardia, a functional systolic murmur at the apex (anemia).
**Endothelial tests** (tourniquet, pinch, hammer — topic 4) — the state of the vascular wall and platelets.

blocks.text: Laboratory investigations

**Complete (clinical) blood count** — from a finger (from the heel in the newborn) or a vein; hemoglobin, erythrocytes, color index, reticulocytes, leukocytes and **the leukocyte differential**, platelets, ESR, hematocrit; on an automated analyzer — the erythrocyte indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC, RDW). **ESR** by the Panchenkov method: the column of plasma (mm) above the erythrocytes that have settled in a capillary in 1 hour.

blocks.label: Figure 11.4
blocks.caption: Determining ESR by the Panchenkov method: normal (1, 2) and raised (3) (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Assessment of hemostasis:

items: **Bleeding time (Duke)** — the finger or earlobe is pricked with a lancet and the drops of blood are blotted onto filter paper every 15–30 seconds; normally **2–4 minutes**. Prolongation — **reduced platelet count or impaired platelet function** (platelet component).

**Clotting time** — assesses the plasma component; the norm depends on the method: **Morawitz** — beginning 3, end 5 minutes; **Bürker** — 2.5 and 5.5 minutes; **Lee–White** (venous blood) — 5–10 minutes; **Sitkovsky** — 1.5 and 4 minutes. Prolongation — **deficiency of coagulation factors** (hemophilia).

**Coagulogram:** activated partial thromboplastin time (**APTT**, 25–55 s), prothrombin index (70–110%) or **INR**, thrombin time (14–16 s), **fibrinogen** (1.7–3.5 g/l), antithrombin III, D-dimers, individual factors (VIII, IX), clot retraction (60–75%), platelet aggregation.

blocks.text: **Other investigations:** iron metabolism parameters, bilirubin and its fractions, hemoglobin electrophoresis (thalassemia), osmotic resistance of erythrocytes (spherocytosis), Coombs test (immune hemolysis), vitamin B~12~ and folate; **myelogram** (bone marrow aspiration) and trephine biopsy; lymph node biopsy; cytochemical, immunophenotypic, cytogenetic and molecular methods (leukemias).

blocks.text: Changes in erythrocytes
**Anemia** — a decrease in the amount of hemoglobin (often also erythrocytes) per unit volume of blood below the age norm. The most common blood pathology in children.

**Anemia cut-offs (WHO):** in the newborn Hb **<145 g/l**; **6 months – 5 years — <110 g/l**; **5–11 years — <115 g/l**; **over 12 years — <120 g/l** (in local practice <120 g/l is often used for children over 5 years).

blocks.text: **Erythrocytosis** — an increase in erythrocytes and hemoglobin: secondary — chronic hypoxia (“blue” congenital heart defects, chronic lung diseases), hemoconcentration (dehydration); primary — **polycythemia vera** (rare in children).

**Erythrocyte morphology:** anisocytosis (different sizes), poikilocytosis (different shapes), micro- and macrocytosis, spherocytes, target cells (thalassemia), sickle erythrocytes; **reticulocytosis and polychromatophilia** — strong regeneration of the bone marrow; **normoblasts** in the peripheral blood — physiological in the neonatal period, later pathological (hemolysis, severe anemia, leukemia).

blocks.text: Changes in platelets

items: **Thrombocytosis** (>400×10^9^/l) — reactive (inflammation, rheumatic diseases, sepsis, iron deficiency, after blood loss, **after splenectomy**), polycythemia.

**Thrombocytopenia** (<150×10^9^/l) — a separate disease (**immune thrombocytopenia — Werlhof disease**) or a syndrome (leukemia, aplastic anemia, DIC syndrome, hypersplenism, infections, drugs). At **<50×10^9^/l** there is a risk of bleeding, at **<20×10^9^/l** a risk of spontaneous severe bleeding (including into the brain).

blocks.text: Changes in ESR

items: **Increase:** increased fibrinogen and globulins (inflammation, infections, sepsis), anemia, connective tissue diseases, kidney diseases (nephrotic syndrome), leukemias, lymphomas, tumors, after vaccination.
**Decrease:** the neonatal period, erythrocytosis and hemoconcentration (hematocrit >50%), hyperbilirubinemia, acidosis.

blocks.text: Changes in hemostasis

items: **Hypocoagulation** (tendency to bleed) — reduced platelets or impaired platelet function, deficiency of clotting factors (hemophilia, liver diseases, vitamin K deficiency, obstructive jaundice), an excess of anticoagulants.

**Hypercoagulation** (tendency to thrombosis) — hereditary thrombophilias (deficiency of antithrombin III, proteins C and S), stage 1 of DIC syndrome, antiphospholipid syndrome, burns, major injuries, after surgery, nephrotic syndrome.

**DIC syndrome** (disseminated intravascular coagulation) — in severe infections (sepsis, meningococcemia), shock, extensive injuries, tumors, hemolysis, exsicosis: first the clotting factors are sharply activated, with **disseminated thromboses** in the small vessels (impaired microcirculation, organ failure), then the factors and platelets are **consumed** (“consumption coagulopathy”) and fibrinolysis is activated, resulting in **bleeding from many sites**.

sections.title: 11.7. Main syndromes of blood system involvement

blocks.text: Anemic syndrome
Signs related to tissue hypoxia due to reduced hemoglobin:

items: **pallor** of the skin and mucous membranes (conjunctiva, lips, nail beds, palms);
weakness, rapid fatigue, lethargy, reduced appetite, dizziness, headache, darkening before the eyes, tinnitus, fainting;
dyspnea on exertion, **tachycardia**, a **functional systolic murmur** at the apex, a “humming top” over the neck veins, reduced BP;
in severe anemia — enlarged cardiac borders, heart failure, anemic coma.

blocks.text: Sideropenic syndrome
Signs of tissue iron deficiency in iron deficiency anemia:

items: dystrophy of the skin and appendages: **dry skin**, **hair loss and brittleness**, **brittle nails, transverse striations, koilonychia** (spoon-shaped nails);
atrophy of the mucous membranes: nose, esophagus (difficulty swallowing), stomach (dyspepsia, malabsorption); **angular stomatitis**, glossitis, “lacquered” tongue, gingivitis;
**distorted taste and smell** — eating chalk, soil, ice, raw meat, dough (**pica**), liking the smell of gasoline, acetone, paint;
muscle hypotonia and pain (myoglobin deficiency), including of the bladder sphincter — **nocturnal enuresis**, urine leakage on laughing and coughing;
reduced memory and attention, emotional lability, drowsiness; delay in the child's psychomotor development;
frequent infections (immunodeficiency).

parts.text: The laboratory triad of iron deficiency anemia: **hypochromia** (color index <0.85, MCH ↓) + **microcytosis** (MCV <80 fl) + **reduced ferritin and serum iron** (raised TIBC). In the blood smear — **the “PHA” syndrome**: poikilocytosis, hypochromia, anisocytosis.

blocks.text: **Hemolytic syndrome:** anemia + **jaundice** (lemon-yellow tint, raised indirect bilirubin) + **splenomegaly** + dark urine (urobilin) + reticulocytosis. In hemolytic crises — fever, weakness, abdominal pain, marked jaundice, deepening anemia.
Hemorrhagic syndrome

**Hemorrhagic syndrome** — a tendency to bleed: bleeding into cavities and/or hemorrhages into the skin, joints and internal organs. According to which component of hemostasis is disturbed: **coagulopathies** (plasma factors), **thrombocytopenias and thrombocytopathies** (platelet component), **vasopathies** (vascular component).

Symmetric, slightly raised (palpable) petechiae and purpura on the limbs, around the large joints and on the buttocks; with joint, abdominal (abdominal crises, intestinal bleeding) and renal (hematuria) syndromes
Recurrent bleeding from one site from angiomatously altered vessels (nose, intestine, lungs); telangiectasias on the skin and mucous membranes

parts.text: **“Hemophilia — hematoma, Werlhof — petechiae, Henoch–Schönlein — symmetric purpura”**. In hemophilia **the clotting time** is prolonged, in thrombocytopenia **the bleeding time** is prolonged.

**Intramuscular injections must not be given to a child with hemophilia** (risk of a large hematoma); aspirin and NSAIDs are prohibited. In hemarthrosis — immobilization of the joint, cold, and most importantly urgent **intravenous** administration of the deficient factor concentrate.

blocks.text: Lymphoproliferative (hyperplastic) syndrome

**Enlargement of the lymph nodes, liver and spleen** (one or several groups of nodes): leukemias, lymphomas, lymphogranulomatosis, histiocytoses, infectious mononucleosis and other infections (see topic 4).

items: **In lymphogranulomatosis (Hodgkin lymphoma)** — the cervical and supraclavicular nodes enlarge and form **a conglomerate (“packet”)**, mobile at first, then adherent, dense, painless; fever, night sweats, weight loss, itching; on biopsy **Reed–Sternberg (Berezovsky–Sternberg) cells**.
**In lymphosarcoma** — large tumor masses growing into the surrounding tissues, immobile, with signs of compression (edema, thrombosis, paralysis).

blocks.text: The syndrome of acute leukemia (disturbed proliferation and differentiation of leukocytes)
Mutation of hematopoietic cells and their malignant proliferation. In children most often **acute lymphoblastic leukemia** (2–5 years).
Clinical syndromes:

items: **intoxication** — weakness, rapid fatigue, unwillingness to play, loss of appetite, fever, frequent tonsillitis and abdominal pain;
**anemic** syndrome — pallor (waxy), tachycardia;
**hemorrhagic** syndrome — petechiae, purpura, bleeding from the nose and gums;
**hyperplastic (lymphoproliferative)** syndrome — enlargement of the lymph nodes, **liver and spleen**, gum hyperplasia, **skin leukemids** (painless dense bluish infiltrates);
**osteoarticular** syndrome — pain in the tubular bones and joints (ossalgia), limping;
**infectious complications** (neutropenia), neuroleukemia (meningeal signs).

blocks.text: **Hemogram:** normochromic anemia, reticulocytopenia, **thrombocytopenia**, leukocytosis (or leukopenia), **blast cells**, **“leukemic hiatus”** (no intermediate forms between the blasts and the mature granulocytes), raised ESR. **Myelogram:** blasts **≥20–25%** (the diagnostic criterion), the normal hematopoietic lineages depressed.

parts.text: Acute leukemia must be distinguished from **a leukemoid reaction**: in a leukemoid reaction there is no “leukemic hiatus”, intermediate and mature forms are present, there are no specific clinical signs (bone pain, leukemids), and the blood picture recovers after the underlying disease is treated. If in doubt — **bone marrow aspiration**.

blocks.text: A child with anemia — diagnostic algorithm

items: **Confirm the anemia** and determine its severity (Hb by the age cut-off).
**Color index and MCV**: hypochromic-microcytic → iron deficiency (ferritin), thalassemia (Hb electrophoresis); hyperchromic-macrocytic → B~12~ or folate deficiency; normochromic → continue.
**Reticulocytes**: high → hemolysis (bilirubin, Coombs, erythrocyte morphology) or acute blood loss; low → bone marrow failure.
**Other lineages**: leukocytes and platelets are also reduced (pancytopenia) or blasts are present → aplastic anemia or **leukemia** — myelogram.
Determine **the cause**: feeding, blood loss (gastrointestinal, helminthiasis), malabsorption, prematurity.

parts.text: **Prevention of iron deficiency anemia:** iron preparations for pregnant and breastfeeding mothers, exclusive breastfeeding up to 6 months, iron-rich complementary foods from 6 months (meat, fortified cereals), no whole cow's milk before 1 year, prophylactic iron preparations for preterm babies from 2–4 weeks.

skills.title: Skill 1. Assessing a complete blood count

items: Determine the child's age and choose the table of age norms.
Assess hemoglobin and erythrocytes; calculate the color index: (Hb × 3) / the first 3 digits of the erythrocyte count.
Assess the reticulocytes, MCV, MCH and MCHC.
Compare the leukocyte count and the differential with the age features (physiological crossovers); detect a left shift.
Assess the platelets and ESR.
Conclusion: “Within the age norm” or “Mild hypochromic microcytic anemia, eosinophilia”, etc.

skills.title: Skill 2. Determining the bleeding time (Duke)

items: Wipe the earlobe or fingertip with alcohol and let it dry.
Prick to a depth of 3–4 mm with a sterile lancet; start the stopwatch.
Every 15–30 seconds touch the emerging drop of blood with filter paper (without touching the skin).
Record the time when no more blood mark remains on the paper.
Assessment: normally 2–4 minutes; prolongation — disturbance of the platelet component.

skills.title: Skill 3. Determining the clotting time (Morawitz or Sitkovsky method)

items: Place a drop of blood from the finger on a dry, clean glass slide; record the time.
Every 30 seconds pass a glass rod (or needle) through the drop.
The appearance of the first fibrin thread — the beginning of clotting; complete clotting of the drop — the end.
Compare with the norm for the method (Morawitz: 3–5 minutes).

skills.title: Skill 4. Examining a child with a hemorrhagic syndrome

items: History: onset of bleeding, relation to injury, delayed bleeding, bleeding in the family (the mother's male relatives), preceding infection or vaccination.
Inspection: type of rash (petechiae, ecchymoses, hematoma), location, symmetry, color; joints (hemarthrosis); mucous membranes.
Perform the endothelial tests (tourniquet, pinch).
Palpate the lymph nodes, liver and spleen.
Determine the type of bleeding (hematoma, petechial-spotted, mixed, vasculitic-purpuric, angiomatous).
Draw up an investigation plan: CBC and platelets, bleeding and clotting time, coagulogram, urinalysis (hematuria), stool for occult blood.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A child aged 1 year 3 months. The mother complains of the child's pallor, rapid fatigue, poor appetite and urge to eat lime plaster and soil. Born at 34 weeks. Fed with cow's milk since 4 months, eats meat poorly. On examination: pale skin and mucous membranes, dry skin, sparse and brittle hair, cracks at the corners of the mouth. HR 132/min, a soft systolic murmur at the apex. The liver and spleen are not enlarged. CBC: Hb 82 g/l, erythrocytes 3.6×10^12^/l, reticulocytes 1.2%, MCV 66 fl, leukocytes 8.0×10^9^/l, platelets 320×10^9^/l, ESR 8 mm/h. Smear: anisocytosis, poikilocytosis.
cases.ask: 1) Calculate the color index. 2) Classify the anemia fully. 3) Which syndromes are present? 4) Presumptive diagnosis and risk factors? 5) Which investigations are needed for confirmation?
cases.answer: 1) CI = (82 × 3) / 360 = 0.68. 2) Moderate (Hb 90–70 g/l), hypochromic (CI <0.85), microcytic (MCV <80 fl), normoregenerative anemia. 3) Anemic (pallor, weakness, tachycardia, functional murmur) and sideropenic (pica, dry skin, brittle hair, angular stomatitis). 4) Iron deficiency anemia: prematurity (small iron store), early feeding with cow's milk, low meat intake. 5) Serum iron (↓), ferritin (↓), TIBC (↑), transferrin saturation coefficient (↓); stool for occult blood and helminthiasis.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 7-year-old boy. He had ARVI 2 weeks ago. This morning his mother saw many “bruises” and a fine punctate rash on his trunk and legs, and he had a nosebleed. On examination: general condition satisfactory, asymmetric petechiae and ecchymoses of different sizes and colors on the skin and mucous membranes, hemorrhages on the oral mucosa. The tourniquet sign is positive. The lymph nodes, liver and spleen are not enlarged. CBC: Hb 118 g/l, leukocytes 7.2×10^9^/l, normal differential, platelets 14×10^9^/l. Bleeding time 12 minutes, clotting time normal.
cases.ask: 1) Determine the type of bleeding. 2) Presumptive diagnosis? 3) Which laboratory signs confirm it? 4) What must be done to exclude leukemia?
cases.answer: 1) Petechial-spotted (microcirculatory) type: asymmetric petechiae and ecchymoses of different colors and sizes (“leopard skin”), bleeding from the mucous membranes. 2) Immune thrombocytopenia (Werlhof disease) — 2–3 weeks after a viral infection. 3) Marked thrombocytopenia (<20×10^9^/l — risk of severe bleeding), prolonged bleeding time, positive endothelial test, normal clotting time, no anemia or changes in other lineages. 4) The absence of hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy and bone pain argues against leukemia, but for definitive exclusion — a myelogram (in Werlhof disease many megakaryocytes, no blasts).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 3-year-old child has been weak for 3 weeks, with fever of 37.5–38.5 °C and pallor, and does not want to walk because of leg pain. On examination: waxy pallor of the skin, petechiae on the legs. Lymph nodes of all groups are enlarged (1.5–2 cm), dense, painless. The liver projects 4 cm and the spleen 5 cm below the costal arch. Pain on tapping the sternum and tibias. CBC: Hb 72 g/l, reticulocytes 0.2%, leukocytes 38×10^9^/l, blasts 62%, band forms 0%, segmented forms 6%, lymphocytes 32%, platelets 28×10^9^/l, ESR 52 mm/h.
cases.ask: 1) Which syndromes do you identify? 2) Assess the hemogram. 3) Presumptive diagnosis and the method of confirming it?
cases.answer: 1) Intoxication, anemic (pallor, Hb 72 g/l), hemorrhagic (petechiae, thrombocytopenia), hyperplastic (lymphoproliferative) (lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly) and osteoarticular (ossalgia) syndromes. 2) Severe normochromic hyporegenerative anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis, blasts 62%, no intermediate forms (band forms) — “leukemic hiatus”, raised ESR. 3) Acute leukemia (at 3 years most often lymphoblastic); confirmation — bone marrow aspiration (myelogram: blasts ≥20–25%), cytochemical and immunophenotypic studies.

topics.title: The digestive system: anatomical and physiological features, history taking, inspection, examination of the oral cavity, palpation and percussion of the abdomen, liver and spleen, auscultofriction

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the embryonic development of the digestive organs and the main periods of formation of congenital defects;
the age-related anatomical and physiological features of the oral cavity, esophagus, stomach, intestines, liver and pancreas;
the features of digestion, intestinal microflora and defecation in children;
the methods of history taking, inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation in digestive diseases;
the age norms for liver size and the pain points of the digestive organs.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: take complaints and history from a child with a digestive disease;
inspect the oral cavity, tongue, teeth, pharynx and abdomen;
perform superficial and deep (Obraztsov–Strazhesko) palpation of the abdomen;
palpate the liver, gallbladder, pancreas and spleen; test the gallbladder signs;
percuss the liver according to Kurlov and detect free fluid in the abdominal cavity;
determine the lower border of the stomach by auscultofriction.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: In an infant, **regurgitation 1–2 times a day** (within 1 hour after feeding, without distress, with good weight gain) is physiological; the causes are a weak cardiac sphincter, the horizontal position of the stomach and swallowing air. Normally a child over 1 year should pass stool at least **1 time in 36 hours**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The Kurlov dimensions in a school-age child — **“9–7–8”** (close to 9–8–7 in adults). Downward displacement of the liver edge with unchanged dimensions — **hepatoptosis** (right-sided pneumothorax, emphysema); upward displacement — ascites, meteorism; in these cases the liver itself is not enlarged.

blocks.text: The digestive organs form at very early stages of embryogenesis: **on day 7–8** the **primitive gut** begins to form from the endoderm, and **on day 12** it divides into an intraembryonic part (the future digestive tube) and an extraembryonic part (the yolk sac).

items: **Foregut** — pharynx, esophagus, stomach, part of the duodenum, the pancreatic and hepatic buds;
**midgut** — duodenum, jejunum and ileum, the right half of the colon;
**hindgut** — the remaining parts of the colon.

blocks.text: In **weeks 4–10** of pregnancy the primitive gut grows rapidly, leaves the abdominal cavity through the umbilical hernia, **rotates 270°** and returns. Disturbance of these processes results in **intestinal rotation anomalies, embryonic hernias (omphalocele), atresias, stenoses, Meckel's diverticulum**. **From week 16–20** the fetus swallows amniotic fluid (up to 500 ml per day) — the digestive organs “train”; **meconium** forms.

sections.title: 12.2. Anatomical and physiological features of the digestive organs

blocks.text: General features:

items: up to 1–1.5 years, especially in the 1st half-year, the digestive system is adapted to **lactotrophic (milk) nutrition**;

along the whole digestive tube the mucosa is **thin, delicate, drier and easily injured**; the submucosa is **rich in blood vessels** and consists of loose connective tissue; **muscle and elastic fibers are poorly** developed;
the sucking and swallowing reflexes are well developed;
the glands have **low secretory activity**: little digestive juice, low enzyme activity;
conditioned reflex activity is easily disturbed by external influences (overheating, chilling, pain, acute illness, separation from the mother) — predisposition to **functional dyspepsia**.

blocks.text: Oral cavity

items: The oral cavity is relatively **small** and filled by the tongue; the tongue is short, wide and thick; the lips and cheeks are thick with well-developed muscles; in the cheeks there are dense **Bichat's fat pads** (rich in solid fatty acids) — the cheeks are not drawn in during sucking; the gums have **ridge-like thickenings** that help sucking, and the lips transverse folds.
The mucosa is **delicate, dry** and rich in blood vessels — it is easily injured and infected (**candidiasis** — “thrush”, aphthous stomatitis).

**The salivary glands** are insufficiently developed in the newborn: saliva is scanty and thick, with a neutral or weakly acidic reaction and little amylase. **From 3–4 months** salivation increases sharply and the child cannot swallow it all — **physiological drooling** (3–6 months). Salivary amylase reaches adult levels at 1 year.

**The act of sucking** consists of three phases: **aspiration** (the lips enclose the nipple and negative pressure is created in the mouth), **compression** (milk is extracted) and **swallowing**. Because the entrance to the larynx lies at the posterior border of the hard palate, the child **can breathe and swallow at the same time**. Absence of the swallowing reflex is a sign of extreme prematurity.

blocks.text: The esophagus and stomach

items: **The esophagus** is funnel-shaped, relatively short (10–12 cm in the newborn) and narrow; its mucosa is thin, with few glands, rich in blood vessels; the muscle layer is weak; the physiological narrowings are poorly expressed.
**The lower esophageal (cardiac) sphincter is poorly** developed, while the muscles of the pyloric part are well developed — predisposition to **regurgitation** and **aerophagia**.

**The stomach** in infancy lies **horizontally** and varies in shape (round, pear-shaped); once the child begins to walk (9–12 months) it takes a **vertical** position; the fundus and muscle layer are poorly developed.

blocks.title: Table 12.1. Stomach capacity by age
head: Age
Physiological capacity
rows: Increases by ≈25 ml each month (≈100–150 ml at 3 months)

items: In the gastric mucosa, the pepsin-producing **chief cells** and the hydrochloric acid-secreting **parietal cells** are few and functionally immature; the cells producing protective mucus are few. The acidity of the gastric juice is low (pH ≈5–6 in the newborn, ≈3–4 at 1 year); it reaches adult levels **at 10–12 years**. Proteins are broken down mainly by **chymosin** (rennin) and gastricsin; **gastric lipase** partly breaks down the fats of breast milk.
Gastric emptying: breast milk — **2–3 hours**, cow's milk and formulas — **3–4 hours** (which is why the intervals are longer with artificial feeding).

blocks.text: The intestines

items: The intestines are relatively **long**: in the newborn **6–8 times** the body length (4–5 times in adults); the small intestine is ≈1 m per 1 kg of body mass. The mesentery is long and mobile and the intestinal loops are poorly fixed — predisposition to **intussusception and volvulus**.
**The duodenum** is ring-shaped, at the level of LI, mobile; it becomes fixed by fatty tissue by 7 years.

The mucosa is thin, rich in blood vessels, with many villi — **a large absorptive surface**, but **high permeability** (weak barrier function): toxins, allergens and microbes easily pass into the blood — predisposition to toxicosis and allergy.
**The ileocecal valve (Bauhin's valve)** is relatively weak — cecal flora may pass into the ileum.
**The appendix** is conical with a wide entrance — at an early age **appendicitis is rare**, but it runs a rapid destructive course and peritonitis develops quickly (the omentum is short).
**The colon** is not fully mature; formation of the cecum is completed at the end of the 1st year; the sigmoid colon is relatively long and mobile — predisposition to **constipation**.

**The rectum** in the newborn is cylindrical, without an ampulla or folds, relatively long and with little fatty tissue — predisposition to **prolapse** of the mucosa (straining, whooping cough); it takes up its final position at 2 years.

**Digestion:** in infancy **membrane (parietal) digestion** predominates over cavity digestion; in the newborn **pinocytosis** (direct absorption of proteins — breast milk immunoglobulins) is preserved. **Lactase** activity is high in the 1st year and then decreases.
**Motility** is active: food passes through the intestine in **4–18 hours** (≈24 hours in adults) — the bowel empties frequently.

blocks.text: The pancreas and liver

items: **The pancreas** is small in the newborn (≈3 g; ≈50 g at 15 years) and insufficiently differentiated; its exocrine activity is low in the 1st year (little amylase and lipase), increases rapidly after complementary foods are introduced and reaches adult levels **at 5–6 years**. The juice contains trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidases, elastase (proteins), amylase and lipase.

**The liver** is **large** relative to body mass: **≈4%** in the newborn (2% in adults), occupying a large part of the abdominal cavity; the left lobe is relatively large (it becomes smaller at 1.5 years); lobulation becomes distinct at the end of the 1st year; its structure approaches that of adults **at 8 years**. It is rich in blood vessels and poor in connective tissue — it **enlarges quickly** in infection and intoxication.

The **detoxifying** and **conjugating** (glucuronyltransferase) functions of the liver are immature — **physiological jaundice**, sensitivity to drugs. Little bile is secreted and there are few bile acids (poor emulsification and absorption of fats — more fat in the stool); taurine conjugates predominate in bile (antibacterial effect), and there is little cholesterol and salts — **gallstones are rare**.
**The gallbladder** in the newborn is cylindrical or pear-shaped and lies deep in the liver; at 10–12 years it resembles that of adults.

blocks.text: Intestinal microflora and stool

items: The fetal intestine is **sterile**. In the first hours after birth the intestine is **colonized** by microbes (the first “aseptic” phase — 10–20 hours; the second — multiplication; the third — stabilization).

In a **breastfed** child **bifidobacteria** predominate from the end of the 1st month (90–99%) — the bifidus factor in breast milk (lactulose, oligosaccharides) supports them; they create an acidic environment, protect against pathogenic flora and synthesize vitamins. **With artificial feeding** there are more E. coli, enterococci, lactobacilli and opportunistic flora.

**Meconium** — the first stool: a dark green, sticky, odorless mass passed in the first **1–3 days** of life (swallowed amniotic fluid, shed epithelium, bile, mucus). **On days 3–5** — **transitional stool** (green-yellow, mucous, frequent). From day 5 — permanent stool.

blocks.title: Table 12.2. Stool of a breastfed and a formula-fed child
head: Sign
Breastfed
Formula-fed
rows: 3–6 times a day in the 1st month (often after each feed), then 1–3
Golden yellow (bilirubin), may turn green in air

parts.text: In an infant, **regurgitation 1–2 times a day** (within 1 hour after feeding, without distress, with good weight gain) is physiological; the causes are a weak cardiac sphincter, the horizontal position of the stomach and swallowing air. Normally a child over 1 year should pass stool at least **1 time in 36 hours**.

blocks.text: Abdominal pain

Small children cannot localize pain: it shows as **general restlessness**, screaming, crying, refusal of the breast, vomiting, drawing up and kicking the legs. Preschool children often point to the pain **around the umbilicus** (regardless of which organ is affected). In older children the following are determined:

items: **location** and **radiation**;
**character** (dull, stabbing, colicky, cutting, “dagger-like”);
**duration**, **periodicity** and **seasonality** (worsening in autumn and spring — peptic ulcer disease);

**relation to food:** during eating; **early** (30–60 minutes after eating); **late** (after 1.5–3 hours); **hunger pain** (6–7 hours after eating, relieved by eating); **night pain** (from 23:00 to 3:00);
relation to defecation;
aggravating and relieving factors, pain-relieving drugs.

Probable diseases

Stomach, body and tail of the pancreas (pancreatitis), the left half of the colon, spleen; left-sided pneumonia, pleurisy, myocarditis

Acute appendicitis, intussusception, Meckel's diverticulum, Crohn disease, mesenteric lymphadenitis; diseases of the kidneys, urinary tract and genitals
Enterocolitis, intestinal colic, the abdominal form of hemorrhagic vasculitis, intestinal infections, helminthiasis, ascites, peritonitis, renal colic, acute infections (viral hepatitis, meningitis)

blocks.text: **Radiation of pain:** to the right shoulder and shoulder blade — the hepatobiliary system; to both hypochondria — duodenitis, pancreatitis; to the lower back, the back (“girdle-like”) — **pancreatitis**; to the sacrum, perineum — the anorectal area.
Dyspeptic signs

items: **Changes in appetite:** reduced (gastritis, hepatitis, pancreatitis, intoxication), lost (**anorexia**), increased (malabsorption, chronic pancreatitis, recovery period), sharply increased (**bulimia** — diabetes mellitus, CNS pathology), distorted (**pica** — iron deficiency), selective appetite (dislike of fatty food — liver and biliary tract diseases).
**Nausea and vomiting:** time of vomiting, relation to food, presence or absence of relief after vomiting, character of the vomit (unchanged food, bile, blood, “coffee grounds”, sour smell), volume.
**Regurgitation** — the return of food to the mouth in infancy without straining of the abdominal muscles.
**Belching** (air, sour, bitter, putrid) and **heartburn** (burning behind the sternum and in the epigastrium) — gastroesophageal reflux, gastritis.
**Swallowing disorder (dysphagia)**, painful swallowing (odynophagia).
**Constipation** — no defecation for more than 36 hours, or difficult, painful defecation, hard stool; **diarrhea** — frequent passage of liquid or mushy stool; **meteorism** — abdominal distension.

**Unusual taste in the mouth:** sour (gastroduodenitis, peptic ulcer disease), bitter or metallic taste (liver diseases); **thirst** (dehydration, diabetes mellitus); **drooling** (ascariasis, pancreatitis, stomatitis; physiological at 3–6 months).

blocks.text: History
**History of the present illness:** onset and course of the disease, results of previous investigations and treatment.

**Life history:** the course of the mother's pregnancy and delivery; the neonatal period (passage of meconium, jaundice); type of feeding and timing of complementary foods, food intolerance (milk, gluten); dyspeptic disorders; allergic history; eating habits (in older children — irregular meals, dry food, fast food); medication; **family history** — peptic ulcer disease, gastritis, gallstone disease, celiac disease, cystic fibrosis, inflammatory bowel diseases.
General inspection

The following are assessed: the child's **general condition**, **position** (with abdominal pain — lying on the side with the legs drawn up to the abdomen; in peritonitis — lying motionless), the degree of **physical development** (hypotrophy — malabsorption, chronic diseases), the color of **the skin and mucous membranes** (pallor, **jaundice**, subicterus), rashes, hemorrhages, **spider angiomas**, **“liver palms”** (palmar erythema), striae, scars, a venous network on the anterior abdominal wall (“**caput medusae**” — portal hypertension).
Examination of the oral cavity
Examination of the oral cavity and pharynx is performed **last** so as not to upset the child. The corners of the mouth are gently pulled with a spatula, and the following are examined in turn:

items: **lips** — color, moisture, dryness, cracks, herpes, **angular cheilitis** (“perlèche” — deficiency of iron and B vitamins);
**oral mucosa** — color (pale, hyperemic, cyanotic, icteric), **aphthae** and ulcers (stomatitis), **candidiasis** (a white cheesy coating), **Filatov–Koplik spots** on the cheeks in measles;
**gums** — looseness, bleeding (gingivitis, leukemia, scurvy);
**teeth** — number (appropriate for age), position, bite, **caries**, enamel changes;

**tongue** — size (macroglossia — hypothyroidism, Down syndrome), moisture, color, state of the papillae, **coating** (white, yellowish, brown), **“geographic” tongue** (exudative diathesis), **“lacquered” tongue** (atrophy of the papillae — iron and B~12~ deficiency, liver diseases), **“raspberry” tongue** (scarlet fever), **short frenulum of the tongue**;
**hard and soft palate** — clefts, “gothic” palate;
**the ducts of the salivary glands** (hyperemia, edema — mumps);
**pharynx** and tonsils;
**breath odor** — acetone (ketoacidosis, acetonemic vomiting), “liver odor” (liver failure), putrid (caries, gastritis, tonsillitis).

blocks.text: Inspection of the abdomen
The abdomen is inspected with the child standing and lying down:

items: **shape and size** — normally slightly protuberant in infancy (weak muscles, relatively long intestine); it flattens after 3–5 years;
**symmetry** — uneven enlargement (hepato- or splenomegaly, tumor, hernia);
**participation in breathing** — lagging of one half (inflammation), **absence of abdominal breathing** (peritonitis, perforation);
**visible peristalsis** — obstruction to passage from the intestine or stomach (in pyloric stenosis, the “hourglass” sign in the epigastrium);
the state of **the umbilicus** (hernia, umbilical wound — in the newborn), **hernia of the linea alba**, separation of the muscles (diastasis);
**venous network** (“caput medusae”).

“Frog belly” — widened to the sides, with meteorism and hypotonia of the abdominal wall

blocks.text: **General rules:** a warm room, the doctor's hands warm and nails short; the child lies on the back with the head slightly raised, the arms along the body, the legs slightly bent at the knee and hip joints (the abdominal press relaxes); the doctor sits on the child's right side, facing the child. Talk to the child to distract attention; a small child may be on the mother's lap. A painful area is palpated **last**. During palpation the doctor watches the child's face (pain reaction).

**Abdominal regions:** two horizontal lines (through the 10th ribs and the anterior superior iliac spines) and two vertical lines (along the outer edges of the rectus muscles) divide the abdomen into **9 regions**: right and left hypochondrium, epigastrium; right and left lateral regions, umbilical region; right and left iliac regions, suprapubic region.

blocks.label: Figure 12.3
blocks.caption: Abdominal regions and the projection of the organs: 1 — right hypochondrium; 2 — epigastrium; 3 — left hypochondrium; 4 — right lateral; 5 — umbilical; 6 — left lateral; 7 — right iliac; 8 — suprapubic; 9 — left iliac region (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Superficial (orienting) palpation

The palm is placed flat on the abdominal wall and gentle pressure is applied with fingers II–V. Order: **starting from the left iliac region, counterclockwise** — left lateral region → left hypochondrium → epigastrium → right hypochondrium → right lateral region → right iliac region → periumbilical and suprapubic regions.

**Determined:** tenderness of the abdominal wall (localized or diffuse), **tension of the abdominal muscles** (local or diffuse — a “board-like” abdomen — peritonitis), separation of the rectus muscles, hernias (umbilical, inguinal, linea alba), superficial tumors, a markedly enlarged liver and spleen, zones of hyperesthesia (**Zakharyin–Head zones**), asymmetry in the thickness of the subcutaneous fat.

Muscle tension may be **active** (the child is afraid, ticklish — it disappears when attention is distracted) or **passive** (inflammation — it persists). In the newborn the umbilical ring, the periumbilical vessels and the umbilical wound (discharge, hyperemia) are palpated.

blocks.label: Figure 12.4
blocks.caption: Superficial palpation of the abdomen: directions of hand movement (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Peritoneal signs:

items: **Shchetkin–Blumberg sign** — a sharp increase in pain when the hand, slowly pressed into the abdominal wall, is **quickly withdrawn** — irritation of the peritoneum (peritonitis, acute appendicitis);
**Obraztsov's sign** — increased pain on palpation of the right iliac region while the straight right leg is raised (appendicitis);
**Rovsing and Sitkovsky** signs (appendicitis) — studied in detail in the surgery course.

blocks.text: Deep (methodical, sliding, topographic) palpation — according to Obraztsov–Strazhesko

**Four steps:** 1) place the fingers parallel to the organ being palpated; 2) move **a skin fold** perpendicular to the organ (toward the umbilicus); 3) during expiration, **plunge the fingers deep** into the abdominal cavity, to the posterior wall; 4) **slide perpendicular** over the organ.

**Order:** sigmoid colon → cecum (with the terminal ileum) → ascending colon → transverse colon → descending colon → liver and gallbladder → spleen → stomach and duodenum → pancreas → mesenteric lymph nodes.

items: **Sigmoid colon** — in the left iliac region, along the bisector of the left lower quadrant; normally a smooth, dense-elastic, painless, mobile, non-gurgling cylinder 1.5–2 cm in diameter.
**Cecum** — in the right iliac region, by the same method; soft-elastic, slightly gurgling, painless, mobile.
**Ascending and descending colon** — in the right and left lateral regions, with the other hand placed under the lower back as “support”.
**Transverse colon** — with both hands, 2–3 cm above the umbilicus, at the outer edges of the rectus muscles, during expiration.
**The small intestine** is usually not palpable (deep and mobile).

blocks.text: For each part of the intestine **the location, shape, size, consistency, surface, mobility, gurgling and tenderness** are assessed.

blocks.text: The greater curvature and pyloric part of **the stomach** are difficult to palpate; first its **lower border** is determined by percussion palpation (Obraztsov's “succussion splash”) or by **auscultofriction**, then the greater curvature is felt above the umbilicus as a soft thin fold by deep sliding palpation. Epigastric pain — a positive **Chernik's sign**.
Palpation of the liver

**Sliding palpation according to Strazhesko** — in infants and young children and when the liver is enlarged, only this method: the fingers of the right hand are placed in a line parallel to the lower edge of the liver and slide gently **from top to bottom**; the whole accessible surface of the liver is palpated.

**According to Obraztsov** (if the liver is not palpable): the right hand is placed flat on the right half of the abdomen at the level of the umbilicus or lower; the left hand encircles the lower right part of the chest (restricting respiratory movement). During expiration the right hand is plunged deep, then the child **takes a deep breath** — the descending edge of the liver strikes the fingers and “slips past” them. Palpation is repeated along the midclavicular, anterior axillary and midline.
**Assessed:** distance below the costal arch (cm), **edge** (sharp, blunt, rounded), **consistency** (soft-elastic, dense, hard), **surface** (smooth, uneven, bumpy), **tenderness**.

blocks.label: Figure 12.8
blocks.caption: Palpation of the liver (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Normally at an early age the liver is **soft-elastic**, smooth, with a sharp edge, painless; at school age — **dense-elastic** (as in adults).

blocks.label: Figure 12.9
blocks.caption: Position of the liver relative to the right costal arch: a — up to 3–4 years; b — from 3–4 to 7 years; c — over 7 years (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: The gallbladder

The gallbladder is normally **not palpable** (it does not extend beyond the edge of the liver). Its projection is the point where the outer edge of the right rectus muscle crosses the costal arch (**Kehr's point**). Palpation of an enlarged painless gallbladder — **Courvoisier–Terrier sign**.
Gallbladder (“cystic”) signs:

items: **Kehr's sign** — pain when a finger is pressed into Kehr's point (on inspiration);
**Murphy's sign** — pain on deep inspiration while the right hypochondrium is pressed (the child stops breathing in);
**Ortner–Grekov sign** — pain on tapping the right costal arch with the edge of the palm (compared first on the left, then on the right);
**Georgievsky–Mussy (phrenicus) sign** — pain on pressure between the heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle on the right;
**Razdolsky–Lepine sign** — pain on light percussion over the gallbladder projection;
**Boas sign** — pain on the right in the area of the transverse processes of ThXI–LI.

blocks.text: The pancreas and mesenteric lymph nodes

**Grott's method** — the child lies on the back, the clenched right fist placed under the lower back, the legs bent; the fingers are plunged during inspiration between the umbilicus and the hypochondria toward the spine at an angle of 45° (rarely used in practice — pain may occur even in a healthy child).
Pain points and zones:

items: **Chauffard's zone** — between the linea alba and the bisector of the right upper quadrant — the head of the pancreas and the duodenum (pyloroduodenal zone);
**Desjardins' point** — on the bisector of the right upper quadrant, 4–6 cm from the umbilicus (halfway) — the head of the gland;
**Mayo-Robson point** — on the bisector of the left upper quadrant, in the outer 1/3 of the distance between the umbilicus and the costal arch — the tail of the gland;
**Gubergrits–Skulsky zone** — on the left, symmetric to Chauffard's zone — the body of the gland;
**Kach's sign** — pain on the left in the area of the transverse processes of ThX–XI;
**Georgievsky–Mussy sign on the left** — pancreatitis.

blocks.text: **Mesenteric lymph nodes** are palpated in **Sternberg's zones** (in the left upper and right lower quadrants, along the outer edge of the rectus muscle); **Porges' point** — the duodenojejunal junction (to the left and above the umbilicus).

blocks.label: Figure 12.13
blocks.caption: Pain points on the anterior abdominal wall: 1 — Kehr's point (gallbladder); 2 — Desjardins' point; 3 — Mayo-Robson point; 4 — Porges' point; Chauffard's zone (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Spleen** — sliding palpation according to Strazhesko, supine and on the right side (see topic 4); normally not palpable.

Over the abdomen there is normally a **tympanic** sound almost everywhere (gas in the intestine); over the liver, the spleen, a stool-filled bowel (sigmoid) and a full bladder — a **dull** sound. Percussion is quiet.
Percussion of the liver
**Up to 5 years** the liver dimensions are determined along the right anterior axillary, midclavicular and midline. In children **over 5 years** — **three dimensions according to M.G. Kurlov**:

items: **The first dimension** — along the right midclavicular line: **the upper border** — from top to bottom, from the clear sound to the dull sound (normally rib VI), marked along the upper edge of the finger; **the lower border** — from the level of the umbilicus upward, from tympanitis to dullness (normally the edge of the costal arch), marked along the lower edge of the finger.

**The second dimension** — along the midline: the upper point is determined conventionally (because it merges with cardiac dullness) by dropping a perpendicular from the upper point of the first dimension to the midline; the lower border is found by percussion upward from the umbilicus (normally at the junction of the upper and middle thirds of the distance between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus).

**The third dimension** — along the left costal arch: the finger is placed perpendicular to the costal arch at the level of the attachment of rib VIII and percussion is performed along the arch toward the sternum; the border is marked along the outer edge of the finger. The distance from the upper point of the second dimension to this point is the third dimension.

parts.text: The Kurlov dimensions in a school-age child — **“9–7–8”** (close to 9–8–7 in adults). Downward displacement of the liver edge with unchanged dimensions — **hepatoptosis** (right-sided pneumothorax, emphysema); upward displacement — ascites, meteorism; in these cases the liver itself is not enlarged.

blocks.text: **Disappearance of liver dullness** — **perforation** of the stomach or intestine (escape of gas into the abdominal cavity) — a sign requiring urgent surgery.
Detecting free fluid in the abdominal cavity

items: **Fluctuation (fluid wave) sign** — the left palm is placed on the lateral surface of the abdomen and a short tap is given on the opposite side with the fingers of the right hand; the vibration of the fluid strikes the left hand as “a wave”. To exclude transmission through the abdominal wall, an assistant presses the edge of the palm on the middle of the abdomen.

**Percussion** — with the child lying on the back, percussion is performed from the umbilicus to the sides (finger parallel to the linea alba); **bilateral dullness in the lateral regions** — free fluid.

**With a change of position** — the child is turned on the side and percussion is repeated: if the dullness in the upper lateral region **disappears** — free fluid (the fluid has flowed down); if it persists — another cause (a full bowel, a tumor).

blocks.text: Other percussion signs

items: **Mendel's sign** — pain on tapping with half-bent fingers over the projection of the greater and lesser curvature of the stomach — peptic ulcer disease, erosive gastritis;
**Razdolsky's sign** — pain on percussion over the gallbladder projection.

blocks.text: **Auscultation of the abdomen:** normally **faint, periodic sounds of intestinal peristalsis** are heard over the abdominal wall. **Increased peristalsis** — enteritis (loud gurgling over a wide area), the part proximal to a stenosis; **absence of peristalsis (“dead silence”)** — intestinal paresis, peritonitis.

**Auscultofriction** — a method of determining the lower border of the stomach: the stethoscope is placed on the epigastric area (over the stomach projection), and at the same time light “stroke-like” rubbing movements are made with one finger along the abdominal skin **from below upward** (toward the stomach) to the left of the linea alba, radially to the stethoscope. As soon as the finger crosses the border of the stomach the sound becomes sharply **louder** — this is the lower border of the stomach. If light percussion taps are used instead of rubbing — **auscultatory percussion** (auscultopercussion). Normally the lower border of the stomach is **2–4 cm above** the umbilicus.

sections.title: 12.8. Examination of the rectum and anal area

blocks.text: **Inspection** — the anus and the surrounding skin: fissures, scratch marks (enterobiasis), maceration, **prolapse of the rectal mucosa**, gaping anus, polyps and hemorrhoidal nodes, fistulas, scars, infiltrates.

**Digital examination** — the child in the knee-elbow position (in a severe condition on the left side, legs drawn up to the abdomen), after defecation; with a gloved little finger (in small children) or index finger lubricated with petroleum jelly. **Determined:** sphincter tone, smoothness of the mucosa, state of the pararectal tissue, pain, tumor, polyp, intussusceptum; after withdrawal of the finger, traces of **blood, mucus, pus** on the glove. This examination is important for excluding **surgical pathology (intussusception, appendicitis)** in abdominal pain.
“Acute abdomen” — alarming signs

parts.text: Signs in abdominal pain that suggest **acute surgical pathology** (appendicitis, intussusception, intestinal obstruction, perforation): refusal of food, change in behavior (intense crying or lying motionless, forced position); waking from pain; vomiting against a background of pain; **no passage of stool or gas**; pallor, cold sweat, **tachycardia out of proportion to the temperature**; **tension of the abdominal muscles**, a positive Shchetkin–Blumberg sign. Such a child is **not given** analgesics, and urgent surgical examination is arranged.

blocks.text: Intussusception

Most often in children **aged 4–12 months** (when complementary foods are introduced); sudden **colicky abdominal pain** (the child cries sharply, draws up the legs, then calms down), vomiting, **a sausage-shaped mass** palpable in the abdomen, later blood-stained mucus like **“raspberry jelly”** from the anus. On digital rectal examination — blood on the glove. Diagnosis — ultrasound; treatment — air reduction or surgery.
Hepatomegaly — is the organ enlarged?

Projection of the liver edge below the costal arch is not always enlargement: **hepatoptosis** (the diaphragm descends in pulmonary emphysema, asthma, right-sided pleurisy, pneumothorax) — the Kurlov dimensions are normal. In true hepatomegaly the dimensions are also increased: hepatitis, heart failure (congestion), storage diseases, hemolytic anemias, leukemias, tumors.

skills.title: Skill 1. Examination of the oral cavity

items: Wash the hands, put on gloves; good light, a sterile spatula.
The child sits (a small child is held by the mother), the head is fixed.
Inspect the lips and the corners of the mouth.
Retract the cheeks and lips with the spatula and inspect the mucosa, gums and salivary ducts.
Assess the number and condition of the teeth and the bite; inspect the tongue (coating, papillae, moisture).
Press the middle third of the tongue with the spatula and inspect the pharynx and tonsils (last).
Assess the breath odor; record the result.

skills.title: Skill 2. Superficial palpation of the abdomen

items: The child lies on the back, legs slightly bent, the doctor on the right; warm hands.
Place the palm flat on the abdominal wall and press gently with fingers II–V.
Palpate all regions symmetrically, starting from the left iliac region counterclockwise; the painful area last.
Detect pain, muscle tension, hernias, separation of the muscles, superficial masses.
Test the Shchetkin–Blumberg sign.
Conclusion: “The abdomen is soft, painless, peritoneal signs negative.”

skills.title: Skill 3. Deep sliding palpation (Obraztsov–Strazhesko)

items: Sigmoid colon: the right hand in the left iliac region, fingers parallel to the axis of the bowel; move a skin fold toward the umbilicus, plunge deep on expiration, slide perpendicular to the bowel.
Palpate the cecum in the right iliac region in the same way.
Palpate the ascending and descending colon with the left hand placed under the lower back.
Palpate the transverse colon with both hands 2–3 cm above the umbilicus.
Record the location, diameter, consistency, surface, mobility, gurgling and tenderness of each part.

skills.title: Skill 4. Palpation of the liver and percussion according to Kurlov

items: In a small child — sliding palpation from top to bottom according to Strazhesko; in an older child — according to Obraztsov on deep inspiration.
Along the midclavicular line determine how far the liver edge projects below the costal arch (cm), its edge, consistency, surface and tenderness.
Test the gallbladder signs (Kehr, Murphy, Ortner, Mussy).
Determine the three Kurlov dimensions by quiet percussion.
Compare the result with the age norm.

skills.title: Skill 5. Detecting free fluid in the abdominal cavity

items: The child lies on the back; test the fluctuation sign (with an assistant).
Percuss from the umbilicus toward both lateral regions; mark the border of dullness.
Turn the child on the side and repeat percussion; assess the shift of dullness.
Conclusion.

skills.title: Skill 6. Auscultofriction

items: Place the stethoscope on the epigastric area, to the left of the linea alba.
With one finger make light rubbing movements along the abdominal skin from below (from the level of the umbilicus) upward, toward the stethoscope.
Mark the place where the sound becomes sharply louder as the lower border of the stomach.
Measure the distance from the umbilicus (normally 2–4 cm above).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 10-year-old girl complains of a dull pain like a feeling of heaviness in the right hypochondrium; the pain increases after fatty and fried food and radiates to the right shoulder; there is a bitter taste in the mouth and nausea. On examination: the tongue is coated with a yellowish coating. The abdomen is soft and tender in the right hypochondrium. The Kehr, Ortner and Murphy signs are positive. The liver is at the edge of the costal arch, 9–7–8 cm according to Kurlov. The spleen is not palpable.
cases.ask: 1) Involvement of which organ do you suspect? 2) Explain the positive signs. 3) Assess the liver dimensions. 4) Which investigations are needed?
cases.answer: 1) The gallbladder and biliary tract (biliary dyskinesia or cholecystitis). 2) Kehr — pain on deep palpation over the gallbladder projection; Ortner–Grekov — pain on tapping the right costal arch; Murphy — pain on deep inspiration — signs of gallbladder irritation. 3) The liver dimensions are within the age norm (9–10, 7, 8 cm) — no hepatomegaly. 4) Abdominal ultrasound (shape and wall of the gallbladder, stones) and ultrasound with a cholekinetic breakfast (gallbladder contraction), blood biochemistry (bilirubin, ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase), stool for Giardia.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: An 8-month-old child. 4 hours ago the child suddenly began to cry intensely, drawing the legs up to the abdomen, calming down after 10–15 minutes, then the attack recurs. Vomited 2 times. Yesterday meat puree was given for the first time. On examination: the child is pale and lethargic between attacks. The abdomen is slightly distended, a sausage-shaped tender mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant, the right iliac region is “empty”. On digital rectal examination there is blood-stained mucus on the glove.
cases.ask: 1) Presumptive diagnosis? 2) Which signs confirm the diagnosis? 3) Why are children of this age predisposed to this condition? 4) The doctor's tactics?
cases.answer: 1) Intestinal intussusception (ileocecal). 2) Age (4–12 months), sudden onset when complementary foods are introduced, colicky pain (attacks of restlessness with quiet intervals), vomiting, a palpable sausage-shaped mass, an empty right iliac region, blood-stained mucus from the rectum (“raspberry jelly”). 3) The long and mobile mesentery, poorly fixed intestinal loops, active motility, and disturbance of the peristaltic rhythm when complementary foods are introduced. 4) Urgent surgical examination, abdominal ultrasound (“target” sign), air or hydrostatic reduction (in the first hours) or surgery; do not give analgesics.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 4-year-old child at a preventive check-up. No complaints. On examination: the abdomen is slightly protuberant, symmetric, takes part in breathing. On superficial palpation the abdomen is soft and painless. The sigmoid colon is palpable in the left iliac region as a smooth, dense-elastic, mobile, painless cylinder 1.5 cm in diameter. The liver projects 1 cm below the costal arch along the midclavicular line, with a sharp, soft-elastic, painless edge. The spleen is not palpable.
cases.ask: 1) Assess the palpation findings. 2) Is the projection of the liver edge pathological? 3) How are the liver dimensions determined at this age?
cases.answer: 1) All the findings correspond to the age norm: the abdomen is soft and painless, the sigmoid colon has normal characteristics, the spleen is not palpable. 2) No, at 3–7 years projection of the liver edge up to 1 cm below the costal arch is physiological; a sharp edge, soft-elastic consistency and absence of pain are normal. 3) Up to 5 years the liver dimensions are determined by percussion along the right anterior axillary, midclavicular and midline (the norm at preschool age is approximately 6–7, 5, 6 cm); the Kurlov method is used from 5 years.

topics.title: Laboratory, functional, radiological and endoscopic methods of examining the digestive system. Semiotics and main syndromes of digestive system involvement

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the laboratory (coprology, biochemistry, bacteriology), functional (pH-metry, duodenal intubation), radiological (ultrasound, X-ray, CT, MRI) and endoscopic methods of examining the digestive system, their indications and contraindications;
the methods of detecting H. pylori infection;
the main signs of digestive system involvement: abdominal pain, dyspepsia, vomiting, regurgitation, diarrhea, constipation, meteorism, jaundice;
the coprological, biochemical and instrumental syndromes;

the main clinical syndromes of digestive system involvement (gastritis, pylorospasm, pyloric stenosis, duodenitis, ulcer, pancreatitis, biliary dysfunction, cytolysis, cholestasis, liver failure, portal hypertension, enteritis, malabsorption, colitis, irritable bowel syndrome).

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: analyze the coprogram and the biochemical parameters of the liver and pancreas;
interpret the results of duodenal intubation and ultrasound;
prepare the patient for instrumental investigations;
distinguish the types of jaundice by laboratory signs;
distinguish pylorospasm from pyloric stenosis by clinical and laboratory signs;
identify the leading syndrome and draw up an investigation plan.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: The color of jaundice: **“Lemon — hemolysis, orange — hepatitis, olive — obstructive”**. Itching and acholic stools are a sign of **cholestasis** (obstructive).

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In Kildiyarova's table, potassium in adrenogenital syndrome is given as “reduced” and the ABB as “metabolic alkalosis”. In salt-wasting adrenogenital syndrome, because of aldosterone deficiency, **hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis** are seen instead — the table has been corrected according to current data. In pyloric stenosis, by contrast, **hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis** is typical because hydrochloric acid-containing gastric contents are lost.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In a newborn, **bilious (green) vomiting** is a sign of obstruction below the duodenum (intestinal malrotation and volvulus, atresia) and is regarded as **a surgical emergency**. Non-bilious “projectile” vomiting at 2–3 weeks — pyloric stenosis; vomiting + dehydration + skin pigmentation + hyperkalemia — the salt-wasting form of adrenogenital syndrome.

blocks.text: Stool analysis (coprology)

**Coprological examination** — macroscopic (amount, color, consistency, odor, visible admixtures — mucus, blood, pus), chemical (reaction, stercobilin, bilirubin, occult blood, soluble protein) and microscopic examination of the stool. The external features of a healthy child's stool depend on the type of feeding and the nature of the food (see topic 12); there are no admixtures; on microscopy **small amounts** of fatty acids, muscle fibers (in children over 1 year), fiber, mucus and **single leukocytes** are found.
**The Bristol scale** is used to assess **stool form**:

blocks.text: Coprological signs:

items: **Steatorrhea** — fat in the stool: **type 1** — neutral fat (pancreatic lipase deficiency); **type 2** — fatty acids and soaps (insufficient bile secretion, intestinal malabsorption); **type 3** — both. Steatorrhea is **the earliest sign of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency**.
**Creatorrhea** — muscle fibers “++” or “+++” — deficiency of gastric and pancreatic enzymes, rapid passage of chyme.
**Amylorrhea** — many starch granules and digestible fiber — impaired carbohydrate breakdown (enteritis).
**Lienteria** — much fiber and connective tissue — rapid passage of chyme, excess plant food.

blocks.text: **The exocrine function of the pancreas** is assessed by stool trypsin, quantitative determination of fats and **fecal elastase-1**: normally **>200 µg/g** in children over 1 month; **<200 µg/g** — exocrine insufficiency.

blocks.text: **Bacteriological examination** (dysbiosis) — the composition of the intestinal microflora (normal, opportunistic or pathogenic); in dysbiosis the anaerobes (bifidobacteria) decrease and opportunistic flora increases. Stool analysis for **helminth eggs and protozoa** (Giardia) and a perianal scraping (enterobiasis) are also performed.
Biochemical investigations

**State of the liver:** proteinogram, lipid profile, total, direct and indirect bilirubin, **ALT, AST, LDH** (cytolysis), **alkaline phosphatase, GGT, 5'-nucleotidase** (cholestasis), prothrombin index, albumin, cholinesterase (synthetic function), thymol and sublimate tests.
**Pancreas:** blood glucose, **amylase** and **lipase**, urinary **diastase**.

rows: Increased ALT, AST, LDH-5, GGT, aldolase, bilirubin
Increased direct bilirubin, bile acids, cholesterol, β-lipoproteins, alkaline phosphatase, GGT
Hypoalbuminemia, reduced prothrombin index (impaired coagulation), reduced cholinesterase
Dysproteinemia (increased γ-globulins), raised thymol test, increased IgM, IgG

blocks.text: **Contraindications to tube methods:** exacerbation of peptic ulcer disease, gastrointestinal bleeding, acute cholecystitis, chronic diseases in the stage of decompensation, diverticula, esophageal anomalies, swallowing disorders, an attack of bronchial asthma, seizure syndrome.
Examination of gastric secretion
**Fractional gastric intubation** (secretory, acid-forming, enzymatic and motor functions) — now hardly used.

**Intragastric pH-metry** — the juice is not aspirated; a probe with pH electrodes measures while in contact with the mucosa. In a 5-sensor probe the sensors are located in the duodenum, antrum, body of the stomach, cardia and esophagus; the measurement lasts 30 minutes before stimulation and 1 hour after stimulation (histamine, pentagastrin). The method allows **gastroesophageal and duodenogastric refluxes** to be recorded and the dose of antacid/antisecretory drugs to be chosen. **24-hour pH monitoring** is the “gold standard” for the diagnosis of GERD.
Fractional duodenal intubation

It gives the most complete information on the biliary system; on an empty stomach, the tube is passed into the duodenum and bile is collected. As a choleretic stimulus, **33% (or 25%) magnesium sulfate** or 20% glucose solution is given at **0.3–0.5 ml/kg** (warm).
