items: **Hyperkinetic (hypermotor)** type — the bile flow rate A >1.5, B >3, C >2 ml/min; the gallbladder reflex time **<5 min**.
**Hypokinetic (hypomotor)** type — slow bile flow, the volume of portion B and the gallbladder reflex time (**>8 min**) increased.

blocks.text: **Microscopy:** in portions B and C — biliary epithelium, **cholesterol crystals, calcium bilirubinate**, mucus, **leukocytoids** (inflammation), **vegetative forms of Giardia**. **Biochemistry:** in cholecystitis and cholangitis protein increases in portions B and C; reduced bile acids and lecithin make the bile **lithogenic** (stone formation). The portions are also sent for bacteriological examination — normally the bile is **sterile**.
Ultrasound examination

Radiological examination of the abdomen **begins with ultrasound** — safe, noninvasive, informative, with no contraindications. The size and structure of the organs are assessed. **Ultrasound signs:** in ascites, free fluid (if little — in the lateral canals and small pelvis) and the intestine floating upward; in acute inflammation the ultrasound conductivity of the liver increases; tumors have clear borders; gallbladder anomalies, bile thickening, **stones**; in portal hypertension **the diameter of the portal and splenic veins increases**; thickening of the gastric wall (gastritis); in acute pancreatitis the gland is enlarged with reduced echogenicity, in chronic pancreatitis it is small with indistinct contours; abscess, hematoma, cysts; in pyloric stenosis the pyloric canal is elongated and the muscle layer thickened; in intussusception **the “target” sign**.

**Ultrasound with a cholekinetic breakfast** — the motor function of the gallbladder: 2 egg yolks or 20 g sorbitol in 100 ml water are given, and the gallbladder volume is measured every 10 minutes for 1 hour. Normally **by 40–50 minutes the gallbladder contracts evenly by 50–60%**; **>60%** — hypermotor, **<50%** and a slow rhythm — hypomotor dyskinesia.
X-ray examination
The main and decisive method for detecting congenital anomalies, developmental defects, acquired organic lesions and complications of peptic ulcer disease:

items: **plain abdominal X-ray without contrast** — fluid **levels** and gas **“arches”** in intestinal obstruction; **free gas** under the diaphragm in perforation (a “crescent-shaped” lucency);

**contrast examination** (barium sulfate suspension) — esophagus, stomach and intestines; in peptic ulcer disease the **“niche” sign**, signs of penetration and stenosis; **irrigography** — colon (Hirschsprung disease, dolichosigma);
**oral cholecystography**, relaxation duodenography, retrograde cholangiopancreatography — special methods.

blocks.text: Computed tomography, MRI and radioisotope investigation

items: **CT** — accurately assesses the state of the stomach, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, spleen and intestine without complex preparation; **40–50 times more sensitive** than classic radiography; it is performed after drinking a contrast medium (enhanced CT).

**MRI** — based on differences in the magnetic properties of tissue molecules; especially effective for studying dynamic processes such as blood flow; **MR cholangiopancreatography** — noninvasive imaging of the biliary and pancreatic ducts.
**Radioisotope scanning (scintigraphy)** — based on uptake of a radiopharmaceutical by hepatocytes, tumor or inflammatory cells (hepatobiliary scintigraphy, detection of Meckel's diverticulum).

blocks.text: **Endoscopy** — viewing the digestive tube with an endoscope; it allows the diagnosis to be clarified, the depth and extent of the process to be assessed, and **a targeted biopsy** to be taken. In children it is performed with special preparation, often under **anesthesia**.

items: **Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGDS)** — viewing the esophagus, stomach, duodenum (and jejunum) in one examination. **Indications:** pain syndrome, recurrent vomiting, bleeding from the upper parts; **therapeutic endoscopy** — removal of foreign bodies, polypectomy, sclerotherapy of esophageal and gastric varices, dilatation of strictures.

**Rectosigmoidoscopy** — the rectum and the distal sigmoid colon; **colonoscopy** — the whole colon. The indication is justified by a specialist (gastroenterologist, proctologist, surgeon); at an early age under anesthesia.

**Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)** — during duodenoscopy the papilla of Vater is cannulated and the biliary and pancreatic ducts are contrasted; disadvantages — complexity, radiation dose, risk of the complication of **acute pancreatitis**.
**Video capsule endoscopy** — viewing the small intestine (Crohn disease, occult bleeding).

blocks.label: Figure 13.3
blocks.caption: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy: endoscopic appearance of the gastric mucosa (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Biopsy** — pathomorphological examination of altered tissue: determining the nature of space-occupying lesions, inflammatory and functional diseases (e.g., villous atrophy of the small intestine in celiac disease, detection of H. pylori). By fine-needle aspiration (cytology) or needle biopsy (a piece of tissue).
Detection of Helicobacter pylori infection
Detection of H. pylori determines the need for **etiotropic (eradication) therapy** in chronic gastric diseases.

items: **Bacteriological** — culture of a gastric biopsy on a special medium;
**morphological** — staining of histological preparations by Giemsa, toluidine blue, Warthin–Starry;
**cytological** — staining of biopsy smear-imprints by Giemsa, Gram;
**urea breath test** — labeled (^13^C or ^14^C) urea is drunk, and the isotope released by bacterial urease is detected in the exhaled air (noninvasive);
**rapid urease test** — the biopsy is placed in a medium with a substrate, buffer and indicator (color change);
**PCR** — the most reliable method;
**screening methods** — ELISA (antibodies in the blood), H. pylori antigen in the stool, rapid tests.

blocks.text: Abdominal pain
The location of pain is given in the table in topic 12. **The relation of pain to food** is important:

blocks.title: Table 13.5. Relation of pain to food intake and defecation
head: Type of pain
Time
Probable pathology
rows: 6–7 hours after eating; relieved after eating

blocks.text: **The “Moynihan rhythm” is typical of duodenal ulcer**: hunger → pain → relief after eating → hunger → pain.

**Character of pain: visceral** (dull, diffuse, poorly localized — distension or spasm of hollow organs); **parietal (somatic)** — sharp, well localized, increased by movement (peritoneal irritation); **referred (radiating)**. Colicky paroxysmal pain — spasm of a hollow organ (intestinal, biliary, renal colic).
Dyspeptic signs

items: **Belching:** of air (aerophagia), **with the smell of rotten eggs** — achylia (hypoacid gastritis); **sour** — increased acidity or fermentation (gastritis, peptic ulcer disease); **bitter** — bile reflux (duodenogastric reflux); **putrid** — decomposition of food residues in stenosis or obstruction of the esophagus, cardia, stomach or duodenum.
**Heartburn** — a burning, hot or pressing sensation spreading from the epigastrium behind the sternum; in gastroesophageal reflux and diseases with excessive acid production.
**Hiccups** — spasmodic contractions of the diaphragm; in acute gastric dilatation, meteorism, diseases of the diaphragm.
**Nausea** — an unpleasant sensation in the epigastrium and pharynx, before or together with vomiting.

blocks.text: Vomiting
**Vomiting** — an act resulting from stimulation of the vomiting center reflexly via the vagus nerve, directly by toxins, or by CNS processes.

items: **Central vomiting** — in CNS pathology; it is not preceded by nausea, is not related to food, is small in volume and **brings no relief**.
**Peripheral (reflex) vomiting** — in damage to the internal organs; sudden, without nausea, brings no relief.
**Gastric vomiting** — 0.5–1.5 hours after eating, preceded by nausea, large in volume, with a sour smell, **brings temporary relief**.
**Acetonemic vomiting** — repeated, acetone breath odor, acetone in the urine.

blocks.text: Regurgitation and rumination

**Regurgitation** — the **weak return, without straining of the abdominal press,** of swallowed food or secretions to the oral cavity and outside. Up to 6–7 months, if it is **infrequent** and occurs not later than 1 hour after feeding — **physiological**.

**Assessed:** time of onset (from birth, from 2–3 weeks, from 3–4 months), frequency (2–3 times a day, after each feed, more than 10 times), provoking factors (feeding, crying, swaddling), volume (small, “a mouthful”, **“projectile”**), the nature of the contents (fresh or curdled milk, bile, sour or sweetish smell), relation to feeding.

**Rumination** — for at least 3 months, gastric contents are returned to the mouth by periodic contractions of the abdominal press, diaphragm and tongue muscles, re-chewed and swallowed; in children aged 3–8 months, often with CNS pathology.
Diarrhea, constipation, meteorism

**Diarrhea** — frequent defecation with altered stool (from mushy to watery). **Acute** — up to 2–3 weeks (intestinal infections, drugs — antibiotics, alimentary causes); **chronic** — more than 3 weeks or recurrent (inflammatory bowel diseases, irritable bowel syndrome, malabsorption — celiac disease, disaccharidase deficiency, cystic fibrosis; pancreatitis, gastrointestinal allergy, parasitoses, endocrine diseases).

Infectious causes

rows: Overfeeding, cow's milk protein intolerance, carbohydrate malabsorption, irritable bowel syndrome, chloride diarrhea, hyperthyroidism, congenital adrenal hyperplasia
Cystic fibrosis, Shwachman syndrome, chronic pancreatitis, intestinal lymphangiectasia

blocks.text: **Constipation** — prolongation of the intervals between defecations relative to the individual norm, or regular incomplete emptying of the bowel. A healthy child over 1 year should pass stool at least **1 time in 36 hours**. At an early age, even if stools occur several times a day, stools passed with strong straining, distress and crying, as **“sheep droppings”** or in lumps, with traces of blood and mucus — constipation. **Chronic constipation** — more than 3 months. Causes: alimentary (little fiber, much protein and fat, excess calcium — the most common at an early age), neurogenic, dyskinetic, psychogenic, endocrine (hypothyroidism), mechanical, colonic anomalies (**Hirschsprung disease**, dolichosigma), drugs.

**Meteorism** — excessive formation, accumulation or impaired passage of gas in the gastrointestinal tract; gurgling in the abdomen, passage of gas; it may also occur in a healthy person after overeating and gas-forming foods.
Jaundice

**Jaundice** — yellowing of the skin and visible mucous membranes as a result of increased bilirubin in the blood and tissues. Yellowing of the skin and sclera becomes visible when bilirubin is **>68.4–85.5 µmol/l** in the newborn and **>26 µmol/l** in older children.

**Physiological (neonatal) jaundice** — appears **after 48 hours** of life, usually disappears **by day 7–10** (at the latest by week 2–3), no hepatosplenomegaly, normal stool and urine color, bilirubin increases at the expense of the indirect fraction (up to 252 µmol/l in term babies, up to 175 µmol/l in preterm babies).

**False (carotene) jaundice** — with a high intake of carrots, oranges, pumpkin and persimmons only **the skin** (palms, soles) turns yellow, **the mucous membranes and sclera are not stained**, bilirubin is normal.

sections.title: 13.6. Main syndromes of digestive system involvement

blocks.text: Syndrome of impaired digestion in the oral cavity

Causes: disturbed sucking and swallowing (prematurity, CNS damage, cleft lip and palate, short frenulum of the tongue), stomatitis, dental pathology, salivary gland diseases. Manifestations — difficulty sucking and chewing, drooling, breath odor, refusal of food, the “oral syndrome” on coprology.
Gastritis syndrome
Classification: by course — acute, chronic; by extent — diffuse, focal; by secretion — with increased or reduced acidity; by depth — superficial, atrophic, erosive, hypertrophic.

**Clinical picture:** dull, distending, pressing or stabbing pain in the epigastrium related to food; night and seasonal pain favor increased acidity, an erosive process and antral location. Dyspepsia: nausea, vomiting after eating, belching of air, food and **with a rotten-egg smell** (hypoacid state), **heartburn** (hyperacid state), a feeling of heaviness, reduced appetite, unstable stool — **diarrhea** (hypoacid) or **constipation** (hyperacid). The tongue is coated with a white coating; epigastric tenderness on palpation.
**Investigations:** coprogram — many unchanged muscle fibers, digestible fiber and connective tissue “+++”; **EGDS** — hyperemia, edema, mucus, fasting fluid, refluxes; H. pylori tests.

**Functional disorder of the stomach (functional dyspepsia)** — short, inconstant, mild epigastric pains of various character, not related to food; no endoscopic, radiological or morphological changes.
Pylorospasm and pyloric stenosis

**Pylorospasm** — **a functional spasm of the gastric outlet** in young children. Predisposition: the cylindrical shape of the stomach, weakness of the cardiac muscles and **strong development of the pyloric muscles**, immaturity of the gastric fundus, pressure of the large liver, imperfect neuroregulatory mechanisms. **From the first days after birth**: inconstant, small-volume, frequent regurgitation and vomiting (immediately or after 15–20 minutes); the volume of the vomit is **less than the milk taken**; weight gain is slow but steady; no exsicosis or oliguria, no visible peristalsis; on X-ray passage is not impaired.

**Pyloric stenosis** — **a developmental defect** of the gastric outlet (hypertrophy of the muscle layer); in 1:2000 births, mainly **in boys**. The pyloric part is thickened in the shape of an olive (“olive”) (2–3.5 cm long, 1.5–3 cm wide), almost cartilage-like in density. The clinical picture appears **from week 2–3**: persistent **“projectile” vomiting**, large in volume, **the volume of the vomit is always greater than the volume of the feed**, immediately after feeding; the vomit **never contains bile**; the child loses weight quickly, dehydration, oliguria, stool retention (“**hunger stools**” — scanty stool resembling meconium); **“hourglass”**-shaped peristalsis in the epigastrium; a dense **“olive” of 2–4 cm** is palpable at the edge of the right rectus muscle, midway between the umbilicus and the xiphoid process. On X-ray barium is retained in the stomach for **24 hours or longer**, and emptying does not begin in the first 15–20 minutes. **Ultrasound** is the main diagnostic method (pyloric muscle thickness ≥3–4 mm, canal length ≥15–17 mm). Treatment — **surgical (pyloromyotomy)**.

Pyloric stenosis
Adrenogenital syndrome (salt-wasting)

parts.text: In Kildiyarova's table, potassium in adrenogenital syndrome is given as “reduced” and the ABB as “metabolic alkalosis”. In salt-wasting adrenogenital syndrome, because of aldosterone deficiency, **hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis** are seen instead — the table has been corrected according to current data. In pyloric stenosis, by contrast, **hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis** is typical because hydrochloric acid-containing gastric contents are lost.

blocks.text: Involvement of the duodenum (duodenitis)

Pains of various intensity related to food, most often **late** (2–3 hours after eating), sometimes night and early, in the right upper half of the abdomen; nausea, vomiting, unstable stool; **autonomic syndrome** (periodic headache, dizziness, disturbed sleep, rapid fatigue, irritability — related to disturbance of the endocrine function of the duodenum). On examination pallor, weight deficit, coated tongue, tenderness in **the pyloroduodenal (Chauffard) zone**. EGDS confirms the diagnosis.
Peptic ulcer syndrome (peptic ulcer disease)
Predisposing factors: hereditary predisposition, stress (emotional strain, CNS diseases), irregular eating, **H. pylori**, long-term intake of ulcerogenic drugs (NSAIDs).

**Duodenal ulcer** — hunger, night and late (2–4 hours) pains, **the Moynihan rhythm**, severe, recurrent, to the right of and above the umbilicus; heartburn, sour belching, nausea, vomiting, constipation; autonomic disturbances are more frequent. **Gastric ulcer** — early pain, slightly above the umbilicus along the midline; nausea and vomiting after eating. On examination: forced position, autonomic lability (distal hyperhidrosis, persistent red dermographism, bradycardia, hypotension), tension of the abdominal muscles, zones of skin hyperesthesia, a positive **Mendel's sign**, **Oppenhowski's points** (pain on percussion over the spinous processes of the thoracic vertebrae). Diagnosis — **EGDS** (the ulcer defect), the “niche” sign on contrast X-ray.

**Complications:** bleeding (“coffee grounds” vomiting, **melena** — black tarry stool), perforation (“dagger-like” pain, “board-like” abdomen, disappearance of liver dullness), penetration, stenosis.
Pancreatitis syndrome

In gross dietary errors, infections (mumps), abdominal trauma, gastrointestinal pathology. Sharp **girdle-like pain** above the umbilicus, nausea, **repeated vomiting** of gastric contents, intoxication, disturbed stool. In the blood — leukocytosis, raised ESR; increased **amylase, lipase, trypsin**; increased urinary diastase. Ultrasound — edema, enlargement and disturbed structure of the gland. In chronic pancreatitis — exocrine insufficiency (steatorrhea, reduced elastase-1).
Biliary tract dysfunction syndrome (biliary dyskinesia)

Causes: long intervals between meals, dry food, abuse of carbohydrate and fatty food, disturbed daily routine; anatomical defects of the gallbladder (kinks, constrictions); reflex, in diseases of other digestive organs. **Gallbladder dysfunction** and **dystonia of the sphincter of Oddi**; by functional state — **hypokinetic (hypomotor)** and **hyperkinetic (hypermotor)** forms.

The main sign is a dull or sharp pain in the right hypochondrium that **increases after eating and after physical exertion**; nausea, vomiting, **a bitter taste in the mouth**, signs of cholestasis, liver enlargement, pain in the right hypochondrium, epigastrium and Chauffard's zone, **positive gallbladder signs**. In the **hyperkinetic** form — short, paroxysmal, colicky pains; in the **hypokinetic** form — constant dull pain with a feeling of heaviness. Diagnosis — ultrasound with a cholekinetic breakfast, duodenal intubation.
Syndromes of liver involvement

**Cytolysis syndrome** — in viral, infectious and noninfectious, parasitic (echinococcus), toxic (drugs, heavy metal salts, benzene) influences, anomalies of the biliary tract, congenital metabolic disorders. **Clinical picture:** pain and heaviness in the right hypochondrium, dyspepsia (reduced appetite, nausea, bilious vomiting, meteorism, unstable stool), astheno-vegetative signs (weakness, rapid fatigue, sweating, headache), signs of cholestasis (itching, subicterus). The skin is pale, sometimes icteric, dry; scratch marks, ecchymoses, petechiae; **spider angiomas** (telangiectasias), **palmar erythema** (“liver palms”); **hepatosplenomegaly** — the liver dense, tender, smooth. **Dark urine (“beer-colored”)**, discolored stool. Laboratory: increased ALT, AST, LDH, bilirubin mainly at the expense of the direct fraction, dysproteinemia, increased IgM; prolonged detection of HBsAg — a sign of chronicity.

**Cholestasis syndrome** — disturbed bile flow: **itching of the skin**, pigmentation, **xanthomas**, inconstant jaundice, dyspepsia, astheno-vegetative syndrome; scratch marks, hepatosplenomegaly. Laboratory: high cholesterol, bile acids, β-lipoproteins, total lipids, **alkaline phosphatase**, leucine aminopeptidase; increased direct bilirubin.

**Hepatocellular insufficiency syndrome** — when only **20–25%** of the liver parenchyma remains functional. The **acute** form (more often at an early age) — viral hepatitis, hepatotropic poisons (death cap, mushrooms, barbiturates) — hepatic necrosis and coma; **chronic** — as a result of cirrhosis, congenital infections, hereditary diseases. **Clinical picture:** change in behavior — lethargy, stupor, adynamia, drowsiness (less often agitation), then confusion and **coma**; intoxication, pale-yellow skin, dystrophy of the muscles and subcutaneous fat, avitaminosis, liver signs (“lacquered” tongue, spider angiomas, palmar erythema), abdominal enlargement (meteorism, hepatosplenomegaly, **ascites**), edema of the legs, **hemorrhagic syndrome** (bleeding from the nose, gums, gastrointestinal tract); laboratory — hypoalbuminemia, reduced prothrombin. **When coma develops the liver begins to shrink** — a poor prognostic sign.

**Portal hypertension syndrome** — increased pressure in the portal venous system; prehepatic, intrahepatic and posthepatic forms. The main signs — **varicose dilatation of the esophageal and gastric veins** (X-ray, endoscopy), **splenomegaly**, hepatomegaly, **ascites**, a venous network on the anterior abdominal wall (“caput medusae”).
Syndromes of impaired digestion in the small intestine

**Enteritis syndrome** — against a background of intestinal infections (coli infection, salmonellosis), food allergy, operations on the small intestine, gross dietary errors, extraintestinal diseases (influenza, pneumonia, otitis). **Diarrhea** (painless, with passage of gas, followed by relief), meteorism, gurgling, pain **around the umbilicus** after eating; signs of intestinal toxicosis and dehydration (gray skin, the fold smooths out slowly). Coprogram: the stool watery, copious, unformed, pale yellow, with a **sour** (fermentation) or **fetid** (putrefaction) odor, mucus mixed with the stool, altered muscle fibers, fatty acids, soaps.

**Dyspeptic syndrome of infants (simple dyspepsia)** — disturbed feeding routine (overfeeding, too frequent feeding), a diet inappropriate for age, too rapid transfer to artificial feeding. Diarrhea (6–8 times a day, liquid, yellow-green, sour-smelling, with a little mucus and **white flakes** — magnesium and calcium soaps of fatty acids), regurgitation, reduced appetite; the general condition is not disturbed, temperature normal, no dehydration, steady weight gain; no pathogenic flora grows.

**Malabsorption syndrome** — **impaired absorption** in the small intestine: recurrent diarrhea, **polyfecalia** and progressive dystrophy. **Causes:** congenital and hereditary diseases (**celiac disease**, **cystic fibrosis**, disaccharidase (lactase) deficiency, exudative enteropathy), food allergy (cow's milk proteins), chronic inflammation (enterocolitis, pancreatitis), tumors, intestinal resection (“short bowel” syndrome), long-term antibiotics, massive giardiasis; secondary — against a background of severe diseases.

**Clinical picture:** the stool watery or frothy, **large in volume**, **gray and clay-like**, fetid (**steatorrhea**), **greasy and shiny**, leaving greasy stains on diapers that are difficult to wash, the potty is hard to clean; vomiting, progressive **anorexia**, abdominal distension, spastic pains, **abdominal enlargement**, emaciation, **lagging physical development** (slowed growth, weight deficit); signs of vitamin and trace element deficiency (anemia, rickets-like changes, hypoproteinemic edema).

blocks.label: Figure 13.5
blocks.caption: Abdominal enlargement and thinning of the limbs in the malabsorption syndrome (celiac disease) (Kildiyarova)

parts.text: **Celiac disease** — intolerance of gluten (the protein of wheat, rye, barley); symptoms begin 1–2 months **after cereals (porridge, bread) are introduced**. Diagnosis: **IgA antibodies to tissue transglutaminase** in the blood (with total IgA), antibodies to endomysium, duodenal biopsy (villous atrophy). Treatment — **a lifelong gluten-free diet**. **Lactase deficiency** — frothy, sour-smelling diarrhea and meteorism after milk intake; stool pH <5.5, carbohydrates >0.25%. **Cystic fibrosis** — fatty diarrhea + recurrent bronchopulmonary infections; sweat chloride >60 mmol/l.

blocks.text: Impaired digestion in the colon (colitis syndrome)

Infections (dysentery, food toxicoinfections), parasitoses (amebiasis), helminthiases (enterobiasis, hymenolepiasis, trichuriasis), candidomycosis, noninfectious diseases (**ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease**). Colicky pains in the lower abdomen increasing with defecation, **tenesmus** (false urges), defecation **brings no relief**; frequent stools (10–12 times a day, 20–30 times in severe cases), **mucus, pus, blood** in the stool; in severe cases the stool loses its fecal character (“rectal spit”). Coprogram: much mucus, leukocytes, erythrocytes; pathogenic flora on bacteriological examination.
Irritable bowel syndrome

**A functional** pathology: abdominal pain or discomfort (usually **relieved by defecation**), dyspepsia (meteorism, gurgling, diarrhea, constipation or their alternation), a feeling of incomplete emptying of the bowel, imperative urges; lasting **at least 3 months**. It is **a diagnosis of exclusion**. **“Red flag” signs** that exclude it: unexplained weight loss, predominance of symptoms **at night**, constant severe pain, fever, hepatosplenomegaly, **blood in the stool**, leukocytosis, anemia, raised ESR, biochemical changes.
Algorithm for examining a child with abdominal pain

items: Exclude **an “acute abdomen”** (see topic 12) — surgical examination. 2) Look for **“red flag”** signs (weight loss, night pain and diarrhea, bloody stools, fever, growth retardation, inflammatory bowel diseases in the family). If they are absent and the pain lasts more than 2 months — most often **functional pain** (functional dyspepsia, irritable bowel syndrome, abdominal migraine). 3) Minimal investigation: CBC and urinalysis, coprogram, helminths and Giardia, **abdominal ultrasound**, biochemistry (ALT, AST, amylase, bilirubin), and if necessary **EGDS** and an H. pylori test.

blocks.text: Approach to a vomiting newborn

parts.text: In a newborn, **bilious (green) vomiting** is a sign of obstruction below the duodenum (intestinal malrotation and volvulus, atresia) and is regarded as **a surgical emergency**. Non-bilious “projectile” vomiting at 2–3 weeks — pyloric stenosis; vomiting + dehydration + skin pigmentation + hyperkalemia — the salt-wasting form of adrenogenital syndrome.

blocks.text: Cholestatic jaundice in a newborn

parts.text: Jaundice lasting more than 2 weeks, **colorless stools** and dark urine — suspect **biliary atresia**; direct bilirubin (>20% of total) is determined and the child is referred to a surgeon immediately: the result is much better if the Kasai operation is performed **before 60 days**.

skills.title: Skill 1. Interpreting a coprogram

items: Macroscopic parameters: amount, form (Bristol scale), color, odor, mucus, blood, pus.
Chemical: reaction (pH), stercobilin, bilirubin, occult blood, soluble protein.
Microscopy: muscle fibers, connective tissue, neutral fat, fatty acids, soaps, starch, fiber, mucus, leukocytes, erythrocytes, helminth eggs, protozoa.
Identify the coprological signs (type of steatorrhea, creatorrhea, amylorrhea).
Identify the coprological syndrome and indicate the probably affected part.

skills.title: Skill 2. Determining the type of jaundice by laboratory signs

items: Assess the ratio of total, direct and indirect bilirubin in the blood.
Assess urinary urobilinogen and bilirubin.
Assess the stool color and stercobilin.
Take into account ALT, AST, alkaline phosphatase, GGT, hemoglobin, reticulocytes.
Conclusion: prehepatic, hepatic or posthepatic jaundice.

skills.title: Skill 3. Preparing a child for instrumental investigations

items: **Abdominal ultrasound:** on an empty stomach (small children 3–4 hours after the last meal, older children 8–12 hours), limit gas-forming foods for 2–3 days beforehand; simethicone in meteorism.
**EGDS:** on an empty stomach, 6–8 hours after the last meal (4 hours in infants); informed consent from the parents; remove dentures and foreign bodies.
**Contrast X-ray:** on an empty stomach; bowel cleansing before irrigography and colonoscopy (diet, cleansing enema or osmotic laxatives).
**Duodenal intubation:** a light supper in the evening, on an empty stomach; insert the tube with the child lying on the right side.
Explain the nature of the investigation to the child and the parents.

skills.title: Skill 4. Clinical examination for pyloric stenosis (“test feed”)

items: Feed the child and observe: time of vomiting, volume (compared with the volume of the feed), bile admixture.
Observe the epigastrium from the side in light to detect **“hourglass”**-shaped peristalsis.
After vomiting (empty stomach), palpate deeply at the edge of the right rectus muscle, midway between the umbilicus and the xiphoid process, to look for **the “olive”**.
Assess the signs of dehydration, diuresis and weight; send for electrolytes and ABB.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 3-week-old boy. For 5 days he has had “projectile” vomiting immediately after each feed; the vomit is larger in volume than the milk taken, sour-smelling, without bile. The baby feeds greedily, but his weight is 250 g less than at birth. The stool is scanty, thick, dark green. Little urine. On examination: dry skin, sunken anterior fontanelle. “Hourglass”-shaped peristalsis is visible in the epigastrium. After vomiting, a dense mobile mass of 2 cm is palpable at the edge of the right rectus muscle. Blood: K 2.9 mmol/l, Cl 85 mmol/l, pH 7.52, BE +9.
cases.ask: 1) Presumptive diagnosis? 2) Which signs distinguish it from pylorospasm? 3) Explain the electrolyte and ABB changes. 4) Method of confirming the diagnosis and treatment?
cases.answer: 1) Pyloric stenosis, dehydration, hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. 2) Onset at 2–3 weeks, vomit volume greater than the feed, “projectile” vomiting, marked weight loss, dehydration, oliguria, “hourglass” peristalsis, palpable “olive”, “hunger stools”, electrolyte disturbances (absent in pylorospasm, where vomiting is from the first days and small in volume). 3) Hydrochloric acid (H^+^ and Cl^–^) is lost with the vomit — hypochloremia and metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.52, BE +9); the kidney excretes K to retain Na — hypokalemia. 4) Abdominal ultrasound (pyloric muscle thickness ≥3–4 mm, canal length ≥15–17 mm); contrast X-ray (barium retained up to 24 hours). After correction of dehydration and electrolytes — pyloromyotomy (Ramstedt operation).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A girl aged 1 year 6 months. Since 10 months (after semolina porridge and bread were introduced) the stools have been copious, 3–4 times a day, gray, shiny, fetid, hard to wash out of diapers. Her appetite is reduced, she is irritable. Weight 8.5 kg (weight deficit), height below the age norm. On examination: the abdomen is markedly enlarged, the limbs thin, the subcutaneous fat layer thinned, the buttocks “bag-like”. Hb 95 g/l. Coprogram: many fatty acids and soaps, starch “++”.
cases.ask: 1) The leading syndrome? 2) Presumptive diagnosis? 3) Confirmatory investigations? 4) Principle of treatment?
cases.answer: 1) Malabsorption syndrome (polyfecalia, steatorrhea, dystrophy, growth retardation, anemia). 2) The onset of symptoms after gluten-containing foods (semolina, bread) were introduced — celiac disease. 3) IgA antibodies to tissue transglutaminase in the blood (together with total IgA), antibodies to endomysium; duodenal biopsy for confirmation (villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia); for differential diagnosis — sweat chloride (cystic fibrosis), fecal elastase-1. 4) A lifelong gluten-free diet (wheat, rye, barley and oat products are excluded; rice, corn and buckwheat are allowed), correction of anemia and vitamin deficiency.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 12-year-old boy has complained for 2 months of pain in the epigastrium and above and to the right of the umbilicus, appearing on an empty stomach and at night; the pain decreases after eating. There is heartburn, sour belching and constipation. His father has peptic ulcer disease. On examination: the tongue is coated with a white coating, the palms are moist, persistent red dermographism. Tenderness on palpation in the pyloroduodenal zone, Mendel's sign positive. Yesterday the stool was black and tarry.
cases.ask: 1) Presumptive diagnosis? 2) What is the pain rhythm called? 3) What does the black stool mean? 4) Which investigations are needed?
cases.answer: 1) Duodenal ulcer disease complicated by bleeding. 2) The Moynihan rhythm: hunger → pain → relief after eating; hunger, night and late pains are typical of duodenal ulcer. 3) Melena — a sign of bleeding from the upper parts (stomach, duodenum); breakdown of hemoglobin gives the black color — an emergency. 4) CBC (anemia), stool for occult blood, urgent EGDS (ulcer defect, hemostasis), H. pylori tests (rapid urease on the biopsy, later the urea breath test, stool antigen), abdominal ultrasound; blood group and coagulogram.

topics.title: The urinary and immune systems: anatomical and physiological features, methods of examination, urine tests and functional tests, semiotics of involvement

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the age-related anatomical and physiological features of the kidneys and urinary tract, the norms of diuresis and voiding frequency;
the methods of history taking, inspection, palpation and percussion of the urinary system;
the urinalysis, the Nechiporenko, Hamburger, Addis–Kakovsky and three-glass tests, the Zimnitsky, Rehberg and McClure–Aldrich tests and their norms;
instrumental investigations (ultrasound, urography, cystography, scintigraphy);
the main symptoms and syndromes of urinary system involvement;
the age-related features of the immune system, the “critical periods”, the methods of assessing immunity and the signs of immunodeficiency.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: detect edema, palpate the kidneys, test the pain points of the urinary tract, determine Pasternatsky's sign, percuss the border of the bladder;
calculate the daily diuresis by age;
interpret the results of urine tests and functional tests;
identify the leading renal syndrome;
assess the parameters of the immunogram and identify the warning signs of primary immunodeficiency.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: At an early age, the width, hypotonia and tortuosity of the urinary tract and the mobility of the kidney lead to **disturbed urodynamics** and the addition of **a microbial-inflammatory process (pyelonephritis)**.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Diuresis: **“600 + 100 for each year”**. A 7-year-old child: 600 + 100 × 6 = **1200 ml**. Number of voidings: newborn **20–25**, 1 year **15**, 3 years **≈10**, school age **6–7**.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: Geppe's textbook gives the norm for leukocytes in the Nechiporenko test as **up to 2000** (not divided by sex); Kildiyarova gives **up to 4000** for girls. In practice **leukocytes <2000, erythrocytes <1000 per 1 ml** are often taken as the norm.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Source of hematuria: **“Erythrocyte cast + protein + dysmorphic erythrocyte = glomerulus”**. Leukocyturia + bacteriuria + fever + positive Pasternatsky = **pyelonephritis**; leukocyturia + dysuria, without fever = **cystitis**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **Critical period 1 — the neonatal period (1st month):** **physiological depression** of the immune system; passive protection by maternal IgG; low phagocytosis, complement and interferon — susceptibility to pyogenic and gram-negative flora and viruses, a tendency of infection to **generalize** (sepsis). The first crossover of the leukocyte differential on day 4–5. **Critical period 2 — 3–6 months:** breakdown of maternal antibodies; the primary immune response (IgM) predominates, **immunological memory is not formed** — whooping cough and measles run an atypical course, reinfection is possible; local immunity is insufficient; allergic reactions and food allergy appear. **Critical period 3 — the 2nd year:** active exploration of the world, increasing contacts; local immunity remains insufficient; the response to the polysaccharide antigens of pneumococcus and Haemophilus is weak; most primary immunodeficiencies become manifest; diseases of the ENT organs and airways recur. **Critical period 4 — 4–6 years:** the second crossover of the leukocyte differential; IgG and IgM reach adult levels, secretory IgA is still low; parasitic invasions, atopic and immune complex diseases, late immunodeficiencies. **Critical period 5 — puberty (12–16 years in boys, 11–15 years in girls):** involution of the thymus, the mass of the lymphoid organs decreases; the influence of sex hormones — autoimmune and lymphoproliferative diseases increase.

summary.label: Caution
summary.text: In an infant with **unexplained fever (>38 °C)**, vomiting, poor appetite, failure to gain weight and restlessness, **urinalysis and urine culture** are mandatory (urinary tract infection is the most common bacterial cause of “occult” fever at an early age). After the first febrile pyelonephritis **renal ultrasound** is performed, and if it recurs — **voiding cystourethrography** (vesicoureteral reflux).

sections.title: 14.1. Anatomical and physiological features of the kidneys and urinary tract

blocks.text: At birth the morphological and functional development of the kidneys is **incomplete**. Defects of the urinary organs make up **≈1/3** of all congenital defects.

blocks.label: Figure 14.1
blocks.caption: Anatomical and physiological features of the urinary system in young children (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: The kidneys

items: **Mass and shape:** at an early age the kidneys are relatively **large**: in the newborn the kidney mass to body mass ratio is **1:100**, in adults **1:200**. Up to 1 year the kidney is **round**, then bean-shaped.

**Position:** because of their relatively large size and the shortness of the lumbar vertebrae, up to 1 year the kidneys lie **lower**: the upper pole at ThXI–XII, the lower pole **below L~IV~** (below the iliac crest); this feature disappears **by 7 years**. At an early age the kidneys lie almost **parallel**.
**Mobility:** the perirenal fat and fasciae are poorly developed — the kidneys are **mobile**; the fixation mechanisms form **at 5–8 years**.

**Structure:** in the 1st year **the lobulated structure** persists (it disappears at 2–5 years); the medulla is thicker than the cortex (1:4; 1:2 in adults). In a term newborn **the number of nephrons is the same as in adults (≈2 million)**, but the glomeruli are small, the nephrons are insufficiently differentiated until 2 years, and the loop of Henle is short. Morphological maturation of the cortex is completed **at 3–5 years**, and full maturation of the kidney **at school age**.

blocks.label: Figure 14.2
blocks.caption: Anatomical structure of the nephron (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: Functional features of the kidneys

items: **Low glomerular filtration:** the visceral layer of the glomerular capsule has **cuboidal epithelium**; the filtering surface is **5 times smaller** than in adults; renal blood flow is low (**5%** of the cardiac output in the newborn, 25% in adults). Filtration approaches adult levels **by 1 year**.

**Tubular reabsorption and secretion** develop gradually: amino acids, phosphates and bicarbonates are excreted in large amounts; glucose reabsorption is good; sodium is actively reabsorbed — **predisposition to edema**; water and NaCl loads cannot be excreted quickly; excretion of K, Ca and Mg is reduced.

**Concentrating function is low** (little ADH, a short loop of Henle, an immature distal tubule) — **low specific gravity** of the newborn's urine; adult concentrating ability develops **at 9–12 months**.
**Regulation of acid-base balance** is immature (low secretion of hydrogen and ammonium ions) — **acidosis** develops quickly in diseases at an early age.

The optimal homeostatic function of the kidney is reached **at 10–11 years**. Therefore **edema and dehydration** develop easily in children; the weak excretion of the kidneys must be taken into account when giving drugs (antibiotics) and solutions.

blocks.text: The urinary tract

items: **The renal pelvises** are relatively wide and up to 5 years often lie **within the kidney**; **the ureters** are relatively long, wide, hypotonic and tortuous, leaving the pelvis at a right angle; the intravesical part of the ureter is **short** (it lengthens at 10–12 years), and the muscle fibers at its orifice are weak — predisposition to **vesicoureteral reflux**.
**The bladder** in infancy lies **high** (it is palpable above the pubis) and descends into the small pelvis with age; its mucosa is rich in blood vessels.

blocks.title: Table 14.1. Physiological capacity of the bladder
head: Age
Capacity

items: **The urethra** in girls is **short and wide** at all ages and close to the anus — risk of **ascending infection**; in boys it is long, with marked curvature in infancy (taken into account during catheterization).

parts.text: At an early age, the width, hypotonia and tortuosity of the urinary tract and the mobility of the kidney lead to **disturbed urodynamics** and the addition of **a microbial-inflammatory process (pyelonephritis)**.

blocks.text: Diuresis and voiding

items: In term newborns the first voiding occurs **on day 1**; in the first **2–3 days** there is little urine — **transient oliguria** (low fluid intake and extrarenal losses). Absence of urine for 1 day is pathological.
The **formula for daily diuresis** up to 10 years: **600 + 100 × (n – 1)** ml (n — age in years); the ratio of day to night diuresis is **2:1 – 3:1**.

items: Voiding is **a reflex act**; toilet training can begin **from 5–6 months**; by the end of the 1st year the child asks for the potty while awake, and in the 2nd year this skill becomes stable. In sleep, during excitement, or during an interesting game, involuntary voiding may occur up to 3 years (in sleep — up to 5 years).

parts.text: Diuresis: **“600 + 100 for each year”**. A 7-year-old child: 600 + 100 × 6 = **1200 ml**. Number of voidings: newborn **20–25**, 1 year **15**, 3 years **≈10**, school age **6–7**.

sections.title: 14.2. Clinical examination of the urinary system

blocks.text: Questioning

**Main complaints:** abdominal and **lumbar pain** (small children cannot localize it); **dysuric disturbances** (frequent or infrequent, painful voiding, incontinence, enuresis); **edema of the face and legs** (the parents notice rapid weight gain); **raised BP**, headache, dizziness; **change in the appearance of the urine** (turbidity, sediment, change of color — “meat washings”); unexplained **fever** or prolonged subfebrile temperature; visual and hearing disturbances; dyspepsia, thirst, itching of the skin; weakness, weight loss.

**History:** onset of the complaints, results of previous urine tests and treatment; **family history** (glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, urinary tract defects, urolithiasis, deafness, renal failure); lagging physical development at an early age; recurrent episodes of fever without signs of infection.
Inspection

Enlarged in ascites, the umbilicus protrudes when standing, it spreads to the sides when lying (“frog belly”); a bulge above the pubis in acute urinary retention

blocks.text: Palpation

**Detecting edema:** the fingers are pressed for 5–10 seconds on the anterior surface of the shin over the tibia — if **a pit** remains, there is edema. To detect **latent edema** the child is weighed daily, the daily diuresis and fluid intake are calculated, and **the McClure–Aldrich test** is performed.

blocks.label: Figure 14.7
blocks.caption: Method of detecting edema of the legs: the fingers are pressed over the tibia (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.label: Figure 14.8
blocks.caption: A pit remaining at the site of pressure (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Palpation of the kidneys** — **bimanual according to Obraztsov–Strazhesko** (lying down): the child lies on the back with the legs slightly bent; the doctor places the left hand under the lower back — in the angle formed by rib XII and the long back muscles; the right hand is placed on the corresponding half of the abdomen, outside the rectus muscle, below the costal arch, plunged deep during expiration, and the hands are made to **“approach”** each other. **According to S.P. Botkin** — standing, bent forward ≈45°. Before palpating the right kidney make sure the liver is not enlarged, and before the left — the spleen; if there is pain, start from the healthy side.

items: **Up to 2 years** (especially in thin children) the kidneys (more often **the right**) may be palpable; **in older children they are normally not palpable**.

Palpability — enlargement (**hydronephrosis, tumor — Wilms tumor, polycystic disease, vicarious hypertrophy of a single kidney**) or displacement (**nephroptosis, dystopia**); in aplasia of the abdominal wall muscles a healthy kidney is also palpable. Painful palpation — **pyelonephritis, paranephritis**.
Assessed: size, mobility, shape, consistency (a healthy kidney is dense-elastic), surface, tenderness.

blocks.label: Figure 14.9
blocks.caption: Bimanual palpation of the kidney (Obraztsov–Strazhesko) (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Pain points** (with the middle fingers, during expiration):

items: **upper ureteral points** — where the outer edge of the rectus muscles crosses the horizontal line through the umbilicus;
**lower ureteral points** — where the inner edge of the rectus muscles crosses the line through the anterior superior iliac spines;
behind — **the costolumbar points** (where rib XII crosses the long back muscles) and **the costovertebral points** (the angle between rib XII and the spine).

blocks.label: Figure 14.10
blocks.caption: Pain points of the urinary tract: 1 — upper; 2 — lower ureteral points (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Palpation of the bladder** — above the pubis; in older children only a **full** bladder is palpable; at an early age an empty bladder may also be palpable. First the time of the last voiding is determined.
Percussion

items: **Pasternatsky's sign (tapping the lumbar region):** the left palm is placed on the lumbar region at the level of rib XII, alternately on the right and the left, and **short, weak blows** are given to it with the edge of the right palm (standing or sitting). If pain appears — **positive** (negative, weakly positive, positive, sharply positive): **pyelonephritis, paranephritis, urolithiasis**. The appearance of new erythrocytes in the urine after tapping — **a true Pasternatsky sign**.

**Upper border of the bladder:** the pleximeter finger is placed parallel to the pubis and quiet percussion is performed along the midline **downward from the umbilicus**; the place where a dull sound appears is the border of the bladder (in acute urinary retention). If dullness is found, it is repeated after voiding.
Free fluid in the abdominal cavity — see topic 12.

blocks.label: Figure 14.11
blocks.caption: Tapping the lumbar region (Pasternatsky's sign) (Navruzova, Geppe)

blocks.text: **Auscultation:** **a systolic murmur** over the projection of the renal arteries (2–3 cm above the umbilicus, lateral to the midline) — renal artery stenosis (renovascular hypertension).
Urinalysis

**Urine collection:** after thorough washing of the external genitals, **the midstream portion of the morning urine** is collected into a clean container; in newborns and infants **urine bags** stuck to the perineum are used. The analysis is performed **no later than 2 hours** after voiding (otherwise it is stored at +4 °C).

blocks.text: Quantitative examination of the urinary sediment
Used to detect latent leukocyturia and erythrocyturia.

items: **Nechiporenko test** — the number of formed elements **in 1 ml of urine** in the midstream portion of the morning urine; convenient at an early age because the urine is easy to collect.
**Hamburger test** — after emptying the bladder in the morning, the urine is collected into one container for **3 hours**; the number of elements excreted **in 1 minute** is calculated.

**Addis–Kakovsky test** — the urine is collected into one container for **24 hours** (from 8–9 a.m. to 8–9 a.m. the next day); for standardization fluid is slightly restricted and protein food is given (the urine is acidic, specific gravity ≈1020 — the cells are well preserved).

Leukocytes

Casts

parts.text: Geppe's textbook gives the norm for leukocytes in the Nechiporenko test as **up to 2000** (not divided by sex); Kildiyarova gives **up to 4000** for girls. In practice **leukocytes <2000, erythrocytes <1000 per 1 ml** are often taken as the norm.

blocks.text: **Three-glass (two-glass) test** — determining **the source** of hematuria and leukocyturia: in the morning, without washing the external genitals, the urine is voided successively into three containers. Changes only in **the 1st portion** — the external genitals or urethra; in **the 3rd portion** — the bladder (neck); **the same in all three portions** — above the bladder (kidney, ureter or bladder).

**Bacteriological examination of the urine** — the midstream portion collected into a sterile container is cultured; the pathogen, its amount and antibiotic sensitivity are determined. **Diagnostically significant bacteriuria:** in free voiding **≥100,000 (10^5^) CFU/ml**; through a catheter **≥10,000 (10^4^)/ml**; on suprapubic puncture — **any** amount; in children under 1 year in free voiding, E. coli **≥50,000/ml**. Proteus, Klebsiella and Pseudomonas aeruginosa are significant even in smaller amounts.
Functional tests

**Zimnitsky test** — assesses the **excretory and concentrating** function of the kidneys and the **circadian rhythm**. During the day the urine is collected into a separate container **every 3 hours** (8 portions; at an early age — at free intervals), **the volume and specific gravity** of each portion are measured, and the fluid intake is taken into account.

items: **Excretory function:** normally **70–80%** of the fluid taken is excreted.

**Concentrating function:** during the day the specific gravity varies within **1008–1025**; in children over 3 years the maximal specific gravity in at least one portion is **1018–1020**; a difference between the maximal and minimal specific gravity of **≥10 units** (optimally 15) — the ability to concentrate and dilute is preserved.
**Circadian rhythm: daytime diuresis (9:00–21:00) is 2/3–3/4 of the daily diuresis**; predominance of night diuresis — **nocturia** (chronic renal failure, pyelonephritis).

**Hyposthenuria** — specific gravity constantly **<1010–1012**; **isosthenuria** — monotonous specific gravity around **1008–1010** (the specific gravity of primary urine) — a severe disturbance of the concentrating function; **hypersthenuria** — >1030 (glucosuria, proteinuria, dehydration).

blocks.text: **Blood creatinine and urea** — easily determined indicators of renal function; an increase indicates impaired filtration function.

**Rehberg test** — assesses **the glomerular filtration rate (GFR)** by **the endogenous creatinine clearance** and **tubular reabsorption** (creatinine is freely filtered in the glomeruli and is almost neither reabsorbed nor secreted in the tubules). The urine is collected over 24 hours (or 2 hours), and venous blood is taken after the last voiding.

items: Clearance: **C = (U × V / P) × (1.73 / S)**, where U and P are the creatinine in the urine and plasma, V is the minute diuresis, and S is the child's body surface area.
**Tubular reabsorption** = [(clearance – minute diuresis) / clearance] × 100% — normally **97–99%**.

In practice GFR is calculated by **the Schwartz formula**: **GFR = k × height (cm) / creatinine (µmol/l × 0.0113)**; k — 0.33 in preterm babies; 0.45 in term newborns and up to 2 years; 0.55 at 2–14 years; 0.70 in boys over 14 years.

**Other investigations:** blood total protein and fractions, cholesterol, electrolytes (K, Na, Ca, P), ABB; in the urine — daily protein, the protein/creatinine ratio (normal ≤0.2 mg/mmol), microalbuminuria; for the proximal tubules — excretion of amino acids, phosphates, glucose, β~2~-microglobulin; for the distal tubules — ammonium and titratable acidity.

blocks.text: Urinary syndrome
**Urinary syndrome** — pathological changes in the urine: proteinuria, hematuria, leukocyturia, cylindruria, bacteriuria, crystalluria.

items: **Proteinuria** — excretion of **>150–200 mg** of protein per day (or more than 0.033 g/l). Degree: **mild** — <1 g/day; **moderate** — 1–2.5 g/day (glomerulonephritis); **marked (nephrotic)** — >2.5–3 g/day or **>50 mg/kg/day**. **Renal (glomerular, tubular)** and **extrarenal** (prerenal — Bence Jones protein; postrenal — inflammation of the urinary tract); **functional** — fever, physical strain, chilling, **orthostatic**. **Selective** (mainly albumin — milder damage) and **nonselective** (large-molecule globulins — deep damage).

**Hematuria** — **>2–3 erythrocytes** per field of view in the morning urine; **microhematuria** (the color does not change) and **macrohematuria** (>25–30, red urine or “meat washings”). **Glomerular** (dysmorphic erythrocytes, erythrocyte casts, with proteinuria — glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, hereditary nephritis) and **nonglomerular** (isomorphic erythrocytes — urolithiasis, cystitis, tumor, trauma). With pain — renal colic; with dysuria — cystitis.

**Leukocyturia** — **>5–6 (>10 in girls)** per field of view in the urinalysis, >2000(–4000)/ml by Nechiporenko, >2 million/day by Addis–Kakovsky; **pyuria** — leukocytes cover the whole field of view. **Neutrophilic** type (on the urocytogram) — microbial inflammation (**pyelonephritis, cystitis**, urethritis); **mononuclear/lymphocytic** — glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, SLE.

**Cylindruria** — **always a sign of renal pathology** (except for single hyaline casts): hyaline — physical strain, fever, nephrotic syndrome; granular and waxy — severe degenerative damage to the tubules; **erythrocyte** — renal hematuria (glomerulonephritis); leukocyte — renal leukocyturia (pyelonephritis).
**Bacteriuria** — the main sign of urinary infection (significant cut-offs above).
**Crystalluria:** urates — urate diathesis (neuro-arthritic diathesis), high meat intake; oxalates — oxalate nephropathy; triple phosphates — urinary tract infection.
**Glucosuria** (diabetes mellitus, **renal glucosuria** — normal blood sugar), **ketonuria** (acetonemic vomiting, diabetes mellitus).

parts.text: Source of hematuria: **“Erythrocyte cast + protein + dysmorphic erythrocyte = glomerulus”**. Leukocyturia + bacteriuria + fever + positive Pasternatsky = **pyelonephritis**; leukocyturia + dysuria, without fever = **cystitis**.

blocks.text: Edema syndrome

Mechanisms of renal edema: **reduced oncotic pressure** of the plasma (hypoalbuminemia); increased capillary permeability; activation of **the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system** (retention of Na and water); **reduced glomerular filtration**. Renal edema appears **in the morning on the face and eyelids** and descends during the day; it is soft and warm, the skin pale (cardiac edema — in the evening on the legs, with cyanosis, firm).
Pain syndrome

items: **Dull, constant lumbar pain** — stretching of the renal capsule (glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, hydronephrosis);
**sharp, paroxysmal pain in the lower back radiating down along the ureter — to the groin and genitals** — **renal colic** (urolithiasis, a blood clot);
**suprapubic pain** — cystitis, bladder stone, urinary retention;
pain in the lower back and one side of the abdomen during voiding — **vesicoureteral reflux**.

blocks.text: Main clinical syndromes

**Nephritic (acute nephritic) syndrome** — **hematuria** (from micro- to macro-, “meat washings”), **arterial hypertension**, moderate **proteinuria** (1–2 g/day), moderate **edema** (face, shins) or latent edema, **oliguria**, cylindruria. Typical of **acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis** (**1–3 weeks** after tonsillitis or pyoderma), Henoch–Schönlein nephritis, SLE.

**Nephrotic syndrome** — **massive edema** (up to anasarca), **marked proteinuria (>50 mg/kg/day or >3 g/day)**, **hypoproteinemia and hypoalbuminemia** (<25 g/l), dysproteinemia (increased α~2~-globulins), **hyperlipidemia** (hypercholesterolemia). **Complete** (all signs) and **incomplete**; **pure** (without hematuria and hypertension — most often “minimal change” — in children aged 2–6 years, steroid-sensitive) and **mixed** (with hematuria and/or hypertension). **Primary** (congenital, idiopathic, glomerulonephritides) and **secondary** (SLE, vasculitides, amyloidosis, diabetes mellitus, hepatitis B and C, HIV, heavy metals).

blocks.text: **Syndrome of urinary tract involvement (infection)** — pyelonephritis, cystitis: pain, dysuria, a positive Pasternatsky sign, **intoxication and fever** (in pyelonephritis); laboratory — **neutrophilic leukocyturia, bacteriuria**, microhematuria; instrumental — dilatation and deformation of the pelvicalyceal system, signs of obstruction. At an early age pyelonephritis often presents with **“unexplained” fever**, vomiting and failure to gain weight.

**Tubular dysfunction (tubulopathy) syndrome** — polyuria, hypo- and isosthenuria; **proximal** — renal glucosuria, **phosphate diabetes** (vitamin D-resistant rickets: severe rickets-like deformities, low blood P, normal Ca, phosphaturia), **de Toni–Debré–Fanconi syndrome** (glucosuria + aminoaciduria + phosphaturia + rickets-like changes); **distal** — **nephrogenic diabetes insipidus** (polyuria, polydipsia, hypernatremia), **renal tubular acidosis** (acidosis in the blood, alkaline urine — calcinosis, stones), pseudohypoaldosteronism.

**Arterial hypertension syndrome** — **renoparenchymal** (glomerulonephritis, pyelonephritis, defects, reflux nephropathy) and **renovascular** (renal artery stenosis, thrombosis, aortoarteritis). The most common cause of secondary hypertension in children is **kidney disease**.

**Acute kidney injury (acute renal failure)** — a sharp, **reversible** decline in renal function: **oliguria/anuria, hyperazotemia (raised creatinine and urea), hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperhydration**. Causes: **prerenal** (shock, dehydration, blood loss), **renal** (hemolytic uremic syndrome — the most common cause at an early age, acute glomerulonephritis, nephrotoxins — aminoglycosides, sepsis), **postrenal** (obstruction). Phases of the course: initial, oligoanuric, polyuric, recovery.

**Chronic renal failure (chronic kidney disease)** — **irreversible** disturbance of homeostasis as a result of a progressive decrease in the number of functioning nephrons. At the onset — **polyuria, nocturia, isosthenuria**, a moderate rise in creatinine; then intoxication, **anemia**, arterial hypertension, acidosis, **renal osteodystrophy**, growth retardation, hyperkalemia; **the terminal (uremic) stage** — GFR <15–20 ml/min/1.73 m^2^, itching of the skin, a grayish-yellow skin color, **ammonia odor**, nausea, vomiting, hemorrhagic syndrome, pericarditis (the “death knell” rub), seizures, uremic coma.

sections.title: 14.6. The immune system: anatomical and physiological features

blocks.text: **The immune system** — the set of organs, tissues and cells that protects the body from **genetically foreign** substances (antigens) entering from outside or formed in the body.

blocks.title: Table 14.14. Organs of the immune system (Geppe)
head: Central
Peripheral
rows: Lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils (Waldeyer–Pirogov ring), Peyer's patches of the intestine, appendix, skin (Langerhans cells), liver (Kupffer cells), tissue macrophages

blocks.text: (Geppe's table lists the spleen among the central organs; in most textbooks it is considered a peripheral organ.)
Innate (nonspecific) defense

items: **Natural barriers:** skin, mucous membranes, ciliated epithelium, the acidic environment of the stomach, the blood-brain barrier.

**Humoral factors: lysozyme** (saliva, tears, breast milk; high in the newborn), **properdin** (low at birth, increases at 1–3 weeks), **interferons** (low production capacity in the newborn, maximal in puberty), **the complement system** (≈**50%** of adult levels at birth, reaching adult levels by the end of the 1st month).

**Phagocytosis** (neutrophils, macrophages): in the newborn the engulfing activity is adequate, but **the final stage (digestion) is imperfect** — it reaches adult levels at 6–12 months; phagocytosis of pneumococcus, Klebsiella and Haemophilus is incomplete — these infections are severe and generalized.

blocks.text: Adaptive (specific) immunity

items: **Cell-mediated immunity** — **T lymphocytes** (mature in the thymus): **CD4^+^ T helpers** (Th1, Th2), **CD8^+^ cytotoxic T lymphocytes (killers)**, T regulators (suppressors). A T lymphocyte recognizes an antigen together with HLA molecules after it has been processed by **an antigen-presenting cell** (macrophage); it acts against intracellular viruses, tumor cells and intracellular pathogens.

**Humoral immunity** — **B lymphocytes** (mature in the bone marrow) become **plasma cells** and produce **immunoglobulins (antibodies)**; they recognize the antigen in its native form; they act against extracellular pathogens.
**Memory cells** — store information about the antigen and ensure a rapid and strong response on re-encounter (the basis of vaccination).

blocks.text: The “critical periods” of immune system development

parts.text: **Critical period 1 — the neonatal period (1st month):** **physiological depression** of the immune system; passive protection by maternal IgG; low phagocytosis, complement and interferon — susceptibility to pyogenic and gram-negative flora and viruses, a tendency of infection to **generalize** (sepsis). The first crossover of the leukocyte differential on day 4–5. **Critical period 2 — 3–6 months:** breakdown of maternal antibodies; the primary immune response (IgM) predominates, **immunological memory is not formed** — whooping cough and measles run an atypical course, reinfection is possible; local immunity is insufficient; allergic reactions and food allergy appear. **Critical period 3 — the 2nd year:** active exploration of the world, increasing contacts; local immunity remains insufficient; the response to the polysaccharide antigens of pneumococcus and Haemophilus is weak; most primary immunodeficiencies become manifest; diseases of the ENT organs and airways recur. **Critical period 4 — 4–6 years:** the second crossover of the leukocyte differential; IgG and IgM reach adult levels, secretory IgA is still low; parasitic invasions, atopic and immune complex diseases, late immunodeficiencies. **Critical period 5 — puberty (12–16 years in boys, 11–15 years in girls):** involution of the thymus, the mass of the lymphoid organs decreases; the influence of sex hormones — autoimmune and lymphoproliferative diseases increase.

blocks.text: **History and inspection:** frequent and severe infections, recurrences, opportunistic infections, reactions to vaccination (complications after BCG), allergic diseases, family history (death from infection at an early age); examination of the lymph nodes, tonsils and spleen (see topic 4); **absence or hypoplasia** of the tonsils and lymph nodes — a sign of humoral immunodeficiency.
Immunogram (laboratory methods):

items: **Cell-mediated immunity:** the number of lymphocytes and T lymphocytes (at 7–14 years T cells make up **≈70%** of lymphocytes, ≈1400/µl), the **CD3, CD4, CD8** subpopulations and **the CD4/CD8 ratio** (normal 1.5–2), the blast transformation reaction with phytohemagglutinin, cytokines; **skin tests** (Mantoux); chest X-ray (thymic hypoplasia or thymomegaly).

**Humoral immunity:** the number of B lymphocytes (CD19, CD20; ≈25%, ≈500/µl), **serum IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE**, secretory IgA (in saliva), circulating immune complexes, specific post-vaccination antibodies.
**Complement system:** total hemolytic activity (CH50), C3, C4, C1 inhibitor.

**Phagocytosis:** the neutrophil count (**neutropenia** — absolute count <1500/µl), the phagocytic index and number, **the NBT test** (nitroblue tetrazolium — bactericidal activity), chemotaxis, adhesion molecules (CD11/CD18).

blocks.text: **3 types** of immune system involvement: 1) quantitative or functional insufficiency of a component of the immune system (**primary and secondary immunodeficiencies**); 2) impaired recognition of self antigens (**autoimmune diseases**); 3) a hyperreactive immune response (**allergic reactions**).
The 10 warning signs of primary immunodeficiency

items: **6–8 or more** episodes of otitis a year.
**4–6** severe sinusitis episodes a year.
**More than 2** severe pneumonias a year.
Recurrent **deep abscesses** of the skin or internal organs.
**More than 2** severe infections (osteomyelitis, sepsis, meningitis).
**Persistent oral candidiasis** or fungal infection of the skin in a child over 1 year.
The need for **2 months or more** of antibiotic treatment (ineffective).
The need for **intravenous antibiotics** to clear an infection.
**Primary immunodeficiency** or deaths from infection at an early age in the family history.
**Failure to gain weight and growth retardation** in an infant.

parts.text: If there are two or more signs — an immunology consultation and an immunogram are needed. **Live vaccines** (BCG, oral poliomyelitis vaccine, measles) are **contraindicated** in cell-mediated and combined immunodeficiency — risk of generalized vaccine infection.

blocks.title: Table 14.17. Clinical features of primary immunodeficiencies (Geppe)
head: Affected component
Clinical signs
Examples
rows: Recurrent purulent otitis, sinusitis, pneumonia and bronchiectasis caused by encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, Haemophilus, streptococcus); begins after 6 months (when maternal IgG is exhausted); lymphoid hypoplasia

Bruton agammaglobulinemia (X-linked, in boys, at 6–9 months), common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency (the most common), hyper-IgM syndrome, transient hypogammaglobulinemia of infancy
Viruses, fungi (candidiasis), mycobacteria, Pneumocystis, protozoa; growth retardation, diarrhea, malabsorption; BCG-itis; risk of tumors
DiGeorge syndrome (22q11: thymic aplasia, hypoparathyroidism — hypocalcemic seizures, heart defects, facial anomalies), chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis

Recurrent bacterial, especially meningococcal and gonococcal (C5–C9), infections; autoimmune diseases (C1–C4 — SLE); C1 inhibitor deficiency — hereditary angioedema

blocks.text: Secondary immunodeficiencies

As a result of a pathological process outside the lymphoid tissue: **malnutrition (dystrophy), avitaminoses**; viral infections (measles, rubella, chickenpox, EBV, **HIV — acquired immunodeficiency syndrome**); bacterial and fungal infections; malignant tumors; conditions with **protein loss** (**nephrotic syndrome, extensive burns, exudative enteropathy**); major surgery; **radiation, chemotherapy, glucocorticoid and cytostatic therapy**; splenectomy; severe physical strain and stress.
Allergic and autoimmune conditions

items: **Allergic (atopic) diseases** — atopic dermatitis (in infancy), food allergy, allergic rhinitis, bronchial asthma (the “atopic march”); raised IgE in the blood, eosinophilia.
**Autoimmune diseases** — rheumatic fever, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, SLE, autoimmune thyroiditis, type 1 diabetes mellitus; they increase in puberty.

blocks.text: Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis

parts.text: **1–3 weeks after tonsillitis, scarlet fever or pyoderma** — the “**nephritic triad**”: **edema** (face and eyelids in the morning), **arterial hypertension** (headache, vomiting; in a severe case — **eclampsia**: seizures, loss of consciousness), **urine the color of “meat washings”** (macrohematuria) and oliguria. Laboratory: proteinuria 1–2 g/l, erythrocyte casts; in the blood **raised ASO**, **reduced complement C3** (recovers in 6–8 weeks), raised ESR. Treatment: bed rest, restriction of salt and fluid, penicillin, antihypertensive drugs; the main dangers are hypertensive encephalopathy, acute heart failure and acute kidney injury.

blocks.text: Urinary tract infection in a young child

parts.text: In an infant with **unexplained fever (>38 °C)**, vomiting, poor appetite, failure to gain weight and restlessness, **urinalysis and urine culture** are mandatory (urinary tract infection is the most common bacterial cause of “occult” fever at an early age). After the first febrile pyelonephritis **renal ultrasound** is performed, and if it recurs — **voiding cystourethrography** (vesicoureteral reflux).

skills.title: Skill 1. Detecting edema

items: Inspect the skin of the face, eyelids, limbs, lower back and abdomen; pay attention to clothing marks.
Press with a finger for 5–10 seconds on the anterior surface of the tibia; assess the pit.
Check for edema in the lumbosacral area and the abdominal wall (in a lying child).
Detect free fluid in the abdominal cavity.
If latent edema is suspected — weigh the child, calculate the diuresis and fluid balance, perform the McClure–Aldrich test.

skills.title: Skill 2. Bimanual palpation of the kidneys (Obraztsov–Strazhesko)

items: The child lies on the back with the legs slightly bent; the doctor on the right; warm hands.
Place the left hand under the lower back, in the angle between rib XII and the long muscles.
Place the right hand outside the rectus muscle below the costal arch and plunge it deep during expiration.
Bring the hands together and try to feel the lower pole of the kidney; on deep inspiration the kidney slides under the fingers.
Palpate the left kidney in the same way; in older children repeat standing according to Botkin.
Assess size, consistency, surface, mobility, tenderness.

skills.title: Skill 3. Pain points and Pasternatsky's sign

items: Palpate the upper and lower ureteral points with the child lying on the back, during expiration.
Palpate the costolumbar and costovertebral points from behind.
With the child sitting or standing, place the left palm on the lumbar region at the level of rib XII.
Give short, weak blows with the edge of the right palm; first on the healthy side, then on the affected side.
Assess the pain (negative, weakly positive, positive, sharply positive).

skills.title: Skill 4. Percussion of the border of the bladder

items: The child lies on the back; determine the time of the last voiding.
Place the pleximeter finger parallel to the pubis at the level of the umbilicus.
Percuss quietly downward along the midline; mark the point where tympanitis changes to dullness.
Measure the distance from the pubic symphysis; repeat after voiding if necessary.

skills.title: Skill 5. Interpreting urine tests and functional tests

items: Compare the urinalysis with the age norms: color, clarity, pH, specific gravity, protein, glucose, sediment.
Compare the Nechiporenko, Hamburger or Addis–Kakovsky results with the norm.
In the Zimnitsky test assess: the ratio of daily diuresis to fluid intake, day/night diuresis, the maximal specific gravity and the range of specific gravity.
Assess the GFR and tubular reabsorption by the Rehberg test or the Schwartz formula.
Identify the leading urinary syndrome and the level of involvement (glomerular, tubular, urinary tract).

skills.title: Skill 6. Performing the McClure–Aldrich test

items: Wipe the lower third of the inner surface of the forearm with alcohol.
With a fine needle inject 0.2 ml of isotonic NaCl strictly intradermally (a “lemon peel” bleb).
Record the time and observe until the bleb disappears.
Compare the result with the age norm.

skills.title: Skill 7. Assessing an immunogram

items: Determine the absolute numbers of leukocytes, lymphocytes and neutrophils.
Compare CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19 and the CD4/CD8 ratio with the age norm.
Compare the levels of IgG, IgA, IgM, IgE with the age norm.
Identify the affected component by comparing with the clinical signs (type of infections, age at onset).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: An 8-year-old boy. He had tonsillitis 2 weeks ago. For 3 days his face and eyelids have been swollen in the morning, with headache, scanty urine the color of “meat washings”. On examination: pale skin, edema of the face and eyelids, pastosity of the shins. BP 140/95 mm Hg. Pasternatsky's sign weakly positive on both sides. Daily diuresis 400 ml. Urinalysis: protein 1.5 g/l, erythrocytes cover the whole field of view (altered), erythrocyte casts 2–3 per field of view, leukocytes 4–5.
cases.ask: 1) The leading syndrome? 2) Presumptive diagnosis? 3) What is the normal diuresis for this child? 4) Which additional investigations are needed?
cases.answer: 1) Acute nephritic syndrome: edema, arterial hypertension, macrohematuria (“meat washings”), moderate proteinuria, erythrocyte casts, oliguria. 2) Acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis (2 weeks after tonsillitis). 3) 600 + 100 × (8 – 1) = 1300 ml; 400 ml is less than 1/3 of the norm — oliguria. 4) Blood ASO, complement C3 (reduced), creatinine, urea, potassium, total protein, albumin, cholesterol; the Nechiporenko, Zimnitsky and Rehberg (GFR) tests; a throat swab (β-hemolytic streptococcus); renal ultrasound; ECG, fundoscopy.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 4-year-old girl. Over 1 week edema gradually increased: first in the eyelids, then in the legs, and the abdomen enlarged. On examination: anasarca, free fluid in the abdomen, pale “ivory”-colored skin. BP 90/60 mm Hg. Urine: protein 6.6 g/l, erythrocytes 0–1, hyaline casts. Blood: total protein 42 g/l, albumin 18 g/l, cholesterol 11.5 mmol/l. Daily proteinuria 2.8 g (weight 16 kg).
cases.ask: 1) The leading syndrome? Assess the degree of proteinuria. 2) Determine the form. 3) The mechanism of the edema? 4) How can latent edema be detected?
cases.answer: 1) Nephrotic syndrome: massive edema, proteinuria 2.8 g / 16 kg = 175 mg/kg/day (>50 mg/kg — nephrotic level), hypoproteinemia, hypoalbuminemia (18 g/l), hypercholesterolemia. 2) Complete, pure nephrotic syndrome (no hematuria or hypertension); by age and clinical picture probably minimal change (steroid-sensitive) idiopathic nephrotic syndrome. 3) Massive proteinuria → hypoalbuminemia → reduced plasma oncotic pressure → fluid moves into the interstitium → hypovolemia → activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and ADH → retention of Na and water. 4) Daily weighing, calculating the balance of daily diuresis and fluid intake, the McClure–Aldrich test (the bleb resorbs quickly).

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 1-year-old boy. Since 6 months he has had purulent otitis 4 times, pneumonia 2 times and purulent (pneumococcal) meningitis 1 time; the effect of antibiotics is short-lived. The mother's brother died of an infection in childhood. On examination: weight deficit, the tonsils and peripheral lymph nodes are hardly detectable. Blood: IgG 0.5 g/l, IgA and IgM not detected; B lymphocytes (CD19) <1%; T lymphocytes normal.
cases.ask: 1) Which immune component is affected? 2) Presumptive diagnosis? 3) Why did the disease begin after 6 months? 4) Principle of treatment and vaccination precautions?
cases.answer: 1) Humoral immunity (B lymphocytes and antibodies) — recurrent purulent infections caused by encapsulated bacteria, lymphoid hypoplasia, a sharp decrease in all Ig classes, absence of B cells, normal T cells. 2) X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton disease) — a boy, a similar condition in the mother's brother (on the maternal side). 3) In the first months of life the child is protected by maternal IgG that crossed the placenta; it is broken down by 3–6 months, and the child's own antibodies are not produced. 4) Lifelong immunoglobulin replacement therapy (intravenous or subcutaneous, keeping IgG at a normal level), active antibiotic treatment of infections; the live oral poliomyelitis vaccine is contraindicated; refer the family for genetic counseling.

topics.title: Feeding the healthy child: breastfeeding, mixed and artificial feeding, complementary foods. Defense of the case history

goals.text: The student should know:

items: the types of feeding and their definitions;
the composition of breast milk, the features of colostrum and transitional milk, the advantages of breastfeeding;
the physiology of lactation, the rules of early breastfeeding and successful breastfeeding, contraindications to breastfeeding;
the causes and degrees of hypogalactia and measures to overcome it;
the principles of mixed and artificial feeding, adapted and therapeutic formulas;
the timing, rules and sequence of introducing complementary foods;
the methods of calculating food volume in children under 1 year, the principles of feeding children over 1 year;
the structure of the case history and the procedure for defending it.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: assess the breastfeeding technique (position, correct attachment) and explain it to the mother;
calculate the daily and single feed volume for a child under 1 year;
draw up an age-appropriate feeding regimen and a plan for introducing complementary foods;
take a feeding history;
write and defend a case history.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Breast milk and cow's milk: **“Protein 1:3, lactose 2:1”** — cow's milk contains **3 times more** protein (mainly the poorly digestible **casein**) and half as much lactose; in breast milk **whey proteins (albumin)** predominate, in cow's milk **casein**.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: **The WHO/UNICEF “10 Steps to Successful Breastfeeding”** (the main ones): train health workers; inform pregnant women about the benefits of breastfeeding; put the baby to the breast **within the first 30 minutes** after delivery; teach mothers to maintain lactation even when separated from their baby; give the newborn **no food or drink other than breast milk** (unless medically indicated); keep mother and baby **together day and night**; breastfeed **on demand**; give breastfed babies **no teats or pacifiers**; establish breastfeeding support groups.

summary.label: Caution

In artificial feeding only **adapted formulas** are used.
