blocks.text: Rational feeding is the basis of the child's physical and mental development, the formation of immune protection and lifelong health. In the 1st year the digestive organs are not yet ready to digest some food ingredients (see topic 12).

blocks.title: Table 15.1. Types of feeding
head: Type
Definition
rows: Breast milk only (breast milk remains the main food even after complementary foods are introduced); exclusive — nothing other than breast milk, not even water, is given
When breast milk is insufficient (hypogalactia), supplementary feeding with an adapted formula; breast milk is more than 1/5 of the daily volume (more than 150–200 ml per day)
Milk formulas only, or breast milk less than 1/5 of the daily volume

blocks.text: Physiology of lactation

items: **The prolactin reflex (milk production reflex):** when the baby sucks, the nerve endings in the nipple are stimulated → **prolactin** is released from the anterior pituitary → milk is produced in the alveoli. Prolactin is produced more **at night** — **night feeding** maintains lactation; frequent feeding increases milk.

**The oxytocin reflex (milk ejection reflex):** under the influence of sucking, seeing the baby and hearing its voice, **oxytocin** is released from the posterior pituitary → the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli contract → milk flows; oxytocin also accelerates **involution of the uterus**. Pain, stress and anxiety **inhibit** this reflex.

blocks.text: Composition of breast milk

items: **Colostrum** — at the end of pregnancy and in **the first 3–5 days** after delivery; yellowish, thick; rich in **protein** (mainly immunoglobulins — **secretory IgA**), leukocytes, vitamin A, carotene and trace elements; high in calories — even a small amount meets the newborn's needs; **“the first vaccination”**, it speeds up the passage of meconium (mild laxative effect).
**Transitional milk** — **from day 4–5 to week 2–3**; protein decreases, fat and lactose increase.

**Mature milk** — **from week 2–3**. Within one feed **“foremilk”** (watery, rich in lactose and water — quenches thirst) and **“hindmilk”** (rich in fat, high in calories — satisfies hunger) are distinguished; therefore the baby should **fully empty** one breast.

head: Type of milk
Proteins, g/l
Fats, g/l
Carbohydrates, g/l
Calories, kcal/l

parts.text: Breast milk and cow's milk: **“Protein 1:3, lactose 2:1”** — cow's milk contains **3 times more** protein (mainly the poorly digestible **casein**) and half as much lactose; in breast milk **whey proteins (albumin)** predominate, in cow's milk **casein**.

blocks.text: Advantages of breastfeeding

items: **Proteins** are finely dispersed (albumin, α-lactalbumin) and easily digested; amino acids (taurine, cystine) are in the optimal ratio for CNS development; there is no antigenic property — **low risk of allergy**.

**Fats** — many **unsaturated fatty acids** (omega-3, omega-6, long-chain — arachidonic and docosahexaenoic acids) — formation of the brain, retina and cell membranes; **breast milk lipase** breaks down fats already in the stomach.
**Carbohydrates** — mainly **β-lactose** and **oligosaccharides (bifidus factor)** — promote the growth of **bifidoflora** and improve calcium absorption.
**Enzymes** (amylase, lipase, proteases) — facilitate digestion.
**Trace elements** (iron, zinc, calcium) with **high bioavailability** (iron bound to lactoferrin is ≈50% absorbed); an optimal Ca:P ratio (2:1).

**Protective factors:** secretory IgA, IgG, IgM, **lactoferrin**, **lysozyme**, interferon, complement, macrophages, lymphocytes, neutrophils, bifidus factor — they reduce the risk of intestinal and respiratory infections, otitis, necrotizing enterocolitis, and later of obesity, diabetes mellitus and allergic diseases.
The milk is **sterile, warm and ready**, and its composition adapts to the baby's needs; it is economically cheap.

**A psychoemotional bond between mother and baby** forms; in the mother the risk of postpartum bleeding, breast and ovarian cancer and anemia decreases; **lactational amenorrhea** (natural contraception).

blocks.text: Rules of early breastfeeding and successful breastfeeding
Putting the baby to the breast **in the delivery room, within the first 30 minutes after delivery** (if there are no contraindications) and **“skin-to-skin” contact**:

items: stimulates the rapid onset and long duration of lactation;
ensures colonization of the skin and intestine with the mother's beneficial microflora; colostrum — immunological protection;
accelerates **involution of the uterus** and reduces postpartum bleeding;
prevents purulent-inflammatory diseases in mother and baby;
quickly establishes the psychoemotional bond.

parts.text: **The WHO/UNICEF “10 Steps to Successful Breastfeeding”** (the main ones): train health workers; inform pregnant women about the benefits of breastfeeding; put the baby to the breast **within the first 30 minutes** after delivery; teach mothers to maintain lactation even when separated from their baby; give the newborn **no food or drink other than breast milk** (unless medically indicated); keep mother and baby **together day and night**; breastfeed **on demand**; give breastfed babies **no teats or pacifiers**; establish breastfeeding support groups.

blocks.text: **Breastfeeding technique — signs of a correct position:** the baby's head and body are in one line, the face is turned to the breast, the body is close to the mother, and the mother supports the baby's whole body. **Signs of correct attachment:** the mouth is wide open, **the lower lip is turned outward**, **the chin touches the breast**, more of the areola is visible above than below; the baby sucks slowly and deeply, swallowing is heard, and the mother feels no pain.
Feeding regimen
Today **“free feeding” — breastfeeding on demand** is recommended (not chaotic): 8–12 (≈10) times a day in the 1st month, including night feeds; later the baby settles into a regimen.

blocks.title: Table 15.3. Breastfeeding regimen for children under 1 year (Kildiyarova)
head: Age
Number of feeds
Interval, hours
Night break, hours

blocks.text: A feed lasts **15–20 minutes** (≈50% of the milk is taken in the first 5 minutes). The WHO recommendation: **exclusive breastfeeding up to 6 months**, then continued breastfeeding together with complementary foods **up to 2 years and beyond**.

**Signs that the baby is getting enough milk:** voiding **more than 6 times a day** (pale urine), regular stools, calm after feeding, **good weight gain** (≥125 g per week, ≥500 g per month in the 1st half-year). “Test weighing” (before and after a feed) is an additional method.
Contraindications and difficulties in breastfeeding

blocks.title: Table 15.4. Contraindications to breastfeeding (Kildiyarova)
head: On the mother's side
On the baby's side
rows: Chronic diseases of the heart, kidneys, liver and lungs in the stage of decompensation
Extreme prematurity (no sucking and swallowing reflexes) — expressed milk is given by tube
Severe cerebral circulatory disturbance, Apgar score <7 (asphyxia, birth trauma, seizures)
Taking cytostatics, some antibiotics (chloramphenicol, tetracycline), radioactive preparations
Defects of the jaws and palate (fed with expressed milk)
HIV infection (when a safe substitute is available)
Hemolytic disease of the newborn (according to some authors, the first 7–10 days)

blocks.text: **Difficulties on the mother's side:** incorrect nipple shape (flat, inverted), **cracked nipples**, **lactostasis**, **mastitis** (breastfeeding from the healthy breast continues), hypogalactia. **On the baby's side:** rhinitis, stomatitis, candidiasis, cleft palate, short frenulum of the tongue, prematurity.

parts.text: **Acute respiratory infection or tonsillitis** in the mother is not a contraindication to breastfeeding — the mother wears a mask while feeding (the milk is a source of antibodies for the baby). **Hepatitis B** — breastfeeding is possible if the newborn has been vaccinated. **In mastitis** breastfeeding is not stopped (in purulent mastitis the milk from the affected breast is temporarily expressed and discarded).

blocks.text: Hypogalactia

**Hypogalactia** — reduced secretory activity of the mammary glands during lactation. **Primary (true)** — hormonal disorders (deficiency of prolactin, oxytocin), endocrine diseases of the mother — rare (≈5%). **Secondary** — the majority: complications of pregnancy and delivery, maternal diseases, **stress**, unwillingness to breastfeed, **violation of the rules of breastfeeding** (late and infrequent breastfeeding, feeding on a strict schedule, a night break, pacifiers and teats, incorrect technique), inadequate nutrition and rest of the mother.

items: **Early** (within 10–14 days after delivery) and **late** (after 2–3 weeks).
**Degrees:** I — milk deficit <25%; II — 26–50%; III — 51–75%; IV — >75%.
**Lactation crises** — temporary unexplained decreases in milk (at 3–6 weeks, at 3, 4, 7, 8 months), lasting 3–4 days.

blocks.text: **Measures:** breastfeeding **frequently, on demand**, from **both breasts** at each feed (keeping night feeds); daytime rest and sleep for the mother, complete and varied nutrition, a warm drink and lactogenic teas 15–20 minutes before feeding; a positive emotional climate in the family; breast massage and a warm shower before feeding. Only when all possibilities have been exhausted, in **grade III–IV** hypogalactia, is **supplementary feeding** with an adapted formula (by spoon, cup or syringe — without a teat) prescribed.
Reasons for transfer to artificial feeding

Grade III–IV hypogalactia or agalactia; contraindications to breastfeeding; absence of the mother; the mother's own choice. **Artificial feeding is a metabolic stress**: protein load, changes in the intestinal microflora, increased risk of infection and allergy.

parts.text: **Whole cow's milk, goat's milk and kefir** are not given to a child under 1 year (according to Kildiyarova at least **until 8 months**, preferably until 2 years): much protein and salts — load on the kidneys; little iron and **diapedetic bleeding** from the intestinal mucosa — iron deficiency anemia; no vitamins or protective factors; risk of allergy. In artificial feeding only **adapted formulas** are used.

blocks.text: Breast milk substitutes

**Principles of adaptation:** reducing the protein content **by 2.5 times**, bringing the whey protein to casein ratio closer to that of breast milk (60:40), adding taurine and nucleotides; optimizing the fat composition with **unsaturated fatty acids** (vegetable oils, ARA, DHA); increasing carbohydrates **1.5–2 times** (lactose, prebiotics — galacto- and fructo-oligosaccharides); fortification with vitamins (12), iron, iodine, zinc, copper and selenium; reducing the content of Ca, K and Na.

items: **Starter (formula 1)** — 0–6 months (highly adapted);
**follow-on (formula 2)** — 6–12 months (more protein and calories);
**formula 3** — over 1 year;
**fermented adapted formulas** — from 3–4 weeks, in a 1:1 or 2:1 ratio with a sweet formula (probiotic effect, in dysbiosis, atopic dermatitis, intestinal diseases);
**therapeutic (special) formulas**.

blocks.text: Rules of artificial feeding

items: Feed with one adapted formula; **do not change the formula often**; switch gradually to a new formula over **5–7 days**.

The formula is prepared **fresh before each feed** according to the instructions on the package, at a temperature of **36–37 °C**; the teat hole is small (milk should drip when the bottle is turned over); the utensils are sterile.
The feeding interval is often **3–3.5 hours** (formula leaves the stomach more slowly), 6–7 times a day, with a 6-hour night break; overfeeding is avoided.
Complementary foods are also introduced to formula-fed children **at 4–6 months** (they may be introduced earlier than in breastfed children).

blocks.text: Rules of mixed feeding

items: First **breastfeed from both breasts**, and only after the breasts are fully emptied give supplementary feeding with formula (**top-up**) — to maintain lactation;
the top-up is given with **a spoon, cup** or a teat with a small hole (a teat weakens the baby's sucking — “nipple confusion”);
the volume of the top-up is determined by **test weighing** or by calculating the food volume;
measures to increase breast milk are continued.

blocks.text: **Complementary foods** — new foods of higher concentration and density introduced into the diet in addition to breast milk (formula): they meet the growing body's increasing needs for protein, energy, iron, zinc and vitamins, develop the chewing apparatus and digestive system, and prepare the child for the family table.

**Timing of introduction:** according to the recommendations of WHO and the Ministry of Health of Uzbekistan — **from 6 months**; according to the Russian national program (Kildiyarova, Geppe) — individually, **at 4–6 months** (not before 4 months and not later than 6 months). **Signs of readiness:** holds the head independently, sits with support, the tongue-thrust reflex (pushing out the spoon) fades, shows interest in food, the weight has doubled since birth.

blocks.title: Table 15.6. Consequences of untimely introduction of complementary foods (Kildiyarova)
head: Early introduction (before 4 months)
Late introduction (after 6–7 months)
rows: Intestinal dysfunction (regurgitation, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, dysbiosis) — immaturity of the digestive organs
Delayed skills of eating thick and solid food, refusal to chew and swallow
Delayed development of taste sensations, habituation to uniform liquid food
Risk of intestinal and respiratory infections
Disturbed growth and development, deficiency of iron, zinc, copper, calcium and vitamin D
Delayed maturation of the digestive system, constipation

blocks.text: Rules for introducing complementary foods

items: Introduced only to a **healthy** child (no new food is introduced during illness or preventive vaccination);
each new food is started in a **small amount** (½–1 teaspoon) and increased to the required volume over **5–7 days**;
a new food is given **in the first half of the day** (to monitor tolerance);
move from **single-component** foods to multi-component ones; only **one** new food at a time;
food is **homogeneous** at first, then gradually thicker; given **from a spoon**;
complementary food is given **before breastfeeding**, then the breast is offered;
a new food is introduced only after the previous one is fully accepted;
until 1 year, **no salt or sugar is added** to food, and **honey and whole cow's milk** are not given.

blocks.text: **Choosing the first complementary food:** for children with adequate weight and a tendency to constipation — **vegetable puree** (cauliflower, zucchini, broccoli, pumpkin — soft fiber); for children with low weight and frequent stools — **cereal (porridge)** (first **gluten-free**: rice, buckwheat, corn; gluten-containing — semolina, oats, wheat — later).

parts.text: **Calculation example:** a 3-month-old child weighing 6000 g, fed 6 times a day. Volumetric method: 6000 / 6 = **1000 ml/day**; single-feed volume = 1000 / 6 ≈ **165 ml**. Caloric method: 115 × 6 = 690 kcal; 690 × 1000 / 700 ≈ **985 ml/day**.

blocks.text: **Features:** stomach capacity increases, saliva and digestive juices increase, the chewing apparatus develops, and the number of teeth grows. **At 1–1.5 years** food is minced (ground, mushy), with a gradual transition to thicker food and pieces; the child is first spoon-fed, then taught **to eat independently**.

items: **Number of meals:** up to 1.5 years **4–5 times** a day, then **4 times** (breakfast, lunch, afternoon snack, dinner); intervals of 3.5–4 hours.

**Dairy products** are the main source of protein and calcium: at 1–3 years **≈600 ml** a day, at older ages **≈500 ml** (milk, kefir, yogurt, cottage cheese, cheese); for children over 1 year, **“growing-up” milk formulas** fortified with vitamins and trace elements are recommended.
**Meat** (beef, poultry, rabbit), **fish** and **eggs** are complete animal proteins; **sausage products** are not recommended.
**Cereal products** (buckwheat, rice, oats, corn) — giving buckwheat together with milk improves the amino acid balance.
**Vegetables, fruits, greens** provide vitamins, minerals and fiber; proteins eaten with vegetables are absorbed better (**85%** instead of 70%).
**Sugar and sweets** are limited; fast food and carbonated drinks are not recommended.

blocks.text: In the case history, the following feeding data are recorded (Geppe):

items: **type of feeding** (natural, mixed, artificial) and its duration;
**time of first breastfeeding** (within 30 minutes after birth or later) and the reason;
how the child took the breast (sucked actively or weakly);
**feeding regimen** (on demand; every 3–3.5 hours; with a night break);
**reason, age and type of formula** when switched to mixed or artificial feeding, and its tolerance;
**complementary foods**: at what age, which foods, in what order, tolerance;
vitamin D and other supplements;
age of transition **to the family table**;
current diet and appetite, food allergy.

sections.title: 15.8. Writing and defending the case history

blocks.text: Structure of the case history
In pediatric propaedeutics, the educational case history reinforces the skill of **complete examination** of the child and **semiotic analysis** of the data obtained.

items: **Title page:** department, patient's full name, age, ward, curator (student) and teacher, period of supervision.
**Passport section:** full name, date of birth and age, sex, address, parents' full names, place of work and occupation, child-care institution, date of admission, referral diagnosis.
**Complaints** (in the words of the patient and parents): main and additional; review of systems.
**History of present illness (anamnesis morbi):** when and how it began, course of development, examinations and treatment received, condition before admission.

**Life history (anamnesis vitae):** antenatal period (mother's pregnancy — which one, course, illnesses, risk factors), **intranatal** (delivery — term, course, Apgar score), **postnatal** — birth weight and length, first breastfeeding, separation of the umbilical stump, neonatal period; **physical and neuropsychological development** (head holding, sitting, walking, first words, teething); **feeding history** (15.7); **past illnesses**; **preventive vaccinations** (according to the national schedule, reactions); **allergy history**; **epidemiological history** (contact with infectious patients); **family history** (genealogical tree); **social and living conditions**.

**Physical examination (status praesens):** general condition (degree of severity), consciousness, position, **anthropometry and assessment of physical development** (centile tables or z-score, harmony); then **by systems** — nervous system and sense organs, skin, subcutaneous fat, lymph nodes, musculoskeletal system, respiratory, cardiovascular, digestive, urinary and endocrine systems (results of inspection, palpation, percussion and auscultation, with figures).
**Semiotic conclusion (identifying pathological changes):** the pathological symptoms found are grouped by systems, combined into **syndromes**, and the **leading syndrome** is identified.
**Preliminary (provisional) diagnosis** and its justification (in the propaedeutics course — a syndromic diagnosis).
**Examination plan:** laboratory and instrumental tests and interpretation of their results (compared with age norms).
**Daily notes (diary)** — dynamics of the child's condition over the days of supervision (temperature, pulse, RR, BP, changes in condition).
**Epicrisis** — a brief summary.
**References used**, curator's signature.

blocks.text: Procedure for defending the case history

parts.text: At the defense the student: 1) gives brief information about the patient (age, sex, when and with what complaints the patient was admitted); 2) presents **the main complaints and the history of the present illness**; 3) identifies the disease-related **risk factors** from the life history; 4) states **the main pathological findings of the objective examination** and must be able to demonstrate them in practice at the bedside; 5) assesses **physical and neuropsychological development**; 6) groups the symptoms into **syndromes** and justifies **the leading syndrome**; 7) interprets the results of laboratory and instrumental investigations by comparing them with the age norms; 8) answers questions from the teacher and the group (on anatomical and physiological features, methods of examination, semiotics).

blocks.text: **Assessment criteria:** completeness and orderliness of the case history, correct use of medical terms, literate and precise writing; practical skill in performing the physical examination; correct identification and justification of syndromes; answers to theoretical questions.

parts.text: The case history is **a medical document**: the **confidentiality** of patient data is preserved, and the rules of deontology are observed in communication with the patient and parents; the examination is carried out with the parents' consent and in their presence.

skills.title: Skill 1. Assessing breastfeeding technique

items: Help the mother choose a comfortable position (sitting, lying on her side, “football hold”).
Assess the child's position: head and body in one line, face toward the breast, body close to the mother, whole body supported.
Assess attachment: mouth wide open, lower lip turned outward, chin touching the breast, more of the areola visible above.
Assess sucking: slow, deep sucks with pauses, swallowing is heard.
Ask the mother about pain and the state of the breasts (cracks, milk stasis); explain mistakes.

skills.title: Skill 2. Calculating feeding volume and drawing up a regimen

items: Determine the child's age, current weight and type of feeding.
In the first 10 days — Finkelstein or Zaitseva formula; after 10 days — calculate the daily volume by the volumetric or caloric method.
Divide the daily volume by the age-appropriate number of feeds to determine the single-feed volume.
Set the feeding times.
If complementary foods are given, replace one feed (then a second) with complementary food and draw up a daily menu.

skills.title: Skill 3. Preparing an adapted formula

items: Wash hands; sterilize the bottle and nipple.
Pour the required volume of boiled water cooled to 40–50 °C into the bottle.
Add the indicated amount of dry formula using the scoop from the package (leveled off).
Shake until homogeneous; check the temperature by dripping onto the inner surface of the wrist (36–37 °C).
Feed the child in a semi-upright position; keep the bottle neck always full of milk (to avoid swallowing air); discard the leftover.

skills.title: Skill 4. Defending the case history

items: Briefly present the passport data and main complaints.
Identify the important factors from the history of present illness and life history.
Demonstrate the pathological findings of the physical examination at the bedside.
Assess physical and neuropsychological development.
Combine the symptoms into syndromes and justify the leading syndrome.
Interpret the laboratory and instrumental results; answer questions.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A 1.5-month-old child. Birth weight 3300 g, now 4300 g. Breastfed strictly every 3.5 hours with a 6-hour night break; only one breast is offered at each feed. In recent days the child is restless, wakes often between feeds, and urinates 5–6 times a day. The mother says milk “is not staying” in her breasts. She is worried about returning to work and sleeps little.
cases.ask: 1) Assess the weight gain. 2) What is happening and what are its causes? 3) Doctor's recommendations? 4) Should formula be prescribed immediately?
cases.answer: 1) Weight has increased by 1000 g in 1.5 months (normally ≈600 g in the 1st month and ≈800 g in the 2nd month — ≈1000–1100 g is expected) — borderline, slightly low. 2) Secondary hypogalactia or a lactation crisis (around week 6); causes: a strict regimen and a long night break (prolactin is produced mostly at night), feeding from only one breast, maternal stress and lack of sleep (the oxytocin reflex weakens). 3) Breastfeed on demand, often, with night feeds and from both breasts at each feed; check breastfeeding technique; adequate rest, sleep, emotional calm and full nutrition for the mother, a warm drink and lactogenic teas before feeding; support from family members; monitor weight and number of urinations after 3–5 days. 4) No — the degree of hypogalactia has not been established; only if all measures fail and grade III–IV hypogalactia is confirmed (control weighing) is supplementary feeding with an adapted formula prescribed, given by spoon or cup.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A 6-month-old child weighing 7500 g, healthy, exclusively breastfed. Psychomotor development is age-appropriate: sits with support, is interested in food. Stools 1 time a day, sometimes 1 time in 2 days, rather hard. The mother asks for advice on complementary foods.
cases.ask: 1) Is it time to introduce complementary foods? What are the signs of readiness? 2) What should the first complementary food be and why? 3) Rules of introduction? 4) Draw up a plan for the next 2–3 months.
cases.answer: 1) Yes, according to WHO, 6 months is the time to introduce complementary foods; signs of readiness: sits with support, holds the head, is interested in food, has doubled the birth weight. 2) Because of the tendency to constipation and adequate weight — a single-component vegetable puree (zucchini, cauliflower, broccoli), then vegetable oil is added. 3) Only to a healthy child, in the first half of the day, before breastfeeding, starting with ½–1 teaspoon and increasing to 150 g over 5–7 days; one new food at a time; from a spoon; without salt or sugar; monitor tolerance (rash, stools). 4) 6 months — vegetable puree (single, then mixed); 6.5 months — gluten-free porridge (buckwheat, rice, corn) + butter; 6.5–7 months — meat puree (5–30 g, then 50 g); 7 months — fruit puree, egg yolk (¼), cottage cheese; 8 months — adapted kefir, bread, rusks; 8–9 months — fish puree (1–2 times a week). Breastfeeding continues.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: A 4-month-old child is artificially fed (the mother stopped breastfeeding at 2 months, saying her milk had “gone”). Weight 6400 g. The child has been fed whole cow's milk diluted with water, 7 times a day. Over the last 2 weeks there has been frequent regurgitation, irregular stools, and redness with itchy rashes on the face and neck. Blood: Hb 98 g/l.
cases.ask: 1) Feeding errors? 2) Causes of the rash and anemia? 3) Calculate the child's daily and single-feed volumes. 4) Recommendations?
cases.answer: 1) Whole cow's milk given to a child under 1 year; no adapted formula used; no measures taken to maintain and restore lactation. 2) Cow's milk proteins (casein, β-lactoglobulin) are highly allergenic — rashes typical of atopic dermatitis (cow's milk protein allergy); cow's milk is low in iron, which is poorly absorbed, and diapedetic bleeding from the intestinal mucosa occurs — iron deficiency anemia (Hb 98 g/l). 3) Volumetric method: at 4 months (on the 2–4-month boundary) 1/6 × 6400 ≈ 1070 ml, but it should not exceed 1000 ml — ≈1000 ml/day; with 7 feeds the single-feed volume is ≈140–145 ml (if switched to 6 feeds — ≈165 ml). 4) Stop cow's milk and switch to a therapeutic formula based on extensively hydrolyzed protein; allergist consultation; iron preparations; once formula tolerance improves, at 4–6 months (cautiously, given the allergy) a hypoallergenic single-component complementary food; advise the mother on the possibilities of relactation.
